title: Privacy Budgets for Test Email in Web Apps
description:
Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. In a web application, it is closer to a small data store: messages can contain personal-looking addresses, sign-in links, verification codes, and enough context to explain what a user did. When a test fails, that data may then be copied into CI logs, screenshots, artifacts, or a developer's laptop.

A useful pattern is to give test email a privacy budget. The budget is not a single number. It is a set of limits for who owns a fixture, how long it lives, what evidence may be retained, and which parts of a message can be exposed to a test. This makes Privacy a design property of Web Development, rather than a cleanup task at the end.

Why test email deserves a privacy budget

Browser and API tests need realistic signals. A signup flow may need to prove that a message is delivered, that the correct link changes account state, and that a second click is rejected. But a test does not need to preserve the entire email forever to prove those things.

Without explicit limits, a shared inbox can let one parallel run read another's message, a failed assertion can print a verification URL into a long-lived log, and a retry can reuse an address or token. A cleanup job can also remove the message before a developer understands the failure.

The first question are not “which temporary inbox is cheapest?” It is “what is the smallest piece of email evidence that proves this behavior?” Search phrases such as tempmailso and temp mail mail may appear in product or test discussions, but the engineering decision should be based on isolation, retention, and access control.

Define the budget before choosing an inbox

Start with the assertion. If the test only checks that a verification message arrived, a receipt may be enough:

{
  "run_id": "ci-1842-attempt-2",
  "fixture_id": "signup-7f31",
  "message_id": "msg-9081",
  "received_at": "2026-10-18T02:20:00Z",
  "subject": "Verify your account",
  "result": "matched"
}

If the test must follow a link, grant the browser step temporary access to the link while keeping it out of ordinary logs. The test helper can return a short-lived value in memory, then replace it with a token identifier once the assertion finishes.

This separation matters because message metadata and authentication material have different sensitivity. A subject and timestamp are useful for diagnosing delivery. A complete URL with a bearer token may be enough to sign in as the test account. It also make the failure record much safer to share with a teammate.

The budget should answer four questions: who owns the fixture, how long the raw message lives, what the test can read, and what survives cleanup. The answers should favor one run attempt per address, bounded retention, narrow access, and a redacted receipt instead of the whole message.

Keep ownership and retention explicit

Give every fixture a run id and attempt number. A retry should get its own address, message correlation value, and token. It is tempting to retry a failed fetch against the same inbox, but that makes old and new messages indistinguishable. A retry should get it's own evidence trail.

The provider adapter should own fixture creation, message lookup, short-lived link claims, and release receipts. The application test should own expected behavior. This division makes it possible to change from a hosted temporary inbox to a local mail capture service without rewriting every test. The runner requests release in a finally-style cleanup step; a janitor removes expired fixtures, and repeated cleanup returns an ordinary “already released” result.

For old fixtures, even a query string like temp gamil com can reveal how legacy test data was generated. A phrase such as temp org mail may also be present in search or compatibility cases. Keep these typo keywords as plain test data only; do not use them as selectors, links, or supported domain examples.

Collect evidence without collecting secrets

Good CI evidence is specific enough to explain a failure and small enough to be safe. A layered receipt works well:

  1. Correlation: run id, attempt, fixture id, and environment.
  2. Delivery: message id, received time, and a normalized subject hash if needed.
  3. Consumption: token id, response status, and whether the token was accepted, expired, or already used.
  4. Cleanup: expiry time, release status, and janitor outcome.

Avoid printing the complete HTML body, query strings, authorization headers, or screenshots of the inbox. Redact before logging, not in a dashboard query after the value has already been copied to several systems. A small allowlist of fields is easier to review than a large blocklist of secret-looking fields.

There is a related lesson in turning API tests into useful CI receipts: the result should describe what happened, not preserve every input. For signup flows, idempotent signup email handling provides another useful boundary. A receipt can say that an event was handled once without retaining the triggering message.

A small implementation contract

Teams do not need a large platform to start. They need a few invariants that are tested alongside the application:

  • A fixture belongs to one run attempt and one environment.
  • A message is accepted only when its recipient and correlation value match.
  • A verification token is single-use, purpose-bound, and short-lived.
  • A retry creates new fixture and token identifiers.
  • Logs contain identifiers and outcomes, never raw links or message bodies.
  • Cleanup is repeatable and a janitor handles crashes.
  • Access to message content is narrower than access to test receipts.

These rules reduce flakiness as well as exposure. The boundary stay understandable when a provider changes or a browser test runs in parallel. It is a modest contract, but it turns email from hidden shared state into an owned test resource.

Review checklist

Before adding an email-dependent test, ask: can two runs claim the same message; does a failure expose a clickable URL; does every retry have a new fixture and token; is raw data deleted after a crash; can a developer diagnose delivery from a redacted receipt; and are screenshots covered by the same retention policy?

If the answers are explicit, the test is checking both product behavior and the safety of its own evidence. That prevent a common failure mode: a green test suite that quietly creates a growing archive of sensitive email.

Questions teams usually ask

Should every test use a hosted temporary inbox?

No. A local mail capture service is often best for application semantics; use a provider-like fixture when delivery integration itself is under test. Keep the same ownership and retention contract in both cases.

title: Ling 3.1 Flash is now available on AI Gateway
description:
Ling 3.1 Flash from InclusionAI is now available on AI Gateway. The model is free to use through October 13, 2026.

Ling 3.1 Flash is a hybrid reasoning language model with 560B total parameters and 25B active per token. It has a 262K-token context window on AI Gateway.

The model is designed for coding, multi-step analysis, and agents that use tools, including workflows involving long documents, code, and extended task histories.

To try Ling 3.1 Flash, use inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash or inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash-free as the model name:

The standard model ID is free during the promotion and begins billing when it ends. The -free model ID stops serving instead of billing when the free promotion ends.

To use Ling 3.1 Flash in a coding agent, follow the AI Gateway coding agents guide and select inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash as the model.

Try Ling 3.1 Flash in the AI Gateway model playground, or explore the model catalog.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring routing, retries, and failover. You can use an AI Gateway API key or bring your own provider key.

title: AWS Transform Now Automates Azure-to-AWS Cloud-Native Code Conversion
description:
Originally published on PkLavc.

Confirmed facts

On October 16, 2026, AWS announced the general availability of Azure-to-AWS SDK code conversion in AWS Transform, a feature designed to automate migration of Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS.

The service identifies Azure service code within submitted .NET source code and converts it to equivalent AWS SDK calls, validating that changes are incorporated into the transformed output.

AWS Transform is available in eight AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London).

Conversion support includes Azure Functions to AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS. Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB conversion is available in preview status.

Technical analysis

The feature operates through an assessment phase where AWS Transform discovers Azure SDK usage in the submitted codebase, presenting conversion options in both an assessment report and modernization plan. Developers can accept these options or modify them before execution.

This approach addresses a significant engineering challenge in cross-cloud application modernization by automating what was previously manual code refactoring. The service's ability to translate service calls between cloud providers reduces migration complexity for .NET applications leveraging serverless and storage services.

The regional availability across eight AWS Regions suggests the service is designed for global enterprise use, though the announcement does not disclose processing requirements, data residency handling, or transformation accuracy metrics. The preview status of Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion indicates ongoing refinement of that specific mapping.

  • Supported conversions: Azure Functions → AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage → Amazon S3, Azure Queue Storage → Amazon SQS

  • Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion is in preview

  • Service requires .NET application source code submission for analysis

title: Local Whisper vs. Cloud Dictation: Privacy, Latency and Accuracy Tradeoffs (Plus a Private Setup)
description:
"Just run Whisper locally" is good advice that skips a lot of detail. Local speech-to-text is genuinely useful, but it is not automatically faster, more accurate, or even fully private, depending on what else sits in your pipeline.

This post breaks the decision into three questions (what leaves the machine, where latency comes from, and how accurate it is for your voice) and ends with a setup where nothing leaves your computer. I use InsertKit as the dictation front end because it supports local Whisper, bring-your-own-key cloud providers, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints in one place. The tradeoffs apply to any stack.

1. Privacy: map the data flow first

A modern dictation pipeline usually has two stages:

mic audio -> [speech-to-text] -> raw transcript -> [LLM formatting] -> text at cursor

Each stage can be local or remote, and people often secure one and forget the other.

  • Speech-to-text. With a cloud engine, your audio is uploaded and processed by that provider. With a local Whisper model, audio stays on your machine.
  • Formatting. Clean-up (removing filler words, fixing punctuation, adapting tone) is usually done by a chat model. If that model is in the cloud, your transcript leaves the machine even when the audio did not.
  • Side channels. Sync features count too. In InsertKit, snippets, clipboard history, custom vocabulary, and API keys sync to your account. If your vocabulary list contains an unreleased product codename, that word list is synced, even if every audio clip stays local.

What InsertKit stores is worth knowing precisely: cloud voice history in Settings → Usage covers the last 30 days and is text only, no audio, with a Clear button. Local voice history stays on the device, and setting its maximum to 0 disables it.

So "private" is not a property of a model. It is a property of the whole path.

2. Latency: where the milliseconds actually go

Local is not always faster. Rough breakdown:

Cloud: upload time + queueing + inference on fast hardware + download. On a good connection, short utterances can come back very quickly, because providers run large models on serious GPUs.

Local: zero network, but inference runs on your CPU or GPU. A small model on a modern laptop is responsive. A large model on an older CPU can take noticeably longer than the time you spent talking.

Two details that matter in practice:

  • Model loading. Expect the first transcription after loading a large model to be slower than the ones that follow.
  • Long dictation. If the tool waits until you finish a three-minute ramble before transcribing, you wait for all of it at the end. InsertKit splits long speech into chunks at natural pauses and transcribes them while you keep talking, which hides much of that delay locally and in the cloud.

3. Accuracy: benchmark your own voice

Published word error rates come from benchmark datasets, not from your accent, your mic, or your jargon. Ten minutes of testing beats any leaderboard.

Here is a quick, tool-agnostic way to compare Whisper model sizes with whisper.cpp:

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j --config Release

for m in base small medium; do
  sh ./models/download-ggml-model.sh $m
done

# Convert a 60-second recording of you reading real work text to 16 kHz mono WAV
ffmpeg -i sample.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le sample.wav

for m in base small medium; do
  /usr/bin/time -p ./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-$m.bin -f sample.wav -otxt -of out-$m
done

Then score each output against what you actually said:

# pip install jiwer
from jiwer import wer

ref = open("reference.txt").read()
for m in ["base", "small", "medium"]:
    hyp = open(f"out-{m}.txt").read()
    print(m, "WER:", round(wer(ref, hyp), 3))

Use real material: a commit message, a ticket description, a paragraph full of service names. Generic sentences flatter every model.

A few patterns you will likely see:

  • Bigger models handle accents and noise better, at the cost of speed and memory.
  • Jargon fails across all sizes. That is a vocabulary problem, not a model-size problem.
  • Whisper can hallucinate on silence or noise, producing text nobody said. Trimming silence and using a decent mic reduce it.

For jargon, a correction layer helps more than a bigger model. InsertKit's Custom Vocabulary has word hints plus "heard as → write as" corrections, like post gres → Postgres, and corrections run before and after formatting so the LLM cannot undo them.

The decision, simplified

  • Audio must never leave the machine: local Whisper.
  • Speed on modest hardware: cloud, or a small local model.
  • Accuracy on difficult audio: a large local model with a GPU, or a strong cloud engine.
  • Zero setup: a hosted engine that needs no key.
  • Air-gapped or offline work: local Whisper plus a local LLM, or formatting turned off.

Many developers end up hybrid: local for anything touching client code or internal docs, cloud for low-stakes chat.

A fully private dictation setup

Here is the setup where audio and text both stay on your machine. Local Whisper is a desktop feature in InsertKit (Windows, macOS, Linux).

Step 1: Local speech-to-text

In the Speech Engine panel, choose Local Offline (Whisper) and download a model inside the app. Sizes go from Tiny (~75 MB) and Base (~140 MB) through Small (~460 MB) and Medium (~1.5 GB) to Large v3 (~3 GB). Use your benchmark results to pick. Small is a sensible starting point on most laptops.

Step 2: A local LLM for formatting

Run a local OpenAI-compatible server. With Ollama:

ollama pull llama3.2
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models

LM Studio exposes a similar server, by default at http://localhost:1234/v1.

In InsertKit, open Settings → API Keys and add a Custom OpenAI-compatible provider: a name, the base URL (for example http://localhost:11434/v1), a key if your server needs one, and the models (auto-fetched or entered by hand). Then choose that model for Smart Formatting.

Smaller local models format well enough for clean-up. If output gets too creative, add a short custom instruction under Use my own instructions, such as "Fix punctuation and remove filler words. Do not add or change content."

Step 3: Decide what happens when formatting is unavailable

Enable Keep working offline so the raw transcript is pasted if the formatter cannot be reached. Or skip formatting for sensitive sessions and rely on vocabulary corrections.

Step 4: Verify, do not assume

Turn off Wi-Fi (or run nmcli networking off on Linux) and dictate a paragraph into your editor. If text still appears and is formatted, both stages are local. Turn the network back on afterwards, because account sync needs it.

Linux note

Check Settings → General → Linux Dependencies. Typing and pasting rely on tools such as xdotool and wtype, and on Wayland the tips point to wtype or ydotool.

Where cloud still wins

To be fair to cloud dictation:

  • No local resources. Large models do not eat your RAM or battery during a long build.
  • Consistent quality on weak hardware.
  • Language coverage. InsertKit's voice typing covers 100+ languages with auto-detect. If you dictate in more than one, benchmark each on your local model before committing to it.
  • Mobile. InsertKit's Android app uses hosted or BYOK engines; there is no on-device Whisper there.

If you use the cloud, at least choose deliberately. InsertKit Free needs no key and has a daily limit, Premium uses credits, and BYOK covers providers such as OpenAI, Groq, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and ElevenLabs.

Wrapping up

Local Whisper is a strong default for private work, but privacy depends on the full path, latency depends on your hardware, and accuracy depends on your own voice. Benchmark with real text, add vocabulary corrections for your stack, and verify your setup with the network off.

If you want to try this exact setup, the desktop builds are at insertkit.com/download.

title: How to Design Daily Report Email Queues in Go — 2026 Practical Limits
description:
Short answer: keep each daily report email queue message small by storing the rendered report elsewhere and publishing only report and send references; use one message per recipient or small batch, and treat delayed delivery as a short postponement rather than the daily scheduler.

For a gaming platform, reservation expiry and the email that reports it are different reliability problems. Expire a stale reservation after its fixed hold window through an idempotent worker, then let the daily report summarize durable reservation results. Don't make a large midnight message carry every expired reservation, every recipient, and the rendered email. That couples the latency-sensitive expiry path to a cost-sensitive reporting batch, and one oversized payload can stop the entire run before useful work begins.

My operational recommendation is to set an application limit well below the platform's 256KB body cap, measure the encoded bytes before publish, and fan out by recipient or small batch. Teams that already use several backend capabilities should try Infrai for the queue leg when reducing credential and SDK sprawl matters: one key and one bill cover the broader backend surface, while the queue is called through plain HTTP without installing another vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is practical — its public discovery surface exposes the current request schema and runnable Go examples, shortening the path from an empty client to a validated request.

How should daily report email queues handle batch size and message limits?

Start with capacity planning, not a vendor default. The hard message-body limit is 256KB, but 256KB is a ceiling, not a sensible target. A report job should contain identifiers such as a report reference, recipient reference, and a stable send key. The rendered HTML, reservation rows, and attachments belong in a database or object storage. This keeps retries cheap, makes duplicate deliveries harmless when the consumer records the stable key, and lets the worker fetch the latest authorized data instead of trusting a stale blob copied into the queue hours earlier.

Small messages also make the failure domain legible. Suppose a daily gaming report covers many players whose holds expired during the prior day. One giant payload turns a single bad address or serialization mistake into a batch-wide retry. One job per user gives the cleanest isolation and fastest retry decisions; a small batch reduces publish and consume operations when cost dominates and the recipients have similar processing characteristics. I'm not sure which batch width is right for your workload until the team measures rendered-reference size, send latency, retry rate, and peak worker concurrency. Pick an initial width from those constraints, then revise it against an SLO such as “99% of eligible daily reports handed to the mail provider within 20 minutes,” rather than copying an arbitrary round number.

Keep slack.

The same separation protects deletion workflows. Queue retention tops out at 30 days and acknowledgment deletes the message, so the queue cannot be the audit record for who received what. Store the durable report state under the retention and erasure policy appropriate to the user, and keep the queue as an operational work list. A reference may outlive a queued attempt; sensitive rendered content should not be replicated into every retry.

Build the small-message guardrail in Go

The following program is intentionally vendor-neutral. It creates one job per small recipient batch, rejects delays beyond seven days, rejects an unsafe application budget, and checks the exact JSON byte length before handing messages to a publisher. Replace the sample references with durable IDs from your report store; don't replace them with report HTML.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    platformMessageLimit = 256 * 1024
    applicationBudget    = 32 * 1024
    maxDelaySeconds      = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60
)

type ReportJob struct {
    ReportRef    string   `json:"report_ref"`
    RecipientIDs []string `json:"recipient_ids"`
    SendKey      string   `json:"send_key"`
    DelaySeconds int      `json:"delay_seconds"`
}

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    header := response.Header.Get("Retry-After")
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if retryAt, err := time.Parse(http.TimeFormat, header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(retryAt); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Second << attempt
}

func getQueue(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey, queue string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.Replace(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/get/{queue}",
        "{queue}",
        url.PathEscape(queue),
        1,
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("build queue request: %w", err)
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read queue response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue returned %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("get queue exhausted retries")
}

func encodeJobs(reportRef string, recipients []string, batchSize, delaySeconds int) ([][]byte, error) {
    if batchSize < 1 {
        return nil, errors.New("batch size must be positive")
    }
    if delaySeconds < 0 || delaySeconds > maxDelaySeconds {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("delay must be between 0 and %d seconds", maxDelaySeconds)
    }

    var messages [][]byte
    for start := 0; start < len(recipients); start += batchSize {
        end := start + batchSize
        if end > len(recipients) {
            end = len(recipients)
        }

        job := ReportJob{
            ReportRef:    reportRef,
            RecipientIDs: recipients[start:end],
            SendKey:      fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", reportRef, start/batchSize),
            DelaySeconds: delaySeconds,
        }
        body, err := json.Marshal(job)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("encode report job: %w", err)
        }
        if len(body) > applicationBudget {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("job %s is %d bytes; reduce batch size", job.SendKey, len(body))
        }
        if len(body) > platformMessageLimit {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("job %s exceeds the platform limit", job.SendKey)
        }
        messages = append(messages, body)
    }
    return messages, nil
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queue := os.Getenv("INFRAI_QUEUE")
    if apiKey == "" || queue == "" {
        log.Fatal("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_QUEUE")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    queueConfig, err := getQueue(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, apiKey, queue)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("verified queue=%s config=%s\n", queue, queueConfig)

    recipients := []string{"player-1042", "player-2088", "player-7710", "player-9901"}
    messages, err := encodeJobs("expired-holds-2026-08-14", recipients, 2, 0)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    for i, message := range messages {
        fmt.Printf("job=%d bytes=%d body=%s\n", i, len(message), message)
    }
}

This guardrail is deliberately stricter than the platform. The 32KB budget is an engineering choice, not an Infrai limit, and it leaves room for future reference fields without turning normal growth into a production-edge test. Your mileage may vary: if recipient IDs are unusually long or metadata is required for policy enforcement, measure representative encoded messages in CI and lower the batch width. Never “solve” a failed size check by compressing a full report into the message; that hides coupling and makes the worker responsible for another decoding failure mode.

No payload rescue.

For Infrai, publish through POST /v1/queue/publish using Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit method, status checks, and exponential retry on HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After. Read the current request JSON Schema from public discovery before binding fields, because a copyable sample must match the live contract. Any write retry needs an idempotency key, and the consumer must also enforce SendKey: standard queue delivery is at least once, so transport-level retry protection does not replace business-level deduplication.

Separate reservation expiry from the daily schedule

A fixed reservation hold and a daily email have different clocks. Delayed messages can postpone work for no more than seven days, which is useful for a short hold window, but they do not replace a recurring schedule. Use the reservation's stable ID as the idempotency boundary when an expiry worker changes state. Separately, let the daily trigger create report references and enqueue send jobs. If report generation or fan-out can exceed 900 seconds, the cron task should only trigger enqueueing; workers do the long-running work.

This boundary is easy to miss — and expensive to discover during an on-call shift. Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers, execution timing can have second-level jitter, and only the first 4KB of run output is retained. Therefore the database must answer “which reporting day is complete?” without interpreting cron history. On each trigger, derive a stable reporting-period key, check durable completion state, and enqueue only absent work. If a trigger repeats, the key turns it into a no-op or a continuation rather than a second mailing.

There is no native fan-out/join primitive here. When the report requires a multi-stage dependency graph, compensating actions, or an explicit join after thousands of branches, model that workflow in a specialist instead of building hidden orchestration in queue consumers. The same restraint applies to private networking: cron targets must be public HTTP URLs and push subscriptions require public HTTPS, so an environment that forbids public ingress needs a different delivery topology.

Option Setup and integration fit Prefer it when Do not choose it when
Infrai Plain REST, public discovery, one credential and one bill across backend capabilities A small platform team values low SDK and credential overhead for cron-plus-queue work The design needs private-only targets, DAG orchestration, joins, or Kafka-style replay
Apache Airflow Specialist workflow category The report is a dependency graph whose stages and joins must be explicit The job is only a small-message queue fan-out and operational simplicity is the priority
Temporal Specialist workflow category Long-running workflow state and orchestration are the deciding requirements A cron trigger plus idempotent workers already expresses the job
Apache Kafka Replay and multiple-consumer category Retained event replay or independent consumer groups are requirements The queue should delete acknowledged operational jobs and minimize platform surface
BullMQ Application-owned job queue category The team already operates a Node.js and Redis stack and accepts that on-call surface Consolidating credentials and backend APIs is the primary integration goal
Celery Application-owned job queue category Python workers and a separately operated broker are established platform choices A plain HTTP integration is more valuable than framework-level task APIs
Sidekiq Application-owned job queue category Ruby workers and their queue operations are already standard in the team The workload should remain language-neutral over REST

This is a buy-versus-build decision, not a feature-count contest. Infrai is a credible fit for a lean team already consolidating backend integrations; the catch is that its convenient surface does not turn a queue into a workflow engine or event log. Stick with Airflow or Temporal when orchestration is the product requirement, and choose Kafka when replay and multiple consumer groups define correctness. Those boundaries matter more than the first-day setup time.

Verify delivery and plan rollback before launch

Verification needs three layers. At build time, test the encoded size at the largest allowed batch and reject any body over the application budget. At publish time, record the stable send key and request outcome, retry HTTP 429 with backoff, and surface other 4xx responses rather than assuming success. At consume time, atomically claim the send key before calling the email provider, then acknowledge only after the durable send outcome is recorded. The queue is at least once. Duplicates are expected inputs, not surprising incidents.

Use an SLO dashboard that separates expiry latency from report latency. Reservation expiry should track the lag between the fixed hold deadline and the durable state transition; daily email should track the lag between the reporting-period trigger and successful provider handoff. Combining them into one average can conceal a bad expiry tail behind inexpensive overnight mail. Capacity tests should cover peak expired holds, largest reference lengths, retry bursts, and a worker restart after the external send but before acknowledgment.

Rollback is boring by design. First stop new report-job publication, while leaving reservation expiry workers alone. Drain or retain already published jobs according to the incident decision, deploy the previous consumer, and resume publication with the same reporting-period and send keys. Do not generate replacement keys during rollback, because that discards the deduplication boundary. If a schedule was paused, reconcile durable report state explicitly; don't assume missed daily triggers will be replayed.

Keep the keys stable.

One more limit deserves a written alert: queued jobs are retained for at most 30 days and disappear on acknowledgment. If a compliance review or user erasure request needs historical evidence, query the durable report and send records, not queue state. Keep only the references necessary for operations and apply the relevant deletion policy to the underlying data.

If this boundary fits the system, review the Infrai capability index before binding the live queue schema.

References

  • Cron overview
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure
  • Infrai capability index and discovery entry point

title: TanStack Start vs Next.js in 2026: Same App, Real Benchmarks
description:
I built the same small store in TanStack Start 1.0 and Next.js 16.4 and benchmarked both on one machine. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

TanStack Start vs Next.js got a lot more interesting on October 13, 2026, when TanStack Start 1.0 went stable. I built the same small store in both frameworks, with the same routes, data, components and Tailwind styles, and measured them on one machine. TanStack Start served 2.9× more server-rendered list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more JSON API calls per second than Next.js 16.4. It also shipped 20% less JavaScript and built 3.9× faster. Next.js still won where it was designed to win: a prerendered page, and a far bigger set of built-in tools.

Here are the numbers, how I got them, and how I'd choose between the two in 2026.

TL;DR: is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes, by a wide margin in my tests. Every route that rendered per request was 2.9× to 8.6× faster on TanStack Start, with much lower tail latency. On the client the gap is smaller: 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript against 135 KB, and an interactive button 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU. Next.js led only on its prerendered home page, because it serves static HTML while Start rendered that page on every request.

Same app, Node 24.22, 2 cores Next.js 16.4.2 TanStack Start 1.169.3 Difference
Home page, req/s 3,220 (static) 2,920 (SSR) Next +10%
Product list, 100 items, SSR, req/s 220 637 Start 2.9×
Product page, SSR, req/s 512 2,341 Start 4.6×
JSON API route, req/s 2,165 18,515 Start 8.6×
p99 latency, product list 754 ms 194 ms Start 3.9× lower
Server memory at idle 94 MB 60 MB Start −36%
Client JS on /products, gzip 135 KB, 7 files 109 KB, 3 files Start −20%
Interactive button, 4× CPU throttle 324 ms 289 ms Start −35 ms
Production build 4.86 s 1.26 s Start 3.9×
Dev server, first page 2.96 s 1.52 s Start 1.9×
Deploy output 38 MB 1.4 MB Start 27× smaller

If you mostly ship content that can be cached, these server numbers matter less. If you run a dashboard, an API-heavy app or anything that renders per user, they matter a lot.

What is TanStack Start?

TanStack Start is a full-stack React framework built on TanStack Router. It adds server-side rendering, streaming, typed server functions, server routes for raw HTTP and middleware, and it builds with Vite (or Rsbuild). The 1.0 announcement calls it ready for production after a long release-candidate phase, and the first stable package was @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0.

The big design difference from Next.js is the component model. In Next.js App Router, pages and layouts are React Server Components by default and you opt into client code with "use client". In Start, components are ordinary React components that render on the server and hydrate on the client. You put work on the server explicitly with createServerFn() or a route loader. Server Components in Start exist, but they are experimental and off by default, so treat them as a preview, not a reason to pick it.

How I benchmarked TanStack Start and Next.js

I wanted a fair app, not a hello world. Both apps have:

  • Home page: a heading and a link. Next.js prerenders it as static HTML; Start has no static prerender by default, so it renders it per request.
  • Product list: 100 products rendered on the server on every request, with a timestamp so neither framework can cache it. In Next.js that's an async Server Component with await connection(). In Start it's a route loader calling a GET server function.
  • Product page: one product plus a client-side "Add to cart" counter, so both frameworks must hydrate interactive code.
  • JSON API: a route returning 20 products. A Next.js route handler with dynamic = "force-dynamic", and a Start server route.

Versions: Next.js 16.4.2 with Turbopack and React 19.3.0, TanStack Start 1.169.3 with Vite 8.3.4, Nitro and React 19.3.1, Tailwind 4 in both. Both ran on Node 24.22 in production mode: Next.js as its standalone server.js, Start as its Nitro Node output. A quick check with next start gave the same results (2,377 req/s on the API, 534 on the product page).

The server was pinned to 2 CPU cores with taskset, and the load generator oha ran on 6 other cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM. Each run used 64 connections for 10 seconds after a 4 second warm-up, and every number is the median of 3 runs on a fresh server process. All runs returned 100% HTTP 200. Client metrics came from Playwright and Chromium: script bytes on each page (gzip level 6), and the time from navigation to a working button click with a 4× CPU slowdown, median of 6 runs.

This is a small synthetic store, not your app. Your database, auth and caching will usually dominate. Treat these as the cost of the framework layer itself.

Server performance: how many requests can each handle?

Server-rendered pages. The product list is where per-request rendering cost shows. Start served 637 pages per second with a p99 of 194 ms; Next.js served 220 with a p99 of 754 ms. On the lighter product page, Start served 2,341 per second versus 512. My reading is that Next.js does more work per request: it renders the Server Component tree to the RSC payload and then renders HTML from it, and it embeds that payload in the page. You can see that in the HTML: the 100-item list was 92 KB raw in Next.js and 60 KB in Start (8.5 KB versus 6.4 KB gzipped).

API routes. This was the biggest gap. A Start server route answered 18,515 requests per second; a Next.js route handler answered 2,165. That's 8.6×. Start's server routes are close to a plain handler on Nitro, while every Next.js request goes through the full Next server and router. For context, Hono on raw Node served 73,000 JSON requests per second on the same 2 cores in my Hono vs Express benchmark, so neither framework is the right place for a hot, high-volume API.

Static pages. Next.js led here: 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second. Next serves the prerendered HTML file, while Start rendered the home page with React each time and still came within 10%. This is the important caveat for Next.js: anything you can make static or cache, with "use cache" or prerendering, skips most of the per-request cost. I covered how to do that in Next.js "use cache".

Memory. Next.js idled at 94 MB and peaked at about 504 MB under the SSR list load. Start idled at 60 MB and peaked at 363 MB. Both are fine for a small VPS, but on a 1 GB box running several apps, Start leaves more room.

Bundle size, hydration and client navigation

On /products, Next.js loaded 7 script files totalling 135 KB gzipped (453 KB raw). Start loaded 3 files totalling 109 KB gzipped (337 KB raw). Most of both is React and React DOM, so the difference is framework runtime: about 26 KB gzipped.

With Chromium's CPU throttled 4×, the "Add to cart" button on a fresh product page became interactive in 289 ms on Start and 324 ms on Next.js. Client-side navigation from the list to a product took 160 ms on Start versus 182 ms on Next.js. Start made 2 requests per navigation (the route chunk and the server function), while Next.js made about 10.

So on the client, Start is faster, but not dramatically. On a real app with a large component library, your own code will outweigh this 26 KB.

Build time, dev server and deployment

Production build: Next.js took 4.86 s (5 clean runs, including its TypeScript check) and Start took 1.26 s with Vite. Running tsc --noEmit separately on the Start app took another 1.54 s, so even with a type check added, Start's build was about 1.7× faster.

Dev server: from launching the dev command to the first fully rendered /products page, Next.js took 2.96 s cold and 2.91 s warm. Start with Vite took 1.52 s cold and 1.45 s warm.

Deploy output: Next.js standalone output was 38 MB because it traces and copies the parts of node_modules it needs, including Next itself. Start's Nitro output was 1.4 MB, fully bundled. In a Docker image that difference is real, but small next to a Node base image. My Next.js Dockerfile guide shows how to keep the Next.js side lean. Installed node_modules were 354 MB for the Next.js app and 152 MB for Start.

Developer experience: what's different day to day?

Numbers aside, the daily work feels different:

  • Data loading. Next.js fetches data inside async Server Components. Start uses route loaders and server functions, usually with TanStack Query for client caching. If you already use TanStack Query, Start will feel natural.
  • Server code. Next.js has Server Actions and route handlers; I compared them in Server Actions vs Route Handlers. Start has createServerFn() with validators, GET or POST, and middleware that runs on both client and server.
  • Type safety. Start's router generates types for every path, param and search param, so a broken link is a type error. Next.js has opt-in typedRoutes, which covers links but not validated search params.
  • Caching. Next.js has a framework cache (Cache Components, "use cache", cacheLife). Start has no server data cache: you use HTTP headers, a CDN, or your own store. That's simpler to reason about and more work for content sites.
  • Built-ins. Next.js ships next/image, next/font, metadata APIs and a huge ecosystem of examples. In Start you bring your own image and font handling.
  • Hosting. Next.js runs best on Vercel and works anywhere with Node or Docker, as I do with Coolify. Start deploys through Nitro or plugins to Node, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

One gotcha I hit in Next.js: my generated project wired Tailwind 4 through a turbopack.rules entry for *.css in next.config.ts (the @tailwindcss/turbopack loader). When I overwrote the config to add output: "standalone", the CSS came out empty and the Tailwind compiler ended up in the client bundle: 280 KB of gzipped JavaScript instead of 135 KB. If you edit that file, keep the rules block, and check your bundle after config changes.

Should I switch from Next.js to TanStack Start?

Pick TanStack Start if:

  • your app renders per user or per request (dashboards, SaaS, internal tools), so server cost matters
  • you want typed routes and search params, explicit server functions and no framework-level cache
  • you like Vite, or want to deploy to Cloudflare Workers or a small VPS without Vercel
  • you already use TanStack Query, Router or Table

Stay with or pick Next.js if:

  • your site is mostly content that can be prerendered or cached, where Next served static pages fastest
  • you rely on React Server Components today, or on next/image, next/font and the metadata API
  • hiring, templates and third-party SDK examples matter more than raw speed
  • you host on Vercel and want its integration

For an existing, healthy Next.js app, I wouldn't rewrite just for these numbers. Cache what you can first. For a new interactive app, Start 1.0 is now a serious default. The official TanStack Start vs Next.js page has a fair feature-by-feature comparison too.

How do I migrate from Next.js to TanStack Start?

The rough steps I'd follow, based on building the same app in both:

  1. Move app/ routes to src/routes/ files using createFileRoute. Dynamic segments change from [id] to $id.
  2. Replace data fetching in async Server Components with a route loader that calls a createServerFn().
  3. Remove "use client" directives. Every component in Start is a normal component.
  4. Turn route handlers into server routes with server: { handlers: { GET } }.
  5. Replace Server Actions with POST server functions, and add an input validator.
  6. Replace next/link with TanStack Router's Link (to plus typed params), and next/image and next/font with your own components or plain tags.
  7. Add Nitro (or a hosting plugin) to vite.config.ts for your deploy target.

Migrate one representative route end to end first, including auth and a mutation, before committing the whole app.

Common mistakes when comparing Next.js and TanStack Start

  • Comparing a static Next.js page to an SSR Start page and calling Next faster. Make the rendering mode the same on both sides, or report it, as I did for the home page.
  • Forgetting to copy .next/static into the standalone folder. Next's standalone server doesn't serve client assets without it, so hydration silently never happens. My first client test showed a 30 second timeout for exactly this reason.
  • Benchmarking dev mode. Always build and run with NODE_ENV=production.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores as the server. Pin them apart or your numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Leaving devtools in production. Check that router and query devtools aren't in your client bundle.

Key takeaways

  • TanStack Start 1.0 went stable on October 13, 2026, and its Server Components support is still experimental.
  • On the same app and 2 cores, Start served 2.9× more SSR list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more API calls than Next.js 16.4.
  • Next.js won on its prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 req/s, so caching closes the gap for content you can cache.
  • Start's p99 on the 100-item SSR page was 194 ms versus 754 ms, and it idled at 60 MB versus 94 MB.
  • Start shipped 20% less client JavaScript (109 KB vs 135 KB gzipped) and became interactive 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU.
  • Start built in 1.26 s versus 4.86 s and its dev server answered in 1.5 s versus 3.0 s.
  • Choose Start for per-request, interactive apps and typed routing; choose Next.js for cacheable content, RSC and its built-ins.

Related: if you're weighing other parts of your toolchain too, see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint and React Compiler in Next.js.

FAQ

Is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes in my tests. With the same app on 2 CPU cores, TanStack Start 1.169.3 served 637 server-rendered list pages per second versus 220 for Next.js 16.4.2, 2,341 product pages versus 512, and 18,515 API requests versus 2,165. Next.js was faster only on a prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second.

Is TanStack Start stable and production ready?

Yes. TanStack Start 1.0 was announced as stable on October 13, 2026, with @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0 as the first stable release. Its React Server Components support is still experimental and off by default.

Does TanStack Start ship less JavaScript than Next.js?

Somewhat. On the same product list page, TanStack Start loaded 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript in 3 files and Next.js loaded 135 KB in 7 files. Most of both is React itself, so the framework difference was about 26 KB gzipped.

Does TanStack Start support React Server Components?

Yes, but experimentally. You opt in with @vitejs/plugin-rsc and rsc: { enabled: true } in the tanstackStart plugin, and the docs say the feature will stay experimental into early v1. Start's normal SSR, loaders and server functions don't need Server Components.

Should I migrate my Next.js app to TanStack Start?

Not just for speed if the app is healthy. Cache or prerender what you can in Next.js first, since static pages were Next's fastest case. Consider Start for new interactive apps, apps that render per user, or teams that want typed routes and search params, Vite and simple hosting.

How much faster does TanStack Start build than Next.js?

In my test app, vite build for TanStack Start took 1.26 s and next build took 4.86 s, averaged over 5 clean runs. next build includes a TypeScript check; adding tsc --noEmit (1.54 s) to the Start build still left it about 1.7× faster.

Can TanStack Start be self-hosted?

Yes. It builds through Nitro to a self-contained Node server, which was 1.4 MB in my test versus 38 MB for the Next.js standalone output. It also deploys to Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

What is the difference between Next.js Server Actions and TanStack Start server functions?

Next.js Server Actions are tied to forms and React's pending and error states. TanStack Start server functions are typed RPC calls created with createServerFn, can use GET or POST, accept an input validator and compose middleware that runs on both client and server. Both need runtime validation and server-side authorization.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.13

We've released version 6.13 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata and data feed files were missing from external storage for chats that ended before the first message from the end-user.

  • Fixed an issue with Kustomer integrations where the caller's information didn't appear on the Incoming call page of the call adapter for direct-line inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue with inbound mobile calls where the end-user leg of the call failed, returning Unknown error, while the agent leg connected normally.

  • Fixed an agent desktop issue where live call and chat data were lost.

  • Fixed an issue that occurred when the receiving agent in an agent-to-agent transfer didn't answer the call. The receiving agent was marked as active on the call indefinitely, even after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where the Dismiss button remained active after an agent sent a message, resulting in a 409 error when clicked.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate "chat finished" events were reported when the end-user left a chat session at nearly the same time that the agent ended the chat session.

  • Fixed an issue where deflected calls were missing from the All Call History and Voice Inbound (IVR) History reports.

  • Fixed an issue that occurred when a direct inbound call was deflected to the agent's overcapacity queue, then that queue redirected to a SIP URI. The SIP redirect didn't include the custom SIP headers.

  • Fixed an issue where an in-queue announcement interval of several minutes for inbound IVR calls was incorrectly reduced to approximately 60 seconds.

  • Fixed an issue where calls that agents were unable to answer due to microphone failures were incorrectly reported as "picked up" in the Agent Activity Timeline report.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly marked agents as still being on a call after it ended, which either prevented them from changing their status to Available or silently blocked them from receiving new calls.

  • Fixed an issue where processing delays for ended calls caused timeout errors.

  • Fixed an issue where a sudden spike in calls bypassed capacity limits, causing agent availability to drop below required minimums.

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Activity Timeline report incorrectly attributed manual agent logins and logouts to System instead of the appropriate agents.

  • Fixed an issue where calls with a missed offer became permanently stuck in the queue, preventing them from being routed to other available agents. This occurred with queues configured with multicast fallback disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where manual or cascade outbound calls that were canceled before connecting were missing from team-filtered Call History reports.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented over-capacity deflection from triggering when an agent warm-transferred an outbound call to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where calls weren't correctly routed to the top-ranked agent when using agent priority overrides.

  • Fixed an issue where escalated voice calls were incorrectly reported as both answered and abandoned.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were missing from the All Call History and Voice Inbound History reports if the caller hung up before leaving a voicemail.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce click-to-dial outbound calls were incorrectly associated with the most recent open case instead of the case from which the call was initiated.

  • Fixed an issue where email accounts remained disconnected indefinitely after a temporary authentication failure.

  • Fixed an issue in Agent Assist where long periods of silence during calls caused connection timeouts, triggering false-positive error alerts.

  • Fixed an issue where the arrow-down-icon and arrow-up-icon arrows on the Agents > Filter Settings page were rendered at an incorrect scale.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls incorrectly created duplicate Salesforce accounts instead of linking to existing accounts.

  • Fixed an issue where the outbound call queue list displayed stale information, potentially causing calls to be placed in a queue that didn't match the agent's selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the menus for transferring calls and forwarding calls to voicemail appeared in English instead of the agent's selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the wrap-up disposition panel froze after a network reconnection even though the submission had completed successfully.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound, click-to-dial calls initiated in Salesforce incorrectly linked to and reassigned ownership of other cases associated with the same phone number.

  • Fixed an issue where the agent adapter went blank and prevented new calls from reaching the agent if an end-user hung up immediately after the agent received the call notification.

  • Fixed an issue where calls that failed to connect got stuck in a silent 'connecting' state in the call adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where Salesforce CRM connections dropped for organizations enforcing OAuth Refresh Token Rotation.

  • Fixed an issue where part of an agent's audio was dropped from recordings when a virtual task assistant ran in the middle of a call.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where menus in the pre-chat and chat screens didn't comply with WAI-ARIA keyboard navigation standards.

  • Fixed a web SDK issue where screen readers couldn't identify the purpose of the Text size options for the chat screen.

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards 6.4

We've released version 6.4 of the advanced reporting dashboards.

Feature

Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard: new Active call ID(s) column

The Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard now has an Active Call ID(s) column in the Live Agent Data table. The column displays the call ID(s) for any call in a connecting, connected, or reconnecting state for the agent. If an agent is handling multiple concurrent calls, the call IDs appear in a comma-separated list. The Active Call ID(s) column reduces the number of steps required for supervisors to identify active calls during live monitoring.

Feature

Improved filtering by team

We made the following changes to team-based filtering:

  • Renamed the Teams filter to Agent Teams to clarify that it filters by the agent team handling the interactions. This change is in the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls, Real-time Queue Monitoring - Chats, Real-time Connected - Calls, and Real-time Connected - Chats dashboards. For more information, see Queue monitoring dashboards, Real-time Connected - Calls dashboard, and Real-time Connected - Chats dashboard.

  • Added a Queue Teams filter to the Real-time Queued - Calls and Real-time Queued - Chats dashboards. This lets you filter queued interactions by the team assigned to the queue.

Feature

Improved the Real-time Calls and Real-time Chats dashboards

We made the following dashboard improvements:

  • Real-time Calls - Calls Connected dashboard. Added the following columns to the Connected Calls table:

    • Total Consumer Talk Time. Total time since the call first connected to a virtual agent or a human agent.

    • Total Hold Time. Total time the call has spent on hold so far, including a hold currently in progress.

  • Real-time Chats - Chats Connected dashboard. Added the following column to the Connected Chats table:

    • Total Consumer Chat Time. Total time since the chat first connected to a virtual agent or a human agent.

Feature

Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard: new Projecting column

The Real-time Calls - Calls Queued dashboard has a new Projecting column in the Call Queued table. Indicates whether the routing engine (deltacast) is currently projecting this queued call to an available agent.

Feature

Advanced reporting available in French Canadian

All advanced reporting dashboards and Explores are now available in French Canadian. When you select French Canadian as your profile language in the CCAI Platform portal, these dashboards and Explores display in that language.

Administrators: There's a new Français (CAN) option when you click Admin > Change Language in the CCAI Platform portal.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the formatting of numeric values was inconsistent across tiles.

  • Fixed an issue where column headers, filter labels, and tile titles didn't immediately switch to a newly selected language.

  • Fixed an issue where the Productive Agents column in the tables of the Queue Group Performance - All dashboard didn't display values appropriate to the queue group settings.

title: Download mode explained: how to enter it, what each screen means, and how to exit safely
description:
If you have ever plugged a Samsung phone into a flashing tool and watched it sit there unrecognized, Download mode is usually the missing piece. It is a low-level state that lets a computer talk to the phone before the normal system starts. That is why tools such as Odin need it: they are not installing an app, they are writing system software, and they need a stable channel to do that work.

What Download mode actually does

Download mode, also called Odin mode, puts the phone in a waiting state. The phone is not booting into its home screen, and it is not running your apps. Instead, it listens for instructions over USB and accepts a firmware package when a trusted tool sends one. When the connection is working, the flashing tool can see the phone, check that it is ready, and start the transfer.

That also explains why the phone can look almost blank in this mode. It is not frozen, and it is not broken. It is simply holding still so the computer can do its job without the normal system getting in the way.

How to enter Download mode on newer Galaxy phones

On most newer Galaxy phones without a physical Home button, use this sequence:

  1. Power the phone fully off.
  2. Press and hold Volume Up and Volume Down at the same time.
  3. While still holding both buttons, plug in a USB cable connected to a computer.
  4. Keep holding the buttons until the warning screen appears, then let go.

If the phone starts charging or boots normally, you probably released the buttons too early or plugged the cable in after the phone had already started. Power it off and try again, keeping both volume buttons held as the cable goes in.

How to enter Download mode on older models

On older models with a physical Home button, the combination is different:

  1. Power the phone fully off.
  2. Press and hold Volume Down, Home, and Power at the same time.
  3. Keep holding them until the warning screen appears, then let go.

The idea is the same on both kinds of phone: start from powered off, hold the right buttons, and wait for the warning screen rather than the normal logo animation.

What the warning screen means and how to continue

The first screen is a warning. It tells you that installing unofficial or custom software can cause problems, and it asks you to confirm that you understand the risk. That warning is there for a reason. Flashing the wrong package, or stopping halfway, can leave the phone unable to boot normally.

Read it, pause, and only continue if you are sure about what you are about to flash. To continue into Download mode, press Volume Up. To cancel and restart the phone instead, press Volume Down. Do not rush this step. If you are unsure, backing out is the safer choice.

What the downloading screen shows

After you press Volume Up, you should see the main Download mode screen. It usually shows the word Downloading, a large icon, and a short block of device details such as the model, product name, and current binary status. On some phones it also shows whether the bootloader is locked or unlocked and whether the device has been modified.

Those details matter. Before you flash anything, check that the model shown matches the phone in your hand and the firmware you prepared. If something looks off, stop and check your files before you connect a flashing tool.

At this point the phone is ready. A flashing tool on the computer should now detect it, and you can load the firmware package you already checked.

How to exit safely

If you have not started a flash, leaving Download mode is simple.

  • Hold Volume Down and Power together until the phone restarts.
  • On some models, a long press of the Power button alone will also restart the phone.

Let the phone restart on its own and reach the normal lock screen. Do not pull the battery on a phone with a sealed battery, and do not force a restart in the middle of a transfer.

If a flash is already in progress, do not exit. Wait until the tool reports that it finished and the phone restarts by itself. Interrupting a transfer is one of the fastest ways to cause a boot problem.

Common mistakes to avoid

Entering Recovery mode by accident

Recovery mode uses a different button combination and shows a menu with options such as reboot, wipe, and apply update. If you see that menu, you did not enter Download mode. Power off and try the Download mode combination again, paying close attention to which volume button you held.

Unplugging the phone mid-flash

Once a flash starts, the cable is part of the process. Unplugging the phone, closing the tool, or letting the computer sleep can break the transfer. Keep the phone still, keep the cable connected, and wait for the tool to finish.

Using a bad cable or loose port

A cable that only charges, a worn connector, or a loose port can drop the connection at the worst moment. Use a good-quality data cable, plug it directly into the computer rather than through a hub when you can, and check that the phone is detected before you start. If the tool keeps losing the phone, swap the cable and try another USB port before you blame the firmware.

A short safety note

Back up anything you cannot afford to lose before you flash. Flashing can wipe data, and it can fail even when you follow the steps carefully. Also use firmware made for your exact model and CSC, which is the region and carrier configuration code. A package for a similar-looking model is not close enough. Check the model number on the phone, check the CSC, and only then start.

Download mode is not something to fear, but it is something to respect. Enter it with the right buttons, read the warning, confirm the details on the screen, and leave it the clean way. If you want a place to check firmware details before you start, SamFware keeps things organized, and you can return to SamFware whenever you need to double-check a model or CSC before flashing.

title: Building a WhatsApp Interactive Button & List Message Handler in TypeScript
description:
Interactive messaging is one of the most effective ways to increase user engagement and eliminate typing friction on WhatsApp. Rather than forcing users to type out responses like "1", "YES", or "MENU", the official Meta WhatsApp Cloud API supports interactive buttons (quick replies, call-to-action buttons) and scrollable list menus (up to 10 options).

In this tutorial, we will build a production-ready, type-safe interactive message handler in TypeScript that parses incoming interactive payloads and routes them into conversational flows.

Understanding WhatsApp Interactive Payloads

When a recipient taps an interactive button or list item, Meta delivers an inbound webhook payload where the message type is set to "interactive".

Inside the interactive object, you will receive either:

  1. button_reply: Contains the id and title of the clicked quick-reply button.
  2. list_reply: Contains the id, title, and optional description of the chosen list row.

Step 1: Defining TypeScript Interfaces

Let's define the strict typings for incoming interactive webhook events:

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveListReply {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  description?: string;
}

export interface WhatsAppInteractiveMessage {
  from: string;
  id: string;
  timestamp: string;
  type: 'interactive';
  interactive: {
    type: 'button_reply' | 'list_reply';
    button_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveButtonReply;
    list_reply?: WhatsAppInteractiveListReply;
  };
}

Step 2: Sending Interactive Quick-Reply Buttons

Here is how to construct and send an interactive button message using Axios and TypeScript:

import axios from 'axios';

interface ButtonPayload {
  to: string;
  bodyText: string;
  buttons: Array<{ id: string; title: string }>;
}

export async function sendInteractiveButtons({ to, bodyText, buttons }: ButtonPayload) {
  const url = `https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/${process.env.WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID}/messages`;

  const payload = {
    messaging_product: 'whatsapp',
    recipient_type: 'individual',
    to,
    type: 'interactive',
    interactive: {
      type: 'button',
      body: { text: bodyText },
      action: {
        buttons: buttons.map(btn => ({
          type: 'reply',
          reply: { id: btn.id, title: btn.title }
        }))
      }
    }
  };

  const response = await axios.post(url, payload, {
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.WHATSAPP_CLOUD_API_TOKEN}`,
      'Content-Type': 'application/json'
    }
  });

  return response.data;
}

Step 3: Dispatching to Conversational CRM and AI Handlers

Once the interactive webhook arrives at your server, you should route it based on the action ID:

export async function handleInteractiveReply(msg: WhatsAppInteractiveMessage) {
  const customerPhone = msg.from;
  const replyType = msg.interactive.type;
  const actionId = replyType === 'button_reply' 
    ? msg.interactive.button_reply?.id 
    : msg.interactive.list_reply?.id;

  console.log(`Received action ${actionId} from ${customerPhone}`);

  switch (actionId) {
    case 'ACTION_BOOK_DEMO':
      // Move customer into 'Demo Scheduled' stage in CRM
      break;
    case 'ACTION_TALK_HUMAN':
      // Trigger human agent assignment
      break;
    case 'ACTION_FAQ':
      // Pass inquiry to AI Knowledge Base
      break;
    default:
      console.warn('Unhandled interactive ID:', actionId);
  }
}

Enterprise Production Considerations

Managing raw button schemas, translation dictionaries, and state machines across hundreds of concurrent chats can quickly become complex.

Platforms like AI Soul provide a visual drag-and-drop conversational designer where interactive buttons, list menus, and AI fallbacks can be configured with zero boilerplate code. Incoming selections are automatically reflected inside the Conversational CRM and can trigger automated WhatsApp Drip Campaigns or AI Chatbot Solutions.

Conclusion

Interactive WhatsApp messages drastically improve completion rates compared to plain text replies. By modeling strict TypeScript contracts and decoupling interactive events from business logic, your integration remains reliable and maintainable.
