title: Pricing Flag Incident Reconstruction — Node.js Uptime Failure Alerts from Health Endpoint Metrics API
description:
For a Node.js pricing rollout, use regional health polling for reachability, a metrics poll for bad outcomes, and a heartbeat for missing work; page only when the evidence agrees, but retain every signal under one rollout identifier for reconstruction. The deciding constraint isn't how quickly one probe can turn red. It's whether an engineer can later answer which flag variant, region, and pricing-rule revision produced a wrong checkout result.

Short answer: a simple uptime alert should combine an outside-in health endpoint, outcome metrics, and a scheduled heartbeat, because each observes a different failure boundary and none can reconstruct a flagged pricing incident alone.

This is an experiment note, not a vendor ranking. The tempting first pass is one poll against /health and one alert on any failure. That approach is easy to demo, yet it confuses transport trouble with pricing correctness and creates almost no evidence for an evaluation harness. The better experiment treats the rollout as the unit of analysis: every observation carries a synthetic checkout case, flag variant, rule revision, region, and timestamp. Then the alert links to the observations that justified it.

No magic here.

The incident record we need to reconstruct

A process-level health endpoint can prove that a caller reached the service and received the expected response shape. It cannot, by itself, prove that a flagged pricing rule selected the intended price. A metrics API can show the count or ratio of evaluated outcomes, but aggregation can hide one region or variant. A heartbeat can show that a scheduled synthetic checkout ran, while saying nothing about whether its assertion was correct unless the payload records that assertion.

The useful question is therefore not “is the app up?” It is “what claim does each signal support?” For this rollout, the external poll supports reachability, the outcome poll supports behavioral change, and the heartbeat supports evaluator liveness. An alert becomes actionable when it names the failed claim and preserves the dimensions needed to replay it.

I first reach for the smallest possible signal set because every label and event has storage and review cost. But prompt-cost awareness offers a useful analogy: dropping context makes an evaluation cheaper until the result can no longer be explained. Observability has the same cliff. Removing rule_revision or flag_variant may reduce cardinality, but it also makes two different pricing behaviors look identical during an incident.

Use a compact event contract before choosing a monitor:

Signal Claim it supports Required reconstruction context Misleading green state
Regional health poll The public path answered as expected region, observed status, latency bucket, rollout ID Pricing output is wrong but the route responds
Outcome metrics poll Evaluated results remain within the rollout's tested bounds variant, rule revision, region, evaluation window Aggregation masks a narrow failure
Evaluator heartbeat The scheduled check completed run ID, expected cadence, last completion, rollout ID The check ran but asserted the wrong thing

That table is also an alert review checklist. If a page cannot identify its supported claim, it probably belongs in a dashboard or deployment record instead.

How should a Node.js health endpoint poll metrics API and heartbeat monitor work?

Run the synthetic evaluator from at least the two deployment geographies named in the rollout plan, EU and US in this example. Each run calls the public Node.js health endpoint, evaluates one fixed cart against the active pricing flag, reads the corresponding aggregate outcome window, and emits a completion heartbeat. The evaluation input must be stable enough to replay: currency, item identifiers, quantities, expected variant, and rule revision belong in the test fixture, while secrets and customer data do not belong in logs.

The collector below is Python because notebook-to-prod work benefits from keeping the evaluation record explicit. It uses only the standard library, accepts observations from generic adapters, and returns an alert decision plus the evidence that produced it. Network calls are intentionally outside the function; the hard part is the decision contract, not an SDK.

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Iterable


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Observation:
    region: str
    rollout_id: str
    flag_variant: str
    rule_revision: str
    health_ok: bool
    pricing_assertion_ok: bool
    completed_at: datetime


def evaluate_rollout(
    observations: Iterable[Observation],
    expected_regions: set[str],
    now: datetime,
    heartbeat_window: timedelta = timedelta(minutes=5),
) -> dict:
    recent = [
        item
        for item in observations
        if now - item.completed_at <= heartbeat_window
    ]
    seen_regions = {item.region for item in recent}
    missing_regions = sorted(expected_regions - seen_regions)
    failed = [
        item
        for item in recent
        if not item.health_ok or not item.pricing_assertion_ok
    ]

    return {
        "alert": bool(missing_regions or failed),
        "missing_heartbeats": missing_regions,
        "failed_observations": [asdict(item) for item in failed],
    }


decision = evaluate_rollout(
    observations=[
        Observation(
            region="eu",
            rollout_id="pricing-rule-42",
            flag_variant="candidate",
            rule_revision="r7",
            health_ok=True,
            pricing_assertion_ok=True,
            completed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        ),
        Observation(
            region="us",
            rollout_id="pricing-rule-42",
            flag_variant="candidate",
            rule_revision="r7",
            health_ok=True,
            pricing_assertion_ok=False,
            completed_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
        ),
    ],
    expected_regions={"eu", "us"},
    now=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
)

The focused failure is deliberately boring: EU completes and passes; US completes but fails the pricing assertion. The heartbeat is healthy, so labeling this “monitor down” would destroy information. The health check is also healthy, so labeling it “uptime failure” alone would send the responder toward networking rather than the flagged rule. The decision keeps all three facts and points at candidate, r7, and pricing-rule-42. That is enough to compare the exact fixture against the control variant and the deployment record without guessing which aggregate moved first.

This example doesn't prescribe the pricing threshold. That number must come from the rollout's eval cases and business invariant, and I'm not sure a global percentage can represent mixed currencies, promotions, and tax paths without more domain evidence. Your mileage may vary. Resolve that uncertainty before deployment by defining expected outputs for representative carts, then make the online assertion use the same versioned fixtures.

A pricing flag failure, replayed backward

A single failed poll should become an observation, not automatically a page. Require a policy that accounts for repeated failure, regional agreement, or a pricing assertion failure tied to the candidate flag. The exact threshold is an operational choice; inventing a universal retry count would hide differences in poll interval, traffic, and recovery objectives.

This matters during a flag rollout because causality is easy to overstate. A health probe might fail near the same moment that a pricing metric changes, yet timestamps alone do not prove the rule caused the probe failure. Preserve the raw observations, clock basis, rollout ID, and deployment event. Then let the incident timeline show what happened rather than embedding a causal claim in the alert title.

Keep the page compact — region, failed claim, first and latest observation, variant, revision, and a link to the retained evidence are enough. Keep the evidence richer. OWASP's logging guidance warns that logs may contain sensitive information and calls for attention to data handling, so synthetic identifiers are safer than customer details for this check. Cart fixtures should be designed for evaluation, not copied from production requests.

There is a second privacy surface in the monitoring toolchain itself. Command-line telemetry should respect the DO_NOT_TRACK convention when supported, especially in local eval and CI workflows where an engineer may reasonably disable ancillary usage reporting. This doesn't replace a data inventory. It makes the intent machine-readable at one boundary.

Privacy and operational boundaries

The simplest architecture is a scheduler, two regional runners, an append-only observation store, and a small decision worker. A free or cheap SaaS may host one or more of those pieces, but price should not choose the evidence model. Free tiers, retention, regional execution, and alert routing can change; verify current terms directly before adopting any service.

The catch is that an external hosted monitor is not suitable when policy forbids sending endpoint metadata or evaluation dimensions to a third party. Use a self-hosted runner and store in that case. Conversely, stick with a hosted check when the team cannot operate an independent scheduler reliably; putting the monitor on the same failure boundary as the application creates a blind spot. For strict data residency, confirm where checks execute and where event data is stored rather than treating an “EU region” label as proof of the whole data path.

Do not force all signals into one retention class. High-volume outcome observations may need short detailed retention plus longer aggregates, while alert decisions and rollout metadata are small and valuable for later review. Also budget label cardinality before exposing metrics: rollout_id and bounded variants are useful, but cart or request identifiers can explode the series count. Detailed per-run context fits an event record better than a metric label.

This architecture is intentionally replaceable. The scheduler, probe adapter, metric reader, and notifier meet at plain records, so a team can move between self-hosted and SaaS components without rewriting the evaluation rule. That's more important than finding one service that claims to cover every box.

The pre-rollout scorecard

Before making this pattern the default, measure detection delay by failure class, the fraction of pages with enough context to identify a variant and revision, duplicate pages per incident, evaluator completion rate, and storage volume by dimension. Also replay known-good and deliberately failing fixtures through the decision function in CI. An alert pipeline without an eval harness is still untested application logic.

Track cost as an engineering constraint, not a victory metric. Poll frequency multiplies requests, regional runners multiply them again, and high-cardinality evidence changes storage. Start from the maximum acceptable detection delay and the incident reconstruction window, then calculate the required cadence and retention. Don't choose a one-minute poll merely because a UI defaults to it.

Finally, run a paper reconstruction after the first staged rollout. Give another engineer only the page and retained evidence, and ask them to identify the affected region, flag variant, rule revision, missing or failed signal, and replay fixture. If they must search chat history or infer a revision from wall-clock time, the experiment failed even if every notification arrived.

Ship the signal contract first.

References

  • https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • https://consoledonottrack.com/

title: Codex Swapped Its Default Model and Retired GPT-5.5 in 15 Days. Did Your Evals Notice?
description:
• Book: Observability for LLM Applications
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On September 29, a pull request merged into Codex gave GPT-6.1 Sol "the highest catalog priority" (#49318). That line made it the model the bundled catalog hands a Codex session when you don't ask for one.

Nine days later, Codex CLI 0.162.0 changed where a fresh terminal thread gets its default model from. Six days after that, GPT-5.5 left Codex for everyone signed in with ChatGPT.

Three changes in 15 days, and none of them showed up in your repo's diff. If your agent runs on whatever the default is, the thing your evals measure may have moved while your code stood still.

My take: a model you didn't choose is a dependency you didn't pin. Pin it per task, and write it down next to every result.

What changed between September 29 and October 14

Here is the sequence, from OpenAI's own release notes and docs:

Date Change Who it hits
Sep 29 Codex CLI 0.159.1: GPT-6.1 Sol becomes the default in the bundled catalog CLI users who never set a model
Oct 7 0.161.0 lists it again: default in the bundled and Amazon Bedrock catalogs The same, plus Bedrock users
Oct 8 0.162.0: new TUI threads respect the server's model defaults TUI users who launch without a model override
Oct 14 GPT-5.5 retires from Codex for ChatGPT sign-ins, at noon PDT (19:00 UTC) Anyone who picked gpt-5.5 and signs in with ChatGPT

The October 8 change is the quiet one. The release note says Codex will "respect server model and reasoning-summary defaults for new TUI threads while retaining explicit launch overrides." The pull request behind it (#50013) puts it more plainly: "Fresh TUI threads should use the app server's model settings unless the launch explicitly overrides them." The server here is the Codex app server the TUI talks to, a local daemon or a remote one (#50913). The same release stopped appending "(default)" to entries in the TUI model picker (#51235).

The October 14 change hits the opposite group: people who did pin a model. OpenAI's models page says the retirement covers ChatGPT sign-ins only and API-key sessions are not affected. It points Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users to GPT-6.1 Sol, and Free and Go users to GPT-6 Luna in the desktop app, both "when available."

To be fair to OpenAI, none of this was hidden. Every change is in a release note or the changelog, the retirement came with an exact time and a named replacement, and 0.162.0 also moved the model and reasoning effort near the top of task details (#50727). GPT-6.1 Sol may well be the better model for you. OpenAI says it nearly matches GPT-6 Astra at about a fifth of Astra's token price (Unite.AI, The Batch), though those are OpenAI's own numbers. An upgrade still moves your numbers, and your evals should say so.

Who picked the default? A catalog file

Look at what "default" meant in #49318. Nobody on your team chose GPT-6.1 Sol. It got the highest priority in a catalog file that ships inside the CLI, so it won.

Codex isn't unusual here. Claude Code's model docs say the aliases opus, sonnet and haiku "point to the recommended version for your provider and update over time." Same doc: "To pin to a specific version, use the full model name, for example claude-opus-5-5." So claude --model opus is a moving target by design, and claude --model claude-opus-5-5 is a pin.

Moving targets are fine for a chat. You want the newest model when you ask a question at 11pm. They are a problem for anything you measure, compare or promise to a teammate.


A default model can change between two eval runs without a single line of your repo changing.

Your evals measure the model, so they need its name

An agent eval can be a formal suite. More often it is a sentence in a team chat: "Codex is worse at migrations than Claude Code." "That AGENTS.md rewrite made the agent better." "This task took 40 minutes last week and 12 this week."

Each of those is a claim about a model. If the model was a default, you don't know which one it was. Did your prompt get better, or did the catalog move? Did Codex get worse at migrations, or did a fresh thread pick up a different server default than the one you tested last month?

The model is not the only hidden variable either. Reasoning effort changes results, and #50013 treats it like the model: if the launch doesn't set it, a fresh TUI thread takes the server's default. The account matters too: the GPT-5.5 retirement hit ChatGPT sign-ins and left API-key sessions alone, so the same gpt-5.5 setting meant two different things depending on how you logged in.

So the minimum record for any agent result is four fields: the model, the effort, the account type and the commit it ran against. Without them, a before-and-after comparison is two numbers with no explanation attached.

Pin it per task, then write it down

For daily work in Codex, a profile is the cleanest pin. Per the advanced config docs, a profile is a file in ~/.codex/ with top-level keys:

# ~/.codex/pinned.config.toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "medium"

Start it with codex --profile pinned. PR #50013 keeps explicit profile launches on the resolved configuration, so the profile's model holds even for fresh TUI threads.

For anything you compare, put the pin and the record in the same script. codex exec takes -m for the model (models page), and -c sets any config key (the config docs say a value that isn't valid TOML is treated as a string):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run-task.sh "<task>" : one pinned run, one logged row
set -u
task="$1"
model="gpt-6.1-sol"
effort="medium"
account="chatgpt"   # or "apikey": how this run signs in

codex exec -m "$model" \
  --sandbox workspace-write \
  -c model_reasoning_effort="$effort" \
  "$task" > last-run.log
agent=$?
npm test > test.log 2>&1
tests=$?

printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
  "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
  "$model" "$effort" "$account" "$agent" "$tests" >> runs.tsv

By default codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox (non-interactive mode docs), so --sandbox workspace-write is what lets the agent edit the checkout before the tests run. The agent column keeps Codex's own exit status, so a failed agent step shows up in the row instead of hiding behind a test result on untouched code.

Swap npm test for your own check, and set account to match how the machine signs in. Every row in runs.tsv now carries all four fields: which model, effort and account produced which test result on which commit.

Pinning has a cost, and October 14 showed it. Anyone pinned to gpt-5.5 with a ChatGPT sign-in had to edit their config. OpenAI's list of what to update covers "workspace defaults, saved model settings, managed configurations, custom agents, scheduled tasks, and scripts that still select gpt-5.5" (changelog).

That is the good kind of break. You change one line in a diff, rerun your tasks, and compare the new rows against the old ones.

Where Hermes IDE fits

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent's own CLI in a real terminal, Codex and Claude Code included, each task on its own branch and worktree.

The part that matters here: when you start a task with ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux), you pick the agent, model, effort and account for that task, and you can save combinations you use often as presets (README). Several accounts per agent are supported, so the sign-in a task runs under is something you choose when you start it.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: agent, project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, the model and effort chips, and a preview of the command Hermes will run.

After launch, every session shows its own spend: the cost the agent reports, or an estimate from its transcript marked as estimated, with token totals. Since 2.3.4, a Claude Code or Codex session keeps showing its own model and cost even when the conversation mentions another company's model. The bar above each session puts Model in the same place for every agent.


Codex and Claude Code side by side in Hermes 2.3.4, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with status, context use, cost and branch per session in the sidebar.

What it doesn't do: Hermes doesn't write your runs.tsv, and it can't stop a vendor from retiring a model you picked. It makes the choice explicit per task and keeps it visible per session. The record is still yours. Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic or any other agent vendor.

So, which model ran your last eval?

Open the last result you shared with your team, a benchmark, a "this agent is better at X" message, a before-and-after on a prompt change. Can you name the model and effort that produced it?

If not, you were testing a catalog entry. Tell me in the comments whether you pin your agent's model, or whether you'd rather ride the default and take the upgrades as they come.

If this was useful

Writing the model next to every result is the smallest piece of LLM observability. Observability for LLM Applications covers the rest of it: tracing each call, running evals that catch quality regressions when a model changes, and tracking cost per feature in production. If you run several agents, Hermes IDE is free and lets you set the model per task (GitHub).

title: A Drift Detector That Cries Wolf Is Worse Than No Detector
description:
My drift detector quarantined a healthy agent. The agent hadn't gotten worse — the benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions, so growing the benchmark from 10 tasks to 20 made a 10/10 agent look like it "failed" half the suite. Corpus growth looked like decay.

I built the drift detector for HivePlane v0.2.0 to catch the failure mode I'd written about in v0.1.0 — "the dangerous agent usually drifted, not got edited." The harder problem turned out not to be detecting drift. It was not detecting drift that wasn't there. A detector that cries wolf trains operators to ignore the signal, and an ignored gate is no gate.

The detector that ate its own benchmark

Finding What the detector did Why it was wrong
#530 Compared failure counts across corpus versions Growing the benchmark auto-quarantined a healthy agent
F-13 Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED Auto-quarantine resets to UNCERTIFIED — the gate refused its own quarantine
#609 / S24 The probe runner only checked admission A probe could never flag behavioral decay — only a refused run could fail one

The scariest line in the release wasn't a missed drift. It was a healthy agent quarantined because the detector compared it to a benchmark that no longer existed.

The benchmark that looked like decay

530 was the one that changed how I think about drift baselines. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions. If the benchmark grew from 10 tasks to 20 — because the learning loop added a reviewed case — a healthy agent that passed 10/10 now "failed" 10 of 20 by the old accounting. Corpus growth looked like decay.

The agent hadn't gotten worse. The benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector couldn't tell the difference, so it quarantined a perfectly good agent.

The fix: drift is measured against the agent's own baseline on comparable corpora. You compare the same tasks across re-evaluations, not different counts. A corpus version change establishes a new baseline, not a drift signal. Growing the benchmark is growth, not regression.

tip: If your drift metric is a count, a benchmark change will look like behavior change. Compare the agent to itself on the same tasks, or any corpus edit becomes a false quarantine.

The reinstatement that refused its own quarantine

F-13 was the symmetry that broke. Drift auto-quarantine resets the certification status to UNCERTIFIED — not QUARANTINED. Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED. So the gate that created the quarantine refused to lift it. A workload could be auto-quarantined and then never reinstated, because the precondition described a state the detector never set.

The fix was removing the stale precondition. An active quarantine record is reinstatable — the workload is re-certified and admission is re-checked. The status field is not the source of truth; the quarantine record is. The gate keyed off the wrong one.

The field test caught this in scenario S5, where reinstatement after S4's auto-quarantine failed in sequence. Two scenarios, one bug, and the lesson: the source of truth for "is this quarantined" is the quarantine record, not the certification status enum.

The probe that couldn't smell decay

609 / S24 was the most subtle. The synthetic probe runner ignored Spec.expected and only checked admission. So a probe could only fail if the run was refused — it could never flag that the agent ran and produced the wrong answer. The probe was a liveness check pretending to be a readiness check.

A probe's job is to catch decay before the drift threshold trips. If the probe only checks "did it run," it can't catch "did it run correctly." The fix: the runner starts the run, waits for terminal, and compares the output to expected. A mismatch fails the probe with a probe.decay warning. Now a probe can smell decay the drift detector hasn't measured yet.

What I learned

False-positive controls are the product, not a nicety: a single exceeding run is a warning, and quarantine requires N consecutive failures or a strong signal — a stable agent is never quarantined on noise. Measure drift against comparable baselines: the same tasks, the same corpus version; a corpus bump is a new baseline, not a regression. The quarantine record is the source of truth, not the status enum — reinstatement keys off the record, or it refuses the very quarantines it should lift. And a probe must assert the expected output, not just that the run was admitted — liveness is not readiness.

The v0.2.0 field test demonstrates the full loop — drift due/assess/probe, auto-quarantine, reinstatement after a fresh certification — as scenarios S4, S5, S8, and S24. The synthetic probe flags decay before the drift threshold in S24. Full evidence in the field-test report; the certification and learning-loop designs are in the certification v2 design and the learning loop design.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Certification v2 design · Learning loop design
  • Operator runbook — drift & quarantine

When was the last time your detector quarantined something that was fine? If your operators have learned to reinstate without reading, your detector isn't a control — it's a checkbox.

title: What a Clinic Website Actually Has to Do in the UAE
description:
Most clinic websites are built like brochures: a hero, a list of services, a contact page. Patients do not use them like brochures. A patient arrives with one job — book the right doctor, fast, on a phone — and every screen that does not serve that job is friction.

We shipped a healthcare solutions page today and had to make these decisions for real, so here is the checklist that survived contact with an actual build:

1. Booking is the product, not a feature

The appointment action has to be reachable from every key screen, not parked on a contact page. On mobile that means the booking/contact action stays in reach while the visitor reads — the same pattern we use for enquiries generally: a lead is a WhatsApp message, a call, or a form submit, and the path to one of those three should never be more than a tap away.

2. Doctor profiles are decision pages

Patients choose people, not departments. A doctor profile needs the things a patient actually compares: specialty, languages spoken, location, and a direct booking route from that profile. A grid of names with no detail forces the patient to call and ask — and many simply book elsewhere instead.

3. Arabic is not a translation toggle

In the UAE, an Arabic version that is a shallow copy of the English page reads as an afterthought to the exact audience it is meant to serve. Proper RTL layout and genuinely reviewed Arabic copy are part of the build, not a plugin. We treat bilingual work as its own scope for this reason.

4. Trust content belongs before the ask

Insurance partners accepted, accreditations, and what happens at the first visit — placed before the booking prompt, not after it. Patients hand over health details and payment information on these sites; the proof has to arrive before the form does.

5. Speed and security are patient-experience issues

A slow mobile page loses the booking. A neglected site — outdated software, no maintenance routine — risks the one incident a clinic cannot afford. Security patching and backups are not IT chores on a healthcare site; they are part of patient trust.

The full breakdown of how we structure this — patient journey, booking flow, doctor profiles, bilingual build, and the maintenance side — is here: clinic and healthcare website solutions in Dubai.

If you run a clinic site, audit it against the patient's job, not the brochure: can a new patient, on a phone, in Arabic or English, reach the right doctor's booking in under a minute? Everything else is decoration.

title: S3 Lifecycle Rules, Step by Step: Move Old Data to Cheaper Storage Without Surprise Fees
description:
Most S3 buckets start the same way. Someone creates a bucket, an app writes files into it, and nobody looks at it again. Months later the bucket holds years of logs, old exports and copies of files nobody remembers. Every byte sits in the default storage class, S3 Standard, and every byte is billed at that rate.

S3 Lifecycle rules fix this. A lifecycle rule tells Amazon S3 to move objects to a cheaper storage class after a number of days, or to delete them when they are no longer needed. You write the rule once, and S3 applies it every day.

The catch is that cheaper classes come with conditions. Some charge for a minimum number of days. Some charge to read data back. Some charge per object moved. A careless rule can cost more than it saves. This guide from CloudSkill Consulting LLC walks through S3 lifecycle rules one step at a time, so you can lower storage cost without surprise fees.

Step 1: Learn the storage classes in plain words

A storage class is a price plan for an object. Each object in S3 has one. The data is the same; what changes is the price to store it, the price to read it, and how fast you can get it back.

Here are the classes this guide uses, in order from "used often" to "almost never used":

  • S3 Standard (STANDARD): the default. No minimum storage time and no retrieval fee. Best for data you read often.
  • S3 Standard-IA (STANDARD_IA): "IA" means infrequent access. Cheaper to store, but there is a fee each time you read data, a 30-day minimum storage charge, and a 128 KB minimum billable size (see the S3 pricing and storage-class pages linked in Sources).
  • S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (GLACIER_IR): for data read about once a quarter, still with millisecond access. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (GLACIER): archive storage. You must restore an object before you can read it, and that takes minutes to hours. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive (DEEP_ARCHIVE): the lowest-cost archive, with restores measured in hours. It has a 180-day minimum.

There is also S3 Intelligent-Tiering (INTELLIGENT_TIERING). It watches how each object is used and moves it between tiers for you, for a small monitoring fee per object. It has no retrieval fees. It is a good choice when you honestly don't know how often data is read.


Figure 1: Each step down is cheaper to store, but has a longer minimum stay and slower or paid reads.

Step 2: Find out what is in the bucket before you write a rule

Never write a lifecycle rule from memory. Look at the data first. Two questions matter:

  1. How big are the objects? Small objects behave differently. By default, S3 Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class. AWS explains why: you pay a transition request for each object, so for small objects the request cost can outweigh the savings.
  2. How often is each prefix read? A prefix is the start of an object key, like logs/ or exports/2025/. Logs written once and almost never read are good candidates. Product images that a website loads all day are not.

AWS gives you tools for this. S3 Storage Class Analysis watches access patterns on a bucket or prefix and helps you decide when to move data from Standard to Standard-IA. S3 Storage Lens shows storage use across buckets. Turn one of them on and give it time before you choose your day counts.

A good habit: write down each prefix, who owns it, how often it is read, and how long it must be kept. "How long it must be kept" is a business question, not a technical one. Ask the data owner.

Step 3: Understand the three rules that cause surprise fees

These three rules are where most lifecycle mistakes come from.

Rule A: minimum storage duration. Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum, Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval have 90 days, and Deep Archive has 180 days (minimum storage charges, per the S3 pricing and storage-class pages). If you delete, overwrite or move an object out before that time, you are charged for the rest of the minimum. A rule that moves logs to Glacier Flexible Retrieval and then deletes them 30 days later still pays for 90 days.

Rule B: small objects. Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill each object as at least 128 KB. Objects archived to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive also carry about 40 KB of extra metadata each: 8 KB billed at the Standard rate and 32 KB at the archive rate. Millions of tiny files can cost more after archiving than before.

Rule C: reads cost money and time. IA and Glacier classes charge per GB retrieved. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects are not readable until you restore them, and while restored you pay for both the archive copy and a temporary Standard copy.


Figure 2: Check every lifecycle rule against these three conditions before you turn it on.

Step 4: Write a first rule that is hard to get wrong

Start with one prefix that is clearly "write once, read rarely", such as application logs. Here is a full lifecycle configuration in the JSON format the AWS CLI expects. It has three rules.

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "logs-tier-then-expire",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 120, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 400 }
    },
    {
      "ID": "old-versions-cleanup",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {
        "NoncurrentDays": 30,
        "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3
      }
    },
    {
      "ID": "abort-stuck-uploads",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

Here is what each part does, in plain words:

  • logs-tier-then-expire applies only to keys starting with logs/. After 30 days the objects move to Standard-IA. After 120 days they move to Glacier Flexible Retrieval. After 400 days they expire. The gaps are chosen on purpose: 90 days in Standard-IA is more than its 30-day minimum, and 280 days in Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more than its 90-day minimum. No early-deletion charge applies. Since July 2026 you can move objects to Standard-IA from day 0. We wait 30 days because new logs are read most often in their first weeks.
  • old-versions-cleanup matters only if versioning is on. When you overwrite or delete an object in a versioned bucket, the old copy stays as a noncurrent version, and you keep paying for it. This rule permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent, but always keeps the 3 newest ones. Be sure that matches your recovery needs, because deleted versions can't be brought back.
  • abort-stuck-uploads cleans up multipart uploads that started but never finished. Their parts are stored and billed, yet they don't appear as normal objects. AWS notes that expiration rules don't remove incomplete multipart uploads; you need this separate action.

An empty Filter ({}) means "every object in the bucket".

S3 rounds lifecycle timing to the next midnight UTC. An object created at 10:30 AM UTC with a 3-day rule becomes eligible at midnight UTC four days later. Transitions to Glacier also run in the background, so the physical move can lag behind the date. You are still billed at the destination rate from the date the rule is met.


Figure 3 (example rule): One object's life under the logs/ rule, with each stay longer than that class's minimum.

Step 5: Apply it safely with the AWS CLI

First, save any rules that already exist. This step matters. The AWS CLI documentation says put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration replaces the whole existing configuration. Any rule you leave out of your file is gone.

# 1. Back up the current configuration (an error here usually means none exists yet)
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data > lifecycle-backup.json

# 2. Check your new file is valid JSON
jq . lifecycle.json

# 3. Apply the new configuration
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

# 4. Read it back and compare
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket example-app-data

If an older rule existed, merge it into lifecycle.json before step 3. A bucket has one lifecycle configuration with up to 1,000 rules.

To see stuck uploads before and after, list them:

aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket example-app-data

Step 6: Check the result, then widen slowly

Lifecycle rules don't act the moment you save them. Give it a few days, then check:

  1. Billing: in AWS Cost Explorer, group S3 cost by usage type. Storage cost for the moved classes should rise while Standard storage falls.
  2. Request and retrieval costs: watch for a jump in transition requests (many small objects) or in retrieval fees (data that is read more than you thought).
  3. Complaints: if someone needs an archived object, they will find it isn't instantly readable. That tells you the day count was too short for that prefix.

When the first prefix looks right, add the next one as a new rule. One prefix at a time keeps every change easy to undo: set its Status to Disabled and apply again.


Figure 4: Grow your lifecycle configuration one prefix at a time.

A short checklist

  • Know each prefix's size, read pattern and required retention.
  • Leave small objects in Standard or Intelligent-Tiering.
  • Make every stay longer than the class's minimum duration.
  • Add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to every bucket.
  • On versioned buckets, decide how many old versions to keep, then expire the rest.
  • Back up the current configuration before every put.

At CloudSkill Consulting LLC, we test lifecycle rules like this on a small prefix before applying them to a whole bucket. Storage tiers are often the first place a cloud bill can shrink. We do this kind of FinOps check for teams on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. If a rule here behaves differently in your account, write to info@cloudskillconsulting.com.

Sources (official documentation, checked Oct 17, 2026)

  • Amazon S3 storage classes and comparison table (minimum storage duration charges): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html
  • Transitioning objects using S3 Lifecycle (128 KB default, minimum durations, archive overhead, billing timing): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html
  • Lifecycle configuration elements (filters, noncurrent versions, multipart uploads, midnight UTC timing, 1,000 rules): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intro-lifecycle-rules.html
  • AWS CLI put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI list-multipart-uploads: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/list-multipart-uploads.html
  • Amazon S3 pricing (minimum storage duration charges): https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • AWS What's New, Jul 16, 2026: S3 removes the 30-day minimum before lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/07/s3-removes-30-day-transitions-standard-ia-one-zone-ia/

title: Accelerator certification speeds VLA models 10
description:
Bounding the risk of acceleration‑induced failure lets practitioners reap order‑of‑magnitude speedups on vision‑language‑action agents. The twist is that a formal guarantee can coexist with those gains, overturning the common belief that safety and performance are mutually exclusive.

Prior VLA accelerators have chased raw latency reductions—action chunking, visual‑token pruning, and similar tricks—while reporting only average task success. Those metrics hide failures that only manifest over closed‑loop trajectories, because a single misstep can cascade into an episode‑level collapse that the average numbers never reveal.

CARE certifies 9.0–10.8× faster inference while guaranteeing that at least 85.8 % of reference‑solved episodes remain successful with 95 % confidence, even under a user‑specified failure budget [1].

The certification process itself requires roughly five times fewer rollouts than exhaustive testing. “care also has the lowest evaluation cost, using 5,263 rather than 25,000 rollouts ( fewer) and reducing H1 evaluation from 1,000 to 113 rollouts.” [1]

The method’s guarantees rely on a static calibration set and have only been demonstrated on four LIBERO suites and two agents (Qwen3.5‑9B, Llama‑3.1‑8B), leaving open how it scales to larger, continually evolving deployments or to online adaptation scenarios [1].

Future VLA benchmark runs should replace naïve latency baselines with CARE‑certified selectors as the default evaluation protocol, and deployment pipelines ought to employ failure‑triggered reference rollouts instead of exhaustive pre‑deployment testing.

References

  1. CARE: Certifying Acceleration for Vision-Language-Action Inference

Example

If prefetch a link to /search?q=shoes, searchParams is resolved from link of URL, cached result of search() is prepared before click. Browser re-uses it untill stale time has passed or searchParams has been changed.

title: Properties Without Witnesses Are Decorations: A Falsifiability Gate for Agent Patches
description:
A property that passes on the patched tree and on the pre-patch tree carries no information. That is the first thing to measure, before you trust any property an agent wrote for you.

Most agent-written property tests fail this way. The agent reads the diff, writes an invariant that the new code obviously satisfies, and the suite goes green in both trees. The test is not wrong. It is simply unable to distinguish the two states, which makes it a decoration, not a check.

This post describes a gate with three rules and one artifact. Properties need a committed witness and a measured detection rate on the baseline. Fixtures must be isolated per sample, verified by transcript hashing. Flaky-frozen tests are forbidden from acting as oracles. The gate is small enough to run on every agent patch.

The three roles, and what each one can lie about

Role What it claims How it lies Gate check
Property "This invariant holds for the domain" Domain is one hand-picked example Fail-rate on pre-patch tree ≥ floor
Fixture "Setup is deterministic" Sample N sees state left by sample N-1 Set of per-sample transcript hashes has size 1
Freeze "This test is temporarily excused" Frozen test becomes the only oracle Freeze list ∩ oracle set = ∅

Each row fails independently. A property with a real domain can still be useless if the fixture leaks state between samples; a clean fixture cannot save an invariant that holds by construction.

Step 1: Commit a witness next to every property

A witness is the concrete input that proves the property can fail. It is not a test case the agent is allowed to invent during the run — it lives in the repository, reviewable, in its own file.

{
  "id": "inv_total_never_negative",
  "seed": 20261018,
  "input": {"lines": [{"qty": 1, "unit_cents": -5}], "discount_cents": 0},
  "expected_on_baseline": "fail",
  "expected_on_patched": "pass"
}

The two expected_* fields are the whole point. On the merge-base tree the witness must reproduce the bug. On the patched tree it must pass. If the witness passes on both, the patch fixed nothing the witness can see, and the review should stop there.

# gate/witness.py — runnable sketch; plugin points are stubbed
import json, subprocess

def replay(tree_dir, prop_id):
    w = json.load(open(f"witnesses/{prop_id}.json"))
    return subprocess.run(
        ["python", "-m", "props.run", prop_id, json.dumps(w["input"])],
        cwd=tree_dir, capture_output=True, text=True,
    ).returncode == 0

Step 2: Measure detection power on the baseline, not on the patch

Passing the witness is necessary and cheap. The expensive question is whether the property generalizes past that one input. Sample the declared domain under a seeded generator on the pre-patch worktree, and count how often the invariant fails.

# gate/power.py
import random

def detection_power(prop, baseline_tree, gen, run_invariant, fixture_hash):
    rng = random.Random(prop.seed)
    fails, transcripts = 0, set()
    for _ in range(prop.samples):
        example, transcript = gen.sample(prop.domain, rng)
        transcripts.add(fixture_hash(transcript))       # rule 2, below
        if not run_invariant(baseline_tree, prop.invariant, example):
            fails += 1
    return fails / prop.samples, transcripts

Set power_floor from your own baseline run, not from this post. A property whose fail-rate on the buggy tree is near zero is a description of the current code, not a check on it. A fail-rate near one usually means the generator produces out-of-domain inputs and the property is failing for the wrong reason.

Rates in between need a human eye. There is no universal threshold; the number is a policy knob your repo owns and reviews.

Step 3: Isolate fixtures per sample and prove it with hashes

Property sampling multiplies whatever your fixture does. If setup writes rows, mutates a module-level cache, or advances a clock, sample 12 is running against sample 11's leftovers — and your fail-rate is measuring ordering, not behavior.

Give each sample a reset hook and hash the setup transcript (touched tables, env keys, temp paths, fake clock value). Across a run, the set of hashes must have exactly one member.

power, transcripts = detection_power(prop, baseline_tree, gen, run_invariant, fixture_hash)
if len(transcripts) != 1:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: fixture state varies across samples → {sorted(transcripts)[:3]}")
if power < prop.power_floor:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: detection power {power:.2f} < floor {prop.power_floor:.2f}")

A set of size greater than one is a deterministic, reproducible red — the kind of failure you can hand back to the agent without a discussion.

Step 4: Freeze the flaky tests, and keep them out of the oracle set

Freezing a flaky test so the suite stays green is a reasonable maintenance move. Letting that frozen test quietly become the only thing validating an agent patch is not.

Pass the freeze list into the property runner explicitly. Any intersection between the frozen set and the tests the property run actually executed is a hard failure, not a warning.

frozen = {l.strip() for l in open("tests/frozen.txt") if l.strip()}
ran    = run_property_suite(patched_tree, prop.id)      # returns test node ids
leaked = frozen & ran
if leaked:
    fail(f"{prop.id}: frozen tests used as oracle → {sorted(leaked)}")

The same list should carry an expiry date per entry. A freeze without an end date silently becomes a permanent hole in coverage.

Step 5: Wire it as one gate with three exit codes

Run the three steps in a fixed order and stop at the first failure. Exit code 0 means the property is falsifiable, its fixture is deterministic, and its oracle is un-frozen. Anything else is a reviewable artifact, not a vibe.

git worktree add ../baseline "$(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)"
python -m gate.run --prop inv_total_never_negative \
  --baseline ../baseline --patched . --samples 200 --power-floor 0.10
# 0 = accepted, 1 = property rejected, 2 = harness error
git worktree remove ../baseline

Per-property cost is samples × setup_time. Two hundred samples across a ten-property patch is a few minutes of wall clock on a modest machine — acceptable per pull request, not acceptable on every keystroke.

The proposal side of this loop does not need a frontier model; scanning a diff and drafting invariants is well inside what free model access handles, and running the sampler on the free server option keeps the 200-sample loop off a laptop that is already running the app under test. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Availability of free tiers is not a guarantee — check the current terms on your own account before wiring it into CI, and do not send proprietary code or credentials to a shared runner.

Limitations and who should skip this

  • Property sampling only works on domains you can generate. Stateful protocols and payment flows usually need a hand-built model first.
  • The power floor is a heuristic. It catches decorative properties; it does not prove the invariant is the right one.
  • Suites with heavy fixtures (containers, seeded production snapshots) will spend the whole budget on setup resets.
  • Teams with data-residency constraints should run the harness entirely in-house; the remote runner is a cost convenience, not a requirement.

Start with the witness registry. It is the cheapest file to commit and the fastest way to discover that half of your agent's properties pass on both trees. When the power floor turns out to be the number you have to lower, that lower number is the finding worth writing down.

title: Go Retrieval Architecture for Multi-Tenant SaaS Help Center Pagination (10k Tenants)
description:
Short answer: paginate a tenant-scoped, immutable retrieval snapshot, then rerank a bounded candidate set once and carry citation lineage through every page. That decision keeps page boundaries stable while the help-center index changes, which is the condition needed for grounded answers.

The unit of work is a retrieval run, not an HTTP page. Normalize the question, bind it to the authenticated tenant and access policy, retrieve candidates, rerank them, and assign a deterministic order before returning page one. A later request slices that same order. Re-running retrieval for every page feels fresh, but it creates gaps, duplicates, and citations that point at a different revision. This also gives the platform team one place to account for work: candidate retrieval, reranking, snapshot storage, and generation can each have a budget, and the run can be rejected before it consumes the rest of the latency SLO when the candidate cap or tenant quota is already exhausted. That is a capacity decision, not a pagination trick.

I treat a cursor like a distributed job handoff. It is state, not authority. A client can decode ordinary base64, so the token must be signed and its tenant, query fingerprint, policy version, snapshot ID, boundary, page size, and expiry must be checked server-side.

How should pagination shape retrieval architecture for a multi-tenant SaaS help center?

Use two orders. The snapshot order controls continuity; the answer order controls how citations are displayed. Never use a displayed citation number as a pagination key. Every item should retain document ID, document revision, chunk ID, and the exact source span supplied to generation. The Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper describes generation conditioned on retrieved passages; preserving that passage identity across pages is what makes the citation claim auditable.

Choose a stable tie-breaker such as chunk ID after the relevance score. If a reranker has any nondeterminism, persist the resulting ordered IDs for the cursor lifetime rather than calculating page two again. A 50-item page is a practical example, not a universal target; capacity planning should set the candidate cap from labeled relevance tests, memory headroom, and the latency budget for the retrieval SLO.

Small boundary, big blast radius.

Measure it.

The snapshot gives consistency, not unlimited freshness. A newly published article may wait until the next query, while current authorization still has to be applied on each continuation. The catch is that this design is not suitable when revoked content must disappear from an already-running answer immediately; in that case, recheck policy per page and accept that a page can shrink.

What signal exposes citation drift before users report it?

The useful alert names an invariant violation, not a vague “pagination failed.” Track overlap between pages, citations outside the authorized result set, revision mismatches, scope-rejected cursors, expired snapshots, and normal exhaustion as separate outcomes. An exhausted result set is healthy; combining it with errors makes an SLO dashboard lie.

Consider a trace for tenant acme-17. Page one ends at chunk billing:rev-8:0042, and page two starts with the same ID. The trace should show the query hash, policy version, snapshot revision, candidate count, page size, cursor age, returned-ID digest, and cited-ID digest. It does not need the customer's full question or document text in routine metrics. Put replayable detail in access-controlled traces with a retention policy that matches the data classification.

The first check is the cursor invariant: the next ID must be strictly after the stored boundary in snapshot order. If that holds, compare the cited revision with the retrieved revision. If both hold, inspect the answer assembly. This ordering keeps an indexing or authorization defect from being misdiagnosed as a model-quality problem.

A signed Go cursor keeps the boundary explicit

The token below is opaque to callers but explicit to the service. HMAC-SHA256 protects integrity; a key ID allows rotation. The decoder validates structural limits before the caller resolves a snapshot.

package cursor

import (
    "crypto/hmac"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/base64"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Payload struct {
    Version      int    `json:"v"`
    KeyID        string `json:"kid"`
    TenantID     string `json:"tenant"`
    QueryHash    string `json:"query_hash"`
    Policy       string `json:"policy"`
    SnapshotID   string `json:"snapshot"`
    NextOffset   int    `json:"next_offset"`
    PageSize     int    `json:"page_size"`
    ExpiresAtUnix int64  `json:"expires_at"`
}

var (
    ErrMalformed = errors.New("malformed cursor")
    ErrSignature = errors.New("invalid cursor signature")
    ErrExpired   = errors.New("expired cursor")
)

func Encode(p Payload, key []byte) (string, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(p)
    if err != nil { return "", err }
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, key)
    _, _ = mac.Write(body)
    enc := base64.RawURLEncoding
    return enc.EncodeToString(body) + "." + enc.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)), nil
}

func Decode(token string, key []byte, now time.Time) (Payload, error) {
    var p Payload
    parts := strings.Split(token, ".")
    if len(parts) != 2 { return p, ErrMalformed }
    enc := base64.RawURLEncoding
    body, err := enc.DecodeString(parts[0])
    if err != nil { return p, ErrMalformed }
    sig, err := enc.DecodeString(parts[1])
    if err != nil { return p, ErrMalformed }
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, key)
    _, _ = mac.Write(body)
    if !hmac.Equal(sig, mac.Sum(nil)) { return p, ErrSignature }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &p); err != nil { return p, ErrMalformed }
    if p.Version != 1 || p.PageSize < 1 || p.PageSize > 50 || p.NextOffset < 0 {
        return p, ErrMalformed
    }
    if now.Unix() >= p.ExpiresAtUnix { return p, ErrExpired }
    return p, nil
}

After decoding, compare TenantID, QueryHash, and Policy with values derived from the current request. Resolve SnapshotID, take the slice at NextOffset, filter it through current authorization, and sign the advanced offset. Because the snapshot is immutable, this offset is not an offset into a changing search index.

Continuation must be idempotent. A network retry can submit the same cursor twice, and both responses should describe the same slice while the snapshot is available. Do not consume a single-use token before the response is durable unless the protocol also has a request idempotency key and replay store.

Verification, rollout, and rollback are part of the design

Test malformed signatures, unknown versions, exact-boundary expiry, tenant and query mismatches, and page sizes 0, 1, 50, and 51. Property tests can generate unique ordered IDs, paginate with random legal sizes, and assert that concatenating pages reproduces the snapshot exactly once. An integration test should update the live index after page one and verify that page two still reads the original snapshot while applying current authorization.

Relevance tests belong beside cursor tests. Use a labeled set from the real help-center intents, evaluate retrieval and reranking before generation, and verify that each answer claim is supported by one cited span. Pagination is correct only when changing the boundary does not change that evidence contract.

Roll out with shadow traces, then a small tenant cohort, then broader traffic. Watch duplicate-result rate, cursor rejection by reason, empty continuation pages, snapshot lookup latency, and citation validity. A rollback should stop issuing the new cursor version while retaining its verification key until outstanding tokens expire.

Set alert thresholds against an actionable SLO. One cross-tenant result is an immediate containment event; one expired cursor usually is not. I'm not sure a single citation-coverage threshold transfers from account recovery to configuration help, because acceptable evidence differs by intent class. Per-intent labels and review are what would resolve that uncertainty.

The operational rule is simple: freeze the evidence order for a traversal, recheck authorization, and make every boundary observable. Stick with fresh per-page retrieval only when freshness is more important than continuity and citation reproducibility.

References

  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Go crypto/hmac package documentation: https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/hmac
  • Go encoding/base64 package documentation: https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/base64

Issue

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the <namespace> segment in these queries.

Queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification. We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases.

Mitigation:

title: Hono vs Express vs Fastify (and NestJS) in 2026: Real Benchmarks on Node 24, Node 26 and Bun
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Hono vs Express in 2026 is a closer race than the benchmark charts you've seen suggest. On Node.js 24, Hono served 1.44× as many JSON requests per second as Express 5 in my tests, and Fastify was right next to it. But Fastify beat Hono on route parameters and POST bodies, and NestJS added 21 to 23% overhead on top of whichever engine it ran on. The biggest jump didn't come from the framework at all: moving Hono from Node to Bun gave another 1.6×.

I benchmarked seven setups (raw node:http, Hono, Express, Fastify with and without response schemas, and NestJS 12 on both its Express and Fastify adapters) across three workloads, two Node versions and Bun. Here's every number, how I got it, and which framework I'd pick for which job.

TL;DR: Hono vs Express vs Fastify, which is fastest?

On Node, Hono and Fastify are tied for first, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express. Hono won the plain JSON test, Fastify won route parameters and POST bodies. Express 5 is the slowest of the three but still served 50,000 requests per second on two CPU cores, which is more than most APIs will ever see. On Bun, Hono pulls clearly ahead at 118,000 requests per second.

Node 24.22, 2 cores, requests/s (median) JSON Route param POST JSON body Startup to first response Install size
node:http (no framework) 78,870 73,049 41,917 76 ms none
Hono 4.13.13 73,067 70,128 36,553 94 ms 3.9 MB, 2 packages
Fastify 5.12.7 71,786 76,746 38,936 153 ms 14.4 MB, 48 packages
Express 5.3.0 50,744 48,335 28,569 116 ms 4.3 MB, 65 packages
NestJS 12.1.3 + Fastify 56,434 59,499 33,418 425 ms n/a
NestJS 12.1.3 + Express 38,893 35,829 23,011 320 ms 22.4 MB, 98 packages

My pick: Hono for new APIs, especially anything that might run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or another edge runtime. Fastify for Node-only services where you want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express when the team and middleware already exist, because it's fast enough. NestJS when the codebase is big enough that structure matters more than 20% of throughput, and then put it on the Fastify adapter.

What are Hono, Express and Fastify?

All three are HTTP frameworks for JavaScript and TypeScript, and they come from different eras.

  • Express is the 2010 original and still the default. Express 5 finally shipped native promise support in route handlers and dropped a lot of legacy API. It has the largest middleware ecosystem by far: 145 million npm downloads in the week of October 6 to 12, 2026.
  • Fastify was built for speed on Node. It compiles JSON schemas into fast serializers and validators, has a strict plugin system with encapsulation, and logs with Pino by default. 15.4 million downloads that week.
  • Hono is built on web standards: handlers take a Request-like context and return a Response. The same app runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda and Vercel. It's tiny and has zero dependencies. 74 million downloads that week, partly because other tools bundle it.
  • NestJS isn't a fourth HTTP engine. It's an application framework with modules, dependency injection and decorators that runs on top of Express (the default) or Fastify. I covered the latest release in my NestJS 12 upgrade guide.

The code looks similar for a simple route. Here are the three handlers I benchmarked:

// Hono
app.get('/users/:id', c => c.json({ id: c.req.param('id'), fields: c.req.query('fields') ?? null }))

// Express 5
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

// Fastify 5
app.get('/users/:id', async req => ({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

How I benchmarked them

Benchmarks of web frameworks are easy to get wrong, so here's exactly what I ran.

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB of RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3.
  3. Versions. Hono 4.13.13 with @hono/node-server 2.1.5, Express 5.3.0, Fastify 5.12.7, and NestJS 12.1.3 with @nestjs/platform-express and @nestjs/platform-fastify. These were the latest npm releases on October 17, 2026.
  4. Workloads. GET /json returns {"message":"Hello, World!"}. GET /users/42?fields=name reads a route parameter and a query string. POST /echo parses a 907-byte JSON body and returns a count.
  5. Fair settings. No logging. ETags off in Express and in NestJS on Express, and x-powered-by off in Express. Fastify ran twice, once without schemas and once with response schemas. Every app returns the same JSON.
  6. Method. Each run started a fresh server, warmed it up for 4 seconds, then measured for 10 seconds. I ran 3 rounds per setup and report the median. Four setups had one noisy round, so I re-ran those with 5 rounds. That's 32 setups and more than 65 million measured requests, with a 100% success rate.

Absolute numbers depend on hardware. The ratios between frameworks are what transfer to your servers.

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. On Node 24, Hono handled 1.44× Express's throughput on plain JSON (73,067 vs 50,744 requests per second), 1.45× on route parameters and 1.28× on POST bodies. Latency followed: p99 on the JSON test was 1.50 ms for Hono against 2.12 ms for Express.

Two details matter more than the headline:

  • Hono came within 8% of raw node:http on the JSON test. There's very little left to optimize in the framework itself.
  • Hono's lead shrinks on POST. On Node, Hono goes through @hono/node-server, which turns Node's request into a web-standard Request before your handler sees it. Parsing a body through that layer costs more than Fastify's native parser. On Bun, where Request is native, the same Hono app did 80,749 POST requests per second, 2.2× its Node result.

Express 5 pays for its flexible middleware pipeline and the extra properties it adds to every request and response. It's still not slow. Fifty thousand requests per second on two cores is about 4 billion requests a day. Your database will give out long before Express does.

Hono vs Fastify: which is faster?

It depends on the route. On Node 24:

Requests/s, Node 24 Hono Fastify Fastify + response schema Winner
JSON 73,067 71,786 74,567 tie (within 4%)
Route param + query 70,128 76,746 75,526 Fastify, +9%
POST JSON body 36,553 38,936 39,045 Fastify, +7%

Fastify's router is a radix tree (find-my-way), and it beat even my hand-written node:http router on the route parameter test (76,746 vs 73,049), because my raw version builds a URL object per request. Adding response schemas, which Fastify compiles into a serializer with fast-json-stringify, was worth only about 4% on these small responses. The bigger value of schemas is validation and documentation, not speed.

So on Node, call it a draw. Pick between them on design: web standards and portability (Hono), or schemas, plugins and Node depth (Fastify).

Fastify vs Express: is it worth switching in 2026?

On raw speed, Fastify was 1.41× faster on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST. Its p99 latency was 25 to 40% lower too.

Whether that justifies a rewrite depends on where your time goes. If a typical request spends 20 ms in Postgres and 0.3 ms in the framework, cutting the framework's share in half changes nothing a user can feel. Switch when profiling shows the framework near the top, when you want schema validation built in, or when you're starting fresh anyway. Don't switch because of a chart, including this one.

How much overhead does NestJS add?

NestJS adds a layer of decorators, guards, pipes and interceptors on top of the engine. In my tests that cost 23% of Express's throughput (38,893 vs 50,744 on JSON) and 21% of Fastify's (56,434 vs 71,786). It also used more memory: about 100 MB idle versus 65 MB for plain Express.

The fix is easy and well documented in the NestJS performance guide: NestJS on Fastify was 1.45× faster than NestJS on Express on JSON and POST, and 1.66× faster on route parameters. It was also faster than plain Express on every test. If you use NestJS and none of your middleware is Express-specific, the Fastify adapter is the cheapest performance win available.

Do Node 26 and Bun change the ranking?

Node 26 made every framework faster without code changes. On the JSON test, Express and Fastify gained about 12%, NestJS 10%, Hono 6% and raw node:http 7%.

JSON requests/s Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Hono 73,067 77,454 118,432
Fastify 71,786 80,220 86,269
Express 50,744 56,627 72,479
NestJS + Express 38,893 42,923 not tested

On Bun, the ranking changes. Hono uses Bun's native server directly, so it ran 1.62× faster than on Node 24 and opened a 37% lead over Fastify. Express and Fastify also got faster on Bun (1.43× and 1.20×) but they run through Bun's node:http compatibility layer instead of calling Bun.serve directly. If you plan to run on Bun, Hono is the obvious choice. I compared the runtimes themselves in Bun vs Node.js in 2026.

Memory, startup time and install size

Throughput isn't the only cost. Startup matters for serverless and autoscaling, and install size matters for container images and cold deploys.

Node 24 Startup to first 200 Peak RSS at startup RSS idle Peak RSS under JSON load
node:http 76 ms 62 MB 58 MB 97 MB
Hono 94 ms 67 MB 63 MB 104 MB
Express 116 ms 75 MB 65 MB 97 MB
Fastify 153 ms 78 MB 72 MB 105 MB
NestJS + Express 320 ms 100 MB 98 MB 143 MB
NestJS + Fastify 425 ms 109 MB 106 MB 138 MB
Hono on Bun 14 ms 24 MB 20 MB 43 MB

Startup is the time from launching the process to the first successful response, measured with hyperfine over 20 runs. Hono on Bun was ready in 14 ms, which is why it's popular for serverless functions. NestJS needed about 2.8 times as long as the plain framework underneath it, because it scans modules and builds its dependency graph at boot.

Install size, measured in a fresh folder with npm: Hono plus its Node adapter is 2 packages and 3.9 MB. Express 5 is 65 packages but only 4.3 MB. Fastify is 48 packages and 14.4 MB. A minimal NestJS app on Express (core, common, platform-express, reflect-metadata, rxjs) is 98 packages and 22.4 MB. If you ship Docker images, my Next.js Dockerfile guide has the same multi-stage tricks that keep a Node API image small.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

If you need... Pick Why
A new API with the fewest moving parts Hono Within 8% of raw Node, zero dependencies, web-standard code
To run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda Hono Same app everywhere; 118k req/s on Bun
The best Node throughput on real routes Fastify Won route params and POST; schemas and plugins built in
An existing team and Express middleware Express 5 50k req/s is plenty; huge ecosystem; easy hiring
Structure for a large team (modules, DI) NestJS on Fastify 1.45 to 1.66× faster than NestJS on Express
End-to-end typed clients Hono (RPC) or Fastify with TypeBox Types flow from routes to clients

Two more points rarely show up in benchmark posts:

  • Ecosystem. Express still has the most middleware, tutorials and Stack Overflow answers. Fastify's plugin ecosystem covers most production needs. Hono's middleware set is smaller but growing, and anything built on web standards tends to just work.
  • Typed clients. Hono's RPC mode lets a frontend import the API's types directly. If your frontend is Next.js, also check whether you need a separate API at all; I covered that in Server Actions vs Route Handlers.

How do I migrate from Express to Hono or Fastify?

You don't need a big-bang rewrite. Both frameworks can sit next to Express while you move routes.

// Fastify: run existing Express middleware during a migration
import Fastify from 'fastify'
import expressPlugin from '@fastify/express'
const app = Fastify()
await app.register(expressPlugin)
app.use(legacyExpressMiddleware)

// Hono: same handler shape on every runtime
import { Hono } from 'hono'
const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', c => c.json({ ok: true }))
export default app // Bun, Workers, Deno; use @hono/node-server on Node

A safe order: move health checks and read-only routes first, measure them in production, then move the routes that write data. Keep the request and response shapes identical so clients never notice. Watch for Express habits that don't carry over: mutating req from middleware, res.locals, and error handlers with four arguments.

Common mistakes when benchmarking web frameworks

  • Running the load generator on the server's cores. Pin them apart, or you measure contention.
  • Benchmarking only /hello. Hono won plain JSON, Fastify won routes with parameters and bodies. One endpoint gives you one answer.
  • Leaving logging on. Fastify with a logger and Express with morgan are both much slower. Compare like with like.
  • Trusting a single run. Four of my 32 setups had one round 10 to 20% below the others. Take the median of several runs.
  • Comparing frameworks on different runtimes. "Hono is 2× faster than Express" is often Hono on Bun versus Express on Node.
  • Ignoring where time actually goes. Profile one real request. The framework is rarely the bottleneck.

Related: if your API is meant for AI agents, read MCP vs API before choosing a framework, because the protocol choice changes more than the framework does.

Key takeaways

  • On Node 24, Hono (73,067 req/s) and Fastify (71,786) are tied on JSON, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express 5 (50,744).
  • Fastify won route parameters (+9% over Hono) and POST bodies (+7%). Hono won plain JSON and came within 8% of raw node:http.
  • NestJS costs about 21 to 23% throughput and about 2.8× the startup time. On the Fastify adapter it's 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express.
  • Node 26 sped every framework up by 6 to 12% with no code changes.
  • On Bun, Hono jumped to 118,432 req/s, 1.62× its Node result, with 14 ms startup and 43 MB under load.
  • Hono installs as 2 packages (3.9 MB). Express is 65 packages (4.3 MB), Fastify 48 (14.4 MB), and NestJS 98 (22.4 MB).
  • Even Express handled 50,000 requests per second on 2 cores. Pick on design and ecosystem first; the framework is rarely your bottleneck.

FAQ

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. In my October 2026 benchmark on Node 24, Hono 4.13.13 served 73,067 JSON requests per second against 50,744 for Express 5.3.0, which is 1.44× faster. It was 1.45× faster on route parameters and 1.28× faster on POST bodies, with lower p99 latency.

Is Hono faster than Fastify?

On Node they're tied. Hono won plain JSON by 2%, but Fastify won route parameters by 9% and POST bodies by 7%. On Bun, Hono pulls ahead: 118,432 requests per second versus 86,269 for Fastify, because Hono uses Bun's native server directly.

Is Fastify faster than Express in 2026?

Yes. Fastify 5.12.7 was 1.41× faster than Express 5.3.0 on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST bodies, with 25 to 40% lower p99 latency. Express still handled about 50,000 requests per second on two cores, which is enough for most APIs.

How much slower is NestJS than Express or Fastify?

NestJS 12.1.3 cost about 23% of Express's throughput and 21% of Fastify's on the JSON test, used about 100 MB of memory at idle, and took about 2.8× as long to start. Using the Fastify adapter made NestJS 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express, and faster than plain Express on every test.

Should I switch from Express to Hono or Fastify?

Only if you have a reason beyond a benchmark. Switch when profiling shows the framework is a real cost, when you want built-in schema validation (Fastify), or when you need to run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or other runtimes (Hono). If most request time is spent in the database, a faster framework won't be noticeable.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

Hono for new APIs and anything that may run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda. Fastify for Node-only services that want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express 5 for teams with existing middleware and experience. NestJS on the Fastify adapter for large codebases that need modules and dependency injection.

Does Node 26 make Express, Fastify and Hono faster?

Yes. With no code changes, Node 26.12 improved JSON throughput over Node 24.22 by about 12% for Express and Fastify, 10% for NestJS, 7% for raw node:http and 6% for Hono.

How did you benchmark Hono, Express and Fastify?

Each server ran on 2 pinned CPU cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM, with oha 1.16.0 on the other cores at 64 connections. Every run started a fresh server, warmed up for 4 seconds and measured for 10 seconds. I report the median of 3 rounds, or 5 rounds for setups with a noisy round, across 32 setups on Node 24.22, Node 26.12 and Bun 1.4.3.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.
