title: avoiding race conditions in async cascade deletes for event‑sourced services
description:
you've got an event‑sourced aggregate that emits a UserDeleted event, and several downstream services react by cleaning up related rows in their own stores. the cleanup runs in background workers, so a second request that references the same user can slip through the cracks and hit a foreign‑key violation.

the race condition

in a typical setup each service subscribes to the UserDeleted topic and issues a cascade delete against its own tables. because the subscription processing is asynchronous, a request that arrives after the UserDeleted event is published but before the worker finishes will see stale data. the DB then throws an error, and the client gets a 500 instead of a graceful "not found".

a deterministic approach

the trick is to make the delete operation idempotent and observable before the request reaches the service. one pattern is to store a tombstone flag in a shared cache (e.g. Redis) as part of the same transaction that publishes the event. workers check the flag before proceeding, and request handlers read it to short‑circuit.

// publish + tombstone atomically
await redis.multi()
  .set(`tombstone:user:${userId}`, '1', 'EX', 300) // 5 min TTL
  .publish('user.deleted', JSON.stringify({ userId }))
  .exec();

workers then do:

const flag = await redis.get(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);
if (!flag) return; // nothing to clean up
await db.transaction(async trx => {
  await trx('orders').where({ userId }).delete();
  await trx('profiles').where({ userId }).delete();
});
await redis.del(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);

trade‑offs

  • latency vs consistency – adding the cache lookup adds a few milliseconds to every request, but it eliminates sporadic DB errors.
  • cache eviction – the TTL must be long enough to cover the slowest worker, otherwise a stale request could still hit the DB.
  • failure handling – if the worker crashes after deleting rows but before clearing the tombstone, subsequent requests will be rejected even though the data is gone. a periodic reconciler that scans for orphaned tombstones can mitigate this.
  • testing – simulate the race by issuing a delete and a read in parallel within integration tests; assert that the read returns a 404 rather than a DB exception.

when to apply

if your service experiences occasional 500 spikes after bulk deletions, or if you already use a message broker for domain events, the tombstone pattern is a low‑overhead way to enforce eventual consistency without locking the DB.

anyone using a similar approach with different stores (e.g. DynamoDB streams) or who prefers optimistic concurrency controls instead? how do you keep the delete path safe without sacrificing throughput?

title: Paid Apps and In-App Purchases in a Google Play Closed Test: What Testers Pay
description:
Disclosure: 12Testers14Day publishes this article and sells Google Play closed-testing help.

If your app costs money, or sells one-time products or subscriptions, a closed test raises a practical question: will your testers be charged? Google's answer depends on the testing track and on whether each tester is a license tester. Getting this wrong can mean testers paying real money, or a 14-day test where nobody ever touches your purchase flow.

The short answer

Based on Google's Play Console Help and Android Developers documentation:

Situation Paid app install In-app purchases and subscriptions
Internal test Free for testers Charged, unless the tester is a license tester
Closed or open test Testers must buy the app Charged, unless the tester is a license tester
License tester on a test track See the note below Test payment methods, no real charge

Google's test setup article says: "Testers must purchase paid apps when participating in open or closed tests. For internal tests, testers can install paid apps for free." It also says internal testers pay for in-app purchases unless you add them to a license testers list.

Google's billing testing guide adds that users "incur actual charges for their test track purchases unless the user is a license tester."

Note on paid apps and license testers: Google's license testing article says your own publishing account can buy your app as a test purchase, and that license testers can buy one-time products and subscriptions without being charged. Before you promise testers a free install of a paid app in a closed test, try it with one license-tester account and check the price shown on the Play Store page.

Why this matters for the 12-tester requirement

If your personal developer account was created after November 13, 2023, Google's testing requirements article says you need a closed test with at least 12 testers opted in continuously for at least 14 days before you can apply for production access. (See our 12-testers requirement explainer for details.)

That has two consequences for monetized apps:

  • A paid price is a barrier to opting in. Every closed tester has to buy the app. Fewer people will agree, and anyone who doesn't install can't give you much feedback.
  • An untested purchase flow is a launch risk. If testers avoid your paywall because they don't want to spend money, your billing code ships with almost no real-device use.

Option 1: Keep in-app purchases testable with license testers

For a free app with in-app products or subscriptions, add your closed testers as license testers as well.

  1. In Play Console, go to Settings > License testing.
  2. Choose testers with an email list (up to 2,000 addresses per list) or a Google Group (no user limit, according to Google).
  3. Save your changes.
  4. Make sure the same people can receive your release. Being a license tester doesn't put someone on your closed track. They still need to be in the track's tester list and opt in through the opt-in link. Our guide to inviting testers and fixing access problems covers the common opt-in issues.
  5. Make sure your one-time products and subscriptions are published. Google says they must be published before they can be tested.

Once that's done, license testers see test payment methods at checkout. Google's billing guide lists several, including:

  • Test instrument, always approves, for a successful purchase.
  • Test instrument, always declines, for a failed payment.
  • Slow test card, approves after a few minutes and Slow test card, declines after a few minutes, for pending purchases.
  • A test instrument that simulates a user-initiated chargeback.

Things that behave differently for license testers

Tell testers about these so their reports make sense:

  • Subscriptions renew fast. A monthly or weekly test subscription renews about every 5 minutes, and a yearly one about every 30 minutes. Test subscriptions renew at most six times, not counting free trials and introductory periods.
  • Unacknowledged purchases are refunded. Google says a license-tester purchase is refunded after 3 minutes if your app doesn't acknowledge it. If testers report that "the purchase disappeared", check your acknowledgement code first.
  • Resubscribe and pause are always on. Google says these features are always enabled for license testers even if you've disabled them in Play Console.

Google also recommends testing with some non-license-tester accounts, either occasionally or after large changes, so your app doesn't depend on test-only behavior.

Option 2: Decide what to do about a paid app price

If your app has an up-front price, you have a few choices. Each has trade-offs.

  • Ask closed testers to buy it. This matches Google's rules, but expect fewer people to agree, and be clear with them about the cost before they opt in.
  • Use internal testing for early paid-app checks. Internal testers install paid apps free, but an internal test doesn't count toward the 12-tester closed-testing requirement. Google also says people who opt in to internal testing aren't eligible for your closed test, even if they're on its tester list. Our internal vs closed testing guide compares the two.
  • Think hard before making a paid app free. Google's pricing article says you can change an app from paid to free, but "once your app has been offered for free, the app can't be changed to paid." To charge again you would need a new app with a new package name. Moving to a free app with an in-app purchase or subscription is a separate product decision, not a testing shortcut.

A pre-test checklist for monetized apps

  • [ ] Decide whether testers should make purchases, and write it in your tester instructions.
  • [ ] Add every closed tester to License testing if you want purchases tested without real charges.
  • [ ] Publish the one-time products and subscriptions you want tested.
  • [ ] Confirm each tester is on the closed track's tester list and has opted in.
  • [ ] Check that your app acknowledges purchases, so test purchases aren't refunded after 3 minutes.
  • [ ] Give testers specific purchase journeys, such as "buy the monthly plan, cancel, then restore purchases".
  • [ ] Run at least one check with a non-license-tester account before production.

Our free closed-testing checklist covers the rest of the setup.

FAQ

Do closed testers pay for in-app purchases?
Yes, unless they're license testers. Google says users are charged for test-track purchases unless they're license testers.

Do license testers count toward the 12 testers?
License testing and the closed-test tester list are separate settings. Google's requirement counts testers who are opted in to your closed test. A license tester who isn't on the track and opted in doesn't count.

Can testers use promo codes instead?
This article doesn't cover promo codes. Check Play Console Help for the current rules before relying on them.

Does a paid-app closed test affect production access?
Google decides production access based on your testing, your app and your answers. The price alone isn't something this article can predict. What helps is a test where testers actually use the app, including the paid features. See what tester activity looks like.

If you'd rather not recruit testers yourself

12Testers14Day provides Google Play closed-testing help: about 14 testers for about 16 days, as a buffer around Google's 12-tester, 14-day requirement. Packages are one-time ($15 Basic for one app, $29 Premium for two, per the pricing page on October 18, 2026). If your app is paid or you want testers to make test purchases, contact the team before you buy so they can confirm what's possible. You can also read how a testing run works.

Official references: Set up an open, closed, or internal test · Test in-app billing with application licensing · Test your Google Play Billing Library integration · Set up your app's prices · App testing requirements for new personal developer accounts

description:

title: LLMs on Consumer Hardware — Part 6: The Orchestration Ceiling — Why a Bigger Coordinator Doesn't Fix the Loop
description:
Part 6 of a series. Previously: Part 5 — Distributing the Workers and the Memory Budget.

Part 5 ended with the 77 GB coordinator finally running as it should — resident, no thrashing, the memory problem resolved by moving the workers to a second machine. That made it possible to answer a question Part 4 had deferred: now that the big model can actually run, does a bigger coordinator fix orchestration? The answer was no, and the reason reshaped how the team was run.

The ceiling persists on the big model

With memory no longer the bottleneck, the coordinator's orchestration could be judged on its own merits. It sequenced delegations more reliably than Gemma had — but it did not escape the same failure modes. On longer plans it still dropped steps, issuing some delegations and silently omitting others before writing its summary. It still, on occasion, emitted a delegation as text rather than executing it — Part 4 showed one such case, a hand-off printed as raw JSON and then abandoned. And it periodically returned nothing at all after a tool call, requiring an automatic nudge to continue:

⚠ Model returned empty after tool calls — nudging to continue

That warning recurred often enough to be diagnostic. These were not the mistakes of a weak model; they were the mistakes of a capable model asked to do something it is structurally poor at — hold a long control loop in its head while also doing the reasoning inside it.

The diagnosis: the ceiling is the loop, not the model

The decisive observation was that all three failure modes — dropped steps, commands narrated instead of executed, empty turns — appeared on the large model exactly as they had on the small one. The common factor was not model size. It was the agentic loop itself.

Asking a language model to orchestrate is asking it to be, simultaneously, the planner that decides the steps, the dispatcher that issues each delegation, the bookkeeper that tracks which delegations are still outstanding, and the evaluator that judges the results as they return. That is a great deal of state to carry across many turns, and carrying state across turns is precisely what these models are weakest at. A bigger model raises the ceiling a little; it does not remove it.

The fix: take the loop away from the model

If the loop is the problem, the loop should not be the model's job. The resolution was deterministic orchestration: a small script owns the control loop. It holds the list of tasks, dispatches each delegation, waits for and collects the result, and decides what runs next. The model is invoked only for the two things it is genuinely good at — planning (what are the steps?) and evaluating (is this result acceptable?) — and never has to remember what it has already dispatched, because the script does that.

The improvement was immediate and measurable. A task sequence that the model-driven loop had stalled on partway through — completing three of five steps before losing the thread — ran all five to completion when the same plan was executed by the script. The model had not become more capable. It had simply been relieved of the one job it could not reliably do.

The lesson

The instinct, when an agent loop is unreliable, is to reach for a bigger model. That instinct was wrong here, and expensively so — it was the reasoning behind the whole coordinator search of Part 4, and the memory wall of Part 5, and in the end it did not solve the problem it was chasing. Orchestration reliability is not a model capability that can be bought in larger quantities; it is a property of how the loop is structured. The durable fix was architectural: move the deterministic part — the loop, the bookkeeping, the dispatch — into deterministic code, and reserve the model for the parts that genuinely require judgment. A control loop is a job for a program, not for a language model, and the sooner that division is drawn the more reliable the system becomes.

What follows

Deterministic orchestration made the team's execution reliable: a plan was now carried out without dropped steps or invented progress. But it did nothing for the moment a plan meets a wall — when the right next step is not in the plan at all, and someone has to rethink the approach rather than merely execute it. Reliable execution and good judgment are different capabilities, and the next entry is about supplying the second without compromising the first.

title: Bun vs Node.js in 2026: Bun 1.4 vs Node 24 and 26, Benchmarked
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself on one machine, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Bun vs Node in 2026 comes down to this: Bun is a JavaScript runtime, package manager, bundler and test runner in one binary, built on JavaScriptCore and now written in Rust. Node.js is the V8-based runtime almost every server, library and hosting platform targets. Bun 1.4 reports Node.js 26 compatibility, so for many apps switching is now a runtime swap rather than a rewrite.

I benchmarked Bun 1.4.3 against Node.js 24.22 (the current LTS) and Node.js 26.12 (LTS from October 28) on one machine. I measured HTTP throughput with Hono, Express and plain node:http, a real Postgres-backed API, a large in-memory heap, startup, TypeScript execution, npm install vs bun install, next build, and native addons like sharp and bcrypt. Every number below comes from those runs.

TL;DR: should I switch from Node to Bun?

Use Bun as your package manager and script runner today: bun install was 13 to 29 times faster than npm in my tests and changes nothing at runtime. Consider Bun as your production runtime for new or dependency-light APIs, CLIs and serverless functions, where it was 1.4 to 1.8 times faster and used 25-70% less memory under load. Stay on Node.js for large existing services that depend on Node-specific APM, long-running stability or exotic native addons, and move to Node 26, which was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on most of my HTTP tests.

Node.js 24.22 Node.js 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Engine V8 V8 JavaScriptCore
Status (Oct 2026) LTS, maintenance from Oct 20 Current, LTS from Oct 28 Stable, 1.x
Hono JSON API, req/s 53,408 60,431 98,145
Express 5 JSON, req/s 35,764 38,530 55,382
Hono + Postgres, req/s 21,749 21,008 32,254 (pg), 33,694 (Bun.sql)
RSS under load, Hono JSON 105 MB 105 MB 36 MB
Startup (-e 0) 28.5 ms 26.3 ms 3.3 ms
Run a .ts file 62.6 ms 59.1 ms 3.8 ms
Install a Next.js app (cold) 15.4 s (npm) 1.15 s (bun)
Native addons tested All work All work All work (sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2)

What is Bun, and how is it different from Node.js?

Bun is an all-in-one toolkit: a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, an npm-compatible package manager, a bundler and a Jest-style test runner in one executable. Node.js is just the runtime and leans on npm, tsc or a loader, a bundler and a test framework from the ecosystem. Bun runs on Apple's JavaScriptCore engine; Node runs on Google's V8.

Bun aims to be a drop-in replacement. It implements Node's built-in modules (node:http, node:fs, node:crypto and the rest), reads package.json and node_modules the same way, and runs N-API native addons. It also adds its own faster APIs such as Bun.serve, Bun.sql and bun:sqlite.

What's new in Bun 1.4?

Bun 1.4 shipped on August 20, 2026, and it is the first Bun written in Rust instead of Zig. Per the Bun 1.4 release post, it adds "+1,517 tests from the Node.js test suite", fixes "over 2,900 issues", cuts idle CPU by 5x and memory by up to 35%, and "starts 50% faster on Linux." Bun now reports itself as Node.js 26 (process.versions.modules is 147).

It also absorbs common dependencies into the runtime: Bun.Image (image processing), Bun.WebView (headless browser), Bun.markdown, Bun.cron(), Bun.Terminal, plus bun run --parallel and bun test --parallel. Upgrading from 1.3 isn't free: the breaking changes list includes stricter TLS verification, YAML 1.2 parsing and no .env auto-loading when Bun is invoked as node. Vercel made 1.4 an explicit opt-in on its platform for the same reason.

How I benchmarked Bun vs Node.js

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3, all official Linux x64 builds.
  3. Apps. The same files ran on every runtime: a node:http hello server, a Bun.serve hello server (Bun only), a Hono 4.13 app, an Express 5.3 app, and a Hono route that reads one row from PostgreSQL 18 through pg 8.23 (or Bun.sql on Bun) with a 10-connection pool, across 10,000 users at random IDs.
  4. Method. For every configuration: start the server, warm up for 4 seconds, measure for 10 seconds, read RSS from /proc. Each configuration ran 3 times and I report the median. Every request returned 200.
  5. CLI timings used hyperfine 2.0.0 (40 runs for startup, 3 to 5 for installs and builds).

Postgres ran on the same machine without pinning, so the database test also measures a shared CPU. That's closer to a small VPS than to a tuned cluster.

Is Bun faster than Node.js?

For HTTP servers, yes, clearly. On the Hono JSON route Bun served 98,145 requests per second against 53,408 on Node 24 and 60,431 on Node 26: 1.84 times Node 24 and 1.62 times Node 26. Bun's advantage held on Express (1.55x Node 24) and on the plain node:http module (1.42x), and Bun.serve reached 128,461 requests per second.

Server (median of 3 x 10 s, 64 connections) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3 Bun vs Node 24
node:http hello 74,200 req/s 83,301 req/s 105,434 req/s 1.42x
Bun.serve hello 128,461 req/s 1.73x
Hono, 10-item JSON 53,408 req/s 60,431 req/s 98,145 req/s 1.84x
Express 5, same JSON 35,764 req/s 38,530 req/s 55,382 req/s 1.55x
Hono + Postgres (pg) 21,749 req/s 21,008 req/s 32,254 req/s 1.48x
Hono + Postgres (Bun.sql) 33,694 req/s 1.55x
600k-entry in-memory cache 53,314 req/s 61,908 req/s 68,134 req/s 1.28x

Latency followed throughput. On the Hono JSON route p99 was 2.10 ms on Node 24, 1.95 ms on Node 26 and 1.17 ms on Bun. On the Postgres route p99 was 4.75 ms, 6.95 ms and 3.98 ms, and 3.50 ms with Bun.sql.

Two results surprised me. First, Bun stayed about 1.5 times faster even with a real database query in every request, which is where many "it's all the database anyway" arguments end. My database was local and fast, though. Over a real network, round trips will shrink that gap. Second, Node 26 alone was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of the five HTTP tests (the Postgres route was a tie), so upgrading Node is the cheapest speedup available.

Does Bun use less memory than Node.js?

Yes. Idle, a node:http server used 58 MB RSS on Node 24 and 23 MB on Bun, while Bun.serve used 16 MB. Under load the Hono app held 105 MB on both Node versions and 36 MB on Bun. On the Postgres route Node 24 grew to 206 MB against 61 MB for Bun with pg and 56 MB with Bun.sql.

RSS (MB): idle / after 10 s load / peak Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
node:http hello 58 / 95 / 95 60 / 97 / 97 23 / 55 / 74
Hono JSON 70 / 105 / 105 66 / 105 / 105 28 / 36 / 45
Express JSON 65 / 97 / 97 66 / 96 / 96 40 / 72 / 81
Hono + Postgres 70 / 206 / 206 66 / 151 / 151 28 / 61 / 69
600k-entry cache 411 / 455 / 455 370 / 410 / 410 261 / 300 / 491

The cache test is the exception worth reading. Bun started with less memory but briefly peaked higher (491 MB) than Node (455 MB). Bun's garbage collector is a known weak spot under large, long-lived heaps. A Bun pull request from this year described a GC "storm" that made allocation-heavy handlers run "at roughly half of Node.js" with a 150 MB live set. That PR #35431 was closed without merging. In my 1.4.3 run with a bigger heap Bun was still 28% faster than Node 24, but test your own workload, not a hello world.

How fast does Bun start compared to Node.js?

Bun starts about 8 times faster. An empty script took a median 3.3 ms on Bun against 28.5 ms on Node 24 and 26.3 ms on Node 26. Running a TypeScript file took 3.8 ms on Bun against 62.6 ms on Node 24. Node's built-in type stripping uses a WebAssembly-based parser, and here it added about 34 ms over an empty script. bun run launched a package.json script in 3.1 ms against 95.1 ms for npm run.

Command (hyperfine median) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Empty script (-e 0) 28.5 ms 26.3 ms 3.3 ms
hello.ts (type annotations) 62.6 ms 59.1 ms 3.8 ms
import('express') 94.1 ms 65.3 ms
Run a no-op package.json script 95.1 ms (npm run) 3.1 ms (bun run)

Startup matters for CLIs, cron jobs, serverless cold starts and test watchers. It barely matters for a long-running API server. Both runtimes run TypeScript directly now: Node's type stripping has been stable since v24.12.0 but only removes erasable syntax and ignores tsconfig.json, while Bun transpiles full TypeScript, including enums.

Is bun install faster than npm?

Much faster. On a Next.js 16.4.2 app with Tailwind, ESLint and TypeScript (458 packages), a cold install with empty caches and no lockfile took 15.4 seconds with npm and 1.15 seconds with Bun, 13 times faster. A CI-style install from a lockfile with a warm cache took 4.6 seconds with npm ci and 0.16 seconds with bun install --frozen-lockfile, 29 times faster.

Install, Next.js 16.4.2 app (458 packages) npm 11.19 bun 1.4.3 Speedup
Cold: no cache, no lockfile (median of 3) 15.4 s 1.15 s 13x
Warm cache + lockfile (median of 5) 4.6 s 0.16 s 29x
Peak memory, warm install 758 MB 13.5 MB

This is the safest win in the whole comparison. bun install writes a normal node_modules, so you can keep running the app on Node. The cold number includes downloads over my server's network, so yours will vary.

# use Bun only as the package manager and script runner
bun install            # writes bun.lock and a normal node_modules
bun run build          # runs your package.json script with Node, as before
node server.js         # production stays on Node.js

Does Next.js work with Bun?

Yes. A Next.js 16.4.2 production build ran fine with bun --bun next build, in a median 3.03 seconds against 3.22 seconds on Node 24, about 6% faster. Turbopack does the heavy lifting in Rust either way, so the runtime matters less for builds than for serving requests. Without --bun, bun run build launches the Next.js CLI with Node because of its shebang.

bun install
bun --bun next build   # build with the Bun runtime
bun --bun next start   # serve with the Bun runtime

If you deploy with Docker, the base image changes from node:24-slim to oven/bun, and the rest of a production Next.js Dockerfile stays the same.

Do native modules work in Bun?

The common ones do. On Bun 1.4.3, sharp (image resize), better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2 and pg all installed from npm and passed the same smoke test as on Node 24. Bun runs N-API addons, which covers most popular native packages. Packages that pick a prebuilt binary by NODE_MODULE_VERSION need a build for 147, the ABI Bun 1.4 reports.

What still bites people is less about compatibility tables and more about operations: APM agents that patch Node internals, rare Node APIs, and memory behavior under months of traffic. The Bun Node.js compatibility page lists module-by-module status.

Is Bun faster at raw JavaScript?

Sometimes. CPU-bound micro-benchmarks were mixed, so don't expect a blanket speedup. Bun was about 3 times faster at parsing small JSON and 1.4 times faster than Node 26 on a 67 KB document, but JSON.stringify tied Node 26. Node 26 made a big jump over Node 24 on JSON, 1.8 times faster on stringify.

Single core, ops/s (mean of 2 runs) Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
JSON.parse, 110 B 1,711,027 1,881,418 5,226,338
JSON.parse, 67 KB 3,854 5,224 7,118
JSON.stringify, 67 KB 6,539 11,634 11,644
SHA-256 of 1 KB (node:crypto) 751,142 751,912 853,054
Sort 100,000 numbers 55 60 90
Map set + get, 100,000 keys 102 134 168

I dropped one test: a regex replace on a constant string ran at 196 million operations per second on Bun, which means JavaScriptCore optimized the work away. That's the trouble with micro-benchmarks. Trust the HTTP and real-app numbers more than these.

Should I use Bun in production in 2026?

For new services, it's a reasonable default now. Bun 1.4 is fast, frugal and broadly compatible, and platforms such as Vercel Functions run it. For existing Node services, migrate only when you can measure the benefit and you have tested memory over days, not minutes. Trigger.dev reported a 5x throughput gain moving a service to Bun and also hit a Bun-only memory leak on the way.

Situation My pick
New API, CLI or worker with mainstream dependencies Bun (runtime + package manager)
Serverless or cron jobs where cold start dominates Bun
Existing large Node service with APM and on-call Node 26 + bun install in CI
Heavy use of exotic native addons or Node internals Node.js
NestJS or Next.js app Node in production for now, Bun for installs and scripts; test Bun in staging

How do I migrate a Node.js app to Bun?

Move in three steps and keep a way back at each one. First swap the package manager, then run your tests on Bun, then switch the production runtime behind a canary.

# 1. package manager only (zero runtime risk)
bun install                 # creates bun.lock next to package-lock.json

# 2. run tests and scripts on Bun
bun run test                # your existing test script
bun --bun run test          # force the Bun runtime even for "node" shebangs

# 3. run the server on Bun, keep the code portable
bun src/server.ts

// portable entry point: Bun.serve on Bun, @hono/node-server on Node
import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', (c) => c.json({ ok: true }))

if (typeof Bun !== 'undefined') {
  Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch: app.fetch })
} else {
  const { serve } = await import('@hono/node-server')
  serve({ fetch: app.fetch, port: 3000 })
}

Frameworks built on Web standards, like Hono, make this painless because the same fetch handler runs on both. For database access, pg worked unchanged on Bun in my test, and Bun.sql is the built-in Postgres client that was 4% faster than pg on Bun in my test. If you're choosing an ORM, see Drizzle vs Prisma. If you self-host, Coolify runs a Bun Dockerfile like any other.

Common mistakes when comparing Bun and Node.js

  • Benchmarking hello world only. Bun.serve vs node:http showed a 1.73x gap; Express showed 1.55x and a large-heap handler 1.28x.
  • Comparing against an old Node. Node 26 was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of five HTTP tests. Compare against the Node you would actually run.
  • Ignoring memory over time. A 10-second run says nothing about a slow leak. Watch RSS for days in staging.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores. Pin the server and the load generator to separate CPUs, or the numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Forgetting --bun. bun run executes scripts whose CLI has a #!/usr/bin/env node shebang with Node unless you pass --bun.
  • Switching runtime and dependencies at once. Swap the package manager first; it gives most of the day-to-day win with none of the runtime risk.

Related: I also ran a NestJS 12 app on Bun 1.4.3: it served 1.49 times Node 24's requests per second on a hello route and started in 264 ms vs 361 ms. See the NestJS 12 migration guide.

Related: framework choice matters on Bun too. In Hono vs Express vs Fastify, Hono served 118,432 JSON requests per second on Bun 1.4.3, 1.62× its Node 24 result, while Express and Fastify gained less.

Key takeaways

  • Bun 1.4.3 served 1.84 times Node 24's requests per second on a Hono JSON API, and 1.48 times with a Postgres query in every request.
  • Bun used 25-70% less memory under load, for example 36 MB vs 105 MB RSS for the Hono app.
  • Bun started in 3.3 ms versus 26-29 ms for Node and ran a TypeScript file in 3.8 ms versus about 60 ms.
  • bun install was 13 times faster than npm cold and 29 times faster with a warm cache and lockfile.
  • Node 26 alone was 8-16% faster than Node 24 on four of five HTTP tests, a free upgrade when it becomes LTS on October 28.
  • sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2, pg and a Next.js 16.4 build all worked on Bun 1.4.3.
  • Adopt Bun as package manager first, then as runtime for new services; keep large existing Node services on Node 26 until you've tested memory over days.

FAQ

Is Bun faster than Node.js?

For HTTP servers, yes. In my tests Bun 1.4.3 served 98,145 requests per second on a Hono JSON API against 53,408 on Node.js 24 and 60,431 on Node.js 26. With a Postgres query in every request Bun was 1.48 times faster than Node 24. CPU-bound micro-benchmarks were mixed, so the gap depends on the workload.

Does Bun use less memory than Node.js?

Usually. Under load my Hono app used 36 MB RSS on Bun versus 105 MB on Node 24 and 26, and the Postgres route used 61 MB versus 206 MB on Node 24. With a large in-memory cache Bun idled lower but briefly peaked higher, at 491 MB against 455 MB, so test memory with your own data.

Is Bun production ready in 2026?

For many services, yes. Bun 1.4 passes 1,517 more Node.js test-suite tests than 1.3, runs common native addons, and is offered on platforms such as Vercel Functions. Teams still report Bun-specific memory issues under long-running load, so canary it and watch memory for days before moving a large existing service.

Is bun install faster than npm?

Yes. On a Next.js 16.4.2 app with 458 packages, a cold install took 15.4 seconds with npm and 1.15 seconds with Bun. A lockfile install with a warm cache took 4.6 seconds with npm ci and 0.16 seconds with bun install --frozen-lockfile. It writes a normal node_modules, so the app can still run on Node.

Does Next.js work with Bun?

Yes. A Next.js 16.4.2 production build succeeded with bun --bun next build in 3.03 seconds against 3.22 seconds on Node 24. Use the --bun flag, because bun run otherwise launches the Next.js CLI with Node due to its node shebang. Turbopack compiles in Rust either way, so builds gain little.

Do native modules like sharp and bcrypt work in Bun?

The popular ones do. On Bun 1.4.3, sharp, better-sqlite3, bcrypt, argon2 and pg installed from npm and passed the same smoke test as on Node 24. Bun runs N-API addons and reports NODE_MODULE_VERSION 147, so packages that select a prebuilt binary by ABI need a build for 147.

Should I upgrade to Node 26 or switch to Bun?

If you have a large existing service, upgrade to Node 26 first: it was 8 to 16 percent faster than Node 24 on most of my HTTP tests and becomes LTS on October 28, 2026. Switch the runtime to Bun when you start a new service or can measure a clear gain in staging.

What changed in Bun 1.4?

Bun 1.4, released August 20, 2026, is the first Bun written in Rust instead of Zig. It reports Node.js 26 compatibility, adds 1,517 Node.js test-suite tests, fixes over 2,900 issues, starts 50 percent faster on Linux, and adds built-ins such as Bun.Image, Bun.WebView, Bun.markdown and Bun.cron. It also has breaking changes worth reviewing.

title: Vercel CDN no longer caches responses with Vary: Cookie
description:
Vercel CDN no longer caches origin responses when Vary includes Cookie.

Vary tells a cache which request headers may change the response. Because cookies often contain visitor-specific values, varying by Cookie can create many cache entries that are rarely reused. The response is still served normally but isn't stored for future requests.

You can identify these responses by checking the x-vercel-cache header and Runtime Logs. The header is set to MISS, and Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie as the cache reason.

If Logs show vary_key_denied:cookie for a route you expect to be cached, check the Vary header returned by your origin:

  • If the response is the same regardless of cookies, remove Cookie from Vary. Vercel CDN can then cache it if it meets the other caching requirements.

  • If the response depends on cookies, keep Cookie in Vary and use Cache-Control: private to prevent personalized responses from being stored in the shared CDN cache.

Caching behavior for other supported Vary headers is unchanged.

Learn more about high-cardinality headers and the vary_key_denied cache reason.

Read more

title: How to keep your smart home running even if the internet goes down
description: Smart home products most often harness Wi-Fi to function. But what can you do if you lose internet frequently?

title: Distributed Cron Jobs
description:
Regular cron runs on one server. What happens when you have 10 servers? Each runs the job 10 times. That's a problem.

The Problem 

Single server cron: ✅ Job runs once at 2am
10-server fleet:    ❌ Job runs 10 times at 2am — duplicate emails, double charges!

Solutions

1. Dedicated Scheduler Node

  • One designated machine runs all cron jobs
  • ✅ Simple
  • ❌ Single point of failure — if this node dies, no cron jobs run

2. Leader Election + Cron

  • Cluster elects a leader (using etcd/ZooKeeper)
  • Only the leader runs cron jobs
  • If leader dies → new leader elected → cron resumes
  • ✅ No SPOF | ❌ Leader election complexity

3. Distributed Lock Before Job Execution 

def run_job():
    lock = redis.set("cron:daily-email", "locked", nx=True, ex=300)  # 5min TTL
    if not lock:
        return  # another node is running it
    try:
        send_daily_emails()
    finally:
        redis.delete("cron:daily-email")
  • ✅ Simple, works with existing Redis
  • ❌ Lock expiry must be > job duration, or use heartbeat extension

4. Dedicated Scheduling Services

  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler — cron without servers
  • Temporal.io — workflow orchestration with scheduling
  • Airflow — DAG-based job scheduling
  • Sidekiq-Cron (Ruby), Bull (Node.js)

Exactly-Once Execution

For critical jobs (billing, emails):

  1. Use idempotency keys in the job itself
  2. Record execution in DB before running: INSERT INTO job_runs (job_id, run_date) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING → if 0 rows inserted, skip
  3. Use a distributed lock with heartbeat

Observability for Cron

  • Alert if a job DIDN'T run (missed heartbeat)
  • Track job duration — sudden increase = something is wrong
  • Log job result (success/failure, records processed)
  • Tool: Healthchecks.io — cron monitoring via ping

title: React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked
description:
I compiled a Next.js 16.4 app with no compiler, the Babel React Compiler and the experimental Rust one, then counted re-renders in Chrome. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes your components and hooks, so you no longer write most useMemo, useCallback and memo calls by hand. In Next.js it is one config flag, reactCompiler: true, stable since Next.js 16.0. Next.js 16.4 adds an experimental native Rust version.

I built a Next.js 16.4.2 test app and compiled it three ways: compiler off, the Babel compiler, and the Rust compiler. Then I counted re-renders in a real browser. With the compiler on, 20 clicks on a counter caused 0 list-row re-renders instead of 20,000, and scripting time fell from about 60 ms to about 7 ms. The Babel version more than doubled compile time. The Rust version cost about a quarter of a second and produced byte-identical output.

TL;DR: should I turn on the React Compiler in Next.js?

Yes, for most App Router projects. Turn it on with reactCompiler: true, run the compiler lint rules first, and try experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler if you build with Turbopack. In my test the compiler removed almost all wasted re-renders for free. It does not replace memo on list items whose parent re-renders, and it skips code that breaks the Rules of React.

Compiler off Babel compiler Rust compiler (experimental)
Config default reactCompiler: true + experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true
Extra install none babel-plugin-react-compiler none
Compile step (median, my app) 2.25 s 5.65 s 2.5 s
Full next build (median) 7.7 s 11.1 s 8.2 s
Client JS, gzip 178,305 B 181,295 B 181,295 B (identical to Babel)
Row re-renders, 20 counter clicks 20,000 0 0
Works with webpack yes yes no (Turbopack only)

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool that rewrites your components so they cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders, and recompute them only when their inputs change. The React Compiler v1.0 announcement calls it "a build-time tool that optimizes your React app through automatic memoization." Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025.

It works with React 17 and later, and on React Native. The introduction docs say that in most cases its memoization "will be as precise, or moreso, than what you may have written." Meta reports that in the Meta Quest Store, "initial loads and cross-page navigations improve by up to 12%, while certain interactions are more than 2.5× faster."

You keep writing plain components. The compiler does the bookkeeping at build time.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js 16?

Install the Babel plugin and set the top-level reactCompiler option in next.config.ts. It moved out of experimental in Next.js 16.0. Next.js does not run Babel on every file: per the reactCompiler docs, "Next.js uses a custom SWC optimization that only applies the React Compiler to relevant files—like those with JSX or React Hooks."

npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

That is the whole setup. New projects can also pick the compiler in the create-next-app prompts.

Can I enable it only for some components?

Yes. Set compilationMode: "annotation" and add the "use memo" directive to the components or hooks you want compiled. This is a good way to start on a large codebase. Add "use no memo" to a component to opt it out in the default mode while you fix it.

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: { compilationMode: "annotation" },
};

export default function Dashboard() {
  "use memo";
  // ...
}

What is the Rust React Compiler in Next.js?

It is a native Rust port of the React Compiler that runs inside Turbopack instead of through Babel in Node.js. It was merged into the React repo in June 2026 (PR #36173) and added to Next.js 16.3 as an experimental option. The Next.js 16.4 release added a fast check that skips files that don't need compiling.

Next.js 16.4 says the Turbopack team's memory changes "reduced the React Compiler's memory usage by 30% and compile time by 15%." To turn it on:

// next.config.ts
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
  experimental: {
    turbopackRustReactCompiler: true,
  },
};

From the turbopackRustReactCompiler docs:

  • It "requires reactCompiler to be enabled". It picks the implementation but doesn't switch the compiler on.
  • It works only with Turbopack. "Using it with webpack will throw an error."
  • You do not need babel-plugin-react-compiler installed.

How I tested it

I wanted numbers from a real Next.js app, not a toy counter, so I measured both build cost and runtime behaviour.

  1. App: Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3.1, Turbopack, Node 24, on an 8-vCPU Linux box. The client dashboard has 1,000 product rows, a filter input, a counter, a stats panel and one deliberately "bad" component. Nothing uses useMemo or useCallback.
  2. Build load: 300 more generated client components on a /gen route, so compile time is measurable.
  3. Three builds: one next.config.ts read an RC_MODE variable (off, babel, rust). I deleted .next before every build, so the Turbopack disk cache never helped, and ran 5 rounds. The tables use the median of rounds 2-5. Round 1 was a cold start: 3.3 s, 12.6 s and 2.9 s of compile time.
  4. Re-renders: each component calls a tiny useRenderCount(name) hook that increments a counter in an effect. Puppeteer drove headless Chrome against next start, and Chrome's ScriptDuration metric measured JavaScript time. I ran each scenario 3 times, and the render counts were identical every run. 
// lib/useRenderCount.ts
"use client";
import { useEffect } from "react";

export function useRenderCount(name: string) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const r = (window.__renders ??= {});
    r[name] = (r[name] ?? 0) + 1;
  });
}

The counter lives in an effect on purpose. Writing to a global during render breaks the Rules of React, and the compiler would skip that component.

Does the React Compiler reduce re-renders?

Yes, dramatically for state that doesn't touch a component's props. Clicking the counter 20 times re-rendered every component on the page with the compiler off: 20,000 row renders. With either compiler, only the two components that actually use the count re-rendered. Rows, stats, the list and even the uncompilable component were all skipped.

Scenario (renders counted) Off Compiler Compiler + memo(Row)
20 counter clicks: Row renders 20,000 0 0
20 counter clicks: JS time 55-62 ms 6-7 ms 6-7 ms
Type "99" in filter: Row renders 290 290 0
Select 10 rows: Row renders 10,000 10,000 19
Select 10 rows: JS time 26-31 ms 14 ms 8 ms

The Babel and Rust builds produced exactly the same render counts, which you would expect from identical output.

The click case is the common one in real apps. Some unrelated state changes high in the tree, and with the compiler off everything below it re-renders.

Why do list rows still re-render with the compiler?

Because the compiler memoizes inside components. It does not turn every component into React.memo. When ProductList must re-render, for example because selectedId changed, its .map() creates new <Row> elements and each row runs. The compiled Row is cheaper to run, since its internals are cached, so JS time still halved from about 28 ms to 14 ms. But all 1,000 rows rendered on each click.

Wrapping the row in memo() fixed it. Selecting 10 rows then rendered 19 rows (1 + 9×2: the newly selected row and the previously selected one).

import { memo } from "react";

function Row({ item, selected, onSelect }: RowProps) {
  return (
    <li style={{ fontWeight: selected ? 700 : 400 }} onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}>
      {item.name}
    </li>
  );
}

const MemoRow = memo(Row); // still worth it for big lists

Without the compiler, the same memo(Row) did nothing: still 10,000 renders. The parent passes onSelect={(id) => setSelectedId(id)} as a new function every render, which breaks memo's prop comparison. The compiler caches that callback automatically. That pairing is what makes memo reliable: compiler for stable props, memo for big lists.

What does the compiled code look like?

The compiler adds a small cache array per component (_c(n) from react/compiler-runtime) and wraps each computation in an "inputs changed?" check. This is what the Babel plugin produced for my Stats component, which totals prices on every render in the source:

function Stats(t0) {
  const $ = _c(10);
  const { items } = t0;
  let onSale, t1, t2, t3;
  if ($[0] !== items) {
    const total = items.reduce(_temp, 0);
    onSale = items.filter(_temp2).length;
    // ...store results in $[1..4]
  } else {
    onSale = $[1]; // reuse cached values
    // ...
  }
  // the returned <p> is cached the same way
}

The expensive reduce and filter run only when items changes. This is the same thing you would do by hand with useMemo, applied to every value in every component.

Does the React Compiler slow down next build?

The Babel version does, the Rust version barely does. In my 300-component app the compile step went from 2.25 s with the compiler off to 5.65 s with Babel, about 2.5 times longer. The Rust compiler took 2.5 s, only 0.25 s more than no compiler at all. Full next build wall time was 7.7 s, 11.1 s and 8.2 s.

Both compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript: the same chunk hashes and the same sizes. Compiled code is larger, because every component now carries cache checks. Raw client JS grew by 213,496 bytes (+28.9%), but after gzip the difference was only 2,990 bytes (+1.7%). The cache checks are repetitive and compress well.

These are numbers from one small app on one machine. Your ratio will differ with codebase size, but the direction should hold: Babel adds noticeable compile time and Rust mostly removes it.

Which code does the React Compiler skip?

Components that break the Rules of React. The compiler checks your code, and if it can't prove a component is safe to memoize it leaves that component uncompiled instead of guessing. The build does not fail. My Bailout component reads and writes ref.current during render, and the Babel plugin's logger reported CompileError: Cannot access refs during render.

export function Bailout({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const renders = useRef(0);
  renders.current += 1; // breaks the rules: ref mutation during render
  return <aside>{label} (render #{renders.current})</aside>;
}

Notice from the render table that Bailout was still skipped on counter clicks. The compiled parent cached the <Bailout label="legacy widget" /> element, so React never re-rendered it. Code the compiler skips simply misses its own internal optimizations. It doesn't break.

How do I find code the compiler can't optimize?

Use the latest eslint-plugin-react-hooks (7.x today). Since React Compiler 1.0, the compiler-powered lint rules ship in the plugin's recommended preset: refs, purity, immutability, set-state-in-effect, set-state-in-render, globals, static-components, incompatible-library and more. You don't need the separate eslint-plugin-react-compiler package any more.

// eslint.config.mjs
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";

export default [
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
];

On my test app, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 flagged the Bailout ref access three times. It also caught a real bug pattern in my generator: 300 components called setState inside useEffect. The rule message says this "can trigger cascading renders". I fixed the generator before benchmarking.

Run the linter before turning on the compiler, fix what it reports, and treat the warnings as a list of components that won't be optimized.

Step by step: adopt the React Compiler in an existing Next.js app

  1. Upgrade. Use Next.js 16.x and React 19.x. The compiler also supports React 17 and 18 through react-compiler-runtime.
  2. Lint first. Add reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended, run eslint . and fix or note the errors.
  3. Install and enable. Run npm i -D babel-plugin-react-compiler, then set reactCompiler: true. On a large app, start with compilationMode: "annotation" and add "use memo" to hot paths.
  4. Try Rust on Turbopack. Add experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true and compare next build times.
  5. Test behaviour. Run your end-to-end tests. Watch effects that depend on memoized values.
  6. Keep memo on big lists. The compiler stabilizes props. memo still decides whether a list item renders.
  7. Remove manual memoization slowly. The React team advises keeping existing useMemo and useCallback or testing carefully before removing them, because removal can change compilation output.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback?

Not in a hurry. For new code, write plain components and let the compiler memoize. In existing code, leave useMemo and useCallback alone until you have tests. The React docs say the hooks "can continue to be used with React Compiler as an escape hatch", for example to keep an effect dependency stable. Removing them can change what the compiler outputs.

Common React Compiler mistakes in Next.js

  • Expecting it to fix big lists alone. It doesn't add React.memo to children. Keep memo() on heavy list items.
  • Mutating during render. Ref writes, global writes or prop mutation make the compiler skip the component, with no build error.
  • Using the Rust flag with webpack. turbopackRustReactCompiler throws with webpack. Remove it or switch to Turbopack.
  • Enabling it without the lint rules. You won't know which components were skipped.
  • Benchmarking with a warm cache. Turbopack's build disk cache hides compile cost. Delete .next between comparison builds.
  • Expecting Server Component wins. The compiler targets components that re-render on the client. Server Components render once per request.

If you are on Next.js 16.4, pair this with the other new client-side features in my guides to React View Transitions in Next.js and the use cache directive.

Related: the React Compiler lint rules from eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7 don't all survive a linter switch. Oxlint ported 12 of 14, Biome none; see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint.

Related: wondering whether to leave Next.js entirely? In TanStack Start vs Next.js I built the same app in both: TanStack Start shipped 111 KB of gzipped JS to Next.js 16.4's 139 KB and built in 1.26 s vs 4.86 s.

Key takeaways

  • React Compiler 1.0 automatically memoizes components and hooks at build time; in Next.js 16 enable it with reactCompiler: true.
  • In my Next.js 16.4.2 test, 20 counter clicks caused 0 row re-renders with the compiler versus 20,000 without, and JS time fell from about 60 ms to 7 ms.
  • The compiler does not make children React.memo; list rows still re-rendered until I wrapped them in memo(), which then cut 10,000 renders to 19.
  • The Babel compiler made the compile step 2.5x longer (2.25 s to 5.65 s); the experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 s.
  • Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript; gzipped size grew only 1.7%.
  • experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler needs reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack, and needs no Babel plugin.
  • Run eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules first; components that break the Rules of React are silently skipped.

FAQ

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes components and hooks. It rewrites your code to cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders and recompute them only when inputs change, replacing most manual useMemo, useCallback and memo calls. Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025, and it supports React 17 and later.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js?

Install babel-plugin-react-compiler as a dev dependency and set reactCompiler: true at the top level of next.config.ts. The option became stable in Next.js 16.0, moving out of experimental. Next.js applies the compiler only to files with JSX or hooks, using an SWC pre-check, to keep build cost down. Use compilationMode: 'annotation' to opt in per component.

What is turbopackRustReactCompiler?

It is an experimental Next.js option, added in 16.3, that runs the native Rust port of the React Compiler inside Turbopack instead of the Babel plugin. It requires reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack and throws with webpack, and needs no babel-plugin-react-compiler install. In my test it compiled in 2.5 seconds versus 5.65 seconds for Babel.

Does the React Compiler make next build slower?

With the Babel plugin, noticeably. In my 300-component Next.js 16.4.2 app the compile step went from 2.25 seconds to 5.65 seconds, and full next build from 7.7 to 11.1 seconds. The experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 seconds to compile and 8.2 seconds in total, so most of the cost disappeared.

Does the React Compiler replace React.memo?

Not for list items. The compiler memoizes inside each component and caches child elements, but when a parent re-renders and maps over data, every child still runs. In my test, selecting a row re-rendered all 1,000 rows with the compiler alone. Wrapping the row in memo() cut 10,000 renders to 19, because the compiler kept its props stable.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback when using the React Compiler?

Not right away. Write new code without them, but keep existing calls until you have tests, because the React team notes that removing them can change compilation output. The hooks still work as an escape hatch, for example to keep an effect dependency stable so the effect doesn't fire repeatedly when its inputs haven't meaningfully changed.

What happens if my code breaks the Rules of React?

The compiler skips that component and leaves it unoptimized; the build does not fail. In my test, a component that mutated ref.current during render produced a 'Cannot access refs during render' compile error in the logger and was left as written. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules report the same problems in your editor.

Does the React Compiler increase bundle size?

Slightly. Compiled components carry cache checks, so in my test raw client JavaScript grew 28.9 percent, by 213,496 bytes, but gzipped size grew only 1.7 percent, by 2,990 bytes, because the generated code compresses well. The Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical bundles in Next.js 16.4.2.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Go 1.27 Finds Leaked Goroutines With the Garbage Collector. Here's What It Misses
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

When researchers pointed a prototype detector at one of Uber's production Go services, it found hundreds of previously hidden partial deadlocks: goroutines parked on a channel or a lock that nothing would ever release. Each one kept its stack and everything that stack pointed to. None of them raised an error.

That detector now lives in the Go runtime. Go 1.26 shipped it as an experimental profile behind GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile. Go 1.27, released on 19 August 2026, made the goroutineleak profile generally available and deleted the experiment flag. You read it from runtime/pprof or from the /debug/pprof/goroutineleak endpoint.

The interesting part is how it decides that a goroutine is leaked. There are no timers and no "blocked for more than ten minutes" heuristics. The runtime asks the garbage collector a reachability question. Once you see the question, you can predict which leaks it will report and which ones it will never notice.

What "leaked" means to the runtime

The release notes define it precisely: a leaked goroutine is one "blocked on some concurrency primitive (channels, sync.Mutex, sync.Cond, etc) that cannot possibly become unblocked."

Think about what it takes to wake a goroutine stuck on ch <- v. Some other goroutine has to run <-ch. To do that, it needs a reference to ch. If no goroutine that could ever run again holds a pointer to that channel, the send can never complete. And "who holds a pointer to what" is exactly what the garbage collector computes on every cycle.

The Go blog post on leak profiles states the rule inductively. A goroutine is live if it is not blocked, or if at least one primitive blocking it is referenced by another live goroutine. Everything else is leaked.

The primitives covered are channel sends and receives (nil channels included), blocking select (empty select {} included), sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.WaitGroup and sync.Cond, per the same post. A goroutine blocked on file or network IO, a raw system call, or a hand-rolled primitive that is not built on those is never reported.

How the mark phase answers "can anything wake this up?"

In a normal GC cycle, every goroutine's stack is a root. A leak-detection cycle changes that. The design document by Georgian-Vlad Saioc and Milind Chabbi lays out the loop:

  1. Treat only runnable goroutines as goroutine roots.
  2. Mark everything reachable from the roots.
  3. Check each unmarked, blocked goroutine. If the primitive it waits on was marked, some live goroutine can reach it, so this goroutine is "eventually runnable." Add it as a root.
  4. Resume marking from step 2. Stop when no new goroutine gets promoted.
  5. Every blocked goroutine that never became a root is leaked. Mark from those too, so the heap ends up marked the same way a regular cycle would mark it, then sweep as usual.

That final step matters for what you expect in production. The profile reports leaks; it does not reclaim them. The blog says the last round lets the GC "mark all the memory it would have marked during a regular run."

There is one wiring problem the loop has to solve. A blocked goroutine is attached to its channel through a sudog, the runtime's record for "a g in a wait list." In runtime2.go, the sudog's channel field is a maybeTraceableChan and its data field is a maybeTraceablePtr. Sudogs are reachable from the global goroutine list and the semaphore table, according to the design doc. If the GC traced those fields normally, every channel with a waiter would be marked through the waiter itself, and nothing would ever look leaked.

So the pointer is stored twice: once as a uintptr (vu, the "source of truth") and once as an unsafe.Pointer (vp, "for liveness only"). When a leak-detection cycle starts, the runtime makes the vp half of every sudog untraceable, so the GC cannot follow the pointer while the address stays recorded. When the cycle ends, it makes them traceable again. The waiter still knows which channel it is parked on, and that knowledge no longer counts as a reason to keep the channel alive.

The blocked goroutine's own stack gets the same treatment by construction. It is not a root until it gets promoted, so the ch variable sitting in its closure does not mark the channel either. A goroutine that survives the whole loop ends up in a new status, _Gleaked, which runtime2.go documents as "a leaked goroutine caught by the GC."

A leak it catches

Here is the classic timeout leak. The worker sends on an unbuffered channel, the caller gives up first, and the send blocks forever.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "runtime/pprof"
    "time"
)

func fetch(ctx context.Context) error {
    ch := make(chan error) // unbuffered: the bug
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        ch <- nil // nobody receives after a timeout
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-ch:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

func main() {
    for range 3 {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
            context.Background(), 10*time.Millisecond)
        _ = fetch(ctx)
        cancel()
    }
    time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond) // senders block

    p := pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak")
    if p == nil {
        fmt.Println("needs Go 1.27, or 1.26 with " +
            "GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile")
        return
    }
    p.WriteTo(os.Stdout, 1)
}

On Go 1.27, go run . is enough. On Go 1.26, build with GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile go run .. Writing the profile triggers a leak-detecting GC cycle and waits for it, as the design doc describes, and debug=1 gives you the text format with function names and line numbers.

Walk through it with the loop above. After each fetch returns, main's frame no longer holds ch. The only remaining references live in the sender's closure and in its sudog. The sender is blocked, so its stack is not a root. The sudog's channel pointer is hidden for the cycle. Nothing marks the channel, so none of the three senders gets promoted, and all three should land in the profile with stacks pointing at the ch <- nil line. I haven't run this exact snippet, so treat that as what the mechanism predicts, not pasted output.

The fix is the one the Go blog gives for its own timeout example: give the channel a buffer of size 1. Then make(chan error, 1) lets the late sender drop its value and exit.

A leak it cannot see

Now move the channel to package level.

var results = make(chan error) // package-level

func fetchGlobal(ctx context.Context) error {
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        results <- nil // same leak as before
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-results:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

The leak is the same: every timed-out call can strand a sender. Sharing the channel also adds a second bug, because a later call can now receive an earlier call's stale result. The profile stays quiet.

Package-level variables are always roots. In step 2 the GC marks results straight from the global, the blocked senders look "eventually runnable" in step 3, and they never reach the leaked set. The Go 1.26 release notes spell this out: "the runtime may fail to identify leaks caused by blocking on concurrency primitives reachable through global variables or the local variables of runnable goroutines."

The second half of that sentence catches more real code than the first. A long-lived worker goroutine that keeps a map of per-request channels in a local variable, and never reads some of them, keeps every one of those channels marked. So does a struct of channels hanging off a server object that a running goroutine still references. The design doc puts it plainly: the detector's "effectiveness is reduced the more heap resources are over-exposed in memory."

That gives you a design rule the detector rewards. Create channels as close to their use as you can, scope them to one request or one call, and do not park them in registries that outlive the work. The narrower the reachability, the more the GC can prove.

Running it in production and in tests

If a service already imports net/http/pprof, Go 1.27 adds the endpoint with no code change. The blog's workflow, with the address left as a placeholder:

# ADDR: wherever net/http/pprof listens in your service
curl "$ADDR/debug/pprof/goroutineleak" > leak.prof
go tool pprof leak.prof

Inside pprof, list fetch (or whatever function spawned the goroutine) shows the blocked line in context.

On cost, the Go 1.26 notes say the feature is designed "to not incur any additional run-time overhead unless it is actively in-use." When you do request it, there is a worst case. The blog describes a leak-free "daisy chain" where runnable G0 references the primitive blocking G1, G1 references the one blocking G2, and so on. Each link only proves live after the previous one, which serializes marking and gives O(n²) steps for one GC cycle, with n the number of goroutines. The blog's answer is to profile periodically, every 4 hours in its example, since a leak that can be observed once stays observable.

The design doc calls the approach "theoretically sound, i.e., there are no false positives," and the blog describes it as "precise" with "little-to-no false positives," so treat a goroutine in the report as a strong signal that it is stuck. The detector also only sees leaks that have already happened. The blog recommends pairing it with goleak in test suites, which flags goroutines still running when a test ends, and with testing/synctest, whose fake clock lets a timeout path run deterministically.

When the profile comes back empty and memory still climbs, check your package-level channels first.

If this was useful

The leak profile makes sense once you know what the runtime does underneath your code: how goroutines park on channels and what the garbage collector treats as a root. The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers the runtime and its concurrency primitives with that picture in mind, including the channel and context patterns that keep a goroutine from getting stranded in the first place.

title: Introducing @zervonex/baileys - A Tailored Fork of the Baileys WhatsApp Web API
description:
As developers working heavily with automation, we often rely on the incredible WhiskeySockets/Baileys library to interact directly with the WhatsApp Web API.

However, maintaining long-term stability, implementing niche patches, and ensuring rapid upstream syncs for specific organizational workloads can sometimes require custom overrides.

To solve this for our production pipelines, we have officially published and open-sourced our custom-tailored ecosystem variant: @zervonex/baileys.

🚀 Why Use @zervonex/baileys

The @zervonex/baileys package is a dedicated, scoped fork built to ensure predictability, seamless integration, and stable session management in Node.js environments. By utilizing a scoped npm package under @zervonex, we ensure that updates are controlled, thoroughly tested, and safe from unexpected upstream breaking changes.

Key Highlights:

  • Fully Scoped & Managed: Eliminates package naming collisions and guarantees clean dependency trees.
  • Production Ready: Built out of a necessity for reliable, automated multi-device connectivity.
  • Seamless Transition: Maintains structural compatibility with the core Baileys API so you don't have to rewrite your codebase.

🛠️ Quick Start & Installation

You can integrate our fork into your Node.js or TypeScript application instantly using your preferred package manager.

# Using npm
npm install @zervonex/baileys

# Using yarn
yarn add @zervonex/baileys

# Using pnpm
pnpm add @zervonex/baileys

Basic Initialization Example 

async function connectToWhatsApp() {
    // Dynamically importing the modules using await import
    const { default: makeWASocket, useMultiFileAuthState } = await import("@zervonex/baileys");

    const { state, saveCreds } = await useMultiFileAuthState('auth_info_zervonex');

    const sock = makeWASocket({
        auth: state,
        printQRInTerminal: true
    });

    sock.ev.on('creds.update', saveCreds);

    sock.ev.on('connection.update', (update) => {
        const { connection, lastDisconnect } = update;
        if(connection === 'close') {
            console.log('Connection closed, reconnecting...');
            connectToWhatsApp();
        } else if(connection === 'open') {
            console.log('Opened connection successfully via @zervonex/baileys!');
        }
    });
}

connectToWhatsApp();

📦 View on Registry

Take a look at the live release, version history, and dependencies directly over on the npm registry:
👉 View @zervonex/baileys on npm

We are actively looking forward to refining this fork. Feel free to leave a comment below if you have any feature suggestions or compatibility questions!

title: VaultExam AI: Mock Tests from Your Notes, Without Uploading Them Anywhere
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

VaultExam AI is a 100% local, privacy-first tool that turns a chapter (In any format) into a ready-to-print question paper + answer key and lets you ask questions of the same document with page-cited answers.

Who would pay for it: independent coaching institutes, test-prep tutors, university professors and corporate trainers. Their curated notes and question banks are their intellectual property, and they don't want to upload them to a cloud API. They also spend hours every week typing up mock tests, DPPs and Set A/B variations by hand.

What it does:

  • Upload Notes in any format. It is chunked and embedded locally, and the file is deleted from disk straight after ingestion.
  • Ask the document: answers come only from your notes, with Page citations.
  • Generate an exam: choose the institute name, exam type (Coaching Mock Test, University Mid-Sem, Corporate SOP Quiz), difficulty (Recall, Application, Analytical/Edge Cases) and the number of MCQs, short answers and long answers.
  • Set A/B/C: each set draws on different parts of the document and avoids repeating earlier questions.
  • Answer key included: MCQ answers with explanations, model answers for short and long questions, marking-scheme key points, and the source page for every question so a teacher can verify it.
  • Print or save as PDF straight from the browser.

Demo

Code

https://github.com/ronitsolanki-01/VaultExam.git

How I Built It

Everything runs on the user's own machine. No cloud calls, no per-token fees.

  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1.1 and Spring AI 2.0.1
  • LLM: an open-weight model (qwen3.5:4b) served by local Ollama
  • Embeddings: nomic-embed-text via Ollama
  • Vector store: PostgreSQL with PGVector (pgvector/pgvector:pg16 via Docker Compose), with metadata filtering by document_id
  • Ingestion: Spring AI's TikaDocumentReader and PagePdfDocumentReader keeps page number on every chunk, then TokenTextSplitter chunks it
  • Frontend: one Next.js page (TypeScript, Tailwind), with window.print() for output

How the exam generator works: it retrieves a sample of chunks from the document, asks the model for MCQs, short answers and long answers in separate structured-output calls, then validates each result (question count, exactly four options, valid answer index) and retries if the local model returns bad JSON. Each set uses a different seeded sample of the document, plus a "don't repeat these questions" list.

Things that bit me on a small local model:

  • Reasoning models like qwen3.5 can spend their whole token budget "thinking" and return an empty answer, which breaks JSON parsing. I fixed it by disabling thinking in the Ollama options.
  • Ollama's default context window silently truncates long RAG prompts, so I set a larger num-ctx and tuned how many chunks each call retrieves.
  • Small models sometimes return a bare JSON array instead of an object, so the parsing and validation code handles that and retries.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A closed API would have made this product impossible to sell to its target customers. A coaching institute's notes are its business, and "send your question bank to a third party" is a dealbreaker.

Open-weight models let the whole pipeline run inside the customer's own machine. That also changes the economics: generating a hundred papers costs electricity, not tokens, so a tutor can regenerate Set B at 11pm without watching a bill. And because the stack is open, institutes can swap the model for a bigger one as their hardware allows.
