title: Retrieval Architecture for Course Tutors: Relevance Tuning Without Lock-In
description:
Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For an online course tutor aggregating listings from several sources, the durable design is a contract around relevance, latency, and access metadata, not a permanent commitment to one vector database.

Start with the bill and the retention decision

The largest operational term is usually retained and re-embedded course material, not the handful of query calls a learner makes. Keep raw listings only as long as the product needs them, and keep a compact source record (source URL, tenant, ACL, version, and chunk hash) beside each vector. A changed chunk gets a new version; an unchanged hash does not get embedded again. That one rule moves the bill more than shaving a few milliseconds from a query.

Retention has a cost beyond storage. If an instructor deletes a lesson, stale chunks can produce a confident but wrong answer until the index is updated. I would retain deletion tombstones for the same audit window as answer traces, then remove vector payloads after that window. You deliberately stop keeping old text; the trade-off is that a later support investigation may have only the hash and citation metadata, not the original chunk. Compliance and course-owner requests should win over a sentimental archive.

Measure twice.

What should a retrieval contract contain for a course tutor?

Write the contract before choosing an engine. It should state the input (learner query, tenant, locale, and access claims), a bounded candidate count, filters that must be enforced before ranking, and the output fields required for citation. The answer service should never receive an anonymous blob of text. It receives source IDs, titles, URLs, versions, and the retrieval scores that led to the context.

Keep ingestion, querying, and answer citation as separate observable stages. Measure recall against a small set of representative documents and deliberate failures: near-duplicate lessons, outdated syllabi, cross-tenant IDs, and a query whose best answer is lexical rather than semantic. Precision matters too. A top-20 full of vaguely related courses makes a tutor sound fluent while missing the exact prerequisite.

For this particular boundary, Infrai is worth a controlled trial early in the adapter. Its discovery endpoint is public and self-describing, with request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so an engineer can inspect a capability before wiring it into the tutor. That shortens the experiment without making the provider the application contract.

I keep the query budget explicit: retrieve a modest semantic candidate set, optionally blend a lexical set, then rerank only that bounded union. The latency budget belongs in the contract, so a slow reranker cannot quietly become the user experience. Your mileage may vary by corpus shape; I am not sure a single top-k works for both short course cards and long transcripts, which is why the evaluation set needs both.

A small, replaceable vector boundary

The application owns a narrow adapter. Below, the payload is intentionally ordinary JSON and the paths are the documented vector operations. The adapter can be swapped for a specialist service without changing tutor logic.

import os
import time
import uuid
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
HEADERS = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}


def post(path, payload):
    urls = {
        "/vector/collection/create": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/collection/create",
        "/vector/upsert": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/upsert",
        "/vector/query": "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
    }
    for attempt in range(4):
        url = urls[path]
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query" if path == "/vector/query" else url,
            headers=HEADERS,
            json=payload,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("vector request remained rate-limited")


collection = post("/vector/collection/create", {
    "name": "course-listings-v1",
    "metadata": {"tenant_scope": "support-course"},
})

item_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
post("/vector/upsert", {
    "collection": "course-listings-v1",
    "items": [{
        "id": item_id,
        "text": "Lesson: HTTP caching and validators",
        "metadata": {
            "tenant_id": "tenant-42",
            "access": "enrolled",
            "source_url": "https://courses.example/lesson/http-cache",
            "version": 3,
        },
    }],
})

result = post("/vector/query", {
    "collection": "course-listings-v1",
    "query": "How do validators reduce stale course content?",
    "top_k": 8,
    "filter": {"tenant_id": "tenant-42", "access": "enrolled"},
})
print(result)

There are two practical Infrai reasons to test this boundary. Its public discovery surface describes each capability and provides runnable examples, so wiring a new backend operation starts with reading a schema instead of learning another SDK. The same platform also exposes a plain REST surface across many backend capabilities, which can reduce the number of authentication and client conventions your adapter has to carry. That is useful during migration; it is not a promise that every corpus or ranking policy fits one service.

How do specialist and general platforms change migration work?

The adapter keeps the comparison honest. Each option is good at a different boundary, and none removes the need for relevance tests.

Option Useful fit Migration consideration
Pinecone Managed vector search with a focused operational surface You still own metadata contracts and export/import procedures
Weaviate Vector plus schema-oriented search and hybrid patterns Its object and module model becomes part of your adapter unless normalized
OpenSearch Teams already operating search clusters and lexical analysis More cluster policy and tuning can mean a larger operations footprint
Infrai A self-describing REST boundary when several backend capabilities share one integration Validate ranking controls and regional requirements against your evaluation set

Stick with Pinecone when a managed vector specialist and its surrounding tooling are the priority. Choose Weaviate when its schema and hybrid model are central to your product. OpenSearch is sensible when existing cluster ownership and BM25-style analysis matter more than a small integration surface. Try Infrai for the course-listing retrieval adapter when self-describing discovery and one consistent REST contract reduce the migration work across your other backend calls.

The catch is portability still depends on what you normalize. Store your own chunk IDs, source metadata, embedding version, and evaluation fixtures. Export a golden query set before switching providers, replay it after the switch, and compare recall, precision, citation completeness, and p95 latency under the same candidate bound. A provider can satisfy the HTTP contract while changing the ordering that your tutor relies on.

Every indexed item carries tenant and access-control metadata. Enforce those filters in retrieval, then re-check authorization before rendering a citation. Log the request ID, collection version, candidate IDs, and final cited IDs; redact lesson text from logs unless policy explicitly permits it. A citation that points to a private source is a security bug in the application layer even when the vector query was technically successful.

The final quality gate is a failure matrix, not a demo. Include empty results, conflicting editions, deleted lessons, multilingual titles, and a query that should abstain. Review false positives with instructors and false negatives with support agents. Relevance tuning becomes a controlled migration when those cases are versioned alongside code.

One more operational detail pays off during a cutover: run the old and new adapters in shadow mode for a sample of sanitized queries, persist only ranked IDs and scores, and compare disagreements by failure class. That lets you change collection versions or ranking weights without exposing an unreviewed answer to learners. When the distributions settle, switch the read path behind a flag and keep the old writer available until deletion and citation checks have completed. It is slower than a one-line provider swap, but it leaves a clear rollback point.

For example, a support team might discover that “course 101 refund policy” retrieves a marketing page above the enrollment policy. Keep that miss in the fixture set, label the expected source, and test the same query after every chunking or reranking change. If a migration improves semantic recall but drops the exact policy below the citation threshold, it has failed the product contract even if a generic relevance score rises. This is the kind of edge case that rate-limit dashboards will never reveal.

Keep the boundary boring.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the vector capability schema and reproducing the evaluation cases above.

References

  • Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc
  • Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks”: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • Pinecone documentation: https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • Weaviate documentation: https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • OpenSearch documentation: https://opensearch.org/docs/latest/

title: Architectural Breakdown: Python performance: native loops, NumPy and the vectorize trap
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+Python+performance%3A+native+loo+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# `np.vectorize` Is Just a For Loop in a Fancy Coat

It was 02:14 AM on a Tuesday when the on-call alert fired. Our ETL layer on an **8 GB RAM** cloud node (Python 3.11, CPython) started timing out normalising a batch of **500 k** feature vectors. The offending line in `transforms.py`:


python
import numpy as np

def normalize_features(records):
# "Vectorized!" , three exclamation points. Nobody believed it.
return np.vectorize(lambda x: (x - np.mean(x)) / np.std(x))(records)


Forty-seven seconds. For what should have been sub-100 ms. This is the kind of thing that keeps senior engineers up at night, not because it is complex, but because it *looks* correct.

What follows is a hardened rewrite that respects hardware limits, bounded-queue design, and race-condition resilience. Production builds from our [full-stack MVP reference codebase](https://www.shipmvp.tech) run variations of this exact pattern without incident.

---

## Why `np.vectorize` Is a Lie

| Tier | Per-element cost | What actually happens |
|------|------------------|-----------------------|
| Native Python loop | ~100 ns | Bytecode, ref-count, GIL |
| NumPy broadcast | ~50 ns | One C-level boundary crossing |
| `np.vectorize` | ~100 ns | Python loop behind a ufunc costume |
| Numba JIT (`nogil`) | ~10 ns | Compiled machine code, SIMD, no GIL |

`np.vectorize` is built on `np.frompyfunc`. It iterates **in Python**, calls your lambda for every element, builds an object array, then casts back to a numeric dtype. Two full passes. No SIMD. No parallelism. It is a slower `for` loop wearing a NumPy tie.

---

## Hardware-Aware Refactor

### Broadcast-First Normalisation


python
import numpy as np

def normalize_broadcast(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
"""True vectorisation, one C-level pass."""
if not arr.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]:
arr = np.ascontiguousarray(arr)

mean = arr.mean()
std  = arr.std()
return (arr - mean) / std


On an 8 GB node, a `float64` array of 500 k by 128 rows occupies roughly 4.9 GB. A single contiguous buffer avoids hidden copies that push us past the RAM ceiling and trigger swapping. Swapping is where the 47-second disaster comes from.

### Numba JIT for Conditional Logic

When the logic cannot be expressed as a chain of ufuncs (clipping, per-row state), Numba gives near-C speed without the GIL.


python
from numba import njit, prange
import numpy as np

@njit(cache=True, nogil=True, parallel=True)
def normalize_numba(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
n = arr.size

# First pass: compute mean
mean = 0.0
for i in prange(n):
    mean += arr[i]
mean /= n

# Second pass: compute variance
var = 0.0
for i in prange(n):
    diff = arr[i] - mean
    var += diff * diff
std = np.sqrt(var / n)

# Third pass: normalise with clipping and NaN guard
out = np.empty_like(arr)
for i in prange(n):
    val = (arr[i] - mean) / std
    out[i] = 0.0 if np.isnan(val) else max(min(val, 3.0), -3.0)
return out


- `cache=True` writes compiled machine code to disk, so there is no JIT warm-up penalty on container restarts
- `nogil=True` lets multiple worker threads run concurrently
- `parallel=True` enables auto-vectorisation and multi-core execution on inner loops

---

## Bounded-Queue Architecture

Production does not process a 500 k by 128 matrix in one shot. We slice it into chunks that fit in memory and keep the queue size bounded.


python
import queue
import threading

CHUNK_SIZE = 64_000 # ~4 MB per chunk (float64)
MAX_QUEUE = 8 # 32 MB buffer, safe headroom on 8 GB node
NUM_WORKERS = 4

def producer(src_iter, q: queue.Queue):
buffer = []
for rec in src_iter:
buffer.append(rec)
if len(buffer) == CHUNK_SIZE:
q.put(np.asarray(buffer, dtype=np.float64))
buffer.clear()
if buffer:
q.put(np.asarray(buffer, dtype=np.float64))

def consumer(q: queue.Queue, out_q: queue.Queue):
while True:
arr = q.get()
if arr is None:
out_q.put(None)
break
try:
out_q.put(normalize_numba(arr))
finally:
q.task_done()


The `maxsize` bound guarantees we never allocate more than roughly 32 MB of raw data plus 32 MB of normalised output. The producer converts once. No repeated allocation tax. Consumers run in a thread pool and the Numba kernel releases the GIL, so they are actually parallel.

Sentinels (`None`) guarantee each consumer exits exactly once. No lost-wake-up bugs. No manual lock handling.

---

## Failure Modes (Because They Happen)

| Failure mode | Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|--------------|---------|------------|-----|
| **OOM** | Process killed by OS | Chunk too big for 8 GB node | Reduce `CHUNK_SIZE`, add `resource` guard |
| **Stalled pipeline** | Workers block forever | Producer throws before sentinel | Wrap in `try/finally`, always emit `None` |
| **Wrong results** | NaNs post-normalisation | Non-contiguous input, dtype mismatch | `np.ascontiguousarray(..., dtype=np.float64)` upfront |
| **CPU thrashing** | 100% usage, no speedup | Numba without `parallel=True` | Enable `parallel=True`, use `prange` |
| **Deadlock** | `q.join()` hangs | Exception skips `task_done()` | Always call in `finally` |

---

## Benchmarks (8 GB node, 500 k by 128 float64)


plaintext
native_python_list 0.34 s ± 0.01
numpy_broadcast 0.018 s ± 0.001
numpy_vectorize 0.29 s ± 0.02 ← same as pure Python
numba_jit (cached) 0.009 s ± 0.001
pipeline (8-chunk, 4-workers) 0.025 s ± 0.003


Peak memory: ~6 GB. Scales linearly with worker count because the GIL is released. The pipeline includes queue overhead and still beats the naive approach by **13×**.

---

The lesson is not about NumPy or Numba. It is about reading what you write, not what it promises. `np.vectorize` says "vectorised" in its docstring. That is the entire pitch. Do not fall for it.

**Open question for the comments:** When you have a per-row transformation that mixes aggregation with conditional clipping, do you reach for Numba first, or do you prefer the readability of NumPy broadcasting even when it means an extra pass over the data?

title: What jstack Misses When Your Java Service Uses Virtual Threads
description:
Take a Spring Boot service with virtual threads enabled, a HikariCP pool of 10 connections, and roughly 5,000 requests in flight. Latency is climbing. You grab a thread dump and find 43 platform threads, most of the scheduler workers waiting in ForkJoinPool.awaitWork, and very little CPU activity.

If you used jstack, the requests you're looking for may never have made it into the file. On JDK 21 through 25, the traditional dump doesn't list virtual threads. You can spend quite a while reading the scheduler's stacks without seeing the requests waiting for your database.

I'll use that connection-pool scenario throughout this article. The numbers and dump excerpts are illustrative. I run ThreadMine, and its support for these formats needs some explanation too; I'll get to that after the commands.

The carrier can be idle while the request waits

jstack and jcmd <pid> Thread.print show platform threads. That includes the carriers, the scheduler workers on which virtual threads run. When a virtual thread unmounts to wait for I/O or another resource, its carrier is free to run something else.

If most requests are waiting, there may be very little for the carriers to do. Low CPU and idle workers are entirely compatible with a large backlog.

The scheduler uses a ForkJoinPool, with default parallelism based on the processors available to the JVM. You can change it with jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, but I'd leave that alone until I knew what the requests were waiting for. More workers won't help requests queued behind the same ten database connections.

A carrier with a virtual thread mounted can include this line in the traditional dump:

Carrying virtual thread #212

From JDK 24 on, the dump also prints that virtual thread's own stack right below the carrier, under a Mounted virtual thread #212 line. Either way it's useful for identifying the mounted thread. For the thousands of unmounted threads, you need another dump.

Use Thread.dump_to_file

This command has been available since JDK 21:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/dump.txt

The JVM writes the file, so /tmp/dump.txt is a path in the target process's filesystem. This matters in containers. The process also needs permission to write there; the capture guide covers those details.

Plain text is the default. For JSON:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json

The documented format names are plain and json. Existing files aren't overwritten unless you pass -overwrite. Use a new filename for each capture so there's something to compare later.

The output also depends on the JDK version. JDK 21 through 24 give you the thread ID, name, a virtual marker, and the stack. JDK 25 adds state, timestamps, and lock information. A shortened JDK 25 entry might look like this:

#412 "" virtual WAITING 2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z
    at java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:582)
    ...
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:179)
    at com.example.orders.OrderRepository.load(OrderRepository.java:48)
    ...

There's the request, waiting to acquire a connection. The empty name is common for virtual threads; an application can assign a name if it needs one.

For our example, suppose the file contains 5,004 virtual threads and 4,962 occurrences of HikariPool.getConnection. You can check those counts without loading the dump into anything:

grep -cE '^#[0-9]+ ".*" virtual' dump.txt
grep -c 'HikariPool.getConnection' dump.txt

The second command counts matching lines. Open a few of the stacks to check the call path, especially if the method occurs more than once per thread.

At this point, I'd look at connection hold time. If each request holds a connection for 18 ms, ten connections would take roughly nine seconds to clear a backlog of 5,000 requests, with no new arrivals. That gives us a plausible scale for the delay. It doesn't calculate p99, but it tells us where to investigate.

Check slow queries and transaction scope before changing the pool size. A connection held during an unrelated HTTP call, for example, reduces the capacity available to every request behind it. The database may support more concurrency, or it may already be struggling. The dump helps locate the queue; pool and database metrics help explain it.

Virtual threads make waiting cheaper. The database still has to do the work.

What I'd compare in the next dump

For a slowdown that lasts minutes, take another capture after about 30 seconds. Look at the large stack groups and compare thread IDs within them.

If the same requests are still waiting in the same place, investigate why they aren't progressing. If the IDs have changed but the group stays large, requests may be completing while new ones refill the queue. Those situations can look almost identical if you only compare totals.

I wouldn't read much into 5,004 threads becoming 5,011. I'd be more interested in whether connection acquisition time is rising and whether throughput has stopped keeping up with arrivals. I've been fooled by a single dump more than once, and the second one has always been cheap.

The state labels need the same treatment. WAITING is expected in a service doing I/O, and it doesn't tell you by itself whether a virtual thread released its carrier. RUNNABLE doesn't establish CPU saturation either. Start with the stack and the resource involved, then check the metrics that could explain the wait.

JSON helps when there are several executors

For a single pile of requests waiting on HikariCP, the text file is enough to get started. JSON becomes useful when you need to separate work created by different executors or structured-concurrency scopes. It groups threads into containers.

On JDK 25, an entry for a mounted virtual thread can also include its carrier's ID. Here's a reduced container with one thread:

{
  "container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@3f1e7a2c",
  "parent": "<root>",
  "owner": null,
  "threads": [
    {
      "tid": "412",
      "time": "2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z",
      "virtual": true,
      "name": "",
      "state": "RUNNABLE",
      "stack": ["..."],
      "carrier": "37"
    }
  ],
  "threadCount": "1"
}

Run these against the complete JDK 25 JSON file to count virtual-thread entries with a carrier and list the container sizes:

jq '[.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[] | select(.virtual == true and .carrier != null)] | length' dump.json
jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threadCount)\t\(.container)"' dump.json

The dump is collected while threads keep running. That carrier count therefore isn't a measurement of how many carriers were busy at one instant. The container breakdown is what I'd use first to find where the threads are accumulating.

Keep the JDK version with the file. Some fields used here aren't available in older releases. Also check for -Djdk.trackAllThreads=false, which can leave some virtual threads out of the dump.

Pinning depends on the JDK version

A request waiting for a connection and a virtual thread blocking its carrier call for different investigations. For the second case, look for VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread: it's the path where a virtual thread parks while retaining the carrier.

On JDK 21 through 23, this code can take that path when the HTTP call blocks:

synchronized (lock) {
    return httpClient.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
}

The relevant part of the stack can look like this:

#37 "" virtual
      java.base/jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(VirtualThread.java:675)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:593)
      ...
      com.example.price.PriceService.lookup(PriceService.java:32)

With JDK 24 and JEP 491, holding a monitor no longer causes this pinning. Native frames and class initialization can still be involved in other cases. Check the runtime version before recommending changes to synchronized code.

For pinning that comes and goes, I'd use JFR. The jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event has been enabled by default with a 20 ms threshold since JDK 21. A recording gives you frequency and duration, which a couple of dumps can easily miss. The old jdk.tracePinnedThreads option was removed in JDK 24.

Finding parkOnCarrierThread is useful evidence of that particular parking path. Its absence doesn't rule out every form of pinning. There's more on the version differences in the pinning reference.

A note on ThreadMine

ThreadMine reads the text file that Thread.dump_to_file writes, in both shapes it has had so far: the JDK 21 to 24 one, with no state in the header and no at on the frames, and the JDK 25 one, which has both. Virtual threads come through as virtual threads, empty names stay empty, and a thread sitting in parkOnCarrierThread is flagged as pinned. I'll be honest about how recent that is: until this week the parser silently dropped every #22 "" virtual line, and I only found out while checking this article against real dumps from JDK 21 through 25. The JSON form is still not accepted, so paste the text; the per-container counts are the one thing jq still does that the analyzer doesn't.

The change I'd make to a team's incident runbook is straightforward: when the service uses virtual threads, capture Thread.dump_to_file as well as the traditional dump. You want the request stacks available before anyone starts drawing conclusions from idle carriers.

Felipe Maschio is the founder of ThreadMine, a free JVM thread dump analyzer.

References

  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads
  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
  • JDK 25 jcmd command reference
  • JDK 25 release notes: thread dump lock information
  • Virtual threads in JDK 25

title: Why I Want My AI Coding Assistant to Ask Before It Acts
description:
Most AI coding tools are built around one promise: speed. Type a prompt, get code, move on.

But after a while I noticed the speed was costing me something. The AI would edit files I didn't expect, delete things I still needed, or run a command I hadn't read. I'd spend the next hour undoing work I never approved.

The problem with "just do it" AI

When an AI agent has full permission to write, delete, and execute, every action is a small act of trust you didn't explicitly give. For a throwaway script that's fine. For a real codebase it's not.

The failure mode isn't dramatic. It's quiet:

  • A helper function gets "cleaned up" and something subtle breaks
  • A config file gets rewritten with slightly different values
  • A dependency gets bumped and nothing works the next morning

What I actually want

I want an assistant that treats my codebase like it belongs to someone else. That means:

  1. Ask before writing. Show me the change, let me approve it.
  2. Show diffs, not summaries. "I updated the auth logic" tells me nothing. A diff tells me everything.
  3. Checkpoint every step. If step 4 was wrong, I want to rewind to step 3 — not start over.
  4. Ask before running commands. A shell command is the most powerful thing an agent can do. It should be the most gated.

The trade-off is worth it

Yes, this is slower per action. But it's dramatically faster per outcome, because I'm not spending my afternoon fixing things I never agreed to.

If you're on Windows and want an AI editor that works this way, that's the idea behind Arcwright — it's free to start. But the principle applies to whatever tool you use: the AI should earn your trust one approved change at a time.

title: css-ghost: find and delete orphaned CSS selectors with zero config
description:
You've been there. You rename a component, move a file, or quietly migrate from one styling approach to another – and the old CSS stays behind. Nobody complains, the build doesn't break, and the dead selectors quietly accumulate.

css-ghost is a small Node.js CLI tool I built to solve that problem. Point it at a folder and it tells you every CSS class defined in your style files that isn't referenced anywhere in your components.

What it does

css-ghost scans your style files (.css, .module.css, .scss, .sass, .less, MUI makeStyles, vanilla-extract), extracts every class selector, then cross-references them against every component file it can find (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, .vue, .svelte).

Anything defined but never actually used gets reported as an orphan – with its line number and the full CSS rule printed inline, so you can see what it does before deciding to delete it.

It also catches orphaned CSS custom properties (--my-token: value defined but never consumed via var(--my-token) anywhere in the codebase), reported in a separate 🔮 section.

Run it now

No install required:

npx css-ghost ./src

Or install globally for repeated use:

npm install -g css-ghost
css-ghost ./src

Interactive folder picker

Run css-ghost with no arguments and an interactive directory picker opens. Navigate with ↑↓ (or j/k), press Enter or → to go into a folder, ← to go back up, [a] to add the current directory to the scan, then [d] when done:

css-ghost

Useful when you're not sure which subfolder to target, or want to scan multiple directories in one pass.

Dynamic class detection

If a component accesses classes dynamically – styles[variable], styles[\${variant}] – css-ghost can't resolve the class name statically. Rather than silently skip those files or report false positives, it flags them with a ⚠️ warning per file:

✅ src/components/Alert/Alert.module.css

   ⚠️  Dynamic class references detected – results may be incomplete.
   Dynamic references in: src/components/Alert.jsx

   👻 .hidden (line 30)
      .hidden { display: none; }

All statically resolvable patterns are still analysed: string literals, ternaries, cx({ active: isOn }) object keys, array literals, and both branches of ternaries.

Deleting orphans

Once you're happy with the report, pass --delete to remove every flagged selector from its source file:

css-ghost ./src --delete

css-ghost prints the full report first, lists what it's about to delete, then asks for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt in CI:

css-ghost ./src --delete --yes

Tip: commit or stash first. There's no undo.

Other useful flags

Flag What it does
--ghost-trail Show the last git commit that touched each orphan
--strict Exit with code 1 when orphans exist (CI / pre-commit)
--install-hook ./src Write a pre-commit hook that blocks commits with orphans
--output <path> Custom path for the markdown report
--ai Append a plain-English AI summary (needs free OpenRouter key)

Ghost trail

Pass --ghost-trail to fetch the last git commit that changed each orphan's occurrence count:

css-ghost ./src --ghost-trail

   👻 .iconRight (line 28)
      🕵️  b5c6efb · Roland Levy · 3 weeks ago – "Refactor Button component"
      .iconRight {
        margin-left: 6px;
      }

Handy for tracking down when and why a class went dead.

Pre-commit hook 

css-ghost --install-hook ./src

Writes .git/hooks/pre-commit (executable, chmod 755) that blocks commits whenever orphaned selectors exist. Remove it with rm .git/hooks/pre-commit.

How is it different from PurgeCSS?

PurgeCSS is a build-time bundler – it hooks into webpack or PostCSS to strip unused CSS from your production output. It's designed for frameworks like Tailwind or Bootstrap where you use a fraction of the utility classes.

css-ghost is a source code auditor – it finds dead selectors in your actual codebase, with no build step and no config file.

PurgeCSS css-ghost
Works on source files ❌ Build output only ✅
Zero config, no build step ❌ ✅
CSS custom property orphans ❌ ✅
Git history per orphan ❌ ✅
Pre-commit hook ❌ ✅
Deletes dead code for you ❌ ✅
Safe with dynamic classes ❌ Silently removes them ✅ Flags with ⚠️

The two tools are complementary – PurgeCSS for trimming framework output at build time, css-ghost for auditing your own hand-written CSS throughout development.

The source is on GitHub and the package is on npm. PRs and issues welcome.

title: Vercel Sandbox creation now returns a ready sandbox
description:
A new Vercel Sandbox is now ready to run commands and read or write files when creation completes.

Sandbox.create() now resolves only after snapshot restoration completes, so the first command or file operation no longer waits for it. Startup errors also reject Sandbox.create() instead of surfacing during that operation.

Snapshot restoration time now counts toward creation instead of the first operation. Creation is about 50 ms longer at p50, with a larger increase possible for uncached snapshots. The total time through the first operation remains the same.

This change applies automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. See the Sandbox.create() documentation for details.

title: Jev for Python engineers
description:
It's simply impossible to not hear about Jev. Seemingly everyone is tinkering with it in some way, from using it to make trading decisions (what could possibly go wrong?) to generating UIs with it (maybe we're onto something here!).

Jev is a new kind of AI model. You feed it data and ask it a set of multiple-choice questions, and it responds with its answers and how confident it is in each. Just like with any other model, Jev can and will make mistakes, but it will make them fast. ​

​The bottom line is: Jev is built for making narrow decisions. Whether it's accurate enough for your use cases is something you'll need to test.

The job of the Python team at Vercel is to make it easy for Python devs to tinker with Jev, among a few other things. So please welcome the latest release of the AI SDK for Python.

Install it with uv add ai to use the new experimental evaluate() API, which talks directly to Jev's nervous system. Then create an AI Gateway key, set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, and try this complete example:

Now, I'd like to explain what Jev is and how to make it work for you using a couple of examples. One is good and one is dumb. Ask Jev which is which. Let's have some fun!

Jev ELI5

Jev is a universal classifier.

Classifiers are the classic primitive of good old machine learning. Say you want a spam filter. You train a classifier on lots of emails, each labeled as spam or not spam, and it learns to tell whether a freshly incoming email looks like spam.

Problem is, for every new classification task you'd have to collect and label new data, and then train a new classifier on it to tune its weights for that task. But you know what else has weights? Large language models! So the team behind Jev figured out how to turn an LLM into a classifier that you don't need to train for a specific domain, because it's already trained on a broad slice of human knowledge.

And while it started as an LLM, Jev still behaves like a classifier. It's cheap and fast, and it returns structured JSON instead of generating text. Its answers conform to the types and choices you define in your questions.

The API

Jev's official API couldn't be simpler, and to keep it that way, we implemented it in the Python AI SDK pretty much verbatim.

There's just one function, evaluate(), and a few supporting types. The function takes a model, state (can be a simple string or complex JSON), and a mapping of questions. A question is an instance of either ChoiceQuestion (choose one answer), ScoreQuestion (rate the state on a scale you define), or NoulQuestion (estimate the probability that a statement is true).

For the complete API reference, refer your agent to the docs. By now, we should have a good idea of what Jev is and how to use it. Time to see what we can build with it!

Example 1: Python or English?

This is a sensible example of using Jev: quite literally as a classifier.

About a year ago I had an idea to make the Python REPL agentic. I wanted it to have a great UX and thought it would be pretty cool if the REPL could tell whether I'm typing English or Python without me explicitly switching between chat and code.

I needed a classifier, so I spent two days training my own on a random selection of Python code and English text.

After a lot of sweat and dumb Opus 4.1 tokens, I concluded I'm not good enough to make a reliable classifier for Python vs. English. The UI felt jittery: typing if i highlighted it as Python, if i i switched it to English, and if i is flipped it back to Python. What seemed like a very simple problem turned out to be a really hard one.

Let's see how Jev does:

These are actual traces of Jev responses to "does this look like English or Python to you?" The code behind them isn't particularly interesting; it's basically the opening code snippet of this post with a different question.

What's more interesting is whether Jev could solve my REPL problem. And while it does seem to fare much better than my hand-rolled classifier did, it still has gaps. For example, "what's" + " up looks like English to Jev, while it's quite obvious to me that it's a partially typed Python expression.

Example 2: Jev writes Python code

How about we regress and make Jev generate text like an LLM? Jev can't write, so one way to get it to type is to have it go letter by letter. At each step, it picks the next character from a set of letters, punctuation, and whitespace. Another way would be to pick one word at a time from a vocabulary of some N English words.

When I saw that, I immediately knew I had to test how good Jev is at writing Python code.

My first attempt used the "letters + Python keywords + whitespace" method, but I quickly realized Jev could barely type an if statement that way. The only way to get anything sensible out of it was to make it generate an abstract syntax tree (AST) of the program instead.

The idea:

  1. Take the user's prompt and use an LLM (GPT-5.6 in this case) to expand it into a concrete set of instructions for Jev. I found that without a detailed "plan", Jev struggles to implement even elementary tasks.

  2. Make Jev build a Python AST through a series of choices. At each step, show it the current program, mark the field being filled, and offer the possible next nodes, like a function call, an arithmetic operation, or a variable. Each option comes with a preview of the code it would produce.

  3. Apply each choice to the tree and render it back into Python. The host code handles punctuation and indentation; Jev decides the program's overall structure and contents. Repeat until Jev finishes the tree.

I did get Jev to generate syntactically valid (yet still mostly incorrect) Python code using this approach. But as you can see, making classifiers do the job of an LLM is quite challenging. The source code is on GitHub if you think you can do better.

Try Jev

Neither experiment worked quite as I'd hoped, but I'm still excited about Jev. We're only beginning to explore what this new class of models can do!

Try it today with the AI SDK for Python and let us know what you build. All you need is uv add ai and an AI Gateway key. Here's a ready to copy/paste prompt for your coding agent:

title: AZ-500 practice, week 1: 4 questions
description:
Four exam-style questions I wrote this week (PIM, Key Vault, storage, NSG), answers hidden, explanations in plain words.

How to use these: read the question, pick your answer before you open Answer, and write it down (or in the comments). Then check the "why not the others" part even if you got it right: that is where the exam traps live. Every scenario, name and number is made up by me; only the question formats follow the real exam.

Table of contents

  • Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval
  • Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret
  • Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later
  • Q004: NSG rules with application security groups
  • Cheat sheet
  • Coming next

Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval

Identity and access · Single choice · standalone page

Your helpdesk lead, Mai, sometimes needs the User Administrator role to fix accounts. Your security team says: "Fine, but only when she asks for it, for at most 4 hours, and someone has to say yes first."

What should you configure?

  • A. A permanent active assignment of User Administrator, plus a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA
  • B. A Privileged Identity Management (PIM) eligible assignment of User Administrator, with role settings: activation maximum duration 4 hours and require approval to activate
  • C. An access review on the User Administrator role that runs every 4 hours
  • D. An administrative unit that contains Mai's account

Answer

B. "Eligible" means Mai does not hold the role until she activates it. In the PIM role settings, the activation maximum duration can be anything from 1 to 24 hours (so 4 is fine), and "Require approval to activate" makes at least one approver say yes first.

Why not the others:

  • A gives her the role 24/7. MFA proves it is really Mai, it does not make the role go away after 4 hours.
  • C checks who has access, after the fact. An access review every 4 hours would mostly annoy the reviewers.
  • D limits which users she can manage, not when she can manage them.

Source: Configure Microsoft Entra role settings in Privileged Identity Management

Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret

Identity and access · Yes/No series ("Does this meet the goal?") · standalone page

Yes/No series: same scenario, a different solution each time. Some scenarios have several right solutions, some have none.

An app on the Azure VM vm-lab-01 must read a database password stored in the key vault kv-lab-01. The vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Goal: no password, key or certificate is stored in the app code or on the VM.

Solution: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on vm-lab-01 and assign it the Key Vault Secrets User role on kv-lab-01.

Does this meet the goal?

  • A. Yes
  • B. No

Answer

A. Yes. The VM gets its own identity in Microsoft Entra ID, so the app asks Azure for a token instead of keeping a secret in a config file. Key Vault Secrets User can read secret contents, and it works here because the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model.

Other solutions you might see in the same series:

  • "Store a client secret for an app registration in appsettings.json" → No. That is a secret sitting on the VM, the exact thing the goal forbids.
  • "Assign the managed identity Key Vault Reader" → No. Reader sees the vault and the names of its secrets (metadata), but it cannot read the secret values. Close, but no password for you.

Source: Provide access to Key Vault keys, certificates, and secrets with Azure role-based access control

Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later

Compute, storage and databases · Hot area · standalone page

Someone set one container in the storage account stlabdata01 to "Container (anonymous read access)". Your boss wants no anonymous reads in any container of this account, now and later, even if someone changes a container setting again next week.

Pick the right value for each line:

Where Setting Your choice
Storage account stlabdata01 › Settings › Configuration Allow Blob anonymous access ▢ Enabled ▢ Disabled
Each container Anonymous access level ▢ Must be changed to Private one by one ▢ Nothing more to do

Answer

Disabled / Nothing more to do. The account setting (property AllowBlobPublicAccess) overrides the container settings: once it is off, containers that were set to anonymous access are no longer reachable anonymously. Flipping containers to Private one by one is nice tidying, but it is not what stops the leak, and the next person can flip a container right back.

Why not the other values: Enabled leaves every container in charge of its own fate. Changing containers one by one only fixes today, not "later".

Bonus: to do this for every storage account at once, use the built-in Azure Policy "Storage account public access should be disallowed" (Audit or Deny). One gotcha: a static website's $web container stays public no matter what, because that is its job.

Sources: Remediate anonymous read access to blob data · Azure Policy built-in definitions for Azure Storage

Q004: NSG rules with application security groups

Networking · Drag and drop · standalone page

The virtual network vnet-shop has one subnet with the network security group nsg-shop attached. The VMs web01 and web02 are in the application security group asg-web. The VMs api01 and api02 are in asg-api. Everything is in the same virtual network.

You need to meet these rules:

  1. People on the internet can reach the web VMs on HTTPS.
  2. Only the web VMs can reach the API VMs, on TCP 8443.
  3. Nothing else inside the virtual network can reach the API VMs. (Yes, that includes the test VM someone "temporarily" created in March.)

Drag the right value into each numbered box. Each value can be used once, more than once, or not at all.

Values: Internet · VirtualNetwork · AzureLoadBalancer · asg-web · asg-api · 443 · 8443 · 3389

Inbound rules on nsg-shop:

Priority Name Source Destination Port Action
100 allow-https-web [1] [2] 443 Allow
200 allow-web-to-api [3] [4] [5] Allow
300 deny-vnet-to-api [6] asg-api Any Deny

Answer

[1] Internet · [2] asg-web · [3] asg-web · [4] asg-api · [5] 8443 · [6] VirtualNetwork

Application security groups let you write rules against "the web VMs" instead of a list of IP addresses, and they work as both source and destination. Rule 300 is the one people forget: the default rule AllowVNetInBound (priority 65000) lets every machine in the virtual network talk to every other one. You cannot delete default rules, but a custom rule with a lower number wins. Rules are checked from the lowest number up and stop at the first match, so the web VMs still get in through rule 200 before rule 300 says no to everyone else.

Why not the other values:

  • AzureLoadBalancer in [6] would block the load balancer health probes, not your test VM. Your API would go "unhealthy" and you would get a very confusing afternoon.
  • VirtualNetwork in [3] would let any VM in the network call the API, which breaks rule 2.
  • 443 in [5] or 3389 anywhere: wrong port. Nobody asked for RDP from anywhere.

Gotcha: all network interfaces in one application security group must be in the same virtual network, and when a rule uses an ASG as both source and destination, both groups must be in that same virtual network.

Sources: Application security groups · Network security groups overview

Cheat sheet

The same four ideas in plain words, for the manager who asks "so what?". Share it with them.

Coming next

Monday and Tuesday bring a SAS question for storage accounts with key access switched off, and a just-in-time RDP question for Defender for Cloud. All questions live in the AZ-500 practice folder.

Got one wrong? Good. That is one fewer surprise in the exam room. Drop your answers in the comments.

title: Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?
description:
Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?

For months, the artificial intelligence trade seemed unstoppable. Giant chipmakers, cloud providers, and data-center builders lifted Wall Street to one record after another. This week, the music stopped — at least temporarily — as a brutal sell-off swept through the technology sector and forced investors to confront a question they had been happy to ignore: what happens if the most expensive technology bet in history stops paying off?

A Week of Red Numbers

The damage was fast and broad. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite posted its first weekly loss in five weeks, and the S&P 500 logged its worst week since June. Chip stocks — the engine of the AI boom — took the hardest hits. Micron Technology fell more than five percent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped over five percent, Broadcom slid more than four percent, and Intel lost close to six percent on Friday alone. AI data-center infrastructure company CoreWeave, a major Nvidia customer, plunged more than seven percent after a double-digit decline earlier in the week.

The rout was global. Seoul's tech-rich Kospi briefly triggered a trading halt after diving more than eight percent, with Samsung sinking over nine percent and SK hynix down more than eleven percent. Tokyo shed close to five percent, dragged down by chip-linked names like Advantest and Kioxia as well as investment giant SoftBank.

Why Now? Inflation and the Cost of Money

The immediate trigger was economic, not technological. US inflation data came in hotter than expected, with the consumer price index jumping to 3.7 percent in September and wholesale inflation surging 6.3 percent year-on-year — its biggest jump since 2022. Those numbers stoked fears that the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in September for the first time in three years, may have to tighten further, with futures markets now pricing in a high probability of another hike by December.

Higher rates matter more to AI companies than to almost anyone else. Tech giants have financed an unprecedented infrastructure spree — data centers, GPU clusters, and power-hungry compute farms — largely through debt markets. With bond yields climbing to their highest levels in years, the cost of financing that buildout is rising exactly as patience with unprofitable AI ventures is wearing thin. A week before the crash, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had called AI "the most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime. Investors this week appeared to decide that consequence cuts both ways.

The IMF's Warning Shot

The market turmoil coincided with an uncomfortable warning from the International Monetary Fund. At the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the fund released a report projecting that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028, and cautioned that "weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction."

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva did not mince words: if confidence evaporates and "money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks" that "would be felt across the world." Yet the same meetings underscored how central AI already is to the global economy. The fund noted that global trade grew 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025 — a figure that would have been closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem put it bluntly: "It is here, and it's just the beginning."

Bubble or Growing Pains?

Not everyone reading the sell-off sees a bubble bursting. The Dow Jones actually rose on Friday, suggesting investors are rotating out of tech rather than abandoning equities altogether. Earnings expectations for the quarter remain strong, and companies at the heart of the AI supply chain — from TSMC to memory makers — have continued to report robust demand. Nvidia shares, though down more than five percent for the week, remain up dramatically over the longer arc of the AI era.

The bear case, though, is no longer fringe. Critics point to debt-financed capital expenditure, stretched valuations, and monetization that still lags the hype. Analysts this week cited "worries about the AI buildout, bubbly valuations, lower-than-expected earnings growth at leading US frontier labs, and Chinese competition" as compounding pressures. Moody's Analytics economists added that a prolonged Middle East conflict, by pushing up energy prices and interest rates, could "puncture" the AI boom by straining the economics behind AI investment.

What to Watch

Three signposts will matter in the coming weeks. First, the Fed's October 28 policy decision, landing a week before the US midterm elections — a hawkish surprise could renew the pressure on rate-sensitive tech names. Second, the ongoing earnings season, where markets will demand evidence that AI revenue is catching up to AI spending. Third, and hardest to measure: confidence. As Georgieva noted in Bangkok, "if there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities."

Whether this week proves to be a healthy correction in a long structural boom or the first crack in a bubble, one thing is clear: the era of unquestioned AI enthusiasm on Wall Street is over. From now on, the market will want receipts.

BigQuery

Change

An updated version of the Simba JDBC driver for BigQuery is now available.

Feature

Feature

BigQuery pipelines provides support for automated metadata enrichment and Knowledge Catalog data quality scorecard integration. These features are generally available.

Bigtable

Feature

Cloud Healthcare API

Feature

title: AI Is Redrawing the US Data Center Map
description:
Power access is shaping where new campuses rise, when they come online, and the networks connecting them.

October 18, 2026

In June 2024, construction began on the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas. Within a year, its first two buildings had been energized. By September 2025, Crusoe said the site was running early training and inference workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The planned campus would eventually contain eight buildings. Crusoe’s account captures both the speed of the AI infrastructure boom and its defining complication: large campuses become useful in stages.

That progression is changing the geography of computing. Developers need sites where land, electricity and equipment can come together on a workable schedule. As established markets fill up, new locations become attractive, and connecting distant facilities becomes an engineering problem of its own.

The spending curve shows how quickly this has become a national construction story. In November 2022, private US data center construction was running at an annualized pace of $13.9 billion. By August 2026, that rate had reached $85.0 billion, roughly six times as much. These Census Bureau figures cover data centers broadly and measure construction work, including fixed electrical and mechanical systems. They exclude racks and servers, whose costs sit on top of the building investment.

Figure 1. Monthly construction spending expressed as a seasonally adjusted annual rate, in current dollars. The August figure is a spending pace, rather than money already spent during 2026. Source: US Census Bureau.

Construction spending was already increasing before ChatGPT’s launch. Because the figures are in current dollars, the curve combines changes in construction prices with changes in the amount being built. It establishes the growing scale of spending without measuring computing capacity.

The next question is where that work can happen. In its August report, JLL placed 77% of North American data center capacity under construction in frontier markets, highlighting West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and the Carolinas. Its market analysis describes a buildout extending well beyond the industry’s established hubs.

Texas illustrates the shift. JLL reported 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity across the state, compared with 13 GW in Virginia. Northern Virginia remained the largest individual market, with nearly 7 GW of inventory. The state totals show the direction of investment while including projects that still have to become operating facilities.

Figure 2. State totals combine existing capacity and capacity under construction, including hyperscalers’ own facilities. They do not measure electricity currently being consumed. Source: JLL, Midyear 2026.

A large pipeline creates a planning problem for utilities. They must decide how much infrastructure to build before they know which projects will arrive, when their servers will be installed, or how quickly customer workloads will fill them. A speculative request can therefore influence planning long before it becomes a substantial electricity load.

AEP Ohio’s experience shows how that pipeline changes as commitments become binding. Its new tariff required developers to advance through paid studies and financial commitments. About one-fifth of the initial requested capacity reached signed contracts. AEP attributed the narrowing to the filtering of speculative or uncertain projects. The utility still had 17.9 GW of total contracted data center projects, including earlier contracts, scheduled to come online progressively through 2035. AEP’s February update distinguishes those future obligations from operating demand.

Figure 3. Successive stages of one AEP Ohio intake cohort, as reported in February 2026. The final bar excludes contracts signed before the tariff. Source: AEP Ohio.

Texas faces its own version of the credibility problem. ERCOT’s September board update documented a pause in energization approvals for relevant new data center and cryptocurrency facilities of at least 75 MW while verification and community-impact reviews proceeded. Projects received provisional classifications; those classifications did not constitute final permission to connect. The operator expected to publish its community-impact report by December 10.

For developers, that makes the location of available power consequential to computing design. Microsoft offers a concrete example. Its Fairwater facilities in Wisconsin and the Atlanta area are linked through a dedicated network intended to let sites cooperate on large AI workloads. Microsoft explicitly identifies land and power availability as reasons to spread work across locations. Its description of the architecture connects the choice of geography to the need for new networking infrastructure.

Distance introduces costs of its own. Large training jobs require frequent communication among processors; slow exchanges can leave expensive hardware waiting. Microsoft describes dedicated fiber and changes to network protocols designed to reduce bottlenecks between sites. Finding land and power therefore creates another task: making the resulting facilities operate efficiently together.

There are also ways to change the terms on which a facility receives electricity. In a report published October 14, the International Energy Agency examines connection agreements that allow consumption to be curtailed, phased in or adjusted to grid conditions. Such arrangements can help projects connect sooner by changing the reliability or timing of their access.

The tradeoff is practical. Interrupting expensive AI hardware can be costly, and a facility operator may have limited control over customers’ workloads. The IEA’s analysis identifies coordination among computing customers, facility operators and electricity networks as a condition for greater flexibility. Onsite generation also brings equipment lead times and engineering requirements of its own.

The buildout is consequently creating an architecture that extends beyond each campus. Transmission studies, substations, fiber routes and electricity agreements increasingly influence where AI work can run. Abilene’s first buildings became useful when several of those pieces came together. Repeating that achievement across a much larger pipeline will determine how quickly the new map translates into computing capacity.

Data: Figures use the research snapshot checked October 18, 2026. Each chart retains its source’s geography, period and definition. Charts are original graphics based on the cited figures.

title: crecheck v6.0 has been released
description:
Antananrivo, Madagascar - October 14, 2026

PostgreSQL credcheck extension

The credcheck PostgreSQL extension provides few general credential checks, which will be evaluated during the user creation, during the password change and user renaming. By using this extension, we can define a set of rules:

  • allow a specific set of credentials
  • reject a certain type of credentials
  • deny password that can be easily cracked
  • enforce use of an expiration date with a minimum of day for a password
  • define a password reuse policy
  • define the number of authentication failure allowed before a user is banned
  • define a delay on authentication failures
  • force users to change their password after first login
  • throw a warning N days before when the password user is about to expire
  • prohibit password changes
  • last login and boot/shutdown information
  • use of authentication failure with PgBouncer

Release 6.0 has been published,

This major release adds some new features and fix issues reported by users since last release.

  • Allow integration of the max_auth_failure feature with pgbouncer. See documentation.
  • Allow use of password_change_first_login with pgBouncer.
  • Add credcheck.password_valid_min setting to force a short VALID UNTIL window on newly created roles. Useful to force new users to change their password quickly when the client (DBeaver, pgAdmin, ...) does not support the error reported when credcheck.password_change_first_login is enabled.
  • Add an optional last-login history modelled on the Unix last(1)/wtmp. Records user sessions (name, login time, duration, backend pid, source IP and port, and optionally the last SQL query) plus PostgreSQL boot/shutdown/crash markers.
  • Change the behavior of the credcheck.no_password_logging to not hide the error statement anymore but instead to replace every PASSWORD '<literal>' clause with dots inplace of the literal to not expose the password in the log.
  • Add function pg_check_password( IN username name, IN password text ) to check a candidate password (and the associated username) against the credcheck username/password policy without creating or altering a role.
  • Fix privilege escalation via self ALTER ROLE when password_valid_until is set.
  • Fix memory leaks and a heap overflow.

Upgrade require a PostgreSQL restart to reload the credcheck library.

Complete list of changes and acknowledgements are available here

Links & Credits

credcheck is an open project under the PostgreSQL license maintained by HexaCluster. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/issues

About credcheck

The credcheck extension is developed and maintained by Gilles Darold at https://hexacluster.ai. If you need more information please https://hexacluster.ai/contact-us/.

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck#readme

title: Our validator checked files, not frames — the first external user taught us the difference
description:
auto-xhs is an open-source system that lets an AI agent (Muse, Dots, or Grok Bot) run a Xiaohongshu account end to end: research, writing, video production, posting, and replying to comments. It works through the browser like a person would — no unofficial APIs. I open-sourced it on Oct 14.

On the same day, a user in Vietnam, axiom3356, ran the pipeline as-is, measured the output videos, and filed issue #1: three reproducible visual flaws that our validator, validate.py, had not caught. Not one of them.

The three flaws:

  1. At a scene change, the picture goes almost blank for about 2 seconds. Cards in the new scene appear one by one, and before the first one lands, there is nothing on screen.
  2. The finished video came out at 585 kb/s. For 1080p that is far too low — edges smear. 2 Mb/s is the floor anyone recommends.
  3. Two annotation cards in the same area, entering with different delays, can overlap each other.

His root-cause note was the part that stung: the validator checked the file — duration, resolution, word counts, silence gaps — but never looked at a single frame.

What we changed, all of it credited to his report:

  • Blank frames are now a check. Every 0.5 seconds we grab a frame, shrink it to a small grayscale image, and ask whether it is nearly one flat color. Two seconds of that in a row raises a warning with the rough position. Only ffmpeg and the Python standard library.
  • Low bitrate is now a check. Below 2000 kb/s the validator warns. Our own weather example, rendered with the old settings, is 844 kb/s — it gets warned too, and that warning is correct.
  • The assembler got a bitrate floor: target 3M, cap 4M. A small trap here: we had -crf 21 and -b:v set together, and in that combination ffmpeg follows crf and the bitrate target is ignored. Dropping crf fixed it.
  • The overlapping cards are NOT a machine check, and I want to be plain about why. A frame is pixels. Pixels cannot tell a full-bleed background (fine) from a card cropped by the frame edge (broken). A check built on that would cry wolf every day. So instead the template rules now say: one delayed entrance per area, and cards sharing an area go into a layout container. Prevention, not detection.

Both new checks are warn-only. A warning respects the person running the pipeline; a hard error from a check that can misfire does not.

The issue is still open, on purpose. If axiom3356 sends a PR, his gets reviewed first and used first — he found the problems and proposed the checks.

If you run it and your videos look wrong in a way the validator misses, that is exactly the report I want. And if you have content that repeats daily — weather, a digest, a ranking — playbooks live in scenarios/ and new ones are welcome.

title: A Green Test Suite Can Still Hide a Broken PR: 5 Questions to Ask Before Merging
description:
AI coding assistants can write implementation code and tests in minutes. The problem is that both can look correct while the behavior that matters remains untested.

A passing test suite is useful evidence, but it isn't proof that a change is correct.

I've been thinking about this problem while building a Java-focused, AI-powered pull request reviewer. These are five questions I believe developers should ask before approving a PR, especially when AI helped write the code or its tests.

1. What behavior is this test actually verifying?

Start with the expected behavior, not the number of assertions.

Imagine a service that should reject a payment when the account has insufficient funds. A test might call the service and verify that it returns a response.

But what if the test never checks whether the payment was rejected?

The test can execute successfully without verifying the important business rule.

Ask yourself:

  • What behavior should this test protect?
  • What result would prove that behavior?
  • Would the test fail if the behavior were broken?

If you cannot answer these questions, the test may provide less confidence than its green status suggests.

2. Could this test pass without checking anything meaningful?

Consider this JUnit example:

java
@test
void shouldRejectInvalidPayment() {
paymentService.processPayment(invalidPayment);

assertTrue(true);

}

The test passes as long as execution reaches the assertion. It doesn't establish that the payment was rejected.

A more meaningful test would verify the expected outcome, using the appropriate assertion for the application's behavior.

For example, if the contract requires an exception:

java
@test
void shouldRejectInvalidPayment() {
assertThrows(
InvalidPaymentException.class,
() -> paymentService.processPayment(invalidPayment)
);
}

This is only an illustration. The correct assertion depends on the actual application contract.

The important principle is simple: an assertion should verify the behavior the test claims to protect.

3. Are mocks hiding the behavior we need to verify?

Mocks are valuable when testing dependencies, failure conditions, and isolated units of code. But excessive mocking can make a test appear meaningful while avoiding the behavior that matters.

Suppose a test claims to verify that an order is saved correctly, but it mocks the repository and only verifies that save() was called.

That may establish that a method was invoked. It doesn't necessarily establish that the order was persisted correctly or that the resulting state is correct.

Before approving a heavily mocked test, ask:

  • Is the test checking an outcome or just an interaction?
  • Is the mocked dependency the behavior being tested?
  • Would an incorrect implementation still satisfy the assertions?
  • Should an integration test verify the real interaction between components?

Don't remove mocks indiscriminately. Choose the test boundary that matches the behavior you're trying to protect.

4. Does the test cover the change described in the PR?

A PR can change behavior without changing the test that originally covered it.

For example, a developer might change the conditions under which a user can access a resource. The existing test may still verify the successful access path while failing to check the newly introduced restriction.

Compare the change with the tests:

  • Which behavior changed?
  • Which existing tests exercise that behavior?
  • What new failure scenario could the change introduce?
  • Are the expected outcomes explicit?

This is also where repository context matters. The affected behavior might involve callers or related files that aren't part of the diff.

A reviewer should consider those relationships rather than treating each changed line as an isolated unit.

5. Would the test catch a deliberately broken implementation?

This is a useful thought experiment.

Imagine the implementation contains a defect that violates the requirement. Would the test fail?

If the answer is no, the test may not protect that requirement.

Mutation testing takes this idea further by making deliberate changes to the implementation and checking whether the tests detect them. It can provide stronger evidence than simply counting assertions, although it has its own limitations and costs.

You don't need a full mutation-testing setup to start asking the question during code review. But actually running tests against controlled mutations is a separate validation step, not something a normal passing test run proves.

The practical takeaway

Before merging a PR, especially one produced with AI assistance, ask:

  1. Does the test verify the intended behavior?
  2. Could it pass without a meaningful assertion?
  3. Are mocks hiding the behavior that matters?
  4. Do the tests cover the changed behavior and relevant regression scenarios?
  5. Would the tests detect a broken implementation?

These checks won't guarantee that every defect is caught. They can, however, help identify tests that create confidence without providing enough evidence.

AI can help write code and tests faster. The review process still needs to establish what those tests actually prove.

Disclosure: I'm building CodeGuard AI, a self-hosted AI-powered pull request reviewer for GitHub. It reviews PR changes alongside repository context and supports custom team review rules. It does not currently run mutation testing or guarantee detection of every weak test assertion.

Learn more about CodeGuard AI

On coding tasks, Gemini 4 Argon builds features, fixes bugs, and researches unfamiliar codebases, carrying longer tasks through multiple steps. title: OpenAI Decisions API now available on AI Gateway
description:
OpenAI’s Decisions API is now available through AI Gateway at /v1/decisions. It uses the same request and response format as OpenAI, so existing OpenAI SDK integrations can switch by changing the base URL, credentials, and model ID.

Decision models answer typed questions about shared input and return structured answers rather than generated text. In one request, you can ask a model to:

  • Estimate the probability that a condition is true with a predicate question

  • Select from supplied options with a choice question

  • Rate the input against an ordered rubric with a score question

Use these answers for tasks such as classification, routing, triage, and rubric-based scoring.

The endpoint works with any decision model on AI Gateway, including Jev, Liquid d1, and Laya. Use openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions for OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions model. This is separate from openai/gpt-6-luna, which generates text.

With OpenAI SDK 7.30.0 or later for JavaScript or 3.26.0 or later for Python, point the client at AI Gateway and call decisions.create:

The response returns answers in question order, each with the corresponding question’s name.

See the OpenAI Decisions API documentation for Python and cURL examples. To use decision models with the AI SDK or /v1/evaluate, see the decision documentation.

title: Turn your REST APIs into MCP tools with Google Cloud API Gateway
description: Google Cloud API Gateway now acts as a native remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, eliminating the need to build and maintain custom middleware to expose REST APIs to AI agents. By simply adding specific annotations (like x-google-api-management.mcp) to existing OpenAPI 3.x specifications, developers can instantly convert standard REST operations into discoverable, agent-ready tools. title: EmbeddingGemma 2: The Developer Guide
description: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-source multimodal embedding model that maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space.
