title: Solid Glass Adds an AI UI Theme to shadcn/ui Projects
description:
Solid Glass is a public GitHub project that packages a glass-inspired design system for AI applications as a stylesheet intended to work with shadcn/ui. For developers building chat and agent interfaces, its practical proposition is narrow but useful: the stylesheet targets the data-slot attributes and classes that existing shadcn/ui components already carry, so adoption is presented as a theme integration rather than a component rewrite. Source: Solid Glass repository

A theme layer, not an AI framework

The project describes its visual treatment as sitting between flat design and “liquid glass”: surfaces retain outlines, borders, highlights and shadows, while avoiding the highly transparent treatment that can interfere with text legibility. Its stated design goals are tactility, precision, physicality and materiality; for interfaces with streaming responses, agent tasks and pending human decisions, it argues that neutral surfaces and reserved use of colour and motion help keep the UI calm and readable. Source: Solid Glass repository

The core distribution is one CSS file. The repository says it defines colours, three glass thicknesses, a state and motion, while also defining shadcn/ui’s variable names. It supports light and dark modes, although the project describes dark mode as the intended material treatment. Source: Solid Glass repository

Installation begins from a shadcn/ui project using React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and Base UI components. Developers add the deeplethe/solid-glass/solid-glass stylesheet through the shadcn CLI, import it after Tailwind and shadcn styles, and remove the :root and .dark colour variables created by shadcn initialization because Solid Glass defines variables with the same names. Source: Solid Glass repository

Components for agent-facing screens

Beyond the theme, the project supplies installable components including status-glyph, panel, tag, dot-loader, turn-status, composer, tool-steps, diff-view, ask-card, context-ring, task-notice and reasoning. The README positions these around an agent workflow: showing activity, accepting a prompt, rendering tool steps and diffs, asking for user input, and displaying context usage. Source: Solid Glass repository

The repository also includes complete screen-level “Blocks,” including an agent-workspace, plus a Create page that exposes controls for thickness, tint, chart colour, type, radius, rim and blur and produces corresponding CSS variable changes. Source: Solid Glass repository

The compatibility trade-off

Analysis: Solid Glass’s most consequential choice is to treat shadcn/ui as the compatibility surface rather than create another self-contained component ecosystem. That should reduce initial adoption cost for teams already on the shadcn stack, because the theme is designed around existing slots and classes. It also leaves an unresolved maintenance question: the approach depends on those structural conventions remaining stable enough for a stylesheet to keep selecting the intended parts. The repository notes that some displayed shadcn/ui components differ slightly from stock versions, while saying the stylesheet does not depend on those differences. Source: Solid Glass repository

This is therefore best read as a focused UI layer, not evidence of a broader agent runtime or application framework. Its value will depend less on the glass treatment itself than on whether its component conventions fit a team’s existing shadcn/ui codebase and the information density of its AI workflows. The repository is licensed under MIT and includes contribution, code-of-conduct and security-policy materials. Source: Solid Glass repository

title: Checkpoints for AI Code Changes: The Feature Nobody Talks About
description:
Everyone compares AI coding tools on model quality. Almost nobody compares them on recoverability — and that's the thing that actually saves your day.

The scenario

You ask an AI to "refactor the payment module." It touches 9 files. Six of them are fine. Three of them break something subtle that you won't notice until production.

With most tools, your options are:

  • Manually figure out which of the 9 changes was wrong
  • git stash and lose everything
  • Revert the whole thing and start over

What checkpoints change

A checkpoint is a snapshot of your code at a specific moment — usually right before each AI action. Instead of one big "before" and one big "after," you get a timeline:

[checkpoint] before refactor
  [checkpoint] after file 1-3
    [checkpoint] after file 4-6   <- the break is here
      [checkpoint] after file 7-9

Now when something breaks, you don't debug the whole change. You rewind to the last good checkpoint and go from there.

Why this matters more with AI

Human commits are usually coherent — you commit when something works. AI changes are exploratory. The agent is guessing, and guesses are wrong sometimes. Checkpoints turn "the AI broke my code" from a disaster into a two-click fix.

The mental shift

Once you have checkpoints, you stop being afraid of letting the AI try things. You can say "go ahead, attempt the refactor" without the usual dread, because you know you can always rewind.

That fearlessness is the real productivity gain — not the typing speed.

Arcwright builds checkpoints into every AI step on Windows, and it's free to start. Whatever tool you pick, look for this feature. It's the difference between an assistant you supervise and one you're scared of.

title: Optimizing Frontend Performance and SEO for Local Trade Services Web Apps
description:
When developers build websites for local service businesses—such as painters, contractors, or renovation experts—the requirements might seem simple at first glance: show the services, display a gallery, and provide a contact form.

However, from an engineering perspective, local service platforms are a demanding use case for modern frontend architecture. They face unique technical challenges:

Mobile-first users on poor connections: High bounce rates occur if heavy media asset bundles delay rendering on cellular networks.

Aggressive Core Web Vitals targets: Google’s local ranking algorithms heavily penalize slow LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) and high CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift).

Location-based entity resolution: Search engines need well-structured JSON-LD data to link physical service areas to digital routes.

In this article, we’ll look at how modern frontend patterns—from image optimization strategies to server-side rendering (SSR) and dynamic schema injection—can turn a local service site into a high-performance web asset.

1. Asset Optimization Strategy for High-Res Media

Local trade sites rely heavily on high-resolution "before & after" image galleries and project portfolios to establish trust. If unoptimized, these assets destroy performance metrics.

Technical Implementation:
Next-Gen Formats: Convert standard PNG/JPEG uploads to AVIF and WebP dynamically via build tools or image CDNs.

Responsive Source Sets: Serve tailored image dimensions based on viewport width using the tag or framework-level image components.

Explicit Dimensions: Always set width and height attributes to reserve layout space and eliminate Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) during image loading.

 <picture>
  <source srcset="renovated-interior-800.avif 800w, renovated-interior-1200.avif 1200w" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="renovated-interior-800.webp 800w, renovated-interior-1200.webp 1200w" type="image/webp">
  <img src="renovated-interior-800.jpg" width="800" height="600" alt="Professional painting and interior wall renovation in Stuttgart" loading="lazy">
</picture>

2. Geo-Localized Schema Markup & Entity Matching

Search engines parse local intent by matching physical service capabilities with structured microdata. For localized trade services (such as painting, plastering, or facade renovation), implementing the HousePainter or LocalBusiness schema via JSON-LD is essential.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "HousePainter",
  "name": "Malerexperten Stuttgart",
  "url": "https://malerexperten-stuttgart.de/",
  "areaServed": {
    "@type": "City",
    "name": "Stuttgart"
  },
  "knowsAbout": [
    "Malerarbeiten",
    "Fassadensanierung",
    "Innenanstrich",
    "Tapezierarbeiten"
  ]
}

By dynamically injecting structured data corresponding to specific routes, search crawlers can instantly identify geographic service boundaries without relying on unstructured text parsing alone.

3. Server-First Rendering for Instant Parsing

Single-Page Application (SPA) architectures built strictly on Client-Side Rendering (CSR) often introduce indexing latency. Search crawlers must execute client-side JavaScript before discovering local content and internal links.

For local service applications, adopting Server-Side Rendering (SSR) or Static Site Generation (SSG) ensures:

Time-to-First-Byte (TTFB) & Initial Render Speed: Pre-rendered HTML allows bots to crawl content on the initial request.

Low Interactivity Latency (INP): Minimizing client-side JS bundle execution keeps the main thread clear for quick user interactions (such as requesting a quote or tapping a phone link).

For regional trade and engineering platforms—such as specialized painting services like Malerexperten Stuttgart in Germany or Alfa Malerei in Austria—serving static or pre-rendered HTML guarantees both rapid indexation and optimal performance for local mobile visitors.

4. Route Architecture & Internal Link Graph

A clean URL and route hierarchy is critical for both user experience and search engine discovery.

Route Design Best Practices:
Avoid Hash Fragments & Query Strings: Avoid URLs like /services?type=painting&city=stuttgart.

Explicit Hierarchical Slugs: Use clear, semantic route structures such as /malerarbeiten-stuttgart/ or /leistungen/fassadensanierung/.

Internal Cross-Linking: Build an internal graph connecting related services (e.g., linking interior painting directly to plastering and wall prep) to pass topical authority throughout the application.

Conclusion

Building a web app for local trade services isn't just about static web design—it's a technical discipline. By applying modern frontend optimizations (AVIF/WebP assets, strict layout reservation, pre-rendered HTML, and JSON-LD entity markup), developers can build web applications that load instantly and achieve maximum visibility in local search ecosystems.

Key Resources
Google Web.dev – Core Web Vitals Optimization

Schema.org – HousePainter & LocalBusiness Specifications

Malerexperten Stuttgart – Professional Painting & Renovation Services

title: React: mide la UX de un inbox de prueba
description:
Cuando un formulario depende de un correo de verificación, solemos medir si el mensaje llegó. Eso es importante, pero no alcanza. La persona también necesita saber si el inbox está cargando, si ya se revisó, si el código expiró o si debe intentar otra vez. Un inbox de prueba puede recibir el mensaje correcto y aun así ofrecer una experiencia confusa.

En proyectos de frontend me funciona tratar esa pantalla como una parte del producto, no como una ventana tecnica que solo sirve para QA. Si la interfaz tiene estados explícitos, foco estable y una lectura clara en móvil, es mas sencillo detectar los problemas del flujo completo. Este enfoque sirve tanto para un correo desechable usado durante una demo como para una bandeja aislada de pruebas automatizadas.

La UX del inbox también se puede medir

Antes de escribir componentes, separo tres preguntas:

  1. ¿La persona sabe qué está esperando?
  2. ¿Puede distinguir un mensaje nuevo de uno viejo?
  3. ¿Tiene una acción segura cuando el correo no aparece?

Un layout con una animación bonita no responde por sí solo a ninguna de ellas. En cambio, un encabezado que dice “Buscando el correo de verificación”, una marca de tiempo y un botón “Comprobar de nuevo” crean un modelo mental bastante mas útil.

También conviene conectar la interfaz con el flujo que la rodea. Por ejemplo, una lista de direcciones de prueba puede seguir las mismas reglas de aislamiento que unas seed lists para onboarding. Cuando el inbox es parte de una prueba de registro, esa relación evita que el equipo culpe al frontend por un mensaje enviado a otra dirección.

Un modelo de estados pequeño en React

No usaría un booleano llamado loading para representar toda la pantalla. Como mínimo, el inbox necesita distinguir entre cargar, vacío, listo, error y expirado. Un tipo pequeño hace visibles esas decisiones:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: "loading" }
  | { kind: "empty"; checkedAt: number }
  | { kind: "ready"; subject: string; receivedAt: number }
  | { kind: "expired" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

function InboxStatus({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "loading":
      return <p role="status">Buscando el correo...</p>;
    case "empty":
      return <p role="status">Todavía no hay mensajes. Puedes comprobar de nuevo.</p>;
    case "ready":
      return <p role="status">Nuevo mensaje recibido: {state.subject}</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <p role="alert">Esta dirección ya no está disponible. Crea otra para continuar.</p>;
    case "error":
      return <p role="alert">No pudimos revisar el inbox: {state.message}</p>;
  }
}

La ventaja no es solo de tipado. El componente obliga a producto y QA a decidir qué se muestra en cada momento. Un mensaje vacío no debería parecer un fallo de red, y una dirección expirada no debería ofrecer un botón que seguirá haciendo polling para siempre. Si el sistema usa un servicio tipo tempail o tempail mail en una prueba manual, esa diferencia de estado ayuda a no confundir una bandeja vacía con una dirección que ya caducó.

Para mantener el foco, el cambio de estado debería actualizar una región de texto, no desmontar todo el formulario. El botón de volver a comprobar puede conservar su posición y su nombre. Eso hace el flujo mas predecible con teclado y tambien simplifica los tests de interacción.

CSS para que esperar no se sienta lento

El rendimiento percibido nace de detalles pequeños. Reservo un espacio para el mensaje y para la lista, incluso cuando todavía no hay datos. Así el contenido recibido no empuja el botón hacia abajo cuando llega.

.inbox-panel {
  min-height: 12rem;
  contain: layout paint;
}

.inbox-status {
  min-block-size: 3rem;
  display: grid;
  align-items: center;
}

.inbox-message {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 0 5rem;
}

No aplicaría content-visibility a un control que debe estar disponible de inmediato, pero puede ser practico en una lista larga de mensajes. Para una bandeja pequeña, lo mas importante es evitar saltos de layout y no mostrar un spinner que ocupa toda la pantalla por una consulta de pocos cientos de milisegundos.

Accesibilidad: anunciar lo necesario

role="status" es útil para cambios informativos como “mensaje recibido”. Reservaría role="alert" para errores que necesitan atención inmediata. Si todo se anuncia como alerta, la experiencia se vuelve ruidosa, sobre todo cuando el polling ocurre cada pocos segundos.

El texto visual no debe depender solo del color. Un estado expirado puede usar un icono, pero también necesita una frase y una acción. El foco visible del botón debe tener contraste suficiente y no desaparecer al usar un reset de estilos. En móvil, además, el área táctil y el orden de lectura importan mas que una tarjeta compacta.

Para los mensajes de incidentes o fallos intermitentes, puede ser útil enlazar la interfaz con runbooks cortos para incidentes de email. El usuario final no necesita ver el runbook, claro, pero el equipo que mantiene la pantalla sí necesita una ruta de diagnóstico coherente.

Qué medir en una prueba real

No hace falta instrumentar veinte eventos. Empezaría con cuatro:

  • tiempo desde “enviado” hasta “recibido”;
  • cantidad de comprobaciones antes de encontrar el mensaje;
  • porcentaje de sesiones que terminan en expiración o error;
  • activaciones de “comprobar de nuevo” después de que el mensaje ya llegó.

El último dato es curioso: si se activa mucho, quizá el mensaje recibido no destaca, la actualización no se anuncia o el usuario no confía en el estado mostrado. Una métrica de backend puede decir que todo está bien mientras la interfaz comunica lo contrario.

Checklist antes de publicar

  • Cada estado tiene texto visible y una acción razonable.
  • El inbox conserva la posición del botón al recibir datos.
  • El foco no salta durante el polling.
  • Los cambios informativos usan una región status y no una alerta global.
  • La lista funciona sin depender del color.
  • Hay una forma de distinguir mensaje nuevo, viejo y expirado.
  • Los errores dejan una siguiente acción clara.

Q&A

¿Necesito un inbox complejo para una prueba de signup?

No. Un panel con estado, asunto, hora de recepción y una acción de reintento suele ser suficiente. La complejidad debe aparecer solo cuando una necesidad concreta la justifique.

¿Conviene consultar cada segundo?

Generalmente no. Un intervalo moderado con un límite de tiempo y una acción manual suele ser mas amable con el navegador y con el servicio de correo. Cuando el mensaje llegue, detén el polling y registra el resultado.

¿Qué pasa si el correo de prueba expira?

Muéstralo como un estado propio, explica la consecuencia y permite crear una nueva dirección. Ocultar la expiración detrás de un “sin mensajes” deja a la persona adivinando por que la prueba no avanza.

On September 21st, 2026, we began maintenance updates of Apigee instances configured for maintenance windows.

If you set a preferred window for maintenance for your instance, and your instance version is below 1-18-0-apigee-4, your instance will be updated to 1-18-0-apigee-4 within the next seven to 21 days. Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Transfer ownership of shared agents

Administrators can transfer ownership of shared employee-made agents to another user or to themselves in the Google Cloud console. This is useful when reassigning agents created by departing employees or when temporary workers hand over agents to full-time staff.

Key characteristics and requirements include:

  • Administrator only: Only users with the Gemini Enterprise Admin role (roles/discoveryengine.agentspaceAdmin or roles/discoveryengine.admin) can transfer agent ownership. Agent owners cannot transfer ownership unless they are also administrators.
  • Shared agents only: Ownership transfer is supported only for agents that are already shared. Private agents cannot be transferred.
  • Single owner: Each agent has only one owner at a time. When ownership is transferred, the selected user becomes the sole owner, and the previous owner is retained as a permissioned user with the agentUser role.
  • Agents with schedules or triggers: If the transferred agent has a schedule trigger or event trigger, the transfer operation marks them as disabled schedules or events. The new owner must enable it before being able to use the agent.

title: 2026 Go Failure Alerts: Logs and Cron Notifications for Small SaaS
description:
Use exception groups as the primary deployment tripwire, add metrics only for rate, latency, and cost thresholds, and run a small poller that owns Slack or email delivery. For an e-commerce AI agent, that split gives rollback logic a narrow input surface and keeps notification code out of checkout.

TL;DR: start with errors, then add a few metrics that can change a release decision. Logs are evidence for investigation, not the easiest alert source. A separate healthcheck must watch the poller and scheduled agent runs, because a system that only reports failures cannot report a job that never started.

Rollback safety is the deciding constraint. Every alert should carry a release identifier, region, and workflow name. Keep the old version deployable until the observation window closes.

What should a small SaaS failure alert stack measure?

A checkout assistant can fail loudly, degrade gradually, or disappear. Those are different signals. A captured exception is the cleanest evidence of a crash. A metric is better for a rising failure ratio, a latency boundary, or an AI cost guardrail. A log line carries richer request context, but turning free-form text into a dependable threshold creates parsing and query maintenance at exactly the moment the team needs a boring rollback decision.

Use logs after the alert to reconstruct the request. Correlate them with trace_id and span_id where those fields exist, but do not mistake correlation fields for a distributed trace query or span tree. Source-map decoding, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, and session replay are separate capabilities. Choose a product that supplies them when the investigation requires them.

The silent case matters most. If the hourly catalog agent never runs, there may be no exception, log, or metric to query. Send a completion ping to an external dead-man switch such as Healthchecks.io. The alert poller itself needs the same treatment.

Use three operational contracts:

  1. A new exception group tied to the candidate release can stop rollout.
  2. Error ratio, latency, or cost crossing a predeclared limit can trigger rollback after enough samples exist.
  3. A missing heartbeat can page the owner, but should not automatically blame the latest release without corroboration.

The last distinction prevents a scheduler problem from causing a blind application rollback.

Put the rollback policy in code

The poller should query on a fixed cadence, convert provider responses into a small internal snapshot, evaluate one deterministic policy, and send a deduplicated notification. It records the last processed window so a retry does not deliver the same Slack alert twice. If delivery fails, retry with backoff and do not advance the checkpoint.

This runnable policy consumes an application-owned normalized snapshot; it makes no claim about a vendor response schema. It refuses incomplete data instead of quietly treating it as healthy.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    Release string `json:"release"`
    Region string `json:"region"`
    Requests int `json:"requests"`
    Errors int `json:"errors"`
    P95LatencyMS int `json:"p95_latency_ms"`
    CostUSD float64 `json:"cost_usd"`
    NewErrorGroups int `json:"new_error_groups"`
}

type Policy struct {
    MinRequests int
    MaxErrorRate float64
    MaxP95LatencyMS int
    MaxCostUSD float64
}

type Decision struct {
    Rollback bool `json:"rollback"`
    Reasons []string `json:"reasons"`
}

func evaluate(s Snapshot, p Policy) (Decision, error) {
    if s.Release == "" || s.Region == "" {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("release and region are required")
    }
    if s.Requests < 0 || s.Errors < 0 || s.Errors > s.Requests {
        return Decision{}, fmt.Errorf("invalid request counters")
    }
    d := Decision{}
    if s.NewErrorGroups > 0 {
        d.Rollback = true
        d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "new exception group")
    }
    if s.Requests >= p.MinRequests {
        rate := float64(s.Errors) / float64(s.Requests)
        if rate > p.MaxErrorRate {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "error-rate limit exceeded")
        }
        if s.P95LatencyMS > p.MaxP95LatencyMS {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "latency limit exceeded")
        }
        if s.CostUSD > p.MaxCostUSD {
            d.Rollback = true
            d.Reasons = append(d.Reasons, "cost limit exceeded")
        }
    }
    return d, nil
}

func fetchErrorGroups() ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            baseURL+"/v1/errors/groups", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("error groups: status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("error groups: rate limit retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    groups, err := fetchErrorGroups()
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "fetched error groups for normalization")
    _ = groups

    var s Snapshot
    if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&s); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    p := Policy{100, 0.02, 2500, 12}
    d, err := evaluate(s, p)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    if err := json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(d); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(2)
    }
}

Those numbers are illustrative policy values, not measurements or universal limits. Derive production limits from the checkout error budget and business guardrails. Keep the minimum sample condition: one failure in two requests says little, while a new crash signature may justify an immediate stop even at low volume.

Do not let the first poller iteration perform rollback directly. Write an immutable decision record and call a narrow deployment-control interface with a client-generated idempotency key covering release, region, window, and policy version. Replaying a window then repeats the same operation rather than creating a second rollback or page.

Choose the stack by the missing capability

Product names hide different operating models. Compare the path from signal to page and from page to rollback.

Option Best fit Operational trade-off
Sentry Exception-first triage where grouped errors drive response Add metrics and heartbeat monitoring when rollback also depends on latency, spend, or missing runs
Datadog Managed logs, metrics, traces, monitors, and notification integrations Control monitor scope, cardinality, and release tags or broad coverage produces ambiguous pages
Grafana Cloud Teams centered on Prometheus-style metrics and Grafana investigation Error grouping and application context require deliberate instrumentation or another error product
Amazon CloudWatch AWS-centered logs, metrics, alarms, and regional operations Log ingestion and query choices affect cost, so review pricing before logs become the alert substrate
Infrai One REST API and one key cover the integration; the API is self-describing, public discovery needs no key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples No native notifier, routing, escalation, synthetic check, or heartbeat monitor; the poller and dead-man switch are mandatory

Healthchecks.io complements these options by answering whether scheduled work checked in. PagerDuty can own routing and escalation when one Slack channel is no longer enough, but it does not improve the rollback signal.

For a small service, start with Sentry plus one metric backend if exception diagnostics are the daily need. Choose Datadog for managed cross-signal correlation, Grafana Cloud when Prometheus-compatible metrics are central, and CloudWatch when AWS-native operation matters more than a vendor-neutral query layer. The compact REST option fits when minimizing integration surface matters, provided owning the poller is an explicit on-call responsibility.

No winner covers every failure class. Pick the missing capability you cannot safely build.

Verify before allowing automatic rollback

Test with a canary release. Emit a known test exception tagged to the canary, feed a synthetic normalized snapshot to the policy, and verify that exactly one decision record and notification appear. Replay the window. Nothing new should be delivered.

Then provide a healthy snapshot above the minimum request count and confirm rollout continues. Provide too few requests and confirm the thresholds remain inconclusive rather than green. Stop the poller in a test environment and wait for the external heartbeat monitor to report the missing check-in. This verifies the detector's detector.

US and EU paths need separate region labels and checkpoints. Evaluate them independently so a healthy high-volume region cannot dilute a failing low-volume region. Send identifiers and decision reasons to Slack, not customer prompts, order details, or full log bodies.

A practical sequence is manual notification, manual rollback from a recorded decision, then automatic rollback for a small canary. Expand only after duplicate-delivery and stale-window tests pass.

Rollback runbook

When the gate fires, freeze promotion and preserve the candidate release identifier. Identify a new exception group, a threshold breach with enough samples, or a missing heartbeat. Confirm region and window freshness.

Rollback to the last known deployable version through the idempotent deployment-control operation. Keep collecting candidate and baseline signals during recovery; failure to restore the signal points toward a dependency, scheduler, or policy problem. Record the policy version, triggering window, reasons, and deployment result for the postmortem.

If notification fails, retry with exponential backoff and leave the checkpoint unchanged. If the query fails, report detector failure through its heartbeat path and make no health claim.

Unknown is not healthy.

References

  • Sentry Alerts: https://docs.sentry.io/product/alerts/
  • Datadog Monitors: https://docs.datadoghq.com/monitors/

title: Push images to Vercel Container Registry from GitHub Actions
description:
You can now push container images from GitHub Actions to Vercel Container Registry (VCR) without storing long-lived registry credentials.

The new vercel/vcr-action/login action authenticates your workflow using GitHub OIDC. It exchanges the workflow’s OIDC token for a short-lived Vercel access token, then uses that token to log in to vcr.vercel.com. When the job ends, the action logs out and revokes the Vercel token.

To start:

  • Create an OIDC policy on your Vercel team that matches the GitHub repository and workflow, and grants read-write access to VCR.

  • Store your Vercel team ID as a GitHub repo variable, for example VERCEL_TEAM_ID, along with the team slug, project slug, and repo name used in the image tag.

  • Give the workflow or job id-token: write permission.

Then add the login step before you build and push and the image:

The action authenticates Docker by default. Pass engines to use Podman or Buildah instead.

After VCR finishes preparing a linux/amd64 image, you can use it as a custom Vercel Sandbox image. Within the same project, reference it as <repository>:<tag>.

Learn more in the VCR documentation and the GitHub Actions guide.

Read more

title: Introducing Support for Local AI Models in the Antigravity SDK
description: The Google Antigravity SDK now empowers developers to execute offline, agentic workflows locally using models like Gemma 4 26B A4B via LiteRT. This update facilitates powerful hybrid orchestration architectures, allowing a cloud model to act as a lightweight planner while local models securely handle token-intensive tasks—like code auditing and patching—directly on-device. Furthermore, the SDK provides drop-in support for OpenAI-compatible inference servers like Ollama and vLLM, enabling the seamless creation of privacy-first, autonomous local utilities.

title: Best Asset Management Software: How Technology Helps Organizations Manage Their Equipment
description:
1. Popular Asset Management Software Solutions

Different software products are designed for different types of organizations. Here are several well-known options.

IBM Maximo Application Suite
IBM Maximo Application Suite is an Enterprise Asset Management (EAM) platform designed to help organizations manage complex equipment and infrastructure.

It is commonly suited to large organizations in industries such as utilities, transportation, manufacturing, and energy.

Its capabilities include asset tracking, maintenance planning, work orders, and integration with other business systems. Depending on the implementation, AI and equipment-condition information can also support maintenance decisions.

For example, an electricity provider could use Maximo to manage equipment at substations, schedule inspections, and maintain repair records.

SAP Enterprise Asset Management
SAP EAM helps organizations manage equipment and maintenance activities within the SAP business software environment.

It is particularly useful for companies that already use SAP for areas such as purchasing, finance, and business operations.

Connecting asset management with these systems can help employees coordinate maintenance work, spare-parts purchases, and costs.

For example, when a factory needs a replacement component, connected systems can help the maintenance team coordinate with purchasing and inventory departments.

IFS Cloud EAM
IFS Cloud EAM combines asset management with maintenance and field-service capabilities.

It can be useful for organizations that operate equipment across many locations and need to coordinate technicians, maintenance activities, and long-term asset planning.

For example, an energy company could use it to organize field technicians who inspect and repair equipment spread across a large geographic area.

Hexagon EAM, now Octave Attune EAM
This software focuses on managing assets and maintenance, particularly in industries such as manufacturing, utilities, and public infrastructure.

Location-based information can help organizations manage assets spread across large areas.

For example, a water utility could use asset records and mapping information to manage pumps, pipelines, and treatment equipment.

eMaint by Fluke
eMaint is a maintenance-management solution that helps organizations schedule repairs, manage work orders, and track equipment condition.

It can be useful for businesses that want to move from spreadsheets or paper records to a more organized maintenance system.

For example, a manufacturing team could record equipment inspections and use condition measurements to help decide when maintenance is needed.

MaintainX
MaintainX focuses on making maintenance work easier for frontline employees using mobile devices.

Technicians can use it to view work orders, follow maintenance instructions, complete checklists, and record repair information.

For example, a technician working on a machine can update the repair status directly from a phone or tablet.

Accruent
Accruent offers software for managing facilities, buildings, and related assets.

It can be useful for organizations that manage many properties, such as hospitals, universities, retail chains, and office buildings.

For example, a company with offices in several cities could use facilities-management software to organize maintenance tasks and track building-related information.

Asset Panda
Asset Panda focuses on tracking physical assets, including computers, tools, equipment, and other valuable items.

Features such as barcode scanning and mobile access can help organizations record where assets are located and who is using them.

For example, an IT department could track laptops assigned to employees and record when equipment is returned or replaced.

Fiix
Fiix is a cloud-based computerized maintenance management system designed to help organizations organize maintenance activities.

It supports tasks such as work-order management, preventive maintenance, and tracking equipment-related information. Its capabilities can help maintenance teams prioritize work and coordinate with production operations.

For example, a factory could schedule maintenance for a production line to reduce the chance of unexpected downtime.

2. How Should a Company Choose the Right Software?

Choosing asset management software is an important decision. A company should consider its size, industry, budget, equipment, existing systems, and technical resources.

Business Requirements
The organization should first identify the problems it wants to solve.

Does it mainly need to track laptops and tools? Does it need to manage thousands of industrial machines? Does it need to coordinate maintenance across multiple locations?

Understanding the problem helps narrow down the options.

Integration with Other Systems
Organizations often use different software for finance, purchasing, inventory, human resources, and maintenance.

Data integration allows these systems to exchange information.

For example, when a technician requests a spare part, the maintenance system may need information from the inventory system to determine whether the part is available.

Good integration reduces duplicate data entry and helps employees make decisions using consistent information.

Ease of Use
Software should be practical for the people who use it every day.

If technicians find the system difficult to use, they may avoid updating records. This can lead to missing information and inaccurate reports.

Mobile access, simple screens, and clear workflows can help employees record information while performing their work.

Implementation Time and Cost
Enterprise software may require planning, configuration, data migration, integration, testing, and employee training.

The total cost includes more than the software subscription or license. Organizations may also need to pay for implementation, customization, support, and ongoing maintenance.

Companies should ask vendors for realistic estimates based on their actual requirements.

Security and Reliability
Asset management systems may contain important operational and business information. Organizations should evaluate access controls, data protection, backup procedures, system availability, and compliance requirements.

They should also ensure that changes to the system are properly tested and approved before being released into production.

3. Why Is Data Quality So Important?

Even the best software cannot provide reliable answers if the information entered into it is incorrect or incomplete.

Imagine that a maintenance system says a spare motor is available in the warehouse, but the motor has already been used. A technician may waste time looking for equipment that is not there.

Similarly, if employees complete repairs but fail to update the work orders, managers may not have an accurate picture of equipment condition.

Organizations need clear procedures for recording inspections, reporting failures, updating inventory, and closing work orders.

Accurate information helps software produce useful reports and supports better decisions.

Final Thoughts

Asset management software helps organizations take care of the equipment and infrastructure they depend on every day.

EAM provides a broad view of assets throughout their useful life, CMMS focuses on maintenance activities, and asset tracking helps organizations locate and monitor equipment.

Solutions such as IBM Maximo Application Suite, SAP EAM, IFS Cloud EAM, and other maintenance and tracking platforms offer different capabilities for different needs.

The best choice depends on what an organization needs to manage, how its existing systems work, and how much time and money it can invest.

As AI, cloud computing, mobile technology, and data integration continue to develop, asset management is becoming more data-driven. These technologies can help organizations identify problems earlier, plan maintenance more effectively, reduce unnecessary costs, and keep important equipment working reliably.

title: October 08, 2026
description:
Cloud SQL for MySQL

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini

Other

Bug fixes in VS Code

Various bug fixes and minor product enhancements.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in Singapore

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in Singapore (sg) with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise Standard and Plus Editions and Gemini Notebook Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • In-console Terms of Service consent flow: Administrators can opt in to Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 directly in Gemini Enterprise > Settings > AI developer tools > Antigravity authorized models in the Google Cloud console without a separate Anthropic account or onboarding. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.
  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.
  • Consumption billing: Third-party model usage is billed as consumption on your Cloud Billing account and counts toward your project's spend cap, which covers all models. Overages must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure overages and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, October 12, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent. To use Advanced Analytics, you must also enable whichever Conversational Analytics toggle corresponds to the content that you are querying (Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents). If both the Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents toggles are turned off, then Advanced Analytics cannot be enabled. If either Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents is enabled, Advanced Analytics can be enabled, but it is turned off by default.

The Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents settings inherit the enablement state of the Conversational Analytics setting in previous versions of Looker.

Conversational Analytics preview features can still be enabled selectively under the Enable Trusted Tester Features setting.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

Conversational Analytics data agents for both user-defined dashboards and LookML dashboards are now generally available.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

You can now apply themes to Looks in addition to internal dashboards.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where duplicating a scheduled plan could fail to retain the custom message value. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table visualizations now proportionally scale left-pinned columns during automatic sizing, which prevents unnecessary horizontal scrollbars. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where enabling subtotals on table visualizations did not automatically disable the Cell Visualizations option. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where previews for Looker charts in Slack integrations could fail to be displayed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where editing and saving a dashboard could cause the dashboard to reload indefinitely, forcing users to refresh the page. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table cell visualizations that included both positive and negative values could display unwanted scrollbars and hide value labels. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the BigQuery JDBC driver could fail to properly parse certain data types, such as BYTES, STRUCT/RECORD, and nested ARRAY structures. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where linked filters on a dashboard could fail to display autocomplete suggestions even when a parent filter is selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to ensure that phase timings (such as connection acquisitions, execution runtimes, and optimistic pivot fallback retry loops) are successfully captured for queries that fail or time out. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity Dashboard Diagnostics dashboard has been updated to fully support statistics, tile run counts, and performance recommendations for LookML dashboards. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the color palette popover in visualization settings failed to dynamically reposition when it expanded, causing controls to overlap or truncate. This feature now performs as expected.

Breaking

When you set up a connection, self-service modeling will now be available only if a role that grants create_self_service_from_table also selects it through that role's model set.

Fixed

The opacity for the comparison bar in short KPI visualizations has been reduced to increase legibility.

Memorystore for Redis

Feature

To help protect your data and provide a baseline level of persistence, RDB snapshots are enabled by default when you create an instance using the Google Cloud console. This feature is generally available.

VPC Service Controls

Feature

General availability support for the following integration:

  • Cloud Storage for Firebase

Feature

VPC Service Controls feature (Status: Preview): Support for automated remediation suggestions is available in the VPC Service Controls violation analyzer.

Remediation suggestions analyze access denial events and generate actionable, narrowly scoped configuration changes to resolve perimeter denials and adhere to the principle of least privilege. The remediation engine can automatically propose ingress rules, egress rules, VPC accessible services updates, and existing or new context-aware access levels.

For more information, see Resolve access denials with remediation suggestions.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.14.9

On October 7, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.14.9.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.14.9.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Fixed

Fixed in this release

Bug ID Description
565072374 Fixed an issue where VerifyJWT policies using a JWKS uriRef could return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the 5-minute JWKS cache TTL expired when the identity provider rotated keys. The cache now refreshes synchronously upon expiration.
564969400 Fixed an issue where variables initialized from an empty <Value/> element in AssignMessage (AssignVariable) were not treated as empty strings when referenced in message template functions such as replaceAll.
558888960 Fixed an issue in distributed tracing where the target URL was omitted from outbound target request span attributes after a request-flow policy step executed.
554114419 Apigee hybrid now allows policies to modify HTTP/2 request pseudo-headers (:path and :authority) when communicating over HTTP/2.
548763108 Hardened Message Processor outbound HTTP validation to block requests to internal Kubernetes cluster hostnames (*.svc.cluster.local).
513032450 Fixed an issue where apigee-connect-agent control-plane connections could hang for up to 2 hours when silently dropped by a network intermediary by restoring a 15-second TCP keep-alive.

title: Building GoRoute: An Ultra-Lightweight (<15MB RAM) LLM Gateway in Go
description:
Most developers using terminal coding agents like Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, or Cursor end up running an LLM router in the background to handle rate limits, multiple accounts, and model failovers.

Popular tools like OmniRoute and LiteLLM work, but running a full Node.js or Python runtime 24/7 just to proxy HTTP requests consumes 150MB to 300MB of RAM and introduces cold-start latency.

I wanted something that idles at < 6MB RAM, starts instantly, and never panics. So I built GoRoute.

What is GoRoute?

GoRoute is a zero-dependency, compiled LLM gateway and multi-agent router written in Go.

It acts as a local reverse proxy (http://127.0.0.1:8128) sitting between your developer agents and AI providers.

+-------------+       +-------------------+       +-----------------------+
| Claude Code | ----> |                   | ----> | Google Antigravity    |
| OpenCode    | ----> | GoRoute (Go Proxy)| ----> | OpenAI / Anthropic    |
| Codex/Cursor| ----> |   (<15MB RAM)     | ----> | Custom Endpoints      |
+-------------+       +-------------------+       +-----------------------+

Key Capabilities

  1. Sub-15MB Memory Footprint: Compiles to a single 16MB binary with zero external dependencies. Idles under 6MB RAM.
  2. Automatic 429 Failover & Round-Robin: Automatically rotates accounts and instantly fails over across keys if rate limits are hit.
  3. Dual Protocol Translation: Speak OpenAI (/v1/chat/completions) or Anthropic Messages API (/v1/messages) seamlessly.
  4. 1-Click Agent Setup: Automatically configures Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex, Cursor, Aider, and Cline with a single command: 
   goroute setup all
  1. Seamless OmniRoute Migration: If you already have OmniRoute configured, import your existing credentials and routes in 1 second: 
   goroute import-omniroute

Installation & Quick Start

You can install GoRoute directly via curl:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ziuus/goroute/main/install.sh | bash

Or run via npm:

npx goroute setup all

Once installed, check status:

goroute status

Check out the GitHub repo here: https://github.com/ziuus/goroute

I'd love to hear your feedback, feature requests, or questions!

title: Go Realtime Channel Semantics for Logistics State You Actually Store
description:
A realtime channel should carry a current logistics device event to authorized dashboard clients; it should not be treated as the system that remembers that event. The operational rule is blunt: commit durable device state to a database or log, publish a small notification that identifies the new state, and make every reconnect read from the durable source before resuming the live stream. Scope each connection token to the tenant, facility, and permitted topic, because a browser holding a token is an untrusted client even when the person using it is trusted.

TL;DR: the channel is a delivery path with connection state, not a database. It may retain bytes briefly in network buffers, and an implementation may offer replay, but neither property proves durable storage, complete history, or recovery after a retention boundary. Set separate SLOs for durable ingestion and dashboard freshness, then test the gap between them.

What does a realtime channel remember?

Usually, much less than the application needs.

A channel is a logical route over a transport: subscribers express interest, publishers send messages, and an intermediary or peer connection moves those messages while the relevant session exists. WebSocket standardizes a two-way connection over a single TCP connection. Server-Sent Events provides a one-way browser event stream over HTTP. WebRTC defines peer connections and data channels, with signaling left to the application. Those mechanisms differ, but none turns a shipment-status message into a durable business record by itself.

It helps to separate four kinds of state that are often collapsed into the word "realtime." Transport state includes sockets, sequence numbers, retransmission buffers, and heartbeats. Membership state answers which clients are presently attached. Delivery state may include a cursor, acknowledgement, or bounded replay window. Business state answers where device unit-4821 last reported, when it reported, and whether that observation supersedes an earlier one. Only the last category belongs in the authoritative store. Put another way, what a channel actually retains is an implementation detail with a boundary; what the logistics operation must remember is an application requirement.

This distinction matters for a fleet dashboard. Suppose a tracker reports in_transit at sequence 8142, the dashboard disconnects in an elevator, and sequences 8143 through 8151 arrive while it is away. A green socket indicator after reconnect says nothing about those nine observations. Unless the client supplies a cursor and the server can replay from durable history, the screen may look live while showing stale state.

Still stale.

No outage is required. A tab can sleep. A mobile network can change. A proxy can close an idle connection. Capacity can be exhausted while the database remains healthy. Designing on the assumption that every connected client observes every event confuses a favorable moment with a contract.

Store first, signal second

The safe write path gives persistence authority to one component and notification duty to another. Validate the device observation, enforce tenant ownership, write it with an idempotency key or monotonic device sequence, then publish an event containing the durable record identifier and enough routing metadata for subscribers to decide whether to refresh. If publication fails after commit, an outbox worker can retry. If publication happens before commit, a fast subscriber can request a record that does not exist yet.

That ordering is not decorative architecture. It defines recovery.

The following Go sketch keeps the contract small. The interfaces are generic on purpose; the database and broker can change without changing what a channel means.

package status

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Observation struct {
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    DeviceID string
    Sequence uint64
    State    string
    SeenAt   time.Time
}

type Event struct {
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    DeviceID string
    Sequence uint64
}

type Store interface {
    CommitWithOutbox(context.Context, Observation, Event) error
    Snapshot(context.Context, string, string, uint64) ([]Observation, error)
}

func Ingest(ctx context.Context, store Store, o Observation) error {
    if o.TenantID == "" || o.SiteID == "" || o.DeviceID == "" {
        return errors.New("missing routing identity")
    }
    if o.Sequence == 0 || o.SeenAt.IsZero() {
        return errors.New("missing ordering data")
    }

    e := Event{
        TenantID: o.TenantID,
        SiteID:   o.SiteID,
        DeviceID: o.DeviceID,
        Sequence: o.Sequence,
    }
    return store.CommitWithOutbox(ctx, o, e)
}

CommitWithOutbox represents one atomic database transaction, not a promise that two unrelated systems can be committed atomically. A relay reads committed outbox rows and publishes them; consumers tolerate duplicates by comparing the per-device sequence. The event is a prompt to fetch or apply a known version. The stored observation remains the recovery source.

The capacity plan must price both paths. For 40,000 connected devices reporting once every 30 seconds, the average ingest rate is about 1,333 observations per second before retries or bursts. If 2,000 dashboard sessions each watch 100 devices, indiscriminate broadcast creates a very different fan-out load from site-scoped delivery. Average rate is inadequate for sizing; test reconnect bursts, shift changes, and buffered device uploads, then define overload behavior before production traffic defines it for you.

Treat every dashboard as an untrusted subscriber

Authentication answers who received a token. Authorization must still constrain what that token can do. A useful channel grant binds at least the tenant, site or fleet partition, allowed operation, intended service, and a short expiry. The server derives subscription permissions from verified claims; it does not accept a tenant ID from the browser and assume the browser chose honestly.

JWT is a token format, not an authorization policy. RFC 8725 calls for validating the algorithm, issuer, and audience and for using explicit typing where confusion between kinds of JWT could occur. OAuth security guidance also warns against bearer-token exposure. A copied bearer token can be used by whoever possesses it until it expires or another control rejects it, so avoid putting it in a URL, log line, analytics payload, or reconnect diagnostic.

Here is a deliberately narrow verifier shape. The cryptographic verifier is injected because key selection, algorithm restrictions, issuer validation, and audience validation belong in a reviewed library-backed boundary, not in handwritten parsing code.

package authz

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Claims struct {
    Subject  string
    TenantID string
    SiteID   string
    Audience string
    CanRead  bool
    Expires  time.Time
}

type Verifier interface {
    Verify(context.Context, string) (Claims, error)
}

func AuthorizeSubscription(ctx context.Context, v Verifier, raw, tenant, site string, now time.Time) error {
    claims, err := v.Verify(ctx, raw)
    if err != nil {
        return errors.New("invalid channel token")
    }
    if claims.Audience != "status-stream" || !claims.CanRead || !now.Before(claims.Expires) {
        return errors.New("token cannot read status stream")
    }
    if claims.TenantID != tenant || claims.SiteID != site {
        return errors.New("subscription is outside token scope")
    }
    return nil
}

Do not send the durable history in the token. Do not let a wildcard subscription become the convenient default either. Wildcards multiply both the confidentiality impact of a mistake and the fan-out cost of a connection. For an operations screen spanning several sites, mint an explicit grant for that view or authorize a server-side group whose membership is controlled outside the client.

Reconnect from facts, not hope

The reconnect sequence is where the architecture admits what the channel does not store. First, the client requests a snapshot or changes after its last durable cursor. Next, it subscribes to the scoped live route. Finally, it reconciles any overlap by record ID and sequence. A server can reverse the first two steps internally, or establish the subscription before serving the snapshot, to close the race; the invariant is that the client has a cursor-backed bridge between history and live delivery.

A timestamp alone is a weak cursor when device clocks drift or multiple observations share the same timestamp. Prefer a server-assigned monotonic position for the log, while retaining the device sequence for per-device ordering and duplicate detection. Late observations still need a declared rule: event time may describe when the device measured something, but commit position describes when the platform accepted it.

Measure two SLOs separately. The ingest SLO covers accepted observations becoming durable. The freshness SLO covers an authorized dashboard reflecting the latest durable state within a target delay. A transport uptime metric cannot substitute for either one; a connection may be open while the consumer is stalled, unauthorized for the intended partition, or caught up to an incomplete source.

Useful alerts follow those boundaries: outbox age, publish retry rate, subscriber lag by partition, authorization denials, active connection count, and snapshot latency. Avoid tenant IDs and tokens as metric labels. High-cardinality identifiers can overwhelm a telemetry backend, while secrets in labels and logs create a separate incident.

Limitations and trade-offs across the layers

The decision is not "managed realtime or self-hosted realtime" as a single unit. Split it into transport, durable log, authorization, and state storage, because their failure domains and lock-in costs differ. The main limitation of a transient channel is intentional: it is not suitable as the sole record for audit, recovery, or delayed consumers. A durable log can cover those needs, but its trade-off is storage, retention governance, and more complex cursor management. Polling is sometimes the better choice for a small dashboard with loose freshness requirements because it removes persistent-connection operations, although it spends request capacity and detects changes later. These boundaries are how the term is best explained; no transport choice erases them.

Layer Managed service favors Self-hosted favors Exit question
Connection fan-out Lower routine on-call work and faster global rollout Protocol control and placement control Can clients move without changing event semantics?
Durable history Operational support for retention and replication Custom retention, locality, and tuning Can records and cursors be exported with ordering intact?
Token issuance Integration with an existing identity control plane Custom policy and isolated environments Are scopes standard claims or provider-specific rules?
State projection Rapid setup for common query patterns Exact schema, indexing, and reconciliation logic Can the authoritative record be rebuilt independently?

I would reject any design review that answers only with connection count. The capacity envelope needs publish rate, peak fan-out, message size, reconnect rate, replay depth, authorization checks per second, and the maximum tolerable lag. On-call load belongs in the same review: a self-hosted broker that saves a line item but requires expertise the team cannot staff is not cheaper in the engineering sense, while a managed layer whose proprietary cursor infects every client raises the eventual migration cost.

The practical middle ground is common: keep the domain record and cursor contract under application control, then choose operational ownership per layer. This preserves an honest recovery path without pretending infrastructure is interchangeable.

Verify failure and keep rollback boring

Test the contract by breaking the channel while leaving ingestion active. Record the last visible cursor, deliver at least three newer device observations, reconnect, and verify that the dashboard converges to the durable state without missing or double-applying an update. Repeat with duplicated messages, reversed device timestamps, an expired token, a valid token for the wrong site, and a reconnect wave large enough to exercise admission control.

The release gate should include a measurable recovery objective: after a channel interruption, a client with a valid scoped token reaches the latest committed cursor within the dashboard freshness SLO. Verify that an unauthorized site never appears in frames, snapshots, logs, or error details. Security correctness is a data-path property, not a successful login screenshot.

Roll back the live delivery component without rolling back the durable schema or accepting writes into an older incompatible format. During rollback, dashboards can poll the authoritative snapshot endpoint at a controlled interval, with jitter and request limits, while ingestion and outbox accumulation continue. Once live delivery returns, clients perform the same cursor reconciliation used for any reconnect. This is why the fallback is designed before the incident: it shares the source of truth instead of inventing a second one under pressure.

The final decision rule remains small. Persist the observation, authorize the route, and treat the channel as an accelerator. If losing a connection can erase the only copy of device state, the system has assigned storage responsibility to the wrong layer.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7519
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8725
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700

title: Why parsing real estate contracts with LLMs is ten times harder than tutorials claim
description:
When we started building the data pipeline for NovAsia (a property catalog and market tool for Southeast Asia), the plan looked embarrassingly simple on paper:

Grab property PDFs and developer contracts (SPAs).

Run them through a modern vision LLM.

Dump structured JSON into PostgreSQL.

Call it a day.

Two weeks in, the pipeline was completely broken. Here is why standard tutorial advice fell apart in production, and what we had to change to get reliable data out of scanned documents.

The stuff tutorials don't warn you about
Most LLM document parsing demos use crisp, born-digital PDFs with clean typography. In emerging markets like Cambodia and Thailand, reality looks very different:

Phone scans: Half the documents are multi-generation scans or photos taken with a phone camera under uneven lighting.

Dual-language layout: Khmer or Thai text mixed with English, often in adjacent table columns where line baselines don't match.

Physical stamps: Red rubber stamps, signatures, and notary seals placed directly over critical numbers (payment milestone dates, sinking fund fees, transfer taxes).

The 40-page prompt trap: If you shove a 35-page PDF into a long-context model and ask for "all fees and payment dates", it will extract 80% correctly and quietly hallucinate the rest with total confidence.

Three practical changes that fixed it
Instead of trying to find one magic model that does everything, we broke the pipeline down into smaller, boring steps:

  1. Aggressive image cleanup before text extraction

Before any model sees the page, we run basic OpenCV passes: deskewing, binarization, and contrast normalization. Removing phone-scan shadows did more for extraction accuracy than upgrading to a larger model tier.

  1. Section-level chunking with rigid schema validation

We stopped asking the model to parse whole documents at once. We chunk by specific section (e.g., "Schedule of Payments", "Maintenance Obligations") and enforce strict Pydantic schemas. If a field fails validation or falls outside expected bounds, the pipeline flags it for manual check rather than guessing.

  1. Treating tables and narrative text as separate problems

Vision models are great at answering qualitative questions ("under what conditions is the deposit refundable?"), but notoriously sloppy with columns in financial tables. We split table extraction into dedicated passes with explicit row-by-row checks.

The takeaway
If you're building with LLMs on messy, physical-world paperwork, raw context window size won't save you. Most of the reliability comes from image hygiene and strict schema boundaries.

Happy to trade notes if anyone else here is wrestling with noisy scans and table extraction.

Fixed
