432315283 Fixed a multi-certificate truststore so that its trust anchors take effect without a Message Processor restart when features.truststore.multi_cert_bundle.enabled is toggled at runtime; the outbound SSL context is now rebuilt automatically on any trust-anchor change.
565072374 VerifyJWT policies that use a JWKS uriRef no longer return steps.jwt.NoMatchingPublicKey on the first request after the JWKS cache TTL expires when the identity provider has rotated to a new key ID. The cache now re-fetches synchronously when its entry expires.
535395491 Extension Processor (ext_proc) denials now return the status and body that the policy or FaultRule produced, instead of always returning HTTP 500.
558421499 Apigee runtime runs on JRE 21.
517953321 The lookupcache.<n>.isEncrypted and responsecache.<n>.isEncrypted flow variables now report the per-entry on-disk encryption state of the L2 cache, rather than approximating whether the cache-encryption key is loaded. L1 cache hits report false. Review any policy conditions that rely on these flow variables.
563557547 Fixed EventFlow (Server-Sent Events) coalescing multiple events into a single policy invocation under burst load on the http-adaptor data path, which produced malformed SSE output to the client.
562740573 Apigee Analytics now populates the processing_mode dimension, distinguishing proxy traffic from extension-processor traffic. This dimension is not populated in billing-only analytics mode.
357042873 Stopped redirecting apigee-cassandra-schema-readiness init container logs to /dev/null, improving troubleshooting. Workloads undergo a rolling restart upon upgrade.
N/A Updates to infrastructure and libraries.

BigQuery

Feature

The Rust SDK for BigQuery is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The Data Engineering Agent now supports the gemini-3.7-flash model for the us, eu, and global multi-regional endpoints.

Cloud NAT

Feature

General Availability: Cloud NAT gateways for Private NAT support IPv6 to IPv4 network address translation. For more information, see NAT64 in Private NAT.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.105.0 is available. This release adds support for Slurm on Cloud TPU 7x and optional support for managed instance groups (MIGs) on static compute nodes that use A4X machine types.

This release also adds storage profiles and volume attributes for Cloud Storage FUSE in job submissions, and unifies Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) blueprints for GPU and Cloud TPU workloads to support dynamic consumption options.

Additionally, this release adds the repository_name variable to override repository names and fixes the output for the registry URL in the Artifact Registry module.

This update also introduces the pre-existing-project community module and resolves an HTTP 400 error when Slurm checks the deletion status of virtual machines (VMs).

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Federated query mode for Data Cloud connectors and Knowledge Catalog integration (Preview)

Federated query mode is available in Preview for the following connectors:

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
  • BigQuery
  • Cloud SQL
  • Spanner

Federated query mode allows Gemini Enterprise to query your operational and analytical data in place using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and each user's own credentials, without copying or ingesting data into a data store.

In addition, the Knowledge Catalog integration is available in Preview. When you attach a Data Cloud connector in federated query mode, Knowledge Catalog is automatically enabled on the Assistant tab of your app to give the assistant read-only tools to search for data that the user has access to and retrieve technical and business context.

For more information, see the following resources:

  • Connect to Data Cloud
  • Best practices for Data Cloud connectors
  • Secure Data Cloud connectors

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.17

We've released version 6.17 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Feature

Warm transfers auto-resume

When an agent performs a warm transfer, the caller is now automatically taken off hold as soon as the transferring agent leaves the call, establishing two-way audio between the receiving agent and the caller without manual action. The caller stays on hold during the consultation between agents so that their conversation remains private. This applies to warm transfers routed through a queue and warm transfers sent directly to a specific agent. This change eliminates the silence that previously occurred when the caller remained on hold after the handoff.

For more information, see Warm transfers.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Call ended card in the session data feed incorrectly displayed a call length of 00:00 despite the actual duration being recorded correctly.

  • Fixed an issue where calls remained stuck on the live dashboard after a caller hung up during the transition from a virtual agent to a queue.

  • Fixed an issue where the Virtual Agent Session Variables section was missing from the call adapter after a successful credit card tokenization handback.

  • Fixed an issue where agents belonging to multiple teams were incorrectly granted access to all communication channels regardless of their team's specific availability settings.

  • Fixed an issue where emails containing specific formatting displayed a full-screen loading screen that prevented agents from viewing the message or interacting with the agent desktop.

  • Fixed an issue where the CCaaS portal displayed an incorrect Off or Not Configured status for Agent Assist after navigating between queues or refreshing the page.

  • Added a checkbox for Salesforce CRM integrations that, when selected, ignores ticket owner updates when an agent is assigned.

  • Fixed an issue where the automatic wrap-up timer didn't release agents when notes or disposition codes were configured as optional.

  • Fixed an issue where agents remained stuck in a busy Wrap-up status after the automatic wrap-up timer expired if they preselected Wrap-up as their next status.

  • Fixed an issue where calls escalated from a virtual agent to an available human agent were incorrectly deflected to the original queue's voicemail upon reaching a timeout.

  • Fixed an issue where callers were left on hold indefinitely during cold transfers to a direct agent extension when over-capacity deflection was enabled.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent interaction outcomes weren't fully mapped, leading to sessions being incorrectly categorized as "Undefined" or "Unknown".

  • Fixed an issue where Agent Assist message analysis background jobs failed and retried excessively for certain profiles.

  • Fixed an issue where transcript message updates caused excessive background processing load.

  • Fixed an issue where the microphone permission error was mistranslated as "Microphone désactivé!" instead of "Microphone turned off!" for agents using French (Canada) localization in the agent adapter.

  • Fixed an issue where calls meeting over-capacity deflection criteria didn't reach their destination queue, leaving callers connected without a route.

  • Fixed an issue where queue duration metrics weren't captured for scheduled callbacks escalating from a virtual agent to a human agent.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent conversations remained open after a call ended due to missing wrap-up events.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent voice sessions remained active after a caller disconnected, resulting in delayed error logs appearing 10 to 15 minutes after the call ended.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly marked as Unresponsive because call offers were sent before their browser finished transitioning from a previous call.

Issue

In GKE control plane versions 1.36.3-gke.1244000 and later, Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver (gcsfusecsi-node) DaemonSet Pods fail to start on specific node pools. The Pods crash and log the following error:

MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "host-proc-sys-fs-fuse" : hostPath type check failed: /proc/sys/fs/fuse is not a directory.

This issue occurs during a version skew when node pools run an older kernel lacking the required host path (earlier than 6.12.67 for Container-Optimized OS, or earlier than 6.13 for Ubuntu). Affected node pool configurations include:

  • All Ubuntu with containerd (ubuntu_containerd) node pools.
  • Container-Optimized OS with containerd (cos_containerd) node pools on GKE versions 1.33 and earlier, 1.34 versions earlier than 1.34.6-gke.1154000, and 1.35 versions earlier than 1.35.3-gke.1389000.

Workaround: For cos_containerd node pools, upgrade the node pool to a version with the required kernel support (for example, 1.34.6-gke.1154000 or later, 1.35.3-gke.1389000 or later, or match the control plane). For ubuntu_containerd node pools, a fix is in progress. Alternatively, downgrade the control plane to a version earlier than 1.36.3-gke.1244000.

title: Integrating OpenAI Function Calling with Meta WhatsApp Cloud API
description:
Traditional chatbot flows rely on static decision trees (Press 1 for Sales, Press 2 for Support). While predictable, they create severe user friction when a prospect wants a personalized answer or needs to check order status, book an appointment, or check flight updates.

By integrating OpenAI's Function Calling (Tools API) directly into your WhatsApp Cloud API webhook, your AI agent can converse naturally while executing backend API calls deterministically.

In this architecture guide, we demonstrate how to connect an LLM tool loop with WhatsApp interactive messaging.

The Function Calling Execution Loop

When a user messages on WhatsApp:

  1. Ingest Inbound Message: Webhook receives the message payload from Meta.
  2. Query Model with Tool Declarations: Pass the user's message along with defined tool schemas (e.g., check_order_status, book_demo_slot).
  3. Model Tool Decision: If the user intends to perform an action, the LLM emits a tool_calls payload instead of raw text.
  4. Execute Internal Business Logic: Run the database lookup or CRM update with the LLM's structured arguments.
  5. Synthesize Final Natural Response: Pass the tool output back to the LLM to format a friendly WhatsApp response.
  6. Dispatch WhatsApp Message: Send the formatted text or interactive button back via WhatsApp Cloud API.

Step 1: Defining the Tool Schema

Declare your functions using JSON schema:

const tools = [
  {
    type: "function",
    function: {
      name: "check_order_status",
      description: "Lookup the real-time shipping status and tracking code for an order",
      parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          order_id: {
            type: "string",
            description: "The 6 to 8 character order tracking ID, e.g. ORD-1092"
          }
        },
        required: ["order_id"]
      }
    }
  }
];

Step 2: The Agentic Execution Function 

import OpenAI from "openai";
const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function handleWhatsAppAgentQuery(customerPhone, userMessage) {
  const messages = [
    { role: "system", content: "You are the helpful customer service assistant for our store on WhatsApp. Keep responses concise, warm, and mobile-friendly." },
    { role: "user", content: userMessage }
  ];

  const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
    model: "gpt-4o-mini",
    messages: messages,
    tools: tools,
    tool_choice: "auto"
  });

  const responseMessage = response.choices[0].message;

  // Check if model decided to call a function
  if (responseMessage.tool_calls) {
    for (const toolCall of responseMessage.tool_calls) {
      if (toolCall.function.name === "check_order_status") {
        const args = JSON.parse(toolCall.function.arguments);

        // Execute real DB query
        const orderData = await queryOrderDatabase(args.order_id);

        messages.push(responseMessage);
        messages.push({
          role: "tool",
          tool_call_id: toolCall.id,
          content: JSON.stringify(orderData)
        });

        // Get final answer from LLM
        const secondResponse = await openai.chat.completions.create({
          model: "gpt-4o-mini",
          messages: messages
        });

        return secondResponse.choices[0].message.content;
      }
    }
  }

  return responseMessage.content;
}

Step 3: Guardrails and Human Agent Handoff

Even the best LLMs can misunderstand complex edge cases. In production:

  • Set strict confidence thresholds: If the user expresses frustration or asks to "talk to human", trigger an immediate handoff flag.
  • Lock session context: Store the conversation history in Redis or PostgreSQL keyed by the user's phone number with a 24-hour expiration window.

Turnkey AI Agents with AI Soul

Rather than maintaining custom OpenAI token budgets, rate limit queues, vector embeddings, and WebSocket handoffs yourself, platforms like AI Soul offer an enterprise-ready solution.

With AI Soul's WhatsApp AI Chatbot, you can train autonomous LLM agents directly on your website URL, product catalogs, and PDFs with zero code. Furthermore, AI Soul's built-in Conversational CRM provides visual Kanban deal pipelines and multi-agent shared team inboxes so your human team can intervene whenever needed.

Summary

OpenAI Function Calling transforms WhatsApp bots from simple FAQ repeaters into autonomous digital employees capable of booking appointments, qualifying B2B prospects, and recovering lost sales.

title: We changed one word in a prompt and broke a feature nobody was watching
description:
The change was one word in a system prompt. "Concise" became "brief." The diff was a single line. What broke: a summarization feature that our team judged by vibes — read the output, seems fine, ship it — had started omitting a detail that mattered, and three weeks passed before anyone noticed. Nobody was to blame individually. There was just no mechanism in place that could catch it, because we treated prompts like config when they behave like code.

30-second takeaway

  • 3-week bug discovery window collapsed to 60 seconds with prompt regression guards
  • "Concise" vs "brief" — one-word diff → feature silently broke for 8% of users (my own users)
  • Prompts are code: same regression-test arguments apply, and almost nobody I know actually gates them in CI (my own observation, not a measured rate)
  • CI-native: eval gates run where ships already get gated, no manual checklists

(Confession: I changed one word in a system prompt — "concise" to "brief" — and a summarization feature silently degraded for 8% of users (my own users). Nobody noticed for three weeks. Three weeks! I treated prompts like config when they behave like code. Same arrogance, different medium.)

(Caveat: your eval set is only as good as the cases you pick. Ship broken tests = ship broken prompt. And eval sets drift too — revisit them quarterly.)

Prompts are code without a test suite

Every argument for regression testing applies to prompts: changes have non-local effects, behavior varies across inputs you didn't test, and "it seems fine on the two examples I tried" is exactly the confidence level that produces three-week-late bug reports. But most teams' prompt testing process is a human squinting at a handful of outputs — slow, inconsistent, and not something that runs before every ship.

Eval checklists instead of vibes

TestPilot turns prompt testing into a repeatable gate: paste your prompt and the expected behavior, get an eval checklist and a version regression guard — so "brief" vs "concise" gets compared across a real set of cases before it ships, not discovered by users after. It's aimed at dev and QA teams shipping LLM-powered features, with CI integration so the check runs where ships already get gated, and version compare so you can see what actually changed when you touched the prompt.

The version-compare framing matters. The unit of change in an LLM app is the prompt+model+params combination, and "what did this change affect" is only answerable if you can diff behavior across versions, not just diff the text.

The realistic version of this practice

Full honesty about costs: building an eval set is real work, the checklist you define is only as good as your understanding of what the feature should do, and LLM outputs are probabilistic — expect some eval noise, and design thresholds with that in mind rather than demanding perfect determinism. Start embarrassingly small: ten cases that capture what "correct" means for your feature, including the inputs that broke it before. Ten good cases beat a hundred mediocre ones, and the set grows every time reality surprises you.

What it is not

It doesn't score abstract "quality" — it checks the behaviors you specify, which means the hard part (deciding what correct looks like) stays with you. It won't catch biases or failure modes absent from your case set. And CI integration gates what you run it against; a feature with no eval cases has no guard, just the vibes you started with.

The one-feature start

Pick the single LLM feature whose silent failure would embarrass you most. Write down what it must always do and must never do. Turn that into ten test cases, and run the next prompt change against them in TestPilot before it ships. Free to try — and if the first regression it catches pays for the hour you spent, that's the moment prompt testing stops being an idea and becomes a habit.

title: Trust Is a Feature: Verification Lessons From Building the Calendrz Mobile Backend
description:
Trust was everywhere in my LinkedIn feed last week. LinkedIn is testing a feature that lets verified members confirm their connections’ work and school history, with enough confirmations earning a profile badge. Its engineering team also explained how it detects low-quality AI content. And in Europe, the AI Act’s transparency rules had their first real effect: OpenAI said it will add invisible watermarks to text generated in the EU.

Each of those is a different problem, but the theme is the same. “Trust me” isn’t good enough any more. Platforms are being asked to prove things: that a person really worked where they say, that a piece of text really came from where it claims, that an account is really who it says it is.

I’ve spent the last couple of weeks on a less glamorous version of the same problem: preparing the Calendrz backend for native iOS and Android apps. Most of that work wasn’t about features. It was about making sure that the thing calling our API really is who it claims to be, and that the trust stops when it should.

Why mobile apps make trust harder

A web app has an easy setup: a session cookie, on a domain you control, in a browser that enforces a lot of rules for you. A mobile app is a public client. It runs on a device you don’t control, it can’t keep a secret (anything shipped in an app binary can be extracted), and it stays signed in for weeks. If a token leaks, you need to know, and you need to be able to shut it down.

Calendrz holds access to people’s work and personal calendars. That’s sensitive data: who you meet, when, and often why. So the bar here isn’t “good enough for a to-do app”.

What we built: verification at every hop

Here’s a quick tour of the trust-related pieces that landed in the Calendrz backend over the past couple of weeks.

1. Proof of who’s calling: PKCE public clients

The iOS and Android apps are registered as first-party OAuth clients with no secret, because a secret in an app isn’t really secret. They sign in with PKCE instead, which proves that the app finishing the login is the same app that started it. A malicious app that intercepts the redirect can’t do anything with the code it grabbed.

2. Proof that the link is really ours: Universal Links and App Links

When a login finishes, the browser has to hand control back to the app. Custom URL schemes can be claimed by any app, so we serve the Apple and Android “well-known” verification files from our own domain. That’s how the operating system knows a link to calendrz.com really belongs to the Calendrz app. If an environment isn’t configured, the files return a 404, so a misconfigured server can never claim links it shouldn’t.

3. Detecting stolen tokens: refresh-token reuse detection

This is the one I’m proudest of. The mobile apps get short-lived access tokens (60 minutes) and a refresh token that rotates: every time it’s used, it’s replaced. The catch is that a plain rotation setup only knows about the current token. If an attacker copied an older one, the server just sees an unknown token and rejects it, but never notices that something is wrong.

So we now keep a record (a SHA-256 hash, never the token itself) of every refresh token that has been rotated out. If one of those shows up again, that’s the signature of a stolen token chain, as described in the OAuth security best-practice RFC (RFC 9700). Calendrz then revokes the whole authorization, so both the attacker and the legitimate app have to sign in again, while the user’s other sessions are left alone. Refreshes for a given authorization are serialized at the database level, so two refreshes racing each other can’t be mistaken for an attack, and can’t undo a revocation.

4. Trust that ends when it should: revoke on account deletion

When you close your Calendrz account, or unlink one of your connected calendar accounts, every OAuth authorization tied to that identity is now removed. That covers the mobile apps and any AI assistants you’ve connected over MCP. Their refresh tokens die with the account. The revocation runs only after the deletion has committed, so a failure can’t leave you half-deleted.

5. Failing honestly instead of failing quietly

A smaller one, but it’s the same idea. When the new mobile event endpoints can’t load your calendar from Google or Microsoft, they now return an explicit “service unavailable” error instead of an empty list. An empty calendar is a claim (“you’re free all day”), and an app or agent would act on it. If we can’t verify the answer, we say so.

Trust is a feature, even if nobody sees it

LinkedIn’s colleague vouching will show up as a badge on a profile. Most of the work I’ve described won’t show up anywhere. Nobody opens an app and thinks “great refresh-token rotation”. But it follows the same principle: don’t take identity on faith; verify it, and be able to revoke it.

There’s also a lot of AI in this story. Much of this backend work was planned, written and code-reviewed with AI agents, and several of the review rounds caught real issues: a race between two concurrent refreshes, a revocation that could have been rolled back, a log line that leaked more than it should have. As more code gets written this way, having automated checks verify the work before it ships is the engineering version of the trust problem LinkedIn and the EU are trying to solve for content.

The Calendrz mobile apps are still in progress, but most of the trust layer underneath them is already in place. That felt like the right order: build the part people need to rely on before the part they’ll see.

Calendrz keeps your work and personal calendars in sync, privately and securely. Find out more at calendrz.com.

title: 12,534 MCP and Agent Skill Repositories, One Conclusion: This Ecosystem Has No Middle Class
description:
Originally published at MCPMarkets. Live numbers and methodology: mcpmarkets.com/insights.

A full-catalog data analysis of the MCP server and agent-skill ecosystem — snapshot: October 17, 2026

We crawled public GitHub data for every MCP server and agent skill we could find, classified it, and measured what the ecosystem actually looks like — not what the launch posts say it looks like. The catalog held 13,598 published entries at snapshot time; this analysis covers the 12,534 deduplicated entries we could pull and verify (5,945 MCP servers, 6,589 agent skills) — about 92% coverage.

The picture that emerges is not a healthy long tail. It is a very tall, very narrow head, a wide lukewarm plain, and a ravine in between.

Three findings up front:

  1. The head is far narrower than most people assume. The top 1% of repositories by stars hold 47.5% of all server-side stars (41.7% on the skill side). The top 10% hold roughly 83%. Gini: 0.867 for servers, 0.882 for skills.
  2. The middle is nearly empty. 62.8% of MCP servers have fewer than 100 stars. Median: 64. Mean/median ratio: 8.4×.
  3. Skills are hotter than servers — and it isn't close. Median stars 160 vs 64 (2.5×); 84.6% of skill repos were pushed to within the last six months, versus 64.2% of servers. One in five servers has been dormant for a year or two.

By the numbers

Metric MCP servers Agent skills
Entries analyzed 5,945 6,589
Total stars 3,211,236 14,168,570
Median stars 64 160
Repos under 100 stars 62.8% 37.1%
Repos under 1,000 stars 93.1% 78.1%
Pushed within 6 months 64.2% 84.6%
Repos with ≥ 10,000 stars 54 256
Gini coefficient 0.867 0.882

Method

Data comes from the MCPMarkets catalog (mcpmarkets.com), sourced from GitHub's public API: stars, license, primary language, last push date, and README content. Three things stated plainly, because they matter for how far to trust the numbers:

  • Snapshot: 2026-10-17. The catalog kept growing while we were pulling it (~690 new entries in a three-hour window), so pagination over a live dataset drifts at the boundaries. We ended up with 12,534 deduplicated entries — about 92% of the 13,598 published at snapshot time. Distribution metrics are barely affected; absolute counts run slightly low.
  • The server/skill split is heuristic. It comes from keyword and README-feature rules at ingestion time. See Limitations for what that costs us.
  • Stars are a proxy for attention, not quality. They follow HN threads, Twitter posts, and awesome-list cross-promotion, not production usage.

Finding 1: Ten repositories hold about a fifth of the sky

Server side: 5,945 repositories, 3,211,236 stars. Here is how those stars are distributed:

Percentile Stars
p25 36
Median 64
p75 166
p90 631
p99 8,841
Max 96,415

Mean over median is 8.4×, which almost always means a handful of extreme values dominate — and they do. The top 10 repositories hold 18.1% of all server-side stars. The top 1% hold 47.5%. Gini: 0.867.

The leaderboard needs a footnote. #1 is punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers at 96,415 stars — an awesome list, which our keyword rules filed as a server (more on this in Limitations). Behind it: headroomlabs-ai/headroom (75,471) and sansan0/trendradar (62,923).

The skill side is more lopsided at the very top: its ten largest repos hold 15.6% of all skill stars, and the single largest repository in the entire catalog is a skill repo — openclaw/openclaw at 392,124 stars, four times the server-side leader. Then vinta/awesome-python (327,970, another awesome list) and obra/superpowers (299,876).

One leaderboard entry is worth pausing on: anthropics/skills — 181,394 stars, no license field set. The company that created the protocol never licensed its own official example repo. That is a thread we pick up in Finding 4.

Finding 2: 62.8% of servers live below 100 stars

The back side of the head story is the long tail. Server-side star histogram:

Star range Entries Share
0 229 3.9%
1–5 122 2.1%
6–10 27 0.5%
11–50 2,072 34.8%
51–100 1,301 21.9%
101–500 1,490 25.1%
501–1,000 296 5.0%
1,001–5,000 292 4.9%
5,001–10,000 62 1.0%
> 10,000 54 0.9%

(Bands are inclusive of their upper bound, so "≤ 100" sums to 63.1%; the 62.8% figure above is strictly under 100.)

This is not a smooth long tail. It is a wide lukewarm plain with a ravine: a third of all servers sit in the 11–50 band, a second cluster at 101–500, a noticeably smaller notch at 51–100 in between, and then a deep gap before the four-digit head.

93.1% of servers have under 1,000 stars. About one in sixteen (6.3%) has under ten, and only 229 (3.9%) have zero. So "nobody looked at it" is the minority case. The typical MCP server is in use, but barely starred — a production dependency for one team, invisible to everyone else.

The skill-side distribution has the same shape, shifted one bracket up: 37.1% below 100 stars, 78.1% below 1,000, median 160.

Finding 3: Skills are the crowded end of the ecosystem

This is the one we did not expect going in: skill repositories are visibly hotter than server repositories.

  • Median stars: 160 (skills) vs 64 (servers) — a 2.5× gap
  • Total stars: 14,168,570 vs 3,211,236 — 4.4×
  • Pushed within the last six months: 84.6% vs 64.2%
  • Dormant for 1–2 years: ≈0% vs 20.4%
  • The ≥ 10,000-star club: 256 skills vs 54 servers

Two explanations, probably both true. Authoring a skill has a lower barrier — a SKILL.md is the deliverable; there is no protocol layer to implement. And skills arrived later, straight into the agent hype cycle.

The practical read is counter-intuitive: the server side looks less crowded to enter, but its median survival environment is colder. If you ship a server, "being genuinely maintained" is already a differentiator (see Finding 6).

Finding 4: Licenses are boringly permissive — the problem is no license at all

Server-side license distribution:

License Share
MIT 58.4%
Apache-2.0 13.5%
Unlabeled (unrecognized by GitHub) 16.1%
NOASSERTION (no match) 5.7%
AGPL-3.0 2.1%
GPL-3.0 1.8%
Other GPL/LGPL/MPL/EPL variants ~2%

Grouped: permissive licenses (MIT, Apache, BSD, ISC, CC0, Unlicense…) account for 73.2% of servers. Copyleft with teeth — AGPL and GPL together — totals just 5.0%. Skills look similar: MIT 53.5%, Apache-2.0 11.6%, permissive 66.4%, copyleft 2.9%.

For anyone consuming these tools, that is good news: closed-source use, commercial embedding, and redistribution rarely hit a license wall.

The real hazard is ambiguity: unlabeled + NOASSERTION together cover 21.8% of servers and 30.4% of skills. "No license" is a question every user has to answer for themselves — and most will answer it wrong. A directory that surfaces the field verbatim, per entry, is doing a small but real service.

Finding 5: Installation is the ecosystem's weakest link

This finding came out of parsing READMEs. For every server, we tried to extract one runnable install command (something like npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-xxx) and one copy-paste-ready mcpServers JSON block:

  • Only 28.7% of servers yield an executable install command.
  • Only 34.5% contain a usable config snippet.

Put plainly: for more than seven in ten MCP servers, the install path is broken. A reader finishes the README and still doesn't know the one command to run — the README links to the source repo, or buries the config in 300 lines of prose, or waves at npm install and moves on.

Skills, by contrast, hit 100% on install-command extraction — because the install path is uniformly npx skillfish add owner/repo/path. One convention, zero ambiguity.

If you maintain a server, this is the cheapest available edge: hoist the install command and the JSON config to the top of the README, in their own fenced blocks. Ten minutes of work. It is the difference between a user and a bounce.

Finding 6: Two-thirds actively developed, one-fifth asleep

By last upstream push (as of 2026-10-17):

Window Servers Skills
< 6 months 64.2% 84.6%
6–12 months 15.3% 13.6%
1–2 years 20.4% ≈0%
No record 0.1% 1.7%

One in five servers hasn't been touched in a year or two. Given that MCP's client config formats and transports have changed more than once in that window, a meaningful share of them are dead on arrival — yet they still sit in every directory's listing, often near the top, because directories rank by stars.

"Maintained" is a more useful filter than "popular." It is also cheap to surface: that is why every entry in our catalog carries a last-push date next to its star count.

What this means if you're building here

Three practical takeaways, in order of expected impact:

  1. Don't target stars. 62.8% of servers live below 100, and the median is 64. A server at 40 stars is not a failure; it is the norm. Optimize for the one team that adopts it, not the timeline.
  2. Fix your install command first. Seven in ten repos ship it broken. A copy-pasteable command plus a ready mcpServers block is the highest-leverage ten minutes in this ecosystem.
  3. Just stay maintained. One in five server repos is asleep. If you ship a real server and keep it working, you are already in the top quintile of "will still work next quarter" — and you can say so, because it shows up in your commit dates.

And one meta-lesson for people reading ecosystem data: the head is a list, the tail is the market. The top repos by stars are, in significant part, curated lists and aggregators (two of the top five across both sides are awesome-lists). The actual supply of working software lives in the 11–50 and 101–500 bands — the part nobody writes launch posts about.

Limitations

Stated plainly, so you can judge how far to push the conclusions:

  1. Classification noise. Entries were ingested by keyword heuristics, and some obvious lists slipped in (punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers as a server; vinta/awesome-python as a skill). This inflates the head numbers; the tail shape is unaffected.
  2. Stars are not quality. They are driven by exposure, not usage. A 30-star server can be a team's production dependency.
  3. Single source. No npm/PyPI download data, so "starred" and "used" cannot be separated.
  4. Snapshot drift. ~92% coverage, as described in Method; absolute counts are conservative.
  5. Our taxonomy is early. 89% of server entries currently land in a single category (developer tools), and skills have no useful category split yet — so no category-level analysis is offered here.

Every number above is reproducible from the public catalog. If you find a discrepancy, tell us — we would rather correct it than defend it.

Explore the data

  • Live numbers & methodology: mcpmarkets.com/insights — the same metrics, recomputed on demand with the page's Refresh button, with daily snapshots you can cite
  • Browse the catalog: MCP servers and agent skills
  • Browse by category: e.g. developer tools — the server list has a category filter
  • Every entry carries install command, quality score, last-push date, and license

This is the first in what we intend to be a quarterly MCP and Agent Skill Ecosystem Report. Next edition: category-level analysis and install-command coverage trends.

About MCPMarkets. We crawl, classify, and maintain a multilingual (EN/ZH/JA/KO/RU) directory of MCP servers and agent skills — 13,000+ entries with install commands, quality scores, and maintenance signals. The point is not to list everything; it is to make the one useful thing findable, with the fields that actually decide adoption.

Data: public snapshot of the MCPMarkets catalog, 2026-10-17. Written by the MCPMarkets team.

This model is available as a research preview with an initial two-week window.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards 6.14

We've released version 6.14 of the advanced reporting dashboards.

Feature

Two new tables in the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls dashboard: Today's Scheduled Calls and Upcoming Scheduled Calls

We've added two new tables to the Real-time Queue Monitoring - Calls dashboard: Today's Scheduled Calls and Upcoming Scheduled Calls. These tables display pending scheduled calls across your allowed scheduling window, regardless of when they were initially created. The tables provide actionable details for each scheduled call, including the time until the call is due, an overdue flag, and a direct CRM link to the scheduled call. With these tables, you can view your full schedule of pending callbacks to help you plan staffing.

For more information, see Queue monitoring dashboards.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue that caused delays when loading and refreshing real-time agent dashboards.

  • Fixed an issue where the Queue Group and Queue Name filters inflated agent counts by including historical, rather than just current, queue assignments. If you have alerts or thresholds based on the previously inflated counts, update them to reflect the new, accurate counts.

  • Fixed an issue where certain queues were incorrectly mapped or dropped entirely from Queue Group filter results.

  • Fixed an issue where the Is Inbound Call and Is Inbound Chat columns in the Live Agent Data table on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard displayed inverted values, incorrectly showing No for inbound interactions and Yes for outbound. This update also standardizes how interaction direction is defined across all reports, ensuring accurate classification and filtering for API-dialed calls, scheduled callbacks, and direct inbound calls. Additionally, it introduces several enhancements to reporting dashboards to ensure accurate timezone formatting, correct CSAT population by direction, and proper queue time tracking for newer call types.

  • Fixed an issue where the Queue Time column of the Queued Calls tile in advanced reporting displayed inflated wait times for calls that re-entered a queue after being answered or transferred.

  • Fixed an issue where agents performing mandatory after-call work were incorrectly classified as "In-Call" instead of "Wrap-up" on real-time reporting dashboards. You can expect a decrease in active "In-Call" agent counts and a corresponding increase in "Wrap-up" statuses across your live monitoring views. This change only affects dashboard reporting and doesn't affect agent routing or historical data. No action is required.

  • Fixed an issue where the SLA Target on the Real-time Channel Performance dashboards appeared blank for queues with no recent activity or when filters matched no configured queues.

  • Fixed an issue where the Missed Interactions dashboards double-counted declined calls and inflated missed chat volumes by incorrectly including agent response-time alerts. You can expect chat volumes to drop and average missed chat time to rise.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting the Subtotals option for call queue metrics for a Look returned an error.

  • Fixed an issue in downloadable call and chat history reports where French-language calls incorrectly appeared under English queue names.

  • Fixed an issue where scheduled calls disappeared from real-time reporting dashboards 12 hours after their creation, which caused the metric to undercount the total number of upcoming scheduled calls.

  • Fixed an issue where filter options for agent and team data in advanced reporting dashboards weren't correctly scoped to the user's assigned permissions.

  • Fixed an issue where the Agents monitoring page became unresponsive when displaying large numbers of agents, causing significant latency when navigating to other pages.

  • Fixed an issue that caused the following problems with raw data exports:

    • Poor export performance due to inefficient database queries.

    • In the call_recordings export, the url field incorrectly contained a timestamp instead of the actual recording URL.

    The url field now contains the correct recording URL, and the timestamp has been moved to a newly added updated_at field. If you ingest call_recordings data using a fixed schema, update your data mappings to accommodate these changes.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

GKE Standard clusters now support up to 512 maximum Pods per node, an increase from the previous limit of 256. Nodes configured for 257 to 512 Pods will now be allocated a /22 Pod CIDR block (1,024 IP addresses).

Fixed an issue where OpenID Connect (OIDC) ID token audience strings were incorrectly converted to lowercase. The audience field now preserves case-sensitivity. This fixes integration failures with external services that require case-sensitive audience values.

title: PolicyPath
description:
PolicyPath: Turning Organizational Policies into Connected Intelligence with FalkorDB

Introduction

What if an organization could do more than store its policies? What if it could understand how each policy connects to risks, controls, and responsible people?

That question inspired me to build PolicyPath, a graph-powered policy intelligence platform, for FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 under the Company Brain track.

The Problem

Organizations often maintain policies, compliance requirements, risk records, and control documentation separately. Understanding how these pieces relate can take time, especially when someone needs to identify which controls enforce a policy, which risks are associated with it, or who is responsible for approval.

Simply storing documents does not make these relationships easy to explore. I wanted to build a tool that makes organizational knowledge more connected and understandable.

My Solution: PolicyPath

PolicyPath transforms policy information into a connected graph that users can explore through an interactive application.

The project models policies, controls, risks, and owners as graph nodes, with relationships connecting them. This structure helps users investigate policy information and understand how different parts of an organization's knowledge fit together.

The application includes:

  • Policy Explorer: Browse and inspect policy information.
  • Graph Explorer: Explore connections between policies, controls, risks, and owners.
  • Risk Heatmap: Review risk information visually.
  • Ask PolicyPath: Ask policy-related questions through a simple assistant.
  • Decision Brief: Generate and download structured decision summaries in JSON format.

My goal was to make policy analysis easier to navigate and more useful for decision-making.

Why I Chose FalkorDB

FalkorDB is central to PolicyPath because the project depends on relationships, not just individual records.

I used FalkorDB as the graph database and Cypher queries to retrieve connected information. For example, a policy can be linked to the control that enforces it, a risk it relates to, and the person responsible for approval.

Representing these connections as a graph makes relationship-based exploration a natural part of the application. Instead of treating every policy as an isolated entry, PolicyPath helps users examine the wider context around it.

How I Built It

I developed the application using Python and Streamlit, with FalkorDB handling the graph data. I also used Pandas and Plotly as part of the data and visualization stack.

The process involved designing the graph model, connecting the application to the database, building the exploration interface, and adding risk and decision-support features.

I also deployed the application online and prepared a public GitHub repository and demo video so others could explore the project.

Project links

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/Monika-2108/PolicyPath
  • Live application: https://policypath-dnr7owzmvjhxfoib9bcmls.streamlit.app/
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/4WEKiY_XiL8

Challenges and Learnings

One of my biggest learnings was that choosing a graph database is not enough by itself. The graph model and relationships must reflect the actual questions users need to answer.

I learned to think about data as connected entities rather than isolated tables or documents, and to use Cypher queries to retrieve information through those relationships.

I also learned how important it is to connect the backend to a usable interface, deploy an application, document the setup, and communicate a technical idea through a working demonstration.

Building PolicyPath also reminded me that prototypes have limitations. Visualizations, question-answering behavior, and deployment configuration all require testing and refinement. Being aware of those limitations is part of building reliable software.

What's Next?

I would like to extend PolicyPath with richer natural-language querying, more advanced graph analytics, improved visualizations, and more comprehensive policy and risk relationships.

These improvements could help organizations move toward more connected, explainable, and accessible policy intelligence.

Final Thoughts

Building PolicyPath gave me practical experience with graph databases and showed me how connected data can support real organizational workflows.

For me, FalkorDB is more than a place to store records in this project. It provides the relationship layer that makes policy exploration possible.

I hope PolicyPath demonstrates how graph technology can help turn disconnected organizational information into knowledge that people can explore and use to make better-informed decisions.

Built for FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 — Company Brain track.

title: Portfolio v2.0: three themes, one headline, and every number checked against the repo
description:
My portfolio just hit v2.0. It's a Django 5.2 + DRF API with a React 19 build embedded and served by Django, PostgreSQL on Neon, deployed on PythonAnywhere.

The visible change is a theme switcher in the top-right corner with three palettes: Cian (the default, a midnight background with a cyan-to-violet aurora), Violeta (light) and Ámbar (warm and sober). The less visible change taught me more: making sure my portfolio, my CV and my LinkedIn tell the same story with the same numbers.

👉 Live: nicolasandrescl.pythonanywhere.com · backend · frontend

Part 1 — A theme system that never re-renders React

Themes as plain data

Every component was already styled with Stitches tokens ($accent, $surface, $syntaxFunction…). So I didn't need a ThemeProvider. A theme is just a set of token values, written as plain data with no Stitches import:

// src/themes/palettes.js (trimmed)
export const THEMES = [
  {
    key: 'cian',
    label: 'Cian',
    dark: true,
    colors: { background: '#070b14', accent: '#22d3ee', onAccent: '#04111a', /* … */ },
    fonts: { heading: "'Space Grotesk', 'Segoe UI', sans-serif", /* … */ },
  },
  // violeta, ambar …
];

Keeping it free of Stitches means I can test it without a styling runtime. This test catches the most common theming bug, a theme that quietly inherits a color from another one because it forgot to define a token:

it('every theme defines the same tokens', () => {
  const base = getTheme(DEFAULT_THEME);
  const colorKeys = Object.keys(base.colors).sort();
  THEMES.forEach((t) => {
    expect(Object.keys(t.colors).sort()).toEqual(colorKeys);
  });
});

One class on <html>

Each palette becomes a Stitches createTheme class, and switching themes just swaps a class on <html>:

export const themes = Object.fromEntries(
  THEMES.map((t) => [t.key, createTheme(themeClass(t.key), { colors: t.colors, fonts: t.fonts })]),
);
Object.values(themes).forEach((t) => t.className); // ← more on this line below

export function applyTheme(key, root = document.documentElement) {
  const theme = getTheme(key);
  THEMES.forEach((t) => root.classList.remove(themeClass(t.key)));
  root.classList.add(themeClass(theme.key));
  root.dataset.theme = theme.key;
  root.style.colorScheme = theme.dark ? 'dark' : 'light';
  // …and updates <meta name="theme-color"> for the mobile browser bar
}

Why <html> and not a wrapper <div>? Radix renders dropdowns in a Portal attached to <body>. If the theme lived on a div inside the app, every menu would open with the wrong colors.

The switcher itself is a Radix DropdownMenu with a RadioGroup. That gives menuitemradio roles, keyboard navigation, Escape to close and focus management for free. The choice is stored in localStorage, wrapped in try/catch: private mode or blocked storage falls back to Cian instead of breaking the site.

No flash on reload

If you apply the saved theme in a useEffect, every reload paints the default theme first and then switches. The fix is a tiny inline script that runs before React loads:

<style>
  html { background: #070b14; color-scheme: dark; }
  html[data-theme="violeta"] { background: #fbf8ff; color-scheme: light; }
  html[data-theme="ambar"] { background: #130d0a; }
</style>
<script>
  (function () {
    var keys = ['cian', 'violeta', 'ambar'];
    var key = 'cian';
    try { key = localStorage.getItem('portafolio-theme') || key; } catch (e) {}
    if (keys.indexOf(key) === -1) key = 'cian';
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = key;
    document.documentElement.classList.add('theme-' + key);
  })();
</script>

I verified it with Playwright: save Ámbar, reload, screenshot immediately. Even the loading spinner was already amber.

Four traps I stepped on

1. Stitches injects themes lazily. A createTheme rule only reaches the stylesheet when something reads theme.className. My inline script added theme-ambar to <html> before any component had touched that theme, so the class existed but styled nothing. That's the reason for the "useless-looking" line above: reading .className for every theme when the module loads forces the injection.

2. Django wasn't serving Vite's index.html. The production page comes from Django's templates/index.html, which resolves the hashed assets from Vite's manifest. Anything I added to Vite's <head> (the anti-flash script, Google Fonts) would never reach production. It now lives in both files, and the keys have to match.

3. A light theme exposes every hard-coded color. Going from dark to light turned up three problems:

  • color: 'white' on buttons became unreadable on the bright cyan accent. That gave me a new onAccent token.
  • Section wrappers with backgroundColor: '$background' hid the aurora painted on <body>. They're transparent now.
  • The Radix <Theme> paints its own background by default. It now uses hasBackground={false}.

4. docker compose restart served the old bundle. The built dist/ is copied into the image, so after npm run build you need up -d --build. I noticed because the index-*.js hash in the HTML hadn't changed.

Part 2 — One headline, verified numbers

While shipping the themes, I noticed something a recruiter would notice first. My portfolio said "Backend Python Developer | Automation & Reliability", my CV said "Backend Python Developer · DevOps & Reliability", and LinkedIn said something else. Three versions of the same person don't build trust.

So LinkedIn became the source of truth: Backend Engineer → SRE | Python · Django · Kubernetes · Terraform · CI/CD. The portfolio, the CV (versioned HTML → PDF via headless Edge) and my GitHub profile now say exactly that.

Then I went further and re-measured every number I publish against the actual repositories (pytest --collect-only, git shortlog, counting the Postman collection). Several were stale. The test count of my main automation project was off by thousands, a Postman collection had grown from 79 to 82 requests, and one coverage claim described a target instead of the 80% floor the CI actually enforces. I also caught my own mistake: I counted 18 releases when there were 19, because two versions only appear in the project's README, not in commit messages.

The lesson: a number on your CV is a claim someone can check. Measure it from the source, write down where it came from, and prefer wording like "2,800+ tests" when the exact count changes every week.

How it ships

  • 35 frontend tests (Vitest + Testing Library) and 49 backend tests (~91% coverage) with mypy.
  • A scripts/verificar.sh in each repo replays the CI on a clean clone of HEAD, with the same Node and Python versions as GitHub Actions. If Python 3.12 isn't installed locally, it runs inside a python:3.12-slim container. The runner only sees what's committed, so that's what gets tested.
  • End-to-end check in Docker (Django + Postgres + the embedded build) with Playwright: all three themes, desktop and 375 px mobile, no horizontal scroll.
  • CD with Jenkins: test gate → image build → deploy → healthcheck → smoke test, with a stage that guarantees the deploy can never point at the production database.

The two themes besides Cian were ported from an internal tool I built earlier (CmdVault), where they were NiceGUI palettes. Same idea, different stack. That's the part of side projects I enjoy most: the ideas move from one project to the next.

If you try the site, tell me which theme you'd keep. And if you have your own trick for flash-free theming, I'd love to hear it. 👇

title: Go's database/sql Has Been Ports and Adapters Since Go 1. Read Its Driver Port
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Drop one line from a Go service's import block and sql.Open answers with sql: unknown driver "postgres" (forgotten import?). The standard library guesses your bug for you. The missing line is import _ "github.com/lib/pq", and that underscore is the visible end of a ports-and-adapters design that has sat in Go's standard library since the language hit 1.0.

The package was exp/sql until the weekly snapshot of 2012-01-20 renamed it to database/sql, and it shipped in Go 1 on 28 March 2012. Alistair Cockburn had written up the ports and adapters pattern in 2005, with the stated intent of letting an application be "developed and tested in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and databases". Fourteen years after Go 1, database/sql is still a clean blueprint of that idea, plus one design decision you should not copy.

The core owns the port

Start with who defines what. The interfaces live in database/sql/driver, and the package doc opens with: "Package driver defines interfaces to be implemented by database drivers as used by package sql." The consumer writes the contract. Postgres, MySQL and SQLite authors implement it.

That is the rule the Go wiki's Code Review Comments gives for every interface: "Go interfaces generally belong in the package that uses values of the interface type, not the package that implements those values." database/sql follows it to the letter. Here is the required surface, abridged from the package docs:

// database/sql/driver (abridged)
type Driver interface {
    Open(name string) (Conn, error)
}

type Conn interface {
    Prepare(query string) (Stmt, error)
    Close() error
    Begin() (Tx, error) // deprecated
}

type Stmt interface {
    Close() error
    NumInput() int
    Exec(args []Value) (Result, error)  // deprecated
    Query(args []Value) (Rows, error)   // deprecated
}

type Rows interface {
    Columns() []string
    Close() error
    Next(dest []Value) error
}

That is small on purpose. The design goals document that sits in the package directory lists a clear split between the driver layer and the user-facing layer, type conversion handled mostly in the sql package so drivers deal with fewer types, and optional interfaces for special cases or faster paths. Your application code never touches driver.Conn. It talks to *sql.DB, *sql.Rows and *sql.Tx, which are concrete types the core controls.


The core defines one socket. Every database driver is a plug shaped to fit it.

Adapters plug themselves in

Each driver is an adapter, and it registers itself. This is the whole init in lib/pq's conn.go:

func init() {
    sql.Register("postgres", &Driver{})
}

go-sql-driver/mysql does the same with sql.Register(driverName, &MySQLDriver{}), and its package comment tells you to use it via import _ "github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql". The official Go database tutorial explains why the underscore is there: if you never call a function from the driver package directly, you need a blank import so the package still loads.

import (
    "database/sql"

    _ "github.com/lib/pq"
)

func open(dsn string) (*sql.DB, error) {
    return sql.Open("postgres", dsn)
}

The blank import runs init, init writes into a map inside database/sql, and sql.Open looks the name up in that map. Your code depends only on the port. The adapter is a line in your import block. The SQLDrivers wiki page lists roughly 60 adapters built this way, from pgx to modernc.org/sqlite, and marks the ones that pass a shared compatibility test suite.

Optional interfaces: capabilities without a fat port

Here is the part worth borrowing first. The required port stayed tiny, but the protocol grew a lot after 2012: context cancellation, named parameters, session resets, connection validation. The Go team did not add those methods to driver.Conn, which would have broken every driver. They added separate, optional interfaces and let the core detect them at runtime.

Go 1.8 brought QueryerContext, ExecerContext, ConnBeginTx and Pinger. Go 1.9 brought NamedValueChecker. Go 1.10 brought Connector, DriverContext and SessionResetter. Go 1.15 brought Validator. An old driver that implements none of them still compiles and still works.

The detection is a type assertion with a fallback. A simplified sketch of what queryDC in sql.go does:

// simplified sketch of database/sql's queryDC
queryerCtx, ok := dc.ci.(driver.QueryerContext)
var queryer driver.Queryer
if !ok {
    queryer, ok = dc.ci.(driver.Queryer)
}
if ok {
    rows, err := ctxDriverQuery(ctx, queryerCtx,
        queryer, query, args)
    if err != driver.ErrSkip {
        return rows, err // adapter handled it
    }
}
// fallback: Prepare, Query, Close the statement

The driver package docs spell out the chain: if a Conn implements neither QueryerContext nor Queryer, DB.Query prepares the statement, runs it, and closes it. And driver.ErrSkip, whose message reads "driver: skip fast-path; continue as if unimplemented", lets an adapter say "I have this capability, but not for this particular call."

Argument checking follows the same idea. According to convert.go, the core looks for NamedValueChecker on the statement first, then on the connection, and falls back to the statement's column converter or its own default checker when neither exists or when the checker returns ErrSkip. pgx's stdlib adapter implements CheckNamedValue, ResetSession and QueryContext. A smaller driver can skip all three and still get correct behaviour from the core.

That gives you a port that can grow for a decade without a breaking change.

The pool lives in the core

The other half of the design is what adapters do not have to write. The sql.OpenDB doc comment says the returned DB "maintains its own pool of idle connections". The DB struct in that same file holds freeConn, connRequests, maxOpen, maxLifetime and maxIdleTime. Idle connections default to defaultMaxIdleConns = 2, and SetMaxOpenConns documents that "The default is 0 (unlimited)."

No driver reimplements pooling, lifetimes or waiting for a free connection. The adapter contributes hooks the core calls at the right moment. If a Conn implements Validator, the driver docs say IsValid runs before the connection goes back to the pool. If it implements SessionResetter, ResetSession runs before reuse. And driver.ErrBadConn tells the core to retry on a fresh connection, with a warning not to return it if the server might already have done the work.

Policy in the core, mechanism in the adapter. When you design your own ports, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking and pooling belong on the core side for the same reason: otherwise every adapter writes its own slightly different version.

The half you should not copy: a global registry

Now the part that breaks the hexagonal rules. In sql.go, the registry is a package-level map behind a mutex:

var driversMu sync.RWMutex
var drivers = make(map[string]driver.Driver)

Adapters are wired by import side effects into global state, not by an explicit composition root, which Mark Seemann describes as "a (preferably) unique location in an application where modules are composed together." Three costs follow from that.

First, the wiring fails at runtime, not compile time. That is the error from the top of this post: the message has to guess at the forgotten import because the compiler never sees the dependency.

Second, names collide globally. Register panics with sql: Register called twice for driver on a duplicate name. pgx works around that in its init: it registers "pgx" only if sql.Drivers() does not already contain it, and always registers "pgx/v5".

Third, the map is now hard to change. The comment above it in sql.go says it should be an internal detail, but that other packages reach into it via linkname, and asks that its type signature not change.


Side-effect registration on the left, an explicit composition root on the right.

Go 1.10 gave you the exit. sql.OpenDB takes a driver.Connector value instead of a name string, so main hands the adapter to the core directly:

// pgx is github.com/jackc/pgx/v5
// stdlib is github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib (pgx's adapter)
cfg, err := pgx.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
db := sql.OpenDB(stdlib.GetConnector(*cfg))

MySQL has the same shape through mysql.NewConnector, which the Go tutorial uses as its example. Importing the package still runs its init, so the registry entry still exists, but your code no longer depends on a magic string or on import order.

Apply the good half to your own ports

Take the three habits that aged well and leave the registry behind. Say a billing service sends notifications. The service package owns the port, a richer capability is optional, and there is always a fallback:

package billing

// Sender is the port. billing owns it.
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, m Message) error
}

// BatchSender is optional. Detected, never required.
type BatchSender interface {
    SendBatch(ctx context.Context, ms []Message) error
}

func (s *Service) notifyAll(
    ctx context.Context, ms []Message,
) error {
    if bs, ok := s.sender.(BatchSender); ok {
        return bs.SendBatch(ctx, ms)
    }
    for _, m := range ms {
        if err := s.sender.Send(ctx, m); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

Retries and rate limits go in Service, not in each adapter, the same way sql.DB owns the pool. And the wiring happens in one visible place:

func main() {
    db := mustOpenDB()
    repo := postgres.NewInvoiceRepo(db)
    sender := smtp.NewSender(loadSMTPConfig())
    svc := billing.NewService(repo, sender)
    runHTTP(svc)
}

No init, no name strings, no blank imports. If you forget an adapter, the code does not compile. For tests, pass a fake Sender into NewService, which is exactly the isolation Cockburn's 2005 write-up was after.

Next time you type import _ for a database driver, read it as the stdlib showing you the pattern, and the one place it cut a corner. Wire your own adapters in main.

If this was useful

database/sql gets the port and the capability detection right, and gets the wiring wrong. Hexagonal Architecture in Go works through both halves for your own services: where ports live in the package layout, how persistence adapters stay behind them, and how to build a composition root in main that the compiler can check. If the billing example above looks like the direction you want your codebase to go, that book is the long version of it.

title: I ran 50 orders at 1 unit of stock. Here’s what stopped the oversell.
description:
Last week I built a small grocery-style order system to learn how event-driven services handle the classic problem: two customers click “buy” on the last item at the same time.

A caveat first. I built this in about 24 hours using AI coding agents (Cursor), and I directed the design. I’m writing this after going back through the code to understand why it works, which is a different thing from writing every line myself. If you’re after a hand-coded reference, this isn’t one. If you want to see how these patterns fit together and how I tested them, read on.

What it is

Three Spring Boot services (order, inventory, payment), each with its own PostgreSQL database, talking only through Kafka. There’s no central coordinator. Each service reacts to events and publishes its own, which is called a choreographed saga. A Next.js storefront sits on top, and an optional ELK stack lets me trace any order by its ID.

Happy path: an order goes PENDING, then RESERVED, then CONFIRMED. If stock runs out or the payment is declined, the order goes to CANCELLED and any reserved stock is released through a compensation event.

The problem

Writing to your database and publishing to Kafka are two separate operations. If the service crashes between them, you either have an order nobody hears about or an event for an order that doesn’t exist.

The three things that handle it

Transactional outbox. The order service writes the order and the event into the same database transaction. A separate step then publishes the event to Kafka. Either both are saved or neither is.
Idempotent consumers. Kafka can deliver a message more than once. Each consumer records the events it has processed (a processed_events table), so a duplicate does nothing the second time.
Atomic stock updates plus per-order keys. Stock is decremented in a single atomic update, so two orders can’t both read “1 left.” Events for one order use that order’s ID as the Kafka key, which keeps them in order.

The test

I wrote a k6 script that resets one item to a stock of 1, then fires 50 concurrent orders at it, one per virtual user. Afterward it checks that available stock never went below zero and that confirmed orders didn’t exceed the starting stock.

On my MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 16 GB), all 50 requests were accepted. After the saga settled, exactly one order was confirmed and stock sat at 0. The whole run, including setup and waiting for outcomes, took about 6.8 seconds. The other orders are designed to end up CANCELLED. [check your database and put the real count here]

What this does and doesn’t prove

It’s a correctness test, not a performance benchmark. It shows the system doesn’t oversell under a burst of 50 on a laptop. It says nothing about throughput at scale, and I haven’t run a long soak test. Payments are simulated too: a token of ok succeeds and fail declines.

What surprised me

[one or two honest sentences: something you learned or got wrong when you traced the code, e.g. what you expected the outbox to do versus what it actually does]

Try it

Everything runs with docker compose up --build. The repo has the architecture notes, the acceptance scenarios, and the benchmark results:

ArnavPoswal15 / orderflow-platform

Event-driven order platform: Spring Boot microservices + Kafka choreographed saga, transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, Redis, PostgreSQL, Next.js storefront, ELK, k6 load test

Orderflow Platform

Event-driven order platform for grocery-style orders: order, inventory, and payment services each own a database and coordinate through Kafka using a choreographed saga (no central orchestrator).

Status: Phases 1–7 complete (saga, storefront, ops, ELK observability, k6 proof load test, GitHub Actions CI, demo docs).

Architecture

flowchart TB

title: Timestamp attributes are now supported in Vercel Flags
description:
Vercel Flags now supports timestamp attributes, so you can target entities by date and time.

Use timestamp attributes to show a campaign page only between two dates, run a Black Friday promotion, or target users who registered before a cutoff.

Configure a timestamp attribute

You can configure timestamp attributes in the dashboard or via the CLI.

In the Vercel dashboard, open Flags, select Entities, and create or select an entity. Add an attribute and set its data type to timestamp.

Or define the attribute with the CLI:

Whether you configure the attribute in the dashboard or CLI, your application must provide its value when evaluating a flag. The entity and attribute names must match your configuration, and the value must be a Unix epoch timestamp in milliseconds.

This Flags SDK example passes the current time as system.time. Date.now() returns the required value in milliseconds. Keeping it inside dedupe() ensures that every flag evaluated during the same request uses the same time:

Add a targeting rule

In the dashboard, open the flag and add a targeting rule using the timestamp attribute. The rule compares the value from your application with a date and time you choose.

Rules support is after, is at or after, is before, and is at or before. The date and time picker uses your local timezone.

To add a time-based targeting rule with the CLI, use after, at-or-after, before, or at-or-before:

Learn how to provide entities in code and release a flag at a specific time, or read the Flags documentation.

title: A Kotlin Data Class Works as a HashMap Key. In a TypeScript Map It Never Matches
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

A Kotlin grid keyed by Point is about as ordinary as code gets: a cell type and a map from cell to whatever lives there.

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val labels = hashMapOf(Point(1, 2) to "spawn")
    println(labels[Point(1, 2)]) // spawn
}

Two different Point instances, one lookup, a hit. The Kotlin compiler derives equals() and hashCode() from every property in the primary constructor, so the second Point(1, 2) lands in the same bucket as the first and compares equal. Java gives you the same deal with records, final since JDK 16.

Now you port it to TypeScript. The compiler is happy, and the lookup returns undefined with no error anywhere.

Why the Map can't see your Point

Here is the port, as most JVM developers write it on day one:

type Point = { readonly x: number; readonly y: number };

const labels = new Map<Point, string>();
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");

labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // undefined
labels.size;                // 1

const seen = new Set<Point>();
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.size;                  // 2

JavaScript's Map compares keys with the SameValueZero algorithm. MDN spells out what that means for objects: "for object keys, equality is based on object identity. They are compared by reference, not by value." Two object literals with the same fields are two objects, so they are two keys. Set works the same way, which is why your "deduplicated" set holds the same point twice.

The JVM reflex is to add an equals method and move on. It does nothing here:

class Pt {
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  equals(o: Pt): boolean {
    return this.x === o.x && this.y === o.y;
  }
}

const m = new Map<Pt, string>([[new Pt(1, 2), "spawn"]]);
m.get(new Pt(1, 2)); // undefined

There is no equals/hashCode protocol in JavaScript collections. Map never calls your method, and there is no hook to make it. On the JVM, the Object contract says equal objects "must produce the same integer result" from hashCode, and HashMap is built on that promise.

The type checker won't save you either. TypeScript's type system is structural: any { x, y } is a valid Point, so labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }) type-checks perfectly.

One more trap while you are here. If you reach for a plain object as a dictionary instead, every property name gets coerced to a string, and every plain object becomes "[object Object]". Now every point matches every other point. You traded "never matches" for "always matches".

Fix 1: derive a string key

The smallest fix is to stop using the object as the key and use a string computed from it:

const keyOf = (p: Point): string => `${p.x},${p.y}`;

const grid = new Map<string, string>();
grid.set(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
grid.get(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"

Strings are primitives, and SameValueZero compares primitives by value, so this works. For numeric fields the comma is safe because a JavaScript number never stringifies with a comma in it.

String fields are where this goes wrong. With a naive template, { org: "a,b", name: "c" } and { org: "a", name: "b,c" } both produce "a,b,c". Encode the fields as a JSON array in a fixed order instead:

type Member = { readonly org: string; readonly name: string };

const memberKey = (m: Member): string =>
  JSON.stringify([m.org, m.name]);

JSON escaping makes the encoding unambiguous, and the array fixes the order. Don't call JSON.stringify(m) on the whole object: property order follows Object.keys(), which is insertion order for string keys, so { org, name } and { name, org } give you two different keys for the same member.

The cost of Fix 1: the map now holds strings. Iterate it and you get "1,2" back, not a Point. And nothing stops a teammate from calling grid.get("1, 2") with a stray space.

Fix 2: a KeyedMap that takes a key function

If you miss HashMap<Point, V>, write the small wrapper that moves hashCode out of the class and into a function you pass in. It keeps the original key next to the value, so iteration hands you real Point objects:

class KeyedMap<K, V> {
  readonly #entries = new Map<string, [K, V]>();
  readonly #keyOf: (key: K) => string;

  constructor(keyOf: (key: K) => string) {
    this.#keyOf = keyOf;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): this {
    this.#entries.set(this.#keyOf(key), [key, value]);
    return this;
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    return this.#entries.get(this.#keyOf(key))?.[1];
  }

  has(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.has(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  delete(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.delete(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.#entries.size;
  }

  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    return this.#entries.values();
  }
}

Using it reads like the Kotlin version again:

const labels = new KeyedMap<Point, string>(keyOf);
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");
labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // "spawn"

for (const [point, label] of labels) {
  console.log(point.x, point.y, label);
}

One JVM rule carries over unchanged. The java.util.Map docs warn that "the behavior of a map is not specified if the value of an object is changed in a manner that affects equals comparisons while the object is a key in the map." Here, if you mutate a key after set, the stored string is stale and the entry is unreachable by its new value. Keep key types readonly, as Point is above.

Fix 3: branded value types

Fixes 1 and 2 still let anyone pass a raw { x, y } or a hand-built string. Branding closes that door at compile time. The TypeScript playground's nominal-typing example intersects a type with a __brand property, a convention that makes a plain value unassignable to the branded type.

Start with the key string. Brand it, and make one function the only way to produce it:

type PointKey = string & { readonly __brand: "PointKey" };

const pointKey = (p: Point): PointKey =>
  `${p.x},${p.y}` as PointKey;

const spawns = new Map<PointKey, string>();
spawns.set(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
spawns.get(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"
// spawns.get("1,2"); // compile error: not a PointKey

The brand exists only in the type system: at runtime a PointKey is an ordinary string and the map behaves exactly as in Fix 1, while a hand-typed "1, 2" is rejected by the compiler because it has no brand.

You can go one step further and brand the value itself. If a factory hands out one canonical frozen object per coordinate, reference equality becomes value equality, and the plain Map from the first snippet starts working:

type GridPoint = Point & { readonly __brand: "GridPoint" };

const pool = new Map<string, GridPoint>();

function gridPoint(x: number, y: number): GridPoint {
  const key = `${x},${y}`;
  let p = pool.get(key);
  if (p === undefined) {
    p = Object.freeze({ x, y }) as GridPoint;
    pool.set(key, p);
  }
  return p;
}

const owners = new Map<GridPoint, string>();
owners.set(gridPoint(1, 2), "spawn");
owners.get(gridPoint(1, 2));       // "spawn"
gridPoint(1, 2) === gridPoint(1, 2); // true
// owners.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // compile error: no brand

This is interning: one shared instance per distinct value. The brand is what makes it safe: a Map<GridPoint, V> refuses object literals, so the day-one bug from the first section can't compile. The trade-off is memory. The pool keeps every point it ever created alive, so use it for bounded domains like grid cells, currency pairs or enum-like tuples, not for arbitrary user input.

Records and Tuples will not fix this for you

For years the answer to "when will JavaScript get value-equal objects?" was the Records and Tuples proposal, with its #{ x: 1, y: 2 } syntax. That proposal is gone. At the TC39 plenary on April 14, 2025, the committee reached consensus to withdraw it; it "was at stage 2 and unable to gain further consensus for adding new primitives to the language." The inactive-proposals list records the rationale as "Subsumed by Composites".

The Composites proposal is the successor, and it is listed at Stage 2 as of October 2026. Its pitch is this exact problem. Composite({ x: 1, y: 4 }) returns an interned, frozen object, so two composites built from the same values are the same object, === is true, and they work as Map and Set keys. It is the gridPoint factory above, proposed as a language feature.

Read the fine print before you wait for it. Stage 2 in the TC39 process means "refining the solution": the design is a draft that may still change significantly. The README mentions experimental implementations and a polyfill, not a shipping engine. Nested plain objects are compared by reference, so Composite({ v: {} }) !== Composite({ v: {} }). Composites can't be WeakMap keys. And every object you get from JSON.parse, a database driver or an HTTP client will still be a plain object, so you'd convert at the boundary anyway, which is what Fix 3 already does.

Which fix to pick

Reach for Fix 1 when the key is used in one function and never iterated. KeyedMap is the one to pick when you want HashMap<K, V> ergonomics and need the original keys back. Use branded keys or interned values when the map crosses module boundaries and you want the compiler, not code review, to catch the raw object literal.

If this was useful

Map keys are one of those places where Kotlin and Java instincts compile cleanly in TypeScript and then fail quietly at runtime. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript walks through these translation gaps one by one: variance, null safety, sealed classes to unions, coroutines to async/await. If you came to TypeScript from the JVM, it's the one to start with.

The rest of the collection, so you can see which one or two fit you:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript stands in for them if you think in JVM terms, and The TypeScript Type System is where branded types like PointKey get the full treatment. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work. Browse all five on the collection page.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.
