title: Cloudflare Hyperdrive Serves MySQL From One Canonical Copy of a Query Result
description:
TL;DR

  • Hyperdrive is a distributed connection pooler that Cloudflare runs for Workers, holding warm database connections on the company's network and caching query results in its global cache, so Worker requests share connections that are already open.
  • MySQL support in Hyperdrive reached general availability on 14 October 2026, roughly eighteen months after the beta that added MySQL to Postgres-only support.
  • The story behind the release is a consistency bug between the two nodes Hyperdrive runs: a Client beside the Worker and an Endpoint beside the database, each with the data-centre cache they can share.
  • The disagreement was about encoding. Each node cached the bytes it wrote back to the Worker, so a result stored in one node's format could be read by the other node and translated wrongly.
  • The failure surfaced as empty query results on about 0.001% of requests for one high-volume customer, and it appeared once caching was enabled, which pointed the investigation at the pooled path.
  • The fix stores one canonical copy of every result, encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node writes it, and the success rate for client connections reached 99.99% after it shipped.
  • General availability also carries the smaller items: twenty fixes in total, among them a handshake that negotiated utf8, an alias limited to three bytes per code point, which broke four-byte characters such as emoji.

Cloudflare's topology figure from the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the two nodes, the two caches and the database behind them.

What Hyperdrive does between a Worker and a database

A Worker runs at the edge, and the database it needs sits in one region. Establishing a connection between the two costs at least five network round trips on Cloudflare's own count, and a platform that opened one per request would spend more time on handshakes than on queries. Hyperdrive exists to keep that connection warm: the Client node runs alongside the Worker's machine, the Endpoint node runs near the database, and the Endpoint holds a pool of open connections that many Worker requests share.

The product also caches. Results for frequently repeated queries can live in the CDN cache local to each data centre, which is where the vendor's own headline numbers come from: three times faster queries from pooling, up to a hundred times on repeated queries, and cached results in under five milliseconds. A connection string swap is the documented migration path, with mysql2 and mysql among the supported Node.js drivers.

Two nodes, one cache, and an encoding disagreement

The architecture puts a cache at each end, and when a Client and its Endpoint sit in the same data centre they share it. Sharing is the right default for performance, because either node can then answer a repeat query without touching the database. It also means two processes write into one keyspace, which is where the bug lived.

Cloudflare's account of the plumbing is specific. A cached entry is keyed on a hash of the query's wire messages with some normalisation, and the value is the result bytes. For that to work, the same response has to be stored as the same bytes no matter which node stored it, and the post is candid that the implementation carried an assumption from the Postgres work: that the bytes written back to the Worker are the bytes worth caching.

Netics editorial diagram: what each node stored before the fix, and the single canonical copy that replaced it.

The MySQL capability mismatch behind the empty results

MySQL makes that assumption unsafe, and the reason is a negotiation detail in its wire protocol. Capabilities are agreed when a connection is established, and one of them, CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF, changes how a result set is terminated: the metadata end-of-file packet disappears and the final packet becomes an OK packet. Server 5.7.5 and later supports the capability, and a client has to ask for the newer behaviour.

The popular Node.js driver mysql2 does not ask. Hyperdrive does, so the Endpoint and the Client are working with different capability sets, and the pooler translates every result set into the shape the Worker's driver expects, inserting end-of-file packets and converting OK packets back. Caching the translated bytes breaks that translation in both directions: a Client that finds the Endpoint's result in Hyperdrive's own encoding sends it to the Worker untranslated, and an Endpoint that reads bytes a Client already translated passes them to a different Client, which translates them a second time and ends up sending an early end-of-file packet or hanging.

The symptom was narrow and the explanation is mechanical. One high-volume customer saw roughly 0.001% of queries return empty results where a non-empty answer was always expected, the problem appeared only on instances with caching enabled, and the investigation had to reach the MySQL protocol documentation before the assumption surfaced.

Netics editorial diagram: the three numbers that frame the release.

The fix stores one canonical copy per result

Cloudflare's correction is a single rule about what goes into the cache: always store a canonical copy of the result bytes encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node produced it. The Client then translates on the way out and the Endpoint reads a format it understands. Once that shipped, the empty-row reports stopped and the client-connection success rate reached the vendor's 99.99% target.

Generalisations from one vendor's bug are cheap, and this one holds up anyway. A shared cache with two writers needs one agreed serialisation, and a translation layer needs to decide which side of the cache it runs on. The same discipline applies to any pooled or cached data path a team operates, including the caches that sit in front of an inference stack.

The smaller bugs that added up to general availability

The post describes the gap between beta and general availability as twenty bug fixes, and the two encoding defects are worth keeping because they show the same class of failure at lower stakes. The startup handshake negotiated utf8, a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 that covers one to three bytes per code point, so emoji written to the database came back broken; the fix was to negotiate utf8mb4.

The second came from a cleanup step. Hyperdrive clears session state between checkouts with COM_RESET_CONNECTION, which returns a connection to the server default rather than the encoding agreed at startup, so a server defaulting to latin1 handed back a latin1 connection and the pooler had to set the encoding again after every reset. Both bugs are the sort that a test suite written against the happy path misses and a customer with unusual data finds.

Cloudflare's header graphic for the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the pooled path between distributed compute and a regional database.

Reading the 99.99% success rate

Cloudflare reports the figure as its success rate for Client connections, and it matches the 99.99% production availability target the beta set out to validate; it is the vendor's own number, and the post cites no independent measurement. For readers planning a migration, Cloudflare's product page and developer documentation state that Hyperdrive supports any MySQL or Postgres database, including managed services and Postgres-compatible engines, and the documentation lists the supported drivers.

For a team running a regional database behind an application that is read-heavy and globally distributed, the operational case is straightforward. Put one read path through the pooler, measure the cache hit rate on real traffic, and watch the two numbers that this release turned on: the rate of empty or malformed responses, and the connection success rate. Netics runs that kind of measurement work with DevOps pipelines and managed monitoring, and the cache-consistency lesson has a harder-edged sibling in what a misplaced cache endpoint exposes, which is how we read the unauthenticated KV cache server earlier in October.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: Agent Mail: Tencent Just Gave AI Agents Their Own Mailbox
description:
Agent Mail: Tencent Gives AI Agents Their Own Mailbox (@agent.qq.com), Open Source & Free in Beta | Lieke AI

  • @agent.qq.comDedicated agent mailbox Apache-2.0Open source 50/dayBeta send quota 6+ platformsMajor agents supported

In one line: why AI agents need their own mailbox

Two old paths for letting agents handle email — grant access to your personal inbox (privacy risk) or run your own SMTP (ops cost). Tencent QQ Mail's answer: give the agent a digital identity independent from humans: an isolated xxx@agent.qq.com address that can never touch your personal QQ/WeChat mail.
Internal beta opened June 23, 2026. Source code is Apache-2.0 on GitHub (Tencent/AgentlyMail); official site: agent.qq.com.

3-step setup, tested in ~5 minutes

Let the agent install it: ask your agent to read https://agent.qq.com/doc/cli-setup.md and follow the steps to install & configure Agent Mail CLI.

  • It runs automatically:npm install -g @tencent-qqmail/agently-clinpx skills add Tencent/AgentlyMail -g -yagently-cli auth loginOpen the printed authorization link in a browser.

  • Scan to authorize: after OAuth, run agently-cli +me — it returns xxx@agent.qq.com when configured.

Works with WorkBuddy, Claude Code, Cursor, Kimi Work, Doubao, Codex, Hermes and other mainstream agents. Read, send, search, attachments and live watch — all via one CLI.

Security: three layers built for agent workloads

Layer What it does
Physical isolation Agent gets a fresh data space; even a compromised agent cannot reach personal mail
Two-stage confirmation Send/reply/forward/delete requires the agent to generate a summary + confirmation token, then the user approves
Prompt-injection defense Malicious instructions inside inbound mail are treated as plain text, never as system commands

Six practical use cases (hands-on)

  • Invoice auto-expense: agent extracts amount/tax ID and files reimbursement reports

  • Newsletter digest: forward newsletters, get a daily AI summary

  • Order reconciliation: agent pulls order numbers into your sheets

  • A2A business email: procurement agent ↔ supplier agent, fully auditable

  • Verification-code relay: use Agent Mail for signups, agent auto-fills codes

  • AI job applications: dedicated address for resumes and interview scheduling

Competitive landscape: the agent-mail race

Agently Mail (Tencent) AgentMail (YC) Mail4Agent
Integration WeChat scan + CLI API + SDK API-first
Pricing Free in beta 3 mailboxes free, $20-200/mo paid Not public
Security Two-stage confirm + injection defense (unique) DIY DIY
China access No VPN needed VPN needed Fair
Ecosystem CLI + Skill path Python/TS SDK, MCP Server, Webhook Multi-framework

Bottom line: Agently Mail is the lowest-friction option for CN developers; AgentMail suits large overseas API/SDK deployments.

Beta limitations (stated honestly): 50 sends/day, 1GB per address — not production-ready until quotas open up; official Skill has Windows HTML-email layout issues (community fixes exist); A2A cross-domain protocol not yet documented; mailbox prefix can be changed only once.

Before your agent can run 24/7, you need reliable cloud compute

Agently Mail is just the first piece of agent infrastructure. The real backbone is elastic cloud servers that keep agents online around the clock. Lieke AI helps you get official promotional pricing.

Check Alibaba Cloud ECS deals →

Does authorization leak my QQ password? No. It uses the standard OAuth device-code flow; the CLI never stores your QQ password.
Install fails or is slow? Make sure npm can reach the public registry; if the auth link won't open, check access to agent.qq.com.
How does this differ from AgentMail / Mail4Agent? Same category, different positioning: Agently Mail focuses on China accessibility + CLI/Skill + unique security; AgentMail targets overseas API/SDK scale.
Production-ready? Beta quotas are tight (50/day, 1GB). Start with daily reports and newsletter digests; wait for quota release for production scale.

title: pg_hint_plan v1.9.0 Released
description:
The pg_hint_plan development team is pleased to announce pg_hint_plan 1.9.0. This release of pg_hint_plan adds compatibility with PostgreSQL 19, and includes various improvements and bug fixes. For more details, see the release notes. This new major version includes support for path generation strategies (PGS).

pg_hint_plan is a PostgreSQL extension that offers the possibility to tweak PostgreSQL execution plans using so-called "hints" in SQL comments. For more information, see the project page.

The documentation of the project is published at this page, and is synced up automatically from the source repository.

A new set of minor releases is available down to PostgreSQL 14, each marked with the following versions:

  • pg_hint_plan 1.8.1, compatible with PostgreSQL 18.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.7.2, compatible with PostgreSQL 17.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.6.3, compatible with PostgreSQL 16.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.5.4, compatible with PostgreSQL 15.
  • pg_hint_plan 1.4.5, compatible with PostgreSQL 14.

This is the last release planned for PostgreSQL 14.

Notable changes in this set of releases include the following bug fixes, where applicable:

  • Fix infinite loop with hint parser and multi-query strings
  • Add CHECK_FOR_INTERRUPTS() in get_hints_from_comment()
  • Ignore indexes without a name, like hypothetical indexes
  • Fix server crash when HintStateDump[2] throws an ERROR
  • Restore query ID after SPI execution in get_hints_from_table()
  • Correct schema-qualification of operators for hint table query
  • Add PG_MODULE_MAGIC_EXT
  • Update Japanese documentation

title: Drizzle vs Prisma in 2026: Benchmarks, Drizzle 1.0, Prisma 8 and Which to Choose
description:
I benchmarked Drizzle 0.45, the Drizzle 1.0 RC, Prisma 7 and the Prisma 8 RC against the same PostgreSQL 17 database. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Drizzle vs Prisma comes down to how you want to write data access in TypeScript. Drizzle is a thin, SQL-shaped query builder: your schema is TypeScript and every query maps closely to the SQL it sends. Prisma is a higher-level ORM: you write a schema file and get a generated, model-based client. Both are type-safe, and both work well with PostgreSQL and Next.js.

In October 2026 both are in the middle of a major version. Drizzle 1.0 is a release candidate while 0.45.4 is still npm latest. Prisma 8 is a release candidate that npm latest already installs. So I benchmarked all five combinations against the same PostgreSQL 17 database. On simple queries the gap was a tenth of a millisecond. On one common query pattern it was 6-19x, and the cause was the shape of the SQL, not the ORM.

TL;DR: Drizzle or Prisma in 2026?

Pick Drizzle if you think in SQL, deploy to serverless or edge, and want the smallest install and fastest cold start: 30 MB and about 35 ms bundled in my test. Pick Prisma 7 if you want the most guided workflow, a generated client and Prisma Migrate. Wait for GA before moving production to Drizzle 1.0 or Prisma 8.

Drizzle Prisma
Stable line 0.45.4 (npm latest) 7.10.1 (npm prev)
Next major 1.0.0-rc.4 (npm rc) 8.0.0-rc (npm latest)
Schema lives in TypeScript (pgTable) schema.prisma (7) or contract.prisma (8)
Code generation None prisma generate (7), prisma contract emit (8)
Query style SQL builder + relational db.query Model client (7), chained db.orm (8)
Migrations drizzle-kit generate / migrate / push Prisma Migrate
Production install (my test) 21-30 MB, 18 packages 329 MB (7), 130 MB (8)
Bundled cold start (my test) ~35 ms ~100 ms (7), ~370 ms (8 RC)

What is the difference between Drizzle and Prisma?

Drizzle defines tables in TypeScript and gives you a typed SQL builder, so db.select().from(users).where(...) reads like the SQL it sends, with no generate step. Prisma defines models in its own schema language, generates a client and hides SQL behind model methods. Drizzle is closer to the database; Prisma is closer to your domain model.

The same table in each:

```ts title="schema.ts (Drizzle 1.0)"
import { defineRelations } from "drizzle-orm";
import { boolean, index, integer, pgTable, serial, text, timestamp } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const users = pgTable("User", {
id: serial().primaryKey(),
email: text().notNull().unique(),
name: text(),
createdAt: timestamp({ precision: 3, mode: "date" }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

export const posts = pgTable("Post", {
id: serial().primaryKey(),
title: text().notNull(),
published: boolean().notNull().default(false),
views: integer().notNull().default(0),
authorId: integer().notNull().references(() => users.id, { onDelete: "cascade" }),
}, (t) => [index("Post_authorId_idx").on(t.authorId)]);

export const relations = defineRelations({ users, posts }, (r) => ({
users: { posts: r.many.posts() },
posts: { author: r.one.users({ from: r.posts.authorId, to: r.users.id }) },
}));






```prisma title="prisma/schema.prisma (Prisma 7)"
model User {
  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
  email     String   @unique
  name      String?
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
  posts     Post[]
}

model Post {
  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
  title     String
  published Boolean @default(false)
  views     Int     @default(0)
  authorId  Int
  author    User    @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

  @@index([authorId])
}

How do queries compare in Drizzle and Prisma?

All four clients can fetch a user with their posts in one call. Drizzle 1.0 uses object filters in db.query, Prisma 7 uses findMany with include, and Prisma 8 chains .include("posts") on a collection. The type-safety level is the same; the difference is whether the code looks like SQL or like method calls.

These are the exact queries from my benchmark, and all of them type-check under strict:

```ts title="Fetch 20 users with their posts"
// Drizzle 0.45 (RQB v1)
db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true }, orderBy: (u, { asc }) => [asc(u.id)], offset, limit: 20 });

// Drizzle 1.0 (RQB v2)
db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, offset, limit: 20 });

// Prisma 7
prisma.user.findMany({ include: { posts: true }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, skip: offset, take: 20 });

// Prisma 8 RC
db.orm.public.User.include("posts").orderBy((u) => u.id.asc()).offset(offset).limit(20).all();




Drizzle also keeps its plain SQL builder (`db.select().from(posts).innerJoin(...)`) for anything the relational API does not cover. Prisma 7 falls back to `$queryRaw` or TypedSQL, and Prisma 8 has its own SQL builder. I covered Prisma 8's query API in detail in my [Prisma 8 guide](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/prisma-8).

## Is Drizzle faster than Prisma?

For single-row reads and inserts, barely. In my test every client answered a primary-key lookup in 0.12-0.20 ms against local PostgreSQL, and over a network that gap disappears. The real difference was in nested pagination: with `OFFSET`, single-query JSON loading got 6-11x slower than Prisma 7's two-query default.

### Benchmark setup

- PostgreSQL 17.11 on the same machine (8 vCPU Xeon, 15 GB RAM), Node.js 24.22.0, 1,000 users and 10,000 posts with an index on `Post.authorId`.
- Each case: 200 warm-up calls, then 2,000 timed calls. Each client ran 3 times, with inserted rows deleted before each run. The table shows the median of the three per-run medians.
- Versions: Prisma 7.10.1 with `@prisma/adapter-pg`, Drizzle 0.45.4, Drizzle 1.0.0-rc.4 (with and without `jit: true`), and Prisma 8 (`@prisma/orm-postgres` 8.0.0-rc.18).
- "Deep page" means 20 users plus their posts at `OFFSET` 0 to 960.

### Results (median, milliseconds)

| Query | Prisma 7.10.1 | Drizzle 0.45.4 | Drizzle 1.0 rc.4 | Drizzle 1.0 `jit` | Prisma 8 rc.18 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Find user by id | 0.150 | 0.129 | **0.121** | 0.136 | 0.195 |
| First page, 20 users + posts | 0.730 | 0.719 | **0.561** | 0.617 | 1.185 |
| Deep page, 20 users + posts | **0.749** | 4.650 | 5.164 | 5.287 | 8.060 |
| Insert one post | 0.168 | 0.146 | **0.139** | 0.164 | 0.208 |
| Process RSS after run | 289 MB | 251 MB | 295 MB | 296 MB | 404 MB |

Two things stand out. Drizzle 1.0 was the fastest at nearly everything, but `jit: true` made no measurable difference here. Drizzle documents it as "just-in-time compiled row mappers," and mapping 20 rows is not where the time goes. And the deep-page row looks like a Prisma win, but it isn't one, as the next section shows.

## Why are nested queries with OFFSET slow?

Drizzle and Prisma 8 load relations in one SQL statement, using a JSON subquery for each parent row. PostgreSQL applies `OFFSET` last, so it builds the JSON for every skipped row and then throws it away. At `OFFSET 960`, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` showed the posts subquery running 980 times to return 20 users.

![Why OFFSET is slow with single-query relation loading: PostgreSQL builds JSON posts for every skipped row before applying OFFSET, while two-query loading and keyset pagination only touch 20 users](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792248750/fabwaseem/blog/drizzle-vs-prisma/diagram-sql.jpg)

This is the SQL Drizzle 0.45 generated (Drizzle 1.0 is nearly identical):



```sql
select "users"."id", "users"."email", "users"."name", "users"."createdAt", "users_posts"."data" as "posts"
from "User" "users"
left join lateral (
  select coalesce(json_agg(json_build_array(...)), '[]'::json) as "data"
  from "Post" "users_posts" where "users_posts"."authorId" = "users"."id"
) "users_posts" on true
order by "users"."id" asc limit $1 offset $2

The PostgreSQL docs warn about this directly: "The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient" (PostgreSQL 17, LIMIT and OFFSET). Here, each skipped row includes a full posts subquery.

Prisma 7 avoided it only because it sent two queries: the 20 users, then SELECT ... FROM "Post" WHERE "authorId" IN (...). When I turned on Prisma 7's relationJoins preview and set relationLoadStrategy: "join", the deep page went from 0.79 ms to 14.8 ms, the slowest result in the whole test. Prisma's relation queries docs say join uses "a combination of LATERAL JOINs and JSON aggregation", which is the same shape.

How do I fix slow nested pagination?

Use keyset (cursor) pagination instead of OFFSET: ask for "the 20 users after id X". PostgreSQL then seeks straight to the right index position and builds JSON for only 20 rows. In my test, Drizzle 1.0 deep pages dropped from 5.16 ms to 0.66 ms and Prisma 8 from 8.06 ms to 1.29 ms.

```ts title="Keyset pagination (both tested)"
// Drizzle 1.0
db.query.users.findMany({ with: { posts: true }, where: { id: { gt: afterId } }, orderBy: { id: "asc" }, limit: 20 });

// Prisma 8 RC
db.orm.public.User.where((u) => u.id.gt(afterId)).include("posts").orderBy((u) => u.id.asc()).limit(20).all();

// Prisma 7
prisma.user.findMany({ include: { posts: true }, cursor: { id: afterId }, skip: 1, take: 20, orderBy: { id: "asc" } });




Prisma's [pagination guide](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/prisma-client/queries/pagination) recommends the same: use cursor-based pagination "when you care more about performance and consistency as the dataset grows." If you need page numbers, run the parent query first and load children with a second `IN (...)` query. That is exactly what Prisma 7's default does.

## Which has a faster cold start, Drizzle or Prisma?

Drizzle, once bundled. With esbuild, importing the client and running the first query took about 35 ms with Drizzle, about 100 ms with Prisma 7 and about 370 ms with Prisma 8 RC. Unbundled, Drizzle was slower than Prisma 7, because Node loaded 425-528 separate Drizzle module files from `node_modules`.

| Median of 5 process starts | Prisma 7.10.1 | Drizzle 0.45.4 | Drizzle 1.0 rc.4 | Prisma 8 rc.18 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unbundled: import + first query | 55 + 89 ms | 400 + 31 ms | 699 + 18 ms | 494 + 30 ms |
| esbuild bundle: import + first query | 21 + 78 ms | 17 + 19 ms | 16 + 18 ms | 342 + 26 ms |
| Bundle size | 5.0 MB | 448 KB | 476 KB | 1.8 MB |

Next.js and most serverless builds bundle server code, so the bundled row is the one that usually applies. Prisma 7's import is fast, but its first query costs about 78 ms; the client ships its query compiler as base64-encoded WebAssembly, which is the likely cost of that first call. Prisma 8 RC's time goes into startup itself. A CPU profile showed the top functions inside arktype's `@ark/schema` and `@ark/util`, which Prisma 8 uses for runtime validation. That is RC behaviour and may change before GA.

## How big is Drizzle vs Prisma in node_modules?

Drizzle installed in 21 MB (0.45.4) or 30 MB (1.0 RC) with 18 packages, including `pg`. With `npm ci --omit=dev`, Prisma 7 came to 329 MB and 345 packages, and Prisma 8 RC to 130 MB and 118 packages. For Docker images and serverless size limits, that is the clearest difference between them.

Where the Prisma weight comes from, according to `npm ls` and `du`:

- **Prisma 7:** `@prisma/client` (72 MB) lists `prisma` and `typescript` as optional peer dependencies. My project had both as devDependencies, so npm kept them in the production tree, along with the CLI, `@prisma/studio-core` (43 MB) and `@prisma/dev`.
- **Prisma 8 RC:** `@prisma/orm-postgres` depends on `@prisma/orm-toolchain`, which brings `typescript`, `prettier` and rolldown into a production install.

If image size matters, bundle the server and copy only the output. My [Next.js AI starter kit](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/nextjs-ai-starter-kit) uses Drizzle partly for this reason.

## How do migrations compare?

Both generate SQL migration files from your schema. drizzle-kit diffs your TypeScript schema and writes plain SQL, and `push` can sync a dev database without a migration file. Prisma Migrate diffs `schema.prisma`, keeps history in `prisma/migrations` and manages a shadow database for `migrate dev`. Both let you edit the generated SQL before applying it.

Drizzle 1.0 changed the folder layout. `npx drizzle-kit generate --name init` created this:



```text
drizzle/
└── 20261017144733_init/
    ├── migration.sql
    └── snapshot.json

There is no meta/_journal.json any more. The Drizzle v1 upgrade guide says this removes "potential Git conflicts with the journal file," and drizzle-kit generate now runs commutativity checks that flag migrations on two branches that change the same thing. Run npx drizzle-kit up once to convert an existing 0.x migrations folder.

Prisma Migrate is still the more guided tool: prisma migrate dev uses a shadow database to detect drift and offers to reset the dev database when history and schema disagree. One Prisma 7 change to know: seeding no longer runs automatically during migrate dev or migrate reset; you run npx prisma db seed yourself. See the Prisma Migrate docs.

What changed in Drizzle 1.0?

Drizzle 1.0 removes the old relational query API (RQB v1) and replaces it with defineRelations() and RQB v2. Filters and ordering become plain objects. Validators move into the package as drizzle-orm/zod and similar, getTableColumns becomes getColumns, and drizzle-kit drops the migration journal. It also adds MSSQL and CockroachDB dialects.

From the official v0 to v1 changes page:

Area 0.x 1.0
Relations relations() per table One defineRelations() call
Filters where: (u, { eq }) => eq(u.id, 1) where: { id: 1 }
Casing drizzle({ casing: "snake_case" }) snakeCase.table(...)
Validation drizzle-zod package drizzle-orm/zod
Migrations meta/_journal.json One folder per migration
push / pull public schema only by default All schemas by default
Introspection ~10 s under 1 s (Drizzle's figure)

The relations v1 to v2 guide covers the query migration step by step. As of October 17, 2026, npm latest is still 0.45.4 (published October 8) and rc is 1.0.0-rc.4 (June 27).

Should I use Prisma 8 or Prisma 7?

For production today, Prisma 7. Prisma 8 is a rewrite with a new contract file, a new runtime package and a chained query API, and it is still a release candidate. In my test it was also the slowest to start and the heaviest per process. Prisma 8 is worth trying on a branch now; plan the switch after GA.

Note that npm install prisma already installs Prisma 8, so pin prisma@7 and @prisma/client@7 in existing projects. The full migration path, with the contract and the new client, is in my Prisma 8 guide.

Which should I choose for Next.js?

Both work in Next.js 16 server components, route handlers and server actions. Choose Drizzle for Vercel functions, edge routes or small Docker images, where cold start and install size matter. Choose Prisma 7 when a team wants one schema file, generated types and Prisma Migrate's guardrails more than they want SQL control.

Your situation Pick
You think in SQL and want queries that map one-to-one Drizzle
Serverless, edge or tight cold-start budget Drizzle
Small Docker image or function size limit Drizzle
Team wants one schema file and a generated client Prisma 7
Guided migrations with drift detection and a shadow DB Prisma 7
Existing Prisma 6/7 app Stay on Prisma 7, pin it, test 8 on a branch
New app starting this month Drizzle 0.45 or Prisma 7, and plan the move to 1.0 / 8
Paginating nested data Either: use keyset pagination, not deep OFFSET

Auth libraries matter here too. Better Auth 1.7 lists both drizzle-orm (0.45.2+ or 1.0 RC) and Prisma (5 to 7) as supported peers, but not Prisma 8 yet.

Common Drizzle and Prisma mistakes

  • Deep OFFSET with nested relations. Both ORMs build JSON for every skipped row. Use keyset pagination or a second query.
  • Turning on Prisma relationJoins everywhere. In my test it was slower for paginated includes. Measure per query.
  • Unpinned prisma installs. latest is Prisma 8 RC. Pin major versions in Prisma 7 projects.
  • Expecting jit: true to fix slow queries. It speeds up row mapping, not the SQL.
  • Running Drizzle unbundled on serverless. It loads hundreds of module files at startup. Bundle the server output.
  • Upgrading to Drizzle 1.0 without drizzle-kit up. Old migration folders must be converted first.

Related: choosing primary keys for these schemas? In UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18 I benchmarked uuidv7() against UUIDv4 and bigint on 10M rows, with tested Prisma and Drizzle setups for a database-side uuidv7() default.

Related: building the API layer with NestJS? My NestJS 12 migration guide covers the v11 to v12 upgrade, Zod validation (28% faster than class-validator in my test) and v11 vs v12 benchmarks.

Key takeaways

  • Drizzle is a SQL-first TypeScript query builder with no code generation; Prisma is a schema-first ORM with a generated client. Both are fully type-safe.
  • On simple queries, all five clients I tested answered within 0.12-0.21 ms of local PostgreSQL, so raw speed rarely decides the choice.
  • Single-query relation loading plus a deep OFFSET was 6-19x slower than two queries, whether it came from Drizzle, Prisma 8 or Prisma 7 with relationJoins. Keyset pagination fixed it.
  • Bundled, Drizzle started in about 35 ms, Prisma 7 in about 100 ms and Prisma 8 RC in about 370 ms.
  • Production installs were 21-30 MB for Drizzle, 329 MB for Prisma 7 and 130 MB for Prisma 8 RC.
  • Drizzle 1.0 and Prisma 8 are both release candidates on October 17, 2026; use Drizzle 0.45 or Prisma 7 in production and pin your versions.

FAQ

Is Drizzle better than Prisma?

Neither is better for everyone. Drizzle suits developers who want SQL-shaped queries, no code generation, small installs and fast serverless cold starts. Prisma suits teams that want one schema file, a generated model client and guided migrations. Both are fully type-safe, and on simple queries their speed was within 0.1 ms in my test.

Is Drizzle faster than Prisma?

Slightly, on most queries. Drizzle 1.0 RC was fastest on lookups, first pages and inserts, but every client stayed between 0.12 and 0.21 ms on simple queries against local PostgreSQL. The bigger differences were cold start (Drizzle about 35 ms bundled vs about 100 ms for Prisma 7) and nested pagination with OFFSET.

Why is my nested query with OFFSET slow?

Drizzle, Prisma 8 and Prisma 7 with relationJoins load relations in one SQL statement, with a JSON subquery per parent row. PostgreSQL applies OFFSET last, so it builds JSON for every skipped row. At OFFSET 960 the posts subquery ran 980 times. Use keyset pagination (WHERE id > lastId) or a second query.

Is Drizzle 1.0 stable?

Not yet. On October 17, 2026, npm latest for drizzle-orm is 0.45.4, published October 8, and the rc tag is 1.0.0-rc.4 from June 27. Drizzle 1.0 replaces relational queries v1 with defineRelations and RQB v2 and changes the migration folder layout, so test it on a branch first.

Should I use Prisma 8 or Prisma 7?

Use Prisma 7 in production for now. Prisma 8 is a release candidate with a new contract file, a new runtime package and a chained query API. In my test it also had the slowest cold start, about 370 ms bundled. Note that npm install prisma already installs Prisma 8, so pin prisma@7 in existing projects.

Which is better for serverless, Drizzle or Prisma?

Drizzle. Bundled with esbuild, importing Drizzle and running the first query took about 35 ms, against about 100 ms for Prisma 7 and about 370 ms for Prisma 8 RC. Drizzle's production install was 21 to 30 MB, while Prisma 7's came to 329 MB with npm ci --omit=dev.

Does Drizzle have migrations like Prisma Migrate?

Yes. drizzle-kit generate diffs your TypeScript schema into SQL migration files, drizzle-kit migrate applies them, and drizzle-kit push syncs a dev database directly. Drizzle 1.0 stores each migration in its own folder with no journal file and checks for conflicting migrations across branches. Prisma Migrate adds a shadow database and drift detection.

Does Better Auth work with Drizzle and Prisma?

Yes, with both. Better Auth 1.7.10 lists drizzle-orm 0.45.2 or newer, including the 1.0 release candidates, and Prisma 5, 6 and 7 as supported peer dependencies. Prisma 8 is not in its supported range yet, so a Better Auth app on Prisma should stay on Prisma 7 for now.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Findings from the $1M Vercel Sandbox challenge
description:
In August, we launched the $1M hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox, inviting security researchers to try and escape Vercel Sandbox. We also coordinated with cybersecurity experts Trail of Bits to review the source code and security architecture.

Here is a summary of the challenge:

  • 1,285 reports over two weeks

  • $242,000 in bounties paid out

  • One Linux kernel zeroday vulnerability uncovered

No reports showed anyone accessing customer data in Vercel Sandbox. The most severe finding was the defect in the upstream Linux kernel.

The kernel zero day

The program's most important report arrived on day three.

Paulos Yibelo (pwn.ai), a HackerOne researcher working from a standard sandbox with no special access, found a defect in the Linux kernel's networking stack. Paulos discovered that specially crafted packets sent from within the microVM enabled three different attacks:

  1. Leak host memory over the network

  2. Crash the host machine

  3. Execute code on the host

Leaking host memory

In the first attack, memory from the host, the machine your sandbox shares with other tenants, shows up in packets the guest sends over the internet. This can happen continuously, for as long as the guest keeps sending.

This attack was demonstrated against Vercel production sandboxes.

Crashing the host and executing code on the host

The researcher also found that by sending specific packets, they could compromise the host.

First, by sending two packets, the researcher crashed the host machine, shutting down every sandbox running on it. Second, using the same flaw, they were able to run commands with full administrator privileges on the host, breaking out of the sandbox’s isolation boundary.

The packet-related crash and code execution attacks were demonstrated on the researcher’s own KVM and Firecracker machines matching Vercel Sandbox configuration.

Responsibly disclosing the kernel vulnerability

Almost every major cloud provider isolates customer workloads on this same layer of the Linux kernel, so any defect is shared-infrastructure risk.

Immediately after being notified, we collaborated with the researcher to understand and mitigate the vulnerability, working with AWS and other industry partners to prioritize a fix, and ensuring that Vercel customers and other developers using the kernel were safe.

The researcher also contacted the kernel maintainers and worked with them to create candidate patches. Fixes are under private review and CVEs are pending, so we are not publishing additional details until the patches are public. We are disclosing the existence of the vulnerability because it was separately disclosed in public.

Our approach to pressure-testing Vercel Sandbox

The HackerOne challenge made bounties available to any researcher, but we also extended our program to include internal evaluations and an independent investigation.

Before launching the public bounty, we performed live security assessments internally with full source access and support from the engineers who created and maintain Vercel Sandbox. We also engaged Trail of Bits, bringing on two engineers to evaluate our security architecture.

Not every finding came from the outside. Marcos Hernanz, a Vercel intern, found a cross-tenant data leak in the Linux device-mapper storage layer. This vulnerability let any sandbox read recycled disk blocks from previously deleted sandboxes.

The white-box deep dive

Trail of Bits spent four engineer-weeks inside our source code, with full access to the repositories and two enterprise test teams. They delivered 20 findings, and each was tested, confirmed, and referenced to the exact code.

They also performed an architectural review and concluded that our virtualization boundary is sound. Each sandbox runs on its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and the device model is deliberately tiny. No guest shares a running kernel with the host, or with another tenant.

On top of that foundation, they gave us three structural recommendations, which we implemented:

  • Find and eliminate all trust in the guest. Our control plane accepted values returned by software running inside the microVM, and every one of those values is tenant input. Anything that crosses the boundary should be derived server-side or signed with a key the guest cannot reach.

  • One policy, one decider. Egress enforcement was split across subsystems that each parsed the same network policy independently, and they did not always agree. We now use one canonicalization routine per data type, one component per decision, and revalidate connections when policy changes.

  • Assume the next zero day. We strengthened the protections around each sandbox to limit the damage if an attacker exploits the virtualization software. We keep host kernels up to date, have disabled nested virtualization, and use Firecracker’s jailer to run each microVM process with restricted permissions and isolate it from the rest of the host.

Vercel Sandbox findings

We received 1,285 reports in two weeks. This volume is only possible because researchers now hunt at AI speed.

Here is a breakdown of reports by category:

  • 877 duplicates

  • 319 not applicable

  • 57 valid

  • 32 informative

In our report triage we have validated:

  • 1 Critical finding

  • 5 High findings

  • 9 Medium findings

  • 42 Low findings

  • 32 Informative findings

We have paid out $242,000 in bug bounties.

The medium, Low, and Informative findings are small policy-boundary gaps, like a firewall rule that behaved differently than documented and a field that trusted the guest more than it should.

The most severe finding was the Linux kernel zero day defect, and no reports showed anyone reading a customer’s files, secrets, or application data.

We were most impressed with the heterogeneity of the reports. It was clear that researchers used different setups and have different obsessions. Some clearly know Linux namespaces and steered their agents straight at the kernel boundary. Others went after the network policies, and many went after areas we didn’t think to put on the menu.

That variety is what you're funding with a public challenge. Here's one of the more interesting findings it produced.

Cross-tenant disk snapshot restore (with limits)

Filed on day one of the challenge, this report is our favorite example of why we run a public bug bounty, even after internal assessments and a white-box engagement.

When you snapshot a sandbox, the control plane has to record where the snapshot data landed: {storage_url, size, checksum}. The flaw the researcher found was subtle: that answer came from software running inside the guest, and services running on the host trusted it. That is a trust-boundary violation. The guest is where our customers (and hackers) run untrusted code, so the host can never take its word as authoritative.

The researcher combined a known, documented container-escape primitive with this trust flaw. They intercepted the snapshot response inside their own sandbox and rewrote it, swapping the storage objects of two snapshots belonging to two separate accounts they owned. That meant restoring "your" snapshot materialized the other account's entire filesystem.

The researcher demonstrated that each account could read and modify the other’s files, verified the results using hashes, and preserved the test resources so we could independently reproduce the findings.

The limits of this attack matter. Aiming the swap at a specific victim required knowing that victim's internal snapshot storage key, a random 96-bit identifier the platform generates per snapshot and never exposes through the API. The only place that key appears is inside the victim's own sandbox. The researcher owned both accounts, which is what made the proof possible; there was no demonstrated path for a stranger to target another tenant. We still treated it as a priority fix, because a boundary that depends on a secret staying secret is not a boundary.

Trail of Bits independently flagged the same root cause in their assessment, which told us the finding was real, important, and discoverable from two completely different angles.

The fix shipped within a week, and the control plane now binds every snapshot object to the project that created it and rejects anything else. Snapshot creation moved out of the guest-reachable environment into a host-side service, and storage paths are project-scoped with strictly validated URLs.

Thank you to the research community

We would like to thank every researcher who filed a report, whether their finding was a zero day or a duplicate. Every technique discovered in the challenge informs how we protect the workloads running on Vercel Sandbox.

Thank you also to Trail of Bits for your comprehensive internal investigation and guidance.

Read the original challenge announcement and learn more about Vercel Sandbox in the documentation.

title: Collections.unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf in Java
description:
Quick Answer: Collections.unmodifiableList in Java creates a read-only view wrapper over an existing collection rather than an immutable copy. If the underlying collection mutates, those changes immediately reflect in the unmodifiable view. To create a true, isolated snapshot of your data that resists changes to the original source, use List.copyOf() introduced in Java 10.

When you pass a list to another component in your application, you usually want to guarantee its state won't change unexpectedly. You might call Collections.unmodifiableList(), hand over the reference, and assume your work is done. But there is a subtle trap in this approach that leads to unexpected side effects in production.

What is the difference between an unmodifiable view and an immutable list in Java?

An unmodifiable view prevents callers from mutating a list through that specific reference, but it remains linked to the original collection. An immutable list, by contrast, is completely decoupled from the original data source and cannot be altered by any reference.

If you pass around an unmodifiable view, you are essentially placing a clear glass shield over a whiteboard. The consumer holding the view cannot write on the glass, but if another thread or service writes directly on the whiteboard behind it, the consumer sees those changes instantly.

How does Collections.unmodifiableList handle underlying mutations?

When you pass a collection into Collections.unmodifiableList(), Java wraps your original list in a lightweight decorator. Any attempt to call write operations like add() or remove() on this wrapper throws an UnsupportedOperationException.

However, because it remains a view, any direct modification to the underlying collection updates what the view renders.

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Alice", "Bob"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(names);

names.add("Charlie"); // Modifying the underlying list

System.out.println(view.size()); // Prints 3, not 2!

If you hand this view to a service expecting a stable collection, background updates to names will leak through, potentially causing silent bugs or race conditions.

How do you create a true snapshot list in Java using List.copyOf?

Introduced in Java 10, List.copyOf() creates an unmodifiable list containing a shallow copy of the source collection's elements. Because this operation creates a brand-new backing store, subsequent modifications to the source collection have zero effect on the copied list.

It is vital to remember that List.copyOf() creates a shallow copy. While the list structure itself is completely immutable and isolated, the objects contained inside it are not cloned. If you store mutable objects inside the list, their internal properties can still be modified elsewhere.

The same concept applies across languages. If you are working in C#, calling .AsReadOnly() on a list produces a ReadOnlyCollection<T>, which behaves exactly like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList() by acting as a view over the backing list.

Comparison of Read-Only and Snapshot Collections

Method / API Type Decoupled From Source? Language Version
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) Read-Only View No Java 1.2+
List.copyOf(list) Immutable Snapshot Yes Java 10+
list.AsReadOnly() Read-Only View No .NET Framework 2.0+

Frequently Asked Questions

Does List.copyOf create a deep copy of objects in Java?

No, List.copyOf() performs a shallow copy of the collection elements. The reference structure of the list becomes immutable and decoupled from the source collection, but the individual elements inside still refer to their original object instances in memory.

Why does Collections.unmodifiableList throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime?

Java's collection framework uses unified interfaces like List for both mutable and read-only structures rather than separate interface hierarchies. Calling mutation methods on read-only wrappers triggers a runtime UnsupportedOperationException to enforce the contract without breaking interface consistency.

How does C# handle read-only list wrappers compared to Java?

C# uses the .AsReadOnly() extension method on List<T>, which returns a ReadOnlyCollection<T>. Just like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList(), this wrapper provides a read-only interface but remains a live view over the underlying list.

title: Go Scheduled Payment Data Cleanup — Compare 4 Cron Scheduler Latency and Cost Tests
description:
Short answer: choose a cron scheduler for nightly payment reconciliation by testing admission latency, duplicate delivery, missed-run recovery, and execution isolation; the cheapest trigger is a poor bargain if it can silently widen the cleanup backlog.

For a customer-support system, the job is deceptively plain: reconcile yesterday's payment-provider records, repair local status drift, and make corrected state available before agents begin answering billing tickets. The scheduling decision should follow the error budget for that outcome. If agents need corrected data by 06:00 UTC, a trigger at 05:59 with a one-minute runtime has no capacity margin. A trigger at 02:00, feeding bounded workers that can replay partitions, converts a brittle deadline into an observable batch SLO.

Don't optimize the clock first.

How should cost govern a cron scheduler comparison for scheduled data cleanup?

I would run four tests against the whole path, not just the timer: trigger admission latency, duplicate invocation, an intentionally unavailable worker, and a cleanup partition that exceeds its normal runtime. This is a capacity-planning exercise — arrival rate, service rate, backlog age, and deadline are the useful variables. A scheduler's dashboard can show a green invocation while the payment cursor remains twelve hours behind.

The bounded production scenario is one nightly reconciliation with 24 hourly partitions. Each partition reads a stable provider time range, compares external payment IDs with local records, and writes an idempotent result. That number is an example of partition shape, not a benchmark: use enough partitions to replay a narrow failure domain, but not so many that scheduling and database overhead dominate useful work. I'm not sure there is a universal best partition duration; provider rate limits, record skew, and the local write path settle it, and a load test with production-shaped distributions is what resolves the uncertainty.

A useful acceptance sheet is short:

Test Evidence to retain Failure decision
Admission latency Intended time and observed start time Does the remaining window preserve the batch SLO?
Duplicate trigger Two runs with the same logical date Do idempotency keys prevent repeated mutation?
Worker unavailable Trigger accepted while workers are stopped Is work durably recoverable without guessing?
Long partition One partition crosses the next tick Does overlap stay bounded by a lease or concurrency rule?

These tests separate a trigger from a job system. A trigger decides when work becomes eligible. A job system owns durable state, acknowledgements, retry policy, concurrency, and backlog. Combining those responsibilities can be convenient for a small workload, but treating them as the same thing makes incident diagnosis muddy: an absent trigger, a rejected enqueue, and a slow consumer create the same visible symptom — stale support data — while requiring different repairs.

Govern the payment data window before touching the clock

Consider a production incident as a tabletop rather than a claimed war story. The 02:00 trigger fires, the payment provider answers with HTTP 429 for several partitions, and the next run begins before the first has drained. If the job means “delete or update everything older than midnight,” the second run can race the first, retry already-applied writes, or move a shared cursor past records that were never reconciled. The invariant revealed by this scenario is more valuable than any scheduler feature list: each unit of cleanup needs a stable identity, a bounded input interval, and a result that can be applied more than once without changing the final state.

The obvious first model is cron -> cleanup(). It is also where SLOs disappear. The safer model is cron -> create logical run -> enqueue partitions -> workers -> reconcile run; its extra durable state costs storage and operational attention, but it gives on-call engineers a ledger of what should have happened, what did happen, and what remains eligible for retry. This doesn't create exactly-once execution. It makes at-least-once execution tolerable through idempotent effects. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation is useful here because it distinguishes consumer acknowledgements from publisher confirms: the broker accepting a message and a worker completing its effect are separate events.

Here is the preventative boundary in Go. The scheduler calls Start, while the repository enforces uniqueness for the logical date and the queue carries partition identities. Implementations can use a database uniqueness constraint and a durable queue; the interface keeps vendor choice outside the reconciliation rule.

package reconcile

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Partition struct {
    RunDate string
    Start   time.Time
    End     time.Time
}

type RunRepository interface {
    CreateOnce(ctx context.Context, runDate string) (created bool, err error)
}

type Queue interface {
    Enqueue(ctx context.Context, key string, p Partition) error
}

type Starter struct {
    Runs  RunRepository
    Queue Queue
}

func (s Starter) Start(ctx context.Context, runDate string, dayStart time.Time) error {
    created, err := s.Runs.CreateOnce(ctx, runDate)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create reconciliation run: %w", err)
    }
    if !created {
        return nil // A repeated trigger refers to the existing logical run.
    }

    var enqueueErrs []error
    for hour := 0; hour < 24; hour++ {
        start := dayStart.Add(time.Duration(hour) * time.Hour)
        p := Partition{RunDate: runDate, Start: start, End: start.Add(time.Hour)}
        key := fmt.Sprintf("payment-reconcile/%s/%02d", runDate, hour)
        if err := s.Queue.Enqueue(ctx, key, p); err != nil {
            enqueueErrs = append(enqueueErrs, fmt.Errorf("enqueue %s: %w", key, err))
        }
    }
    return errors.Join(enqueueErrs...)
}

One detail matters: after CreateOnce succeeds, failed partition enqueues must remain discoverable in the run ledger so a reconciler can enqueue the missing work. Returning an error is necessary for observability, but it isn't the recovery mechanism. A periodic sweeper can compare expected partition identities with accepted ones and fill gaps; because identities are stable, that repair is safe to repeat.

Slow down here.

Test each trigger boundary with the same harness

GitHub Actions scheduled workflows are attractive when cleanup already lives beside repository automation. Its documentation says scheduled workflows run from the latest commit on the default branch, can be delayed during high load, and may be dropped under sufficiently high load; the shortest interval is five minutes. Those properties can fit a non-urgent maintenance task, but they make the workflow history an inadequate system of record for a deadline-bound reconciliation unless the job also records durable run intent elsewhere. Repository access and workflow permissions also expand the blast radius beyond “wake a worker.”

Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers invoke a Worker's scheduled handler on UTC time. Cloudflare documents that trigger changes can take several minutes, up to 15 minutes, to propagate. This model keeps the trigger close to lightweight edge code, while the execution limits and the need for durable reconciliation state still determine whether the work belongs in one invocation or should be handed to another worker path. It is a boundary choice, not a guarantee that a large batch finishes because the clock fired.

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler exposes one-time and recurring schedules, flexible time windows, retry policy, and dead-letter queue configuration. Those controls make delivery policy explicit, with the trade-off of cloud IAM, target configuration, and another provider-specific control plane. For teams already operating that environment, those dependencies may be normal; for a portable or self-hosted stack, they are lock-in and on-call surface that must earn their place.

BullMQ represents a different boundary. It is a Redis-backed Node.js queue with job scheduling and worker semantics, so choosing it means owning or buying the Redis layer and operating consumers rather than selecting a remote trigger alone. RabbitMQ can supply durable messaging and acknowledgement semantics, but cron eligibility remains a separate concern. These aren't rankings. They are different allocations of responsibility between source control automation, edge execution, a cloud scheduler, and an application-owned queue.

Option shape Best evidence from the four tests Operational cost to count
Repository-scheduled workflow Workflow start history plus external run ledger Repository permissions, variable start time, runner use
Edge cron handler Trigger event plus durable handoff record Execution limits, deployment propagation, state service
Cloud scheduler targeting a worker Delivery attempts, retry policy, dead-letter records IAM, target policy, provider control plane
Application queue with repeatable jobs Queue state, acknowledgements, backlog age Data-store operations, consumers, upgrades, paging

Price should be measured from the current official calculators against expected invocations, execution duration, storage, logs, egress, and on-call ownership; a trigger's sticker price alone excludes most of the system. Published rates and free allowances change, so hard-coding a winner into an architecture review ages badly. The latency side is equally contextual: nightly work rarely needs millisecond admission, but it does need enough recovery time before the support-data deadline.

A Go implementation for idempotent partition admission

The worker needs a lease or equivalent concurrency guard, an idempotency key at the mutation boundary, retry classification, and a checkpoint that advances only after the partition's effects are durable. A 429 response is retryable under the provider's policy; malformed input or an impossible state transition usually needs quarantine and review. Don't turn every error into an immediate retry. Correlated retries can consume the remaining batch window faster than ordinary processing.

For observability, retain logical run date, partition identity, attempt count, intended trigger time, accepted time, worker start time, completion time, and a low-cardinality outcome. From those fields, derive admission delay, queue delay, processing duration, oldest incomplete partition age, success ratio, and projected finish time. Alert on user impact or a threatened deadline rather than on one failed attempt; the retry can be healthy while the backlog trend is not. Logs help explain a partition, metrics show the fleet, and the run ledger answers the awkward audit question: which payment intervals were actually reconciled?

Capacity planning closes the loop. Let W be the available window in seconds, R the sustained records processed per second after rate limiting, and N the expected record count. Require N/R to sit comfortably below W, then test the margin with skew and retries. The exact headroom is an SLO policy decision, not a universal constant. If a provider permits only modest concurrency, earlier scheduling or incremental reconciliation can buy more safety than a larger worker fleet.

Deployment deserves the same skepticism. Pin the cleanup binary or image version, make schema changes backward compatible with in-flight workers, test duplicate and out-of-order partitions, and rehearse replay from the durable ledger. A scheduler configuration change should pass review and emit an auditable event. For a nightly job, a staging clock that runs every few minutes can validate orchestration, but test data must preserve the production invariants: stable external IDs, overlapping updates, pagination, and rate-limit responses.

No mystery metrics.

When should the deployment stay small?

Stick with a simple repository or host cron when the cleanup is disposable, quick, idempotent as a whole, easy to rerun, and has no hard completion deadline. A small cache purge whose next run safely catches up does not automatically justify a queue, run ledger, leases, and another pager. The catch is that “small” must be supported by observed duration and backlog, not by the current row count.

A managed scheduler is not suitable when provider-specific IAM and targets violate portability requirements, while a self-hosted queue is a poor fit when the team cannot own its data store, upgrades, and consumer capacity. An edge handler is the wrong execution home for work that exceeds its documented resource model, though it may still be a clean trigger. Repository automation should remain repository automation when production credentials or unpredictable start delay would breach the service boundary.

The decision rule is deliberately unbranded: define the reconciliation deadline, make run intent durable, test the four failure conditions, and choose the least operational machinery that still preserves the invariant under replay. Cost matters. So do the pages created by the architecture.

References

  • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/what-is-scheduler.html
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/scheduler/latest/UserGuide/managing-schedule-flexible-time-windows.html
  • https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • https://docs.bullmq.io/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585#section-4

title: Vercel Sandbox now supports memory observability
description:
Vercel Sandbox observability now includes memory usage data.

You can access sandbox memory usage data in the dashboard and through the CLI via the vercel metrics command.

Sandbox observability memory in the dashboard

The Memory Usage card reports average, P75, and P95 memory across your sandboxes, alongside the existing CPU usage and data transfer metrics on the sandbox overview page and the project and team-level pages.

On the sandbox detail page, charts are designed to show how close a sandbox is running to its memory ceiling by:

  • Automatically scaling the y-axis to sandbox's memory limit

  • Adding a dashed reference line at 85% of that limit

Sandbox memory is also available in the Observability query builder as the memoryUsedBytes measure on the sandbox usage event. You can build custom queries against it and create alerts from the chart.

Sandbox memory observability in the CLI

Sandbox observability data is also available through the Vercel CLI via the vercel metrics command under vercel.sandbox.memory_used_bytes. Run the command in a linked project for project-specific data, or append --all to see aggregate data across all projects in your team.

The CLI returns:

  • The metric

  • The reporting period

  • The measurement interval

  • The project the sandbox is associated with

  • A graph of memory usage, with min, max and avg values

Learn more in the Sandbox documentation.

title: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant: Benchmarked for RAG in 2026
description:
I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings into pgvector and Qdrant and measured recall, latency, index build and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its docs only, since I didn't run it. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that stores embeddings in a vector column and searches them with HNSW or IVFFlat indexes, next to your normal tables. Qdrant is an open-source vector database you run yourself or use as a managed cloud. Pinecone is a fully managed, serverless vector database you only reach through an API.

For a RAG app, the real question is whether you need a separate vector database at all. I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings (1,536 dimensions) into pgvector 0.8.7 on PostgreSQL 18.6 and into Qdrant 1.19.2 on one machine. Then I measured recall, latency, build time and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its official docs and limits only, because I didn't run it and I won't invent numbers for it.

TL;DR: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant, which should I use?

Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres and have up to a few million vectors. One database, SQL joins, transactions and backups you already have. Choose Qdrant when vector search is the core workload and you need the best recall per millisecond or heavy filtering. Choose Pinecone when you want zero infrastructure and accept a managed service with usage pricing.

pgvector Qdrant Pinecone
What it is Postgres extension Vector database (open source) Managed vector database (closed)
Hosting Anywhere Postgres runs Self-host or Qdrant Cloud Pinecone's cloud only
Index HNSW, IVFFlat HNSW per segment Managed (serverless, object storage)
Max indexed dims 2,000 vector, 4,000 halfvec 1,536 tested here 20,000 dense
Filtering SQL WHERE (post-filter, iterative scans) Payload indexes + filter-aware HNSW Metadata filters (40 KB per record)
Consistency Transactional (ACID) Upserts readable after wait=true Eventually consistent
Recall@10 at ~2.6 ms, my test 0.978 (ef_search 100) 0.985 (hnsw_ef 40) not tested
Cost to start Your Postgres Free binary / free cloud tier Free Starter; Standard $50/month minimum

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Usually not at first. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, pgvector adds vector search without a second system to deploy, secure, back up and keep in sync. In my test it answered top-10 queries over 100,000 OpenAI embeddings in 1.5-4 ms, with 95-99% recall. A dedicated database starts to pay off at very large scale, under heavy filtering, or when search load needs to scale separately.

The hidden cost of a separate vector store is synchronisation. Every document insert, update and delete has to reach two systems, and a failed write leaves them disagreeing. With pgvector the embedding sits in the same row and the same transaction as the document it describes.

What is pgvector?

pgvector is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec types, distance operators like <=> (cosine) and <-> (L2), and approximate HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. Per the pgvector README, it "performs exact nearest neighbor search, which provides perfect recall" by default. An index trades a little recall for speed.

CREATE EXTENSION vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
  id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id int NOT NULL,
  content   text NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- top 5 chunks for a question, inside one tenant
SELECT id, content
FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 5;

Index limits matter for model choice. HNSW can index a vector of "up to 2,000 dimensions" and a halfvec of "up to 4,000 dimensions". A 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large needs a halfvec index or a shorter output size.

What are Qdrant and Pinecone?

Qdrant is an open-source vector search engine written in Rust. It stores points (vectors plus a JSON payload), builds an HNSW index per segment, and adds payload indexes so filters run inside the graph search. You can run a single binary, Docker or Qdrant Cloud.

Pinecone is a managed, serverless vector database. Per its architecture docs, "all your vector data is stored in highly efficient, distributed object storage." Pinecone "separates write and read operations into different paths, with each scaling independently based on demand." There is no self-hosted version.

How I benchmarked pgvector and Qdrant

  1. Data. The first 100,000 rows of the public DBpedia OpenAI embeddings dataset: 1,536-dimension text-embedding-ada-002 vectors of Wikipedia entities, a typical RAG shape. 1,000 held-out rows from the same dataset served as queries.
  2. Ground truth. Exact cosine top-10 for every query, computed with NumPy. Recall@10 is the share of those 10 that each engine returned.
  3. Machine. One 8-vCPU, 15 GB Linux box, everything on localhost, no Docker.
  4. pgvector. PostgreSQL 18.6 with pgvector 0.8.7, shared_buffers = 2GB, maintenance_work_mem = 2GB. HNSW with defaults (m = 16, ef_construction = 64), loaded with binary COPY through psycopg 3.
  5. Qdrant. The Qdrant 1.19.2 release binary, cosine distance, m = 16 and ef_construct = 64 to match pgvector, default optimizer settings (it made 4 segments). Loaded with the official Python client over gRPC from a single process.
  6. Queries. One client, sequential, 50 warm-up queries, then 1,000 timed queries. Latency includes the Python client round trip on both sides.
  7. Filters. Every vector got a random category from 0 to 9, about 10% of rows each. Filtered queries asked for the top 10 inside one category.

Is pgvector fast enough? Recall and latency results

Yes, at this scale both engines are fast. pgvector reached 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms median with default settings, and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with hnsw.ef_search = 200. Qdrant reached 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms median and 0.999 at 5.4 ms. At roughly equal recall (about 98.5-98.8%), Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster: 2.6 ms against 4.0 ms.

Engine and setting Recall@10 p50 latency p95 latency Queries/s (1 client)
pgvector, ef_search = 40 (default) 0.948 1.45 ms 2.16 ms 683
pgvector, ef_search = 100 0.978 2.60 ms 3.70 ms 389
pgvector, ef_search = 200 0.988 4.02 ms 5.82 ms 249
pgvector halfvec index, ef_search = 100 0.973 2.33 ms 3.30 ms 433
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 40 0.985 2.63 ms 3.56 ms 368
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 100 0.997 3.73 ms 4.66 ms 255
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 200 0.999 5.37 ms 6.99 ms 176
pgvector exact (no index) 1.000 380 ms 445 ms 3
Qdrant exact (no index) 1.000 24.7 ms 32.6 ms 39

Why does Qdrant get higher recall at the same ef? It splits the collection into segments (4 here) and searches each one with that ef, so it explores more candidates in total. Compare the engines at equal recall, not equal settings.

How fast do they load and index?

Qdrant indexed faster: 30.8 seconds from the first upload to a fully indexed collection, with the upload itself taking 20.2 s from one Python process. pgvector loaded the rows with COPY in 3.9 s, then needed 69.1 s to build the HNSW index with the default 2 parallel workers.

pgvector Qdrant
Load 100k vectors 3.9 s (COPY) 20.2 s (Python client, gRPC)
Build HNSW index 69.1 s included, indexed at 30.8 s
Table / data size 798 MB —
HNSW index size 781 MB (vector), 391 MB (halfvec) —
Server memory after test Postgres buffers + OS cache 1,293 MB RSS

Use the halfvec trick in pgvector: indexing embedding::halfvec(1536) halved the index from 781 MB to 391 MB and cost about half a point of recall (0.973 against 0.978 at ef_search = 100). Query the index with the same cast:

CREATE INDEX ON documents
  USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(1536)) halfvec_cosine_ops);

SELECT id FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding::halfvec(1536) <=> $1::halfvec(1536)
LIMIT 10;

How does filtered vector search compare?

Qdrant handled filters best. With a payload index on category, filtered top-10 queries returned 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms median. pgvector gave three very different results depending on the plan Postgres picked, so you need to know how its filtering works.

Filtered query (10% of rows match) Rows returned (of 10) Recall@10 p50
pgvector, planner's choice (B-tree on category, exact sort) 10 1.000 44.2 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = off 3.92 0.389 1.77 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = strict_order 10 0.915 3.62 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = relaxed_order 10 0.953 3.37 ms
Qdrant, payload index 10 0.993 2.11 ms

Why does pgvector return fewer rows with a filter?

Because HNSW filters after the index scan. The README explains: "If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average." I measured 3.92. Since pgvector 0.8.0, iterative index scans keep walking the graph until enough rows match.

-- once per session or per transaction (SET LOCAL)
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

SELECT id, content FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 10;

Postgres often picks the exact plan by itself for a selective filter. In my test it used the category B-tree and sorted about 10,000 rows exactly: perfect recall, but 44 ms instead of about 3 ms. That is fine for one tenant with a few thousand chunks. For large tenants, check EXPLAIN and turn on iterative scans. If one filter dominates, consider a partial index or partitioning by tenant.

What does Pinecone offer that pgvector and Qdrant don't?

Fully managed, serverless scaling with nothing to run. Reads and writes scale separately, storage lives in object storage, and you never tune ef or m. The trade-offs are documented:

  • Eventual consistency. The known limitations page says "Pinecone is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records are available to query."
  • Operation limits. Per the operation limits: dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions, 40 KB of filterable metadata per record, 1,000 records or 2 MB per upsert batch, and top_k up to 10,000.
  • Plans. The object limits give the free Starter plan 2 GB of serverless storage and 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Pinecone pricing lists the Standard plan at a $50/month minimum.
  • Network hop. Every query leaves your VPC. Expect your cloud region's round-trip time on top of search time. My localhost latencies are not comparable to Pinecone and I did not measure it.

When should I choose each one?

Decide by what you already run and what dominates your workload. The pgvector default is strong for product teams. Move when you measure a reason, not before.

  1. Choose pgvector when your data lives in Postgres, you need joins, row-level security or transactions with your embeddings, and you have up to a few million vectors per index. Add pgvectorscale (StreamingDiskANN) if the index outgrows RAM.
  2. Choose Qdrant when search is the product: tens of millions of vectors, many filters, multi-vector or hybrid search, or quantization to cut memory. Its quantization guide says scalar quantization achieves "4x compression with minimal accuracy loss."
  3. Choose Pinecone when nobody on the team should run a database, traffic is spiky, and a usage bill plus eventual consistency are acceptable.

How do I move from pgvector to Qdrant later?

Keep embeddings and IDs portable from day one. Use the same primary key in both systems, store the embedding model name and dimensions with each row, and write a re-sync job that streams rows by ID. Qdrant accepts integer or UUID point IDs, so a UUIDv7 primary key maps across directly.

Then run both side by side, compare recall on a fixed set of real queries, and switch reads before you stop writing to Postgres.

Common mistakes with vector search in production

  • Indexing 3,072-dimension vectors as vector. HNSW on vector stops at 2,000 dimensions. Use halfvec or a smaller output dimension.
  • Forgetting iterative scans. Filtered HNSW queries in pgvector can silently return fewer than LIMIT rows.
  • Comparing engines at equal settings. ef means different work in different engines. Compare at equal recall.
  • Measuring recall on random vectors. Use real embeddings from your model. Random data hides graph quality.
  • Creating Qdrant payload indexes after loading. The indexing docs say payload indexes should be created before ingesting data, so filter-aware HNSW edges get built.
  • Ignoring re-embedding cost. Switching embedding models means re-embedding everything, whichever store you use.

If you want a working starting point, my open-source Next.js AI starter kit, Forgekit, ships RAG on pgvector. For self-hosting Postgres or Qdrant next to your app, see self-hosting Next.js with Coolify.

Key takeaways

  • With 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector 0.8.7 hit 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms with defaults and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with ef_search 200.
  • Qdrant 1.19.2 hit 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms, about 1.5x faster than pgvector at roughly equal recall.
  • pgvector's HNSW filters after scanning: a 10% filter returned only 3.92 of 10 rows until iterative scans were enabled.
  • Qdrant's payload index gave the best filtered search in my test: 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms.
  • A halfvec HNSW index halved pgvector's index size (781 MB to 391 MB) for about half a point of recall.
  • Pinecone is serverless and eventually consistent, supports 20,000-dimension vectors, and its Standard plan has a $50/month minimum.
  • Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres; move to Qdrant or Pinecone when measurements show a need.

FAQ

Is pgvector as good as Pinecone or Qdrant?

For most RAG apps up to a few million vectors, yes. In my test of 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector reached 0.988 recall@10 at 4.0 ms median, and Qdrant reached 0.985 at 2.6 ms. Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster at equal recall and better at filtered search, but pgvector keeps embeddings in the same transactional database as your data.

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Not usually at the start. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, the pgvector extension adds vector columns and HNSW indexes without a second system to deploy, back up and keep in sync. Consider a dedicated vector database when you reach tens of millions of vectors, need heavy filtering at low latency, or need to scale search separately.

Why does pgvector return fewer results than my LIMIT?

Because pgvector's HNSW index applies WHERE filters after scanning the index. With a filter matching 10 percent of rows and the default ef_search of 40, about 4 rows match on average; I measured 3.92. Set hnsw.iterative_scan to relaxed_order or strict_order, available since pgvector 0.8.0, so the scan continues until enough rows match.

How many dimensions can pgvector index?

pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat indexes support the vector type up to 2,000 dimensions, halfvec up to 4,000 and bit up to 64,000. For a 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large, index the column as halfvec or request a smaller output dimension. Pinecone supports dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions.

Is Qdrant faster than pgvector?

In my single-machine test, yes, at equal recall. Qdrant 1.19.2 returned 0.985 recall@10 at 2.6 ms median against pgvector's 0.988 at 4.0 ms, and indexed 100,000 vectors in about 31 seconds against pgvector's 69-second HNSW build. With default settings, pgvector was faster per query but at lower recall, 0.948 at 1.45 ms.

How much does Pinecone cost?

Pinecone has a free Starter plan with 2 GB of serverless storage and up to 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Its Standard plan for production has a $50 per month minimum, after which you pay as you go for usage, according to Pinecone's pricing page. Qdrant's open-source build and pgvector are free to self-host.

What is halfvec in pgvector?

halfvec is pgvector's half-precision vector type, storing each dimension in 2 bytes instead of 4. Indexing an expression like embedding::halfvec(1536) halves the HNSW index size; in my test it shrank from 781 MB to 391 MB with recall dropping from 0.978 to 0.973. It also raises the indexable limit to 4,000 dimensions.

Is Pinecone eventually consistent?

Yes. Pinecone's documentation states that it is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records can be queried, and suggests checking index stats to confirm counts. pgvector writes are transactional and visible on commit, and Qdrant upserts sent with wait=true are applied before the call returns.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.
