title: GitView CodeAudit: Go security reviews that never leave your laptop
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

GitView CodeAudit is a security review for Go backends that runs on your laptop. A static analyzer finds the problems and collects the evidence; an open-weight model, Gemma running on Ollama, explains a finding when you ask, but it never decides one.

GitView started as my terminal tool for watching Git changes and studying Go code: call graph, data flow, SQL operations and HTTP routes, each with the evidence behind it. This week I built CodeAudit on top of those analyses.

Who would pay for it? Freelancers and small agencies that build Go APIs for clients. Clients ask for a security review before a launch, a funding round or a big customer's due diligence, and they pay for it. But that code usually comes under an NDA, and pasting it into a cloud AI tool is exactly what the contract forbids. CodeAudit lets one developer do that review on their own laptop and hand over a real deliverable: an offline HTML report with each finding, the path that reaches it, the evidence, and the reviewer's decision with its justification.

That is the side hustle: the client pays for the review, and producing it costs nothing per token.

Every finding answers the questions a client will ask:

  • Where? File, line and function.
  • Why? The rule, and the data that reaches the line, for example c.Query("q") → "... LIKE '%" + term + "%'" → db.QueryContext.
  • How is it reached? Every HTTP route that leads there, through each middleware, marking the one that authenticates.
  • How sure are we? Severity, confidence and verdict are separate fields. A possible IDOR is shown as Review Required — Authorization Not Established, never as "IDOR confirmed".
  • How do I fix it, and how do I test the fix?
  • What did we decide? Open → Investigating → Confirmed / False Positive / Accepted Risk / Fixed, with a history of every change: its date, its justification and the commit it refers to.

Demo

GitView is a local tool, so there is no deployed link: everything below runs on your machine. The repository ships a small vulnerable API, with safe variants of each case, that the tests use. You can reproduce these screenshots with it:

git clone https://github.com/Darrkkens/gitview && cd gitview && go install .   # Go 1.25
gitview audit scan --module internal/audit/testdata/app
gitview audit serve --module internal/audit/testdata/app   # opens 127.0.0.1 in the browser

A SQL injection: the route, the middleware chain and the handler lead to the query, and the inspector shows the evidence.

The same finding explained by Gemma. Each evidence ID the model cites is checked against the analysis.

A possible IDOR is a review, not a verdict. The resource ID comes from the request and the query has no owner or tenant condition, but authorization could live somewhere the static analysis cannot see.

The report you hand to the client is a single offline HTML file. It has no network access, a strict CSP, and only bounded, redacted excerpts of the code.

Code

Darrkkens / gitview

GitView

Monitor de alterações Git em tempo real no terminal. Cada arquivo modificado pode ser expandido ou recolhido individualmente, e os diffs se atualizam sozinhos. Inclui busca global nos diffs, exportação de relatórios, execução de testes, Code Flow e o Go Deep Inspector, para estudar código Go com evidências verificáveis.

go install .
gitview [opções] [diretório]
Opção Descrição
--delta Renderiza diffs com git-delta (alternável com d)
--expand Expande automaticamente arquivos novos
--interval 2s Intervalo do polling de segurança
--no-watch Desativa fsnotify e usa apenas polling
--export-dir DIR Diretório padrão dos relatórios (também GITVIEW_EXPORT_DIR)
--test-timeout 10m Tempo limite de uma execução de testes
--ascii Símbolos ASCII (também GITVIEW_ASCII=1)

Atalhos

? mostra a ajuda da tela atual.

Mouse: a roda rola o diff; clicar numa dica do rodapé (por exemplo x Exportar) equivale a pressionar a tecla; na exportação, clicar num formato, escopo ou caixa [x] escolhe ou…


View on GitHub


  • internal/audit: the rules, the taint paths, the review store, the audit diff and the report.
  • internal/audit/ai: the Ollama client, the context builder and the validator of the model's answers.

How I Built It

Static analysis first. CodeAudit has 18 deterministic rules for injection, authentication, authorization, sensitive data, configuration and dependencies. They run over analyses GitView already had: go/packages, go/types and SSA for the call graph and the data flow, the SQL operations, and the HTTP routes with their middleware chains.

  • Taint: a taint finding is the shortest path in the data flow graph from an HTTP input to a sink.
  • Sanitizers: they only count when their meaning is known. strconv.Atoi neutralizes everything and filepath.Base neutralizes paths; an arbitrary function call is not a sanitizer.
  • Checks: an if that dominates the sink and examines the value, like if !allowed(origin), turns "vulnerable" into "review", because the analyzer cannot prove the check is sufficient.
  • Authorization: a 403 only counts as authorization when the request is already authenticated. A 403 from a CORS filter is shown as a request filter instead.
  • Dependencies: they are checked only against a local copy of the Go vulnerability database (OSV format). Without one, the report says "dependencies not checked" instead of pretending, and a database older than 30 days is flagged as possibly out of date.

Gemma on Ollama, kept on a short leash.

  • Model: by default GitView picks the smallest installed Gemma model (gemma3:4b on my machine). It never downloads one, and it refuses any endpoint that is not on this machine unless you pass --ai-allow-remote.
  • Context: the context sent to the model is built from the analysis, not from a file dump. It holds the finding, its evidence, the route path and the function's code, within a budget of about 6,000 tokens. Secrets are redacted, and the repository's comments and strings go in as data, never as instructions.
  • Answer: Ollama's structured outputs (format with a JSON schema) shape the reply. Every evidence ID, file, line and symbol the model cites is validated against the context, and a citation that does not exist is shown as rejected.
  • Cache: answers are cached by context hash, model digest and prompt version.
  • No authority: the model can recommend a review state, but it cannot change one. The reviewer decides.

Being honest about the model. On my CPU-only laptop, one explanation from gemma3:4b took between three and a half and five minutes (215 s and 310 s in two runs), and gemma3:12b did not fit in the free memory. The prose is useful but not perfect; in one test the model expanded "IDOR" incorrectly. That is exactly why the model is not allowed to decide anything and why its citations are checked.

Testing without a model. The test suite never needs a real model. It runs against a simulated Ollama, including answers that cite evidence that does not exist. The fixture app has one case per rule plus its safe variant (Atoi before the query, filepath.Base, a tenant filter, an admin route that answers 403, a secure cookie…), and the test fails on any unexpected finding.

Dogfooding found my own false positives. Running CodeAudit on GitView itself flagged three "hardcoded secrets". They were descriptions like credential = "Authorization header". The rule now skips values with spaces, the fixture has that case, and the rule documents what it misses because of it: a hardcoded passphrase.

I built this with Claude Code as my pair, from the spec to the browser tests.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The code cannot leave. For a review under an NDA, a model I run myself is the only way AI can touch the code at all. A closed API is simply not an option here.
  • The economics work. A fixed-price review cannot absorb a per-token bill that grows with the size of the codebase. On a local model, each explanation costs electricity.
  • No lock-in. Swapping models takes one flag (--model), and the validator does not trust any model, so a better open model is a drop-in upgrade.
  • The client can audit the auditor. The investigator's prompt, the answer schema and the validator are in the repository. A client can check exactly what was sent to the model: a bounded, redacted context built from the evidence.

My First User

The first real codebase it audited was my own: the Go backend of a production SaaS I maintain, with 134 HTTP routes. The whole analysis took about a second and a half, and CodeAudit reported 16 findings, none of them a confirmed vulnerability:

  • 4 public routes of the authentication flow that write to the database, shown as Review Required — No Authentication Identified. A login route is public by design, which is exactly why the rule asks instead of accusing.
  • 1 CORS middleware that reflects the Origin with credentials, but only after an allow-list check. It is a review, and the inspector points to the check itself.
  • 11 SQL statements built at runtime whose origin the data flow could not determine. They are reported as info instead of being silently dropped, so the reviewer knows where the analysis stopped.

The first version was much noisier, and fixing it on real code shaped the rules:

  • A CORS filter that answers 403 counted as authorization on every route, which hid the authorization rule entirely. A 403 now only counts after authentication.
  • Once that was fixed, the authorization rule flagged login routes, webhooks and reference-data tables. It now skips handlers that authenticate themselves, and it reads the SQL migrations to know which tables have an owner or tenant column.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma, running locally on Ollama, is the AI Security Investigator. It explains findings and paths from the static evidence, its answers are schema-constrained, and every citation is validated.

This post and the code it describes were written with the help of AI (Claude Code).

title: Heuristic Evaluation Playbook for Product Teams
description:
• How heuristic evaluation protects your release schedule
  • Preparing the team and scope: pick heuristics and tasks
  • A rigorous, step‑by‑step usability checklist for reviewers
  • Synthesis and prioritization: severity, reporting, and alignment
  • Actionable templates and a ready-to-run heuristic audit protocol

Heuristic evaluation is the fastest, highest-leverage way to surface UX debt before it becomes customer-facing. When you structure that inspection around Nielsen’s 10 heuristics and a disciplined, timeboxed process, the exercise turns guesswork into concrete, fixable usability issues.

The symptoms are familiar: teams patch UI problems reactively, support tickets spike for the same flows, analytics show drop-offs but not the “why,” and designers iterate blind because there’s no common method to classify severity. That pattern wastes engineering cycles and creates recurring regressions that manual QA keeps catching — but never fully eliminating.

How heuristic evaluation protects your release schedule

Heuristic evaluation buys you early detection at low cost. Expert reviewers inspect flows against a compact set of principles, so you catch both obvious breakages (missing confirmation, broken links) and subtle design failures (poor error messaging, inconsistent affordances) before you reach user testing or a production rollout. The method is fast, repeatable, and scales with scope: run a focused sweep on a single task or a broader UX audit across a product surface.

Why QA and product teams should treat it like a gate:

  • It reduces late discovery of UX regressions that become expensive to rework during a release freeze.
  • It complements exploratory testing: findings feed reproducible test cases for manual and regression suites.
  • It clarifies what to fix first by mapping issues to business-impacting flows (checkout, onboarding, admin tasks).

Important: Always pair a heuristic evaluation with a defined task (e.g., “complete checkout with a promo code”) and the relevant user profile. Heuristics are context-dependent; scope keeps them actionable.

Sources for the practice and rationale appear in the Nielsen guidance and government UX playbooks.

Preparing the team and scope: pick heuristics and tasks

Preparation makes or breaks the outcome. Use this short checklist before any evaluation.

Who to involve

  • 3–5 experienced evaluators is the classic recommendation for heuristic evaluations. This gives a high finding yield while keeping cost low.
  • When the domain or user base is diverse or the site is complex, be prepared to increase evaluators or run multiple segmented sweeps; research shows larger samples can be necessary for complex web tasks.
  • Mix roles when possible: one UX researcher/designer, one QA/exploratory tester, and one product engineer give complementary perspectives.

Which heuristics to use

  • Start with Jakob Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics as your canonical set. Use domain-specific addenda for accessibility, safety-critical flows, or localized interfaces.
  • For regulated or safety-critical products, introduce domain heuristics (e.g., safety checks, clear escalation paths) alongside Nielsen’s list.

Scope and artifacts to prepare

  • Define: user persona, device type, task scenario, environment (logged-in state, test data).
  • Provide: test accounts, credentials, variations (guest vs. signed-in), relevant analytics slices or crash reports.
  • Provide a standard evaluation sheet (spreadsheet, workbook, or Miro board) so findings are recorded uniformly.

Training and timeboxing

  • Run a 20–30 minute calibration/practice round with a simple app to align reviewers on what constitutes a heuristic violation.
  • Timebox independent evaluations to ~1–2 hours per evaluator for a single task or a focused section; longer sessions drop signal-to-noise.

A rigorous, step‑by‑step usability checklist for reviewers

This is the operational usability checklist you can hand an evaluator. Use numbered steps and concrete acceptance criteria.

  1. Context setup (10–15 min)

    • Confirm persona, device, network speed, and the task expected. Record analytics slices if available.
    • Open the evaluation sheet and note the scope and the heuristic set (Nielsen heuristics).

  2. Walkthrough #1 — familiarization (10–15 min)

    • Perform the task once to learn the flow. Don’t annotate yet; learn the edge cases and expected system responses.

  3. Walkthrough #2 — heuristic pass (45–90 min)

    • For each screen/interaction, ask: which heuristic does this element relate to? Log one problem per row with a screenshot. Use this per-heuristic checklist:
      • Visibility of system status — Are loading states visible? Do actions provide immediate feedback?
      • Match to the real world — Does language match user mental models? Any jargon?
      • User control and freedom — Can users undo or exit quickly? Are confirmations clear?
      • Consistency & standards — Are similar actions labelled or styled consistently across pages?
      • Error prevention — Are forms validated proactively? Do confirmations prevent destructive actions?
      • Recognition vs recall — Are key items visible or hidden behind multiple layers?
      • Flexibility & efficiency — Are accelerators available for power users (shortcuts, saved defaults)?
      • Aesthetic & minimalist design — Is content noisy? Does the layout obscure primary actions?
      • Help diagnose & recover from errors — Are error messages actionable and specific?
      • Help & documentation — Is help discoverable when needed? Is it task-focused?

  4. Problem capture (for each issue)

    • Required fields: ID, Title, Flow, Page/Screen, Heuristic, Description, Repro steps, Screenshot, Estimated frequency (1–5), Severity (0–4), Suggested fix (brief), Owner, Estimated effort (T-shirt or days). Use the CSV/JSON templates below.

  5. Severity and evidence

    • Rate problems on frequency, impact on task performance, and persistence (recurring vs one-off). Record these factors separately when possible to justify prioritization.

  6. Repeat for each task segment

    • When scope includes multiple user journeys, repeat steps 1–5 for each flow.

  7. Independent finish then consolidation

    • Submit files but don’t share evaluations with other reviewers until all are done. This avoids groupthink.

Quick red‑flags to watch for (examples you can scan in 5 minutes)

  • Missing confirmation after destructive actions.
  • Form fields that fail silently.
  • Hidden primary navigation behind a hamburger icon with no indication.
  • Multiple CTA styles on the same page.
  • Error messages that show raw codes (e.g., "ERR_502").

Table: Selected heuristics → quick checks

Heuristic Quick checks Red flag
Visibility of system status spinner/progress, success messages No feedback after submit
Consistency & standards consistent labels/styles Same action uses different verbs
Recognition vs recall visible options, clear defaults Important menu items hidden
Error recovery inline errors, suggested fixes Generic "something went wrong"

[Caveat: this mapping is derived from Nielsen’s heuristics and practical QA patterns.]

id,title,flow,page_or_screen,heuristic,severity(0-4),frequency(1-5),repro_steps,screenshot,suggested_fix,owner,effort_days
HE-001,No save confirmation,Profile>Edit,Profile>Save,Visibility of system status,3,4,"Edit name -> Save -> no confirmation","/screenshots/HE-001.png","Add toast confirmation & spinner",product,0.5

{
  "id": "HE-001",
  "title": "No save confirmation",
  "flow": "Profile > Edit",
  "heuristic": "Visibility of system status",
  "severity": 3,
  "frequency": 4,
  "repro_steps": ["Edit profile", "Change name", "Click Save"],
  "screenshot": "/screenshots/HE-001.png",
  "suggested_fix": "Add toast confirmation and spinner",
  "owner": "product",
  "effort_est_days": 0.5
}

Synthesis and prioritization: severity, reporting, and alignment

A disciplined synthesis converts a long list of findings into a prioritized to-do list that engineering will act on.

Severity scale (common, 0–4)
| Score | Label | What it means | Action |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 0 | Not a problem | No usability issue identified | No action |
| 1 | Cosmetic | Little/no effect on task performance | Fix if time allows |
| 2 | Minor | Causes occasional confusion/delay | Schedule in backlog |
| 3 | Major | Frequently blocks or frustrates users | High priority fix |
| 4 | Catastrophic | Prevents completion of critical tasks | Fix before release |

This 0–4 scale and the contributing factors (frequency, impact, persistence) are standard in heuristic workflows.

Aggregation and prioritization protocol

  1. Consolidate issues (affinity cluster) and remove duplicates. Note how many evaluators found each problem.
  2. Compute a mean severity across evaluators and list reproducibility (always/sometimes/rare). Use the reproducibility and frequency estimate to re-weight severity for prioritization.
  3. Add an effort estimate and compute a simple priority score, for example: PriorityScore = MeanSeverity * (Frequency / 5) / EffortDays. Use this as a sorting heuristic, not as an absolute decision.
  4. Present a triage board with three buckets: Critical (fix before release), High (next sprint), Backlog (research / low ROI).

Reporting deliverables (minimum)

  • Consolidated issue tracker (CSV/JSON) with screenshots and repro steps.
  • Priority matrix (severity × effort).
  • UX map showing problem clusters by flow (visual).
  • A 1–2 page executive summary linking top issues to metrics (drop-off, support volume, conversions).

Meeting choreography for alignment (30–60 minutes)

  • Quick readout of top 5 issues (1 minute each).
  • Assign owners and effort bands.
  • Lock in which issues must be triaged into the next sprint and which require user research before changing.

Important: Don’t treat heuristic evaluation as the only signal. Use it to triage design debt; validate contentious fixes with targeted user testing or telemetry after remediation.

Actionable templates and a ready-to-run heuristic audit protocol

Use this deployable protocol for a focused 2‑day sweep on a single user journey.

Example schedule (compressed)

  • Day 0 — Kickoff (30–45 min): scope, heuristics, roles, practice round.
  • Day 1 — Independent evaluations (1–2 hours each per evaluator): each evaluator completes the workbook and logs issues.
  • Day 2 AM — Consolidation and affinity mapping (60–90 min): cluster duplicates and compute mean severities.
  • Day 2 PM — Prioritization and handoff (60–90 min): create tickets, assign owners, decide critical fixes.

Minimum artifacts to deliver at close

  • heuristic-findings.csv (template above)
  • priority-matrix.xlsx (severity × effort, ranked)
  • A one-page readout mapping top 3 issues to business impact (e.g., funnel step, estimated lost conversions, or support cost).

A short, practical triage template (use in your sprint planning)

  • Tag each issue with: fix-by (release), sprint (number), owner (team), risk (high/med/low), notes (research needed: yes/no).

When documenting, use clear language in tickets: state the offending element, the heuristic violated, steps to reproduce, and an example of a desirable outcome (a one-liner recommendation). That makes it easier for engineers to scope work and for product to prioritize.

Table: Sample trade-off guidance for triage
| Category | Action |
|---|---|
| Severity 4 + Low Effort | Stop release; fix immediately |
| Severity 3 + Low Effort | Prioritize in next sprint |
| Severity 3 + High Effort | Split into research + incremental fixes |
| Severity 1–2 | Document and batch as design debt |

Practical QA integration points

  • Turn reproducible heuristic findings into manual test cases for regression suites.
  • Use exploratory test sessions to validate severity and repro rate across real user data.
  • Track UX debt in JIRA or your backlog with a ux:heuristic label and link to the consolidated evidence artifact.

Closing thought
Treat heuristic evaluation as a repeatable quality gate: run small, frequent sweeps aligned to your most important journeys, translate findings into prioritized work, and measure whether the number of critical heuristic violations drops release-to-release. The discipline converts subjective impressions into objective, actionable UX fixes that save engineering time and protect your metrics.

Sources:
How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation — Nielsen Norman Group - Step-by-step process, recommended team size (3–5 evaluators), timeboxing guidance, and the NN/g workbook used for documentation and consolidation.

10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design — Nielsen Norman Group - Canonical list of the 10 heuristics with examples and tips used throughout the checklist.

ISO 9241-11:2018 — Usability: Definitions and concepts - Usability definition (effectiveness, efficiency, satisfaction) and the emphasis on context of use.

Reading 20: Heuristic Evaluation — MIT course material - Severity rating guidance and contributing factors (frequency, impact, persistence) used to justify the 0–4 scale and aggregation approach.

Refining the Test Phase of Usability Evaluation: How Many Subjects Is Enough? — Robert A. Virzi (1992) - Empirical study that supports small-sample discovery rates (4–5 subjects) in specific contexts.

Testing web sites: Five Users Is Nowhere Near Enough — Jared Spool & Will Schroeder (CHI 2001) - Evidence that complex web tasks may require larger samples or segmented testing; useful as a counterpoint on sample-size assumptions.

Heuristic evaluation — 18F Guides - Government guidance on running heuristics, including a recommended 3–5 person team and practical documentation notes.

How to Conduct a Heuristic Evaluation — Maze guide - Practical checklist and template suggestions for capturing issues and linking them to tasks.

title: pg_utl_smtp v2.0 released
description:
Antananarivo, Madagascar - October 06, 2026

PostgreSQL UTL_SMTP compatibility extension

pg_utl_smtp is a PostgreSQL extension to create, manage and use Oracle-style UTL_SMTP package. The use and behavior is just like with the UTL_SMTP Oracle package. This work is released from the HexaRocket project.

This extension allows email notifications to be sent from triggers or stored procedures. By integrating the extension directly into the database, you can trigger data-driven actions without waiting for application intervention. Examples include security alerts or notifications when certain minimum thresholds are reached.

pg_utl_smtp v2.0.0 has been released, this new major version adds an asynchronous mode with setting pg_utl_smtp.asynchronous enabled. The Oracle version doesn't support asynchronous mode but this feature can be useful if you want to port the MSSQL sp_send_dbmail() procedure using pg_utl_smtp.

Other changes in this release:

  • Raise an error when the SMTP server returns an error to HELO/EHLO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, end of DATA or QUIT.
  • Fix duplicate EHLO sent at connection
  • Implement SSL/TLS connections (secure_connection_before_smtp).
  • QUIT releases the connection, a second QUIT raises an error.
  • When the connection can not be established the WARNING gives the reason.
  • Add regression tests by GitHub Actions.

To upgrade an installed version 2.0.0 execute:

  ALTER EXTENSION pg_utl_smtp UPDATE;

This extension uses plperl stored procedures based on the Net::SMTP Perl module to provide the procedures of the UTL_SMTP package.

Links & Credits

pg_utl_smtp is an open project under the PostgreSQL license created by Gilles Darold at HexaCluster Corp. as part of the HexaRocket migration solution. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/issues

The pg_utl_smtp extension is an original work of HexaCluster Corp., HexaCluster is specialized in migration to PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL support. If you need more information please contact us

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp#readme

title: How to Get Google Trends Data in Python Without 429 Errors (a pytrends Alternative for 2026)
description:
If you've ever written pytrends.build_payload(...) and seen TooManyRequestsError: The request failed: Google returned a response with code 429, you're not alone. pytrends was archived, Google's official Trends API is still invite-only alpha, and Trends now rate-limits automated traffic aggressively. This tutorial shows a dependable way to pull interest over time, interest by region and related queries for hundreds of keywords from Python, and explains why the usual fixes stop working.

Why pytrends gets 429s

The Google Trends front end calls a handful of internal endpoints:

  1. /trends/api/explore returns a list of "widgets", each with a short-lived token.
  2. /trends/api/widgetdata/multiline returns the timeline.
  3. /trends/api/widgetdata/comparedgeo returns regions.
  4. /trends/api/widgetdata/relatedsearches returns related queries and topics.

Every response starts with an anti-JSON-hijacking prefix ()]}'), and every call needs a valid NID cookie. When you send many requests from one IP, Google returns 429 or redirects you to /sorry/. The common advice of time.sleep(60) plus retries=3 works for ten keywords. It doesn't work for a thousand, and it doesn't work from cloud IPs at all, because those are often blocked from the very first request.

What actually works is:

  • a fresh session (cookie plus new tokens) after each block,
  • rotating egress IPs,
  • per-widget retries, so one failed section doesn't throw away the whole query,
  • honest status reporting, so you know which rows are complete.

You can build that yourself, or use a hosted Actor that already does it.

Option A: a hosted API (about 5 minutes)

Reliable Google Trends API on Apify handles the warmup, proxy rotation, retries and residential fallback. It charges $0.002 per successful query, and failed queries are free. In our 34-query gate runs on Apify, it returned 34 of 34 results in every proxy mode we tested.

Install the client:

pip install apify-client pandas

Run a comparison:

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/reliable-google-trends").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": [
        "chatgpt, claude, gemini",     # one query comparing 3 terms
        "air fryer",                   # a second query
    ],
    "geo": "US",
    "timeframe": "today 12-m",
    "interestOverTime": True,
    "interestByRegion": True,
    "relatedQueries": True,
})

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
for r in rows:
    print(r["keywords"], r["status"], r["errors"])

Turn the timeline into a DataFrame 

def timeline_df(row):
    recs = [{"date": p["time"], **p["values"]} for p in row["interest_over_time"]]
    return pd.DataFrame(recs).set_index("date")

df = timeline_df(rows[0])
print(df.tail())
df.plot(title="ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini, US, 12 months")

Rising queries (breakouts) 

for kw, rq in rows[1]["related_queries"].items():
    for q in rq["rising"][:10]:
        print(kw, "->", q["query"], q["formatted_value"])

Bulk keyword lists

Each searchTerms entry is its own query, so you can pass 500 entries in one run. To set different options for each query, use customQueries:

run_input = {"customQueries": [
    {"keywords": "bitcoin, ethereum", "geo": "GB", "timeframe": "today 5-y", "property": "news"},
    {"keywords": "lofi music", "property": "youtube"},
]}

Every run also writes a RUN_SUMMARY record to the key-value store with the success rate and block counts:

summary = client.key_value_store(run["defaultKeyValueStoreId"]).get_record("RUN_SUMMARY")["value"]
print(summary)

Option B: roll your own (what you need to handle)

If you'd rather run it yourself, here's the minimum:

import httpx, json, time, random

def warm(client):
    # A headers-only request is enough to obtain an NID cookie
    with client.stream("GET", "https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?geo=US") as r:
        pass

def explore(client, kw, geo="US", tf="today 12-m"):
    req = {"comparisonItem": [{"keyword": kw, "geo": geo, "time": tf}],
           "category": 0, "property": ""}
    r = client.get("https://trends.google.com/trends/api/explore",
                   params={"hl": "en-US", "tz": 0, "req": json.dumps(req)})
    if r.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("blocked")
    return json.loads(r.text[r.text.index("{"):])["widgets"]

From here you still need to: call each widget endpoint with its token; rotate the session and the IP whenever you get a 429 or /sorry/; back off with jitter; and treat related topics as optional (Google often withholds them from sessions it labels USER_TYPE_SCRAPER). In practice the proxy bill and the maintenance cost far more than the code.

Gotchas that apply either way

  • Values are relative (0–100), not search volume. Only compare keywords that were in the same query.
  • More than 5 keywords? Use a shared anchor term in every batch (for example "weather") and rescale each batch against it.
  • Timeframe strings follow the Trends URL format: now 7-d, today 3-m, today 5-y, all, 2024-01-01 2024-06-30.
  • Last data point is often is_partial: true. Drop it before you fit a forecast.

Schedule it

In the Apify console, open the Actor, save your input as a Task, and add a Schedule (for example, daily at 06:00). Then use a webhook or the n8n/Make/Zapier Apify app to push new rows into Google Sheets or your warehouse.

Wrap-up

pytrends taught a generation of analysts to love Trends data, but the 429 wall is real. If you need a few queries a week, a careful DIY script with backoff can be enough. If you need hundreds of keywords on a schedule, without babysitting proxies, try Reliable Google Trends API. It's pay-per-result, and failed queries are free.

title: Easy Full Stack Authentication and Login in the Style of Spring
description:
Three requests leave your app just as its access token expires. If each refreshes independently, the first exchange can invalidate the refresh token the other two are about to use. A login feature becomes a race between requests.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

This week's security work joins the Codename One client and backend around those transitions. The client can coordinate renewal, the server can rotate tokens, and tests can verify what happens after a real request is refused.

Put the access rule beside the route

The backend has Spring-style security chains under com.codename1.backend.security. A chain chooses which requests it handles, then authenticates and authorizes them. This excerpt from the security guide example protects an API using JWT scopes:

@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:read")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .sessionManagement(session ->
            session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

Configure the trusted issuer and the audience your API expects. The guide's configuration keys include cn1.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri and cn1.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences. Audience checking is optional unless configured, so set it deliberately when several services share an issuer.

A backend with no SecurityFilterChain bean has no security layer. Adding a dependency does not secure the routes. A stateless chain also has no CSRF filter unless you request one. Session-based browser applications have a different threat model and need the corresponding session and CSRF configuration.

Method rules such as @PreAuthorize are compiled into checks. They can apply to self-calls and private methods because the build weaves them into the method, rather than relying on calls passing through a runtime proxy. The expression language is a supported subset; ACLs, @PostAuthorize and arbitrary expression evaluation are outside it.

Give the client one owner for renewal

Register an installed app as a public OAuth client with an exact redirect URI and PKCE. A client secret embedded in an app would not remain secret. After configuring OidcClient, install an authorizer for the API base URL:

OidcRequestAuthorizer authorizer =
        new OidcRequestAuthorizer(client).install("https://api.example.com/v1");
authorizer.addSignInRequiredListener((source, reason) -> showSignIn());
authorizer.load().ready(saved -> {
    if (saved == null) {
        showSignIn();
    } else {
        showNotes();
    }
});

This is an application excerpt: client is configured with your provider and token store; showSignIn() and showNotes() are your UI methods. Use SecureStorageTokenStore for platform-protected persistence. Plain storage fallback is an explicit option, not something the app should silently enable to make an error disappear.

The authorizer matches the scheme, host and port, then whole path segments. /v1 includes /v1/notes, but not /v10. It covers ordinary ConnectionRequest calls, the REST builder and generated clients through the network layer.

Renewal starts before expiry by default. Requests queued during the exchange wait for its result. If a token-bearing request receives 401, the authorizer can refresh and retry it once; the caller receives the eventual response. A refused refresh ends the session, clears stored tokens and calls the sign-in listener. If your request writes a body from a stream, verify that your implementation can supply it again before depending on a retry.

For redirects followed by Codename One, the token is removed outside the registered origin or path. The current iOS port lets the system follow redirects before application code sees them. Keep protected API redirects within hosts you control; do not infer that every transport has the same redirect interception point.

Choose the state your deployment can share

The backend includes form login, HTTP Basic, API keys, JWT resource servers, OAuth login and authorization-server support. MFA includes TOTP and recovery codes; passkey endpoints use WebAuthn. These are separate mechanisms with separate configuration, not one switch that makes every deployment secure.

Several instances cannot share an in-memory token repository or rate limiter. Declare the database-backed stores when that is your deployment shape. cn1.security.schema.enabled=true belongs in the module's build-time application.properties; it registers the security migrations. It creates tables, but does not select JDBC stores for you.

Refresh tokens and one-use codes must be consumed atomically. Otherwise two instances can both accept the same secret. The JDBC implementations use conditional database operations and their affected-row counts for those decisions. TOTP secrets are sealed under the configured encryption key; password hashes and one-use recovery codes have their own storage rules.

The packaged server links the mechanisms its chains reach. A token-verifying API need not carry login pages and a password store. That is a useful consequence of explicit configuration and dead-code removal, although it does not reduce the need to review the rules you enabled.

Test the failure after the successful login

The end-to-end client tests connect to the HelloCodenameOne backend. BackendTokenRefreshTest deliberately replaces an access token with one the server did not sign. It checks that the generated client receives one successful response after renewal, that the refresh token rotates, and that reusing a spent refresh token ends the session.

That proves more than a mock that always supplies an authenticated user. It exercises the client's networking and token state together with the server's token endpoint and protected route.

Test layer What it can establish What it does not establish
Backend MockMvc and mock identities Route and method authorization decisions A provider login or signature verification when identity is injected
Native client integration tests Requests, token exchange, renewal and denial against the backend Every external identity provider or device sign-in surface
Browser-specific tests Browser networking and credential APIs, including the virtual-authenticator vault test Passing the native credential/redirect harness unchanged
Port test matrix The declared cases on each supported target Every security mechanism on every port

The credential/redirect tests explicitly report a browser skip because the browser owns those cookies and redirects. A green port suite must be read with those skips. WebAuthn PRF bridge coverage uses Chromium's virtual authenticator; it is not a claim that every hardware authenticator supports that extension.

SAML, LDAP, opaque-token introspection and several authorization-server extensions are outside this release. The backend security guide and client identity guide specify the supported surface. PR #5961 connects those pieces; tomorrow we will look at the migrations underneath their persistent stores.

Discussion

Which failure is hardest to reproduce in your sign-in flow: renewal, revocation, or returning from the provider?

title: A Control Plane for an AI-Run Firm: Workflow, Agent and Human Lanes
description:
"Autonomous company" sounds like a model choice. In practice it is a control-plane design. This post sketches one for a small service firm doing lead intake. The firm is illustrative, not a customer story, and I have no results to share.

The idea

Split every task into one of three lanes and enforce the lane in code.

from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass

class Lane(Enum):
    WORKFLOW = "fixed steps, no model decisions"
    AGENT = "model picks steps, inside limits"
    HUMAN = "person decides"

@dataclass
class Task:
    name: str
    lane: Lane
    tools: list[str]
    needs_approval: bool = False

TASKS = [
    Task("capture_lead",   Lane.WORKFLOW, ["crm.create"]),
    Task("send_reminder",  Lane.WORKFLOW, ["email.send_template"]),
    Task("draft_reply",    Lane.AGENT,    ["crm.read", "email.draft"]),
    Task("quote_price",    Lane.HUMAN,    []),
]

Anthropic's guide says coded workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks, and that agents bring higher cost and compounding errors, so test them in sandboxes with guardrails. Salesforce describes "hybrid reasoning" that combines deterministic logic and adaptive AI. The lanes above are one simple way to do that.

The router 

def route(task: Task, payload):
    log("start", task.name, payload)
    if task.lane is Lane.HUMAN or task.needs_approval:
        return queue_for_human(task, payload)
    if task.lane is Lane.WORKFLOW:
        return run_steps(task, payload)
    return run_agent(task, payload, allowed_tools=task.tools)

Three things live here and not in a prompt: which tools a task may touch, which tasks need approval, and what gets logged.

Incident handling 

PAUSED = set()

def pause(task_name: str, who: str):
    PAUSED.add(task_name)
    log("paused", task_name, who)

Check PAUSED at the start of route. Someone must own the pause, and the log must say who used it.

Red lines to code first

  • Money, contracts and customer promises always go to a person.
  • Every agent action has a log entry with inputs and outputs.
  • Every task has a named owner and an off switch.

What this is not

It is not proof that a company can run itself. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index describes humans setting direction and "checking in as needed". The control plane is how that check-in becomes real.

Tej Pandya, founder of GrowEasy.ai.

title: TIL: What the User Count Option Really Affects in GBase Database
description:
During a typical installation of GBase Database (GBase 8s), the installer asks you to select an expected user count:

1 - 1–100
2 - 101–500
3 - 501–1000
4 - 1000+

It's tempting to accept the default 1–100 and move on. For a quick test, that may be perfectly reasonable. But this option is worth understanding before you initialize an instance for a larger workload.

What Does the User Count Option Affect?

The expected user count helps the installer choose initial instance configuration parameters appropriate for the anticipated workload.

Depending on the installation script and configuration template, these settings may include resource limits related to concurrent connections and other instance resources.

In other words, you're giving the installer a rough indication of how many users the database is expected to serve. It is a sizing input, not a guarantee that the instance will support exactly that number of concurrent connections.

Important: The selected range should not be treated as a direct connection limit. Actual connection capacity depends on the resulting configuration, available system resources, workload, and other relevant limits.

Which User Count Should You Choose?

A simple rule of thumb can help:

  • Feature validation: The default 1–100 range is generally a reasonable starting point.
  • Development and functional testing: Choose a range that reflects the expected test environment.
  • Concurrency testing: Select a range based on the planned workload, then verify the resulting connection and resource settings.
  • Larger deployments: Review the generated configuration and size the instance according to actual workload requirements rather than relying on the installer choice alone.

For example, if you're only validating SQL syntax or checking whether an application can connect, a small user-count range may be sufficient.

If you're preparing a concurrency test with hundreds of simulated users, accepting the default without checking the resulting configuration could leave the instance poorly suited to the test.

Don't Stop at the Installation Wizard

After the typical installation finishes, inspect the generated instance configuration to understand which values were selected.

Check the relevant resource and connection parameters, and confirm that they match your testing or deployment requirements. The exact parameters to review depend on the configuration produced by your GBase Database installation.

For production environments, also consider memory, CPU, storage performance, connection behavior, and workload characteristics. The user-count selection is only one part of database sizing.

Final Takeaway

The user-count option in the GBase Database (GBase 8s) typical installer is more than a cosmetic question. It helps guide the initial instance configuration based on the expected scale of use.

For quick feature validation, the default may be enough. For concurrency testing or larger deployments, choose the range deliberately and verify the resulting settings.

A useful installation habit: don't just ask what value the wizard wants. Ask what configuration that choice will produce.

Have you ever discovered that an installation default affected your database testing or deployment? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React
description:
title: "Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-10T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [webdev, react, nodejs, websockets]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Websocket Protocol Handshakes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Broadcasting Cursor Positions And Canvas Events: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Operational Transformation Basics: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Managing Reconnects: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: WebSocket protocol handshakes, broadcasting cursor positions and canvas events, operational transformation basics, and managing reconnects."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: The trust account invariant: one bank balance, many owners, and the check that catches commingling
description:
A property manager's trust account obeys one invariant: bank balance = every owner's balance + every security deposit held, at every moment. A second rule catches quieter commingling: no single owner's balance may go below zero, because if it does, another owner's money paid that owner's bill. Check both after every posting, not only at month end.

I work on ZeraBooks, and this is the cleanest data model I know for trust money. Below is a Python sketch. All figures are fictional and match the worked month on our property management page.

How do you model a trust account in code? 

from collections import defaultdict
from decimal import Decimal as D

class Trust:
    def __init__(self):
        self.bank = D("0")
        self.owner = defaultdict(lambda: D("0"))     # owed to each owner
        self.deposits = defaultdict(lambda: D("0"))  # held for each owner's tenants

    def post(self, owner: str, amount: D, kind: str):
        """amount is signed from the bank's view: + in, - out."""
        self.bank += amount
        if kind == "deposit":
            self.deposits[owner] += amount
        else:
            self.owner[owner] += amount
        self.check(owner)

    def check(self, owner: str):
        held = sum(self.owner.values()) + sum(self.deposits.values())
        assert self.bank == held, f"bank {self.bank} vs held {held}: does not reconcile"
        assert self.owner[owner] >= 0, f"{owner} is negative: another owner's money was used"

The first assertion is the reconciliation. The second is the one most spreadsheets don't have.

What does a clean month in the trust account look like?

Twelve units, three owners, an 8% fee on rent collected. The trust opens May with $9,600 of deposits.

t = Trust()
for owner, amt in [("Maple", "4800"), ("Elm", "3200"), ("Cedar", "1600")]:
    t.post(owner, D(amt), "deposit")                 # opening deposits, 9,600

t.post("Maple", D("8700.00"), "rent")
t.post("Elm",   D("6400.00"), "rent")
t.post("Elm",   D("75.00"),   "late fee")            # owner's under this agreement
t.post("Cedar", D("4200.00"), "rent")
t.post("Cedar", D("2100.00"), "deposit")             # new tenant

for owner, fee in [("Maple", "696.00"), ("Elm", "512.00"), ("Cedar", "336.00")]:
    t.post(owner, -D(fee), "fee to operating")

t.post("Maple", D("-640.00"), "repair")
t.post("Elm",   D("-380.00"), "repair")

for owner, paid in [("Maple", "7364.00"), ("Elm", "5583.00"), ("Cedar", "3864.00")]:
    t.post(owner, -D(paid), "owner payout")

print(t.bank, dict(t.owner), sum(t.deposits.values()))
# 11700.00, every owner balance 0.00, deposits 11700.00
Trust account, May Maple Court Elm Street Cedar Lane Total
Rent collected 8,700.00 6,400.00 4,200.00 19,300.00
Late fee 0.00 75.00 0.00 75.00
Management fee at 8% (696.00) (512.00) (336.00) (1,544.00)
Repairs paid (640.00) (380.00) 0.00 (1,020.00)
Paid out to owner (7,364.00) (5,583.00) (3,864.00) (16,811.00)
Owner balance, May 31 0.00 0.00 0.00 0.00

Every post passes both assertions. On May 31 the bank shows $11,700.00, exactly the deposits held.


The bank side of the same idea in ZeraBooks: deposits, withdrawals and net must agree with the statement before a month is signed off.

How does commingling show up in the data?

Run the same month in a different order. Pay the Elm Street plumber on May 2, before Elm's rent has come in:

t = Trust()
# ...opening deposits as above...
t.post("Elm", D("-380.00"), "repair")
# AssertionError: Elm is negative: another owner's money was used

The bank balance is still positive, and the first assertion still holds, because the bank doesn't know whose money is whose. The $380 came out of money that belongs to Maple's owner or Cedar's tenants. In many states, that is what trust account rules prohibit, even if Elm's rent arrives the next day.

A month-end reconciliation can pass even when an owner went negative for two weeks in the middle. Check after every posting.

No code fixes this after the fact. The practice does: pay a repair from trust only when that owner's balance covers it, or have the owner fund a reserve first.

Which design choices keep the model honest?

  1. Keep deposits separate from owner balances. Both are liabilities, but deposits belong to tenants. An owner payout should never reach into the deposit total.
  2. Move fees out of trust as a transfer. The 8% fee is the manager's income only once it has moved to the operating account. In the trust model it is money leaving that owner's balance.
  3. Check after every post. Month-end checks miss mid-month negatives.
  4. Use Decimal for money. The invariant is an equality to the cent, and float sums drift.

Key takeaways

  • Invariant: trust bank balance = owner balances + deposits held, always.
  • Second rule: no owner below zero, or another owner's money paid their bill.
  • In the worked May, $1,544.00 of fees moved to operating and the trust closed at $11,700.00, all deposits.
  • Assert after every posting; month-end reconciliation alone can hide commingling.

FAQ

Why can the bank balance be fine while trust rules are broken?

Because the bank balance is a total. It can't tell whose money paid a bill. Only per-owner balances show that.

Is a security deposit an owner's money?

No. It is a liability to the tenant until the lease ends, so it is tracked apart from what is owed to the owner.

Does ZeraBooks keep tenant ledgers?

No. ZeraBooks is a general ledger, not property management software. It has no tenant ledgers, rent collection or portals; managers send reports from their property software.

The full month, with the owner statement mapped to Schedule E lines, is in the guide to bookkeeping for property management. Disclosure: I'm on the ZeraBooks team. ZeraBooks bookkeeping services reconcile trust and operating accounts monthly from uploaded statements, from $150 a month in U.S. dollars.

title: UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18: uuidv7() vs UUIDv4 vs bigint Primary Keys, Benchmarked
description:
I loaded 10 million rows into PostgreSQL 18 tables keyed by bigint, UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 and compared load time, WAL, index size and insert throughput. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

UUIDv7 is a UUID that starts with a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, so new IDs sort in creation order. PostgreSQL 18 generates it natively with uuidv7(). As a primary key it keeps the B-tree index compact like a bigint sequence does, while staying globally unique like a random UUIDv4.

I loaded 10 million rows into three otherwise identical PostgreSQL 18.6 tables, keyed by bigint, uuidv4() and uuidv7(). UUIDv7 matched bigint on load time (37.3 s each), while UUIDv4 took 84.2 s and wrote 2.2x more WAL. I also found one trap: filtering with uuidv7(interval ...) directly in a WHERE clause skips the index.

TL;DR: should I use UUIDv7 primary keys in Postgres?

Yes, if you want UUID primary keys and the IDs do not need to hide when a row was created. On PostgreSQL 18, use id uuid primary key default uuidv7(). On PostgreSQL 17 or older, generate UUIDv7 in your app. Keep UUIDv4 for tokens and IDs whose creation time must stay private, and keep bigint if you never need IDs outside one database.

bigint identity UUIDv4 UUIDv7
Size 8 bytes 16 bytes 16 bytes
Generated by One sequence in the database Anyone, anywhere Anyone, anywhere
Sort order Insert order Random Creation time (ms)
Reveals Row count, insert order Nothing Creation timestamp
10M-row load (my test) 37.3 s 84.2 s 37.3 s
PK index after load 214 MB 385 MB 301 MB
Postgres built-in Always gen_random_uuid() / uuidv4() uuidv7() since 18

What is UUIDv7?

UUIDv7 is the time-ordered UUID version defined in RFC 9562, published in May 2024. The first 48 bits hold the Unix timestamp in milliseconds, then 4 version bits, then random or counter bits. Because the timestamp comes first, sorting UUIDv7 values as bytes sorts them by creation time, which B-tree indexes handle well.

The RFC describes it as featuring "a time-ordered value field derived from the widely implemented and well-known Unix Epoch timestamp source," and says "implementations SHOULD utilize UUIDv7 instead of UUIDv1 and UUIDv6 if possible."

A UUIDv7 from my test database, read left to right:

01a14a80-6c02-7160-b932-6c5ecd65f3c7
└──────┬─────┘ │
  timestamp    version 7   (rest: sub-millisecond precision + random)

Does PostgreSQL support UUIDv7?

Yes, since PostgreSQL 18, released on September 25, 2025. It added uuidv7(), an alias uuidv4() for gen_random_uuid(), and uuid_extract_timestamp(), which reads the timestamp back out. The PostgreSQL 18 docs say the timestamp uses "millisecond precision + sub-millisecond timestamp + random." PostgreSQL 17 and older have no uuidv7().

```sql title="PostgreSQL 18.6"
SELECT uuidv7(), uuidv4();
-- 01a14a74-450a-7a7e-a2f5-713a6b1da251 | 8c13f904-b813-4570-92de-5622dbb59443

SELECT uuid_extract_version(uuidv7()), uuid_extract_timestamp(uuidv7());
-- 7 | 2026-10-17 20:21:36.266+05

SELECT uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'); -- a UUIDv7 with a timestamp shifted one hour back




On PostgreSQL 17 the same call fails with `ERROR: function uuidv7() does not exist`. There, generate UUIDv7 in your application (Prisma's `uuid(7)` or the npm `uuid` package's `v7()`), or upgrade.

The [PostgreSQL 18 release announcement](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-18-released-3142/) calls it "the database-friendly uuidv7() function that provides better indexing and read performance for UUIDs." Here is what that looked like in my test.

## Is UUIDv7 faster than UUIDv4?

For inserts, yes. Loading 10 million rows took 37.3 s with UUIDv7 and 84.2 s with UUIDv4, and UUIDv4 wrote 4.6 GB of WAL against 2.1 GB. With 8 clients each inserting one row per transaction, UUIDv4 managed about 15% fewer inserts per second. UUIDv7 was within 2% of a `bigint` sequence on every insert test.

![UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 B-tree inserts: random UUIDv4 keys land on any leaf page and split pages across the index, while time-ordered UUIDv7 keys append to the rightmost leaf like a bigint sequence](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792251441/fabwaseem/blog/uuidv7-postgres/diagram-btree.jpg)

### Benchmark setup

- PostgreSQL 18.6 with default settings (`shared_buffers` 128 MB), on an 8 vCPU Xeon with 15 GB RAM.
- Three tables: `id` (the key under test), `created_at timestamptz default now()` and a 64-character `payload`.
- Bulk load: one `INSERT ... SELECT` of 10,000,000 rows per table after a `CHECKPOINT`. WAL is measured with `pg_current_wal_lsn()` and index density with [pgstattuple](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstattuple.html)'s `pgstatindex()`.
- Concurrent inserts: `pgbench`, 8 clients, 60 seconds of single-row `INSERT`s into the preloaded tables, 2 rounds. The table shows the average of the two rounds.



```sql title="The three tables"
CREATE TABLE t_bigint (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE t_uuidv4 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv4(),                created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE t_uuidv7 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),                created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);

Results

Metric bigint UUIDv4 UUIDv7
10M-row bulk load 37.3 s 84.2 s 37.3 s
WAL written by the load 1,964 MB 4,598 MB 2,098 MB
Table (heap) size 1,116 MB 1,202 MB 1,202 MB
Primary key index size 214 MB 385 MB 301 MB
Index leaf density 90.0% 70.3% 90.0%
Index leaf fragmentation 0.0% 49.8% 0.0%
Single-row inserts, 8 clients 49,528/s 41,331/s 48,690/s

UUIDv7's index is 41% larger than bigint's, because each key is 16 bytes instead of 8, but it is packed just as tightly (90% leaf density). UUIDv4's index is 28% larger again than UUIDv7's, because random inserts split pages all over the tree and leave them about 70% full.

Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys slow?

Each new UUIDv4 lands at a random position in the B-tree, so inserts touch pages spread across the whole index. Once the index is larger than memory, every insert can mean reading a cold page, dirtying it, and logging a full-page image to WAL after each checkpoint. UUIDv7 keys always go to the rightmost leaf, the same hot page a sequence uses.

That explains each number in the table. The 2.2x WAL comes from full-page writes for thousands of different leaf pages. The 70% leaf density comes from 50/50 page splits in the middle of the tree. In my test the UUIDv4 index (385 MB) was three times shared_buffers (128 MB), so the gap in single-row inserts (15%) was smaller than in bulk loading (2.3x). It will grow as the table and index outgrow memory.

How do I use UUIDv7 as a primary key in PostgreSQL 18?

Declare the column as uuid with DEFAULT uuidv7(). Keep the native uuid type, not text: it stores 16 bytes instead of 36 characters plus overhead. Existing UUIDv4 rows can stay. Both versions share one uuid column, and new UUIDv7 keys simply sort after the old random ones.

```sql title="New table"
CREATE TABLE orders (
id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
total_cents integer NOT NULL,
created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);






```sql title="Existing table: new rows get UUIDv7"
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN id SET DEFAULT uuidv7();

Changing the default does not rewrite old rows or rebuild the index. It only changes how future keys are generated, so the right edge of the index starts behaving like a sequence from then on.

How do I use UUIDv7 with Prisma and Drizzle?

In Prisma, use @default(uuid(7)) to generate the ID in Prisma Client, or @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) to let PostgreSQL 18 generate it. In Drizzle, use uuid().primaryKey().default(sql\uuidv7()). I tested all three on PostgreSQL 18.6. Every ID came out as version 7, and 1,000 sequential creates sorted exactly in creation order.

```prisma title="prisma/schema.prisma (Prisma 7.10.1)"
// UUIDv7 generated by Prisma Client in Node.js
model Order {
id String @id @default(uuid(7)) @db.Uuid
total Int
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}

// UUIDv7 generated by PostgreSQL 18
model Invoice {
id String @id @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) @db.Uuid
total Int
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}




The two Prisma options are not equivalent. `prisma migrate dev` created `"id" UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7()` for `Invoice` but no default at all for `Order`. So a raw SQL insert into `Order` failed with `null value in column "id" ... violates not-null constraint` (code 23502), while the same insert into `Invoice` worked. If anything other than Prisma Client writes to the table (SQL scripts, another service, a queue worker), use `dbgenerated("uuidv7()")`. The [Prisma schema reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-schema-reference) documents both.



```ts title="schema.ts (Drizzle 0.45.4)"
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { integer, pgTable, timestamp, uuid } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const invoices = pgTable("invoices", {
  id: uuid().primaryKey().default(sql`uuidv7()`),
  total: integer().notNull(),
  createdAt: timestamp({ withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

drizzle-kit generate turned that into "id" uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7() NOT NULL. Drizzle's .defaultRandom() still means gen_random_uuid(), which is UUIDv4. For which ORM to pick in the first place, see my Drizzle vs Prisma benchmark.

Can I query by time using a UUIDv7 key?

Yes, because UUIDv7 order is time order: ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 returns the newest rows from the primary key alone. For a time range, compare against uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'), but wrap it in a subquery. Used directly, the volatile function forced a full parallel scan of 15.8 million rows in my test.

```sql title="Rows from the last 30 seconds"
-- Slow: uuidv7() is VOLATILE, so it cannot be an index condition
SELECT count(*) FROM t_uuidv7 WHERE id >= uuidv7(interval '-30 seconds');
-- Parallel Seq Scan, Rows Removed by Filter: 5,280,621 per worker, 3,430 ms

-- Fast: a scalar subquery is evaluated once (InitPlan) and used as the index bound
SELECT count(*) FROM t_uuidv7 WHERE id >= (SELECT uuidv7(interval '-30 seconds'));
-- Parallel Index Only Scan using t_uuidv7_pkey, Index Cond: (id >= (InitPlan 1).col1), ~42 ms




Both queries returned the correct count. The fix only changes the plan. The boundary is approximate within a millisecond, because the bound has random bits after the timestamp, so keep a real `created_at` column for exact cut-offs and reports. `ORDER BY id DESC` on a UUIDv4 table also runs fast, but its "latest" rows are random ones.

## Is UUIDv7 safe to expose in URLs?

Only if creation time is not sensitive. Anyone can decode the timestamp from a UUIDv7: `uuid_extract_timestamp()` returned `2026-10-17 20:32:57.748+05` for a row whose `created_at` was 10 ms earlier. RFC 9562 says "if UUIDs are required for use with any security operation within an application context in any shape or form, then UUIDv4 SHOULD be utilized."

Practical rules:

- **Fine as UUIDv7:** orders, posts, messages, events, internal IDs, anything you would happily sort by date.
- **Use UUIDv4 or a random token:** password reset tokens, invite links, API keys, session IDs, and records where signup time is private (for example, user IDs in a service where account age matters).
- **Never rely on any UUID for authorization.** Unguessable is not the same as access control.

## UUIDv7 vs bigint vs ULID: which should I use?

Use `bigint` identity when IDs are created only by one database and never leave it: smallest index, fastest joins. Use UUIDv7 when clients, services or offline devices create IDs, or when you merge data across databases. ULID gives similar time-ordered properties, but it needs a text column or a conversion, while UUIDv7 fits the native 16-byte `uuid` type.

![Decision chart: bigint identity for single-database internal IDs, UUIDv7 for distributed or client-generated IDs, UUIDv4 for secrets and tokens, ULID only when you need its text format](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792251442/fabwaseem/blog/uuidv7-postgres/diagram-decision.jpg)

| Need | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| Internal IDs, one database, maximum speed | `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` |
| IDs generated in the app, mobile or other services | UUIDv7 |
| Merging rows from several databases or regions | UUIDv7 |
| IDs that must not reveal creation time | UUIDv4 |
| Secrets: tokens, reset links, API keys | Random token (UUIDv4 or longer) |
| Existing ULID system | Keep ULID, or store it as `uuid` (both are 128 bits) |

Before relying on `uuidv7()`, run `SELECT version();` on every environment, including CI and local Docker containers, since a server still on 17 will reject it. If you self-host Postgres next to your app as in my [Coolify self-hosting guide](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/self-host-nextjs-with-coolify), the major version is set by the database image you choose.

## Common UUIDv7 mistakes

- **Storing UUIDs as `text` or `varchar(36)`.** Use the `uuid` type: 16 bytes, faster comparisons.
- **Calling `uuidv7(interval ...)` directly in `WHERE`.** Wrap it in `(SELECT ...)` or compute the bound in the app, or the index is skipped.
- **Using Prisma `uuid(7)` when other writers exist.** It sets no database default. Use `dbgenerated("uuidv7()")`.
- **Expecting `uuidv7()` on PostgreSQL 17.** It does not exist there. Generate in the app or upgrade to 18.
- **Exposing UUIDv7 where timing is private.** Its first 48 bits are the creation time.
- **Dropping `created_at`.** The UUID timestamp is approximate and set by whoever generated the ID. Keep a real column for reporting.

## Key takeaways

- UUIDv7 starts with a 48-bit millisecond Unix timestamp, so IDs sort by creation time; PostgreSQL 18 generates it with uuidv7().
- In my 10M-row test, UUIDv7 loaded as fast as bigint (37.3 s) while UUIDv4 took 84.2 s and wrote 2.2x more WAL.
- UUIDv4's primary key index ended 28% larger than UUIDv7's, with 70% leaf density and 50% fragmentation.
- With 8 concurrent clients, UUIDv4 inserted about 15% fewer rows per second than UUIDv7.
- Wrap uuidv7(interval ...) in a scalar subquery for time-range filters; called directly, it forced a full table scan.
- Prisma's uuid(7) generates IDs in the client with no database default; dbgenerated("uuidv7()") puts the default in Postgres.
- UUIDv7 reveals creation time, so keep UUIDv4 or random tokens for secrets and private timestamps.

## FAQ

### What is UUIDv7?

UUIDv7 is the time-ordered UUID version from RFC 9562, published in May 2024. Its first 48 bits are a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, followed by version bits and random or counter bits. Because the timestamp comes first, UUIDv7 values sort by creation time, which keeps B-tree indexes compact when they are used as primary keys.

### Does PostgreSQL support UUIDv7?

Yes, since PostgreSQL 18, released on September 25, 2025. It added the uuidv7() function, an optional interval argument that shifts the timestamp, uuidv4() as an alias for gen_random_uuid(), and uuid_extract_timestamp() to read the time back. PostgreSQL 17 and older return an error that uuidv7() does not exist.

### Is UUIDv7 faster than UUIDv4 in Postgres?

For inserts, yes. In my PostgreSQL 18.6 test, a 10-million-row load took 37.3 seconds with UUIDv7 and 84.2 seconds with UUIDv4, and UUIDv4 wrote 2.2 times more WAL. With 8 clients inserting single rows, UUIDv4 managed about 15 percent fewer inserts per second. UUIDv7 stayed within 2 percent of bigint.

### Should I use UUIDv7 or bigint as a primary key?

Use bigint identity when one database creates every ID and the IDs never leave your system, because its index is smallest and joins are fastest. Use UUIDv7 when the app, mobile clients or other services create IDs, or when you merge data across databases. In my test UUIDv7's index was 41 percent larger than bigint's.

### How do I use UUIDv7 with Prisma?

Use @default(uuid(7)) to generate the ID in Prisma Client, or @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) on PostgreSQL 18 to generate it in the database. Add @db.Uuid for the native type. The uuid(7) option sets no database default, so raw SQL inserts fail with a not-null error; dbgenerated works for every writer.

### How do I use UUIDv7 on PostgreSQL 17?

PostgreSQL 17 has no uuidv7() function, so generate UUIDv7 in your application and store it in a uuid column. Prisma's uuid(7) default and the npm uuid package's v7() both produce RFC 9562 version 7 values. When you upgrade to PostgreSQL 18, switch the column default to uuidv7() without rewriting old rows.

### Is it safe to expose UUIDv7 in URLs?

Only when creation time is not sensitive. Anyone can decode the first 48 bits, and uuid_extract_timestamp() returns the time in PostgreSQL. RFC 9562 says UUIDv4 should be used if UUIDs are involved in any security operation. Keep UUIDv4 or random tokens for reset links, invites, API keys and private user records.

### Can I query a time range using UUIDv7 ids?

Yes. Compare the key against uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'), but wrap the call in a scalar subquery such as id >= (SELECT uuidv7(interval '-1 hour')). Because uuidv7() is volatile, calling it directly in WHERE forced a full parallel scan of 15.8 million rows in my test, about 3.4 seconds instead of about 42 milliseconds.


---

*Originally published on [fabwaseem.com](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/uuidv7-postgres).*
