title: RingBreaker: An AI Agent That Breaks UPI Mule Rings on FalkorDB
description:
RingBreaker is an AI agent that investigates UPI mule rings inside a FalkorDB graph, freezes the ring only after a human approves, and then proves with one more graph query that no money path is left.

  • Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com
  • Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker
  • Built for: Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (FalkorDB), Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data. Solo, built Oct 15 to 18, 2026.
  • The loop in one line: investigate → verdict → human approval → freeze → verify ("13 open routes, then 0").

The problem

A scam victim pays a "KYC update" fee over UPI. Within hours the money has hopped through four accounts and is gone.

  • Each hop looks harmless. A Rs 8,000 transfer between two accounts is normal on its own.
  • The pattern lives in the connections. Brand-new accounts, minimal KYC, shared phones and devices, money fanning in and out within minutes.
  • Tables hide it. Following money four hops deep in SQL means four self-joins, and the query has to know the shape in advance.
  • Most fraud demos stop at "flagged". Nobody acts on the alert, and nobody checks that the action worked.

In simple words

Think of a bucket brigade passing stolen water down a line of people. You could question each person on their own, and each one would only say "I passed a bucket."

  • RingBreaker looks at the whole line at once: who passed to whom, who stands on the same spot (a shared phone or device), and where the water ends up.
  • It then asks a person: "Remove these five from the line?"
  • After they say yes, it checks again that no bucket can still reach the end. That last check is the point of the project.

The stack

  • FalkorDB: the only datastore. Accounts, transactions, devices, alerts, verdicts and the audit trail all live in one graph. Docker locally, FalkorDB Cloud in production.
  • Node.js + Express: the API, the agent loop and the tools, using the official falkordb client.
  • Groq (groq-sdk) with function calling: openai/gpt-oss-120b as the main model, qwen/qwen3.8-27b as a fallback when the daily quota runs out.
  • React + Vite + react-force-graph-2d: the three-pane dashboard and the live graph canvas.
  • Server-Sent Events: each tool call streams to the browser as it happens.
  • Render: one Docker image serves the API and the built UI on a single URL.

The agent reaches FalkorDB only through read-only tools; the single write path runs from the API after a person approves.

How it actually works, step by step

  1. You click an alert, for example a victim complaint: "paid ~25,000 for a fake KYC update; money moved on within hours."
  2. The API starts the agent and streams every step over SSE. The agent picks graph tools (get_alert, money_trail, fan_stats, shared_identity, expand_ring and others). Each one runs a parameterized Cypher query.
  3. The canvas lights up the exact nodes and edges each query touched. A "Show Cypher" toggle reveals the query behind every step.
  4. The agent submits a structured JSON verdict: ring_confirmed, suspicious or benign, ring members with roles (victim, layer, collector, cashout), evidence citing graph facts, and recommended freezes.
  5. The server validates the verdict and saves it as a Case node in the graph.
  6. You review the evidence, untick anything you disagree with, type your name and press Approve freeze.
  7. The server freezes the approved accounts, writes an audit edge for each, re-runs the verify query and shows the result, for example 13 open routes → 0. The alert then moves to Closed.

The agent proposes; a person decides; the graph proves it.

The dashboard: alert queue with live status on the left, the graph canvas in the middle, the agent trace on the right, and the four-stage tracker in the header.

Mid-investigation on ALT002 (Ring B, the device farm). Every account, device and phone the agent touched is on the canvas, with its latest step glowing. The trace shows each tool call, its arguments and timing, and the switch to the fallback model when the daily quota ran out.

The graph and the agent's tools

One FalkorDB graph, ring, with 7,847 nodes and 25,962 edges, all synthetic and generated from a seeded random generator so every demo is reproducible.

  • Nodes: Account (1,911), VPA, Device, Phone, Alert (7), plus Case nodes written at run time.
  • Edges: SENT (20,007, one per transaction, with amount and ts), USES_DEVICE, LINKED_PHONE, HAS_VPA, ABOUT, and the audit edges INCLUDES {role} and ACTION {type, ts, approved_by}.
  • Transactions are edges, not nodes. A trail of N transfers is an N-hop path, so -[:SENT*1..4]-> answers "where did the money go?" in one query.
  • Planted scenarios:
    • Ring A, a layering chain: 4 victims → 3 first-layer mules → 2 second-layer mules → 1 collector → 1 cash-out, with amounts split into chunks minutes apart.
    • Ring B, a device farm: 6 accounts on 2 devices and 1 phone, each collecting small payments from many senders, then sweeping to one account.
    • Ring C, a decoy: 3 accounts on a shared device but with no money link. The right answer is "suspicious, monitor", not a freeze.
    • Benign look-alikes: a busy merchant with high fan-in, and a family sharing one phone. Neither may be flagged.
  • Tools the model can call (read-only):
Tool What it asks the graph
money_trail Follow money forward or backward up to N hops, with all(r IN relationships(p) WHERE r.ts >= $since) on every edge
shared_identity Who else uses this device or phone: `(a)-[:USES_DEVICE\
{% raw %}fan_stats In/out degree, totals and pass-through ratio
expand_ring Grow a candidate ring along money and identity links at once (UNION ALL)
account_profile Age, KYC level, and how many accounts share each device or phone
get_alert The alert and its target account
run_readonly_cypher A guarded free-form fallback for anything else
  • Every tool starts from an indexed lookup (Account.id, Device.id, Phone.number, VPA.handle, Alert.id, Case.id). Queries take 5 to 30 ms locally and 230 to 470 ms from Render to FalkorDB Cloud.
  • Every tool call emits a trace event: tool, arguments, the exact Cypher, a one-line summary, and the node and edge IDs it touched. The canvas highlights from those IDs.

Act, then prove it

Flagging is half the job. RingBreaker acts on the verdict and then checks its own work.

  • The model cannot freeze anything. Action tools (create_case, freeze_account, verify_cutoff, close_case, generate_report) are never offered to the LLM. Only the approval API calls them.
  • The approval gate is one Cypher statement. It freezes an account only if the case proposed it and it is still active, and writes the audit edge in the same query: 
MATCH (c:Case {id: $case_id}), (a:Account {id: $account_id})
WHERE $account_id IN c.proposed_freezes AND a.status = 'active'
SET a.status = 'frozen'
CREATE (c)-[:ACTION {type: 'freeze', ts: $now, approved_by: $approved_by, reason: $reason}]->(a)
  • Verify counts open money routes into the ring's end account that avoid every frozen account: 
MATCH p = (src:Account)-[:SENT]->(m:Account)-[:SENT*0..5]->(t:Account)
WHERE m.id IN $ring AND t.id IN $terminals AND NOT src.id IN $ring
  AND none(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n.status = 'frozen')
RETURN count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id]) AS routes
  • It counts distinct routes, not raw paths. Each transaction is its own edge, so split payments multiply paths: Ring A has 1,488 raw paths but 13 distinct routes. After the freeze: 0.
  • A leak check stops the proof from fooling itself. It counts ring money that already reached an active account the case never named. The cut-off counts as verified only when routes and leaks are both 0.
  • Alerts close themselves from graph state. Each alert shows Open, Awaiting approval, Closed, Needs review, Monitoring or Dismissed, derived from its latest case.
  • A report is generated from graph data only: accounts and roles, the agent's evidence, every approved action with approver and time, and the live verify result.

Safety: an agent that writes Cypher on untrusted data

The agent reads text it cannot trust and writes queries, so safety lives in code, not in the prompt.

  • Reads physically cannot write. Every read tool runs as GRAPH.RO_QUERY, so FalkorDB itself refuses any write. A test bypasses our own guard and confirms the database still blocks it.
  • Free-form Cypher passes a guard (guard.js): it rejects CREATE, MERGE, DELETE, SET, REMOVE, DROP, CALL, LOAD, FOREACH and multiple statements, enforces a LIMIT of at most 100, and runs with a server-side timeout.
  • Every query is parameterized. Values arrive as $parameters, never spliced into query text, including the seed script.
  • Verdicts are grounded. The validator rejects ring members no tool returned, freezes on victims or non-members, and any freeze on a verdict weaker than ring_confirmed. An invalid verdict gets one retry.
  • Graph text is data. Holder names, UPI handles and alert text are marked untrusted in the system prompt. Even a successful prompt injection could not freeze anything: the model has no action tools.
  • Hard limits per run: 10 model steps, a 10-minute timeout, a 120K-token cap, and one investigation at a time.
  • Public demo hygiene: investigations and approvals need a demo passcode, resetting the graph needs an admin secret, both compared in constant time. No secrets in the repo.

Built to run on a free tier

The whole project runs on Groq's free tier: about 8K tokens per minute and 200K tokens per day, per model. The agent loop is designed around that.

  • Compact tool results. Tools return summaries and distinct transactions, not hundreds of near-duplicate paths.
  • Context trimming. Once the prompt passes about 5.5K tokens, older tool results shrink to their one-line summaries.
  • Model fallback mid-run. When the main model's daily quota runs out, the loop switches to the fallback model and continues from the same step. The trace shows the switch.
  • Self-adjusting requests. If a model rejects a request as too large (Qwen allows 7K input and 1K output tokens per minute), the loop trims the context or lowers the output cap and redoes the step.
  • Malformed tool calls are retried with a hint to send shorter arguments, so a truncated verdict does not fail the same way twice.
  • The report is a template, not LLM prose. It costs zero tokens and can only contain facts that are in the graph.
  • Cost of one investigation: roughly 18K to 35K tokens and 1 to 5 minutes, almost all of it waiting on rate limits. The graph queries are a rounding error.

What fought back

  • The proof could fool itself. In the final test the agent stopped at the collector and missed the cash-out account, which still held Rs 65,202. Verify still said "11 routes → 0". The route count only looks at paths through the case's own members, so freezing everything proposed always gives 0. The fix: a leak check that asks whether ring money already sits in an active account the case never named. That run now reads "Routes cut, but money leaked" instead of a false pass.
  • One transaction, one edge, hundreds of paths. Split payments multiply paths fast: 1,488 raw paths for 13 real routes. Counting distinct sequences of account IDs (count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id])) made the number something a reviewer can read.
  • Some things cannot be Cypher parameters. Edge direction, variable-length bounds and labels cannot be $params. money_trail pre-builds one query per (direction, hops) pair from constants, so user input never becomes query text.
  • Epoch milliseconds vs date strings. The agent compared ts to '2026-10-07' in free-form Cypher and got empty results. The tool description now says times are epoch ms.
  • Free-tier walls. A daily quota that runs out mid-investigation, a fallback model with 1K output tokens per minute, and verdicts cut off mid-word (tool_use_failed). Each became a handled case in the loop, with a test that replays the real error.
  • Prompting is not free. Telling the agent to also trace forward from the collector raised Ring A recall from 0.57 to 0.71. A stricter "run both trails" rule made it loop until the step cap, so it was dropped. Every prompt change was measured, not assumed.

What it does now

npm run eval runs the agent on all 7 alerts and scores it against a ground-truth file. 7 of 7 verdicts correct, 0 unsafe freezes: no victim, merchant or family account was ever recommended for freezing.

Alert Scenario Expected Got Freeze precision / recall
ALT001 Ring A complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 0.71
ALT002 Ring B complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT003 Ring B fan-in ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT004 Ring C decoy suspicious suspicious, no freeze
ALT005 Merchant benign benign
ALT006 Family benign benign
ALT007 Noise benign benign
  • Live run on the deployed site: Ring A's complaint named all 8 accounts (the victim plus all 7 mules, including the cash-out); after approval, verify went from 13 open routes to 0 with no leak, and the alert closed.
  • 53 automated tests: the Cypher guard, the read-only backstop, the approval gate, verify and the leak check, the passcode, verdict validation, and every free-tier failure mode, replayed with a fake LLM client so they cost no tokens.
  • The dashboard: an alert queue with live status, the graph canvas with role-colored rings and a step-by-step HUD, the agent trace with each step's Cypher, the verdict card with a confidence meter and run stats, and a before/after proof card.

The live demo after approval: Ring A frozen (red) with roles on the canvas, each proposed freeze and its reason, and the proof card: 13 open routes before the freeze, 0 after, no leak.

Who this is for

Fraud and risk teams at banks, payment apps and UPI providers who already get alerts but spend hours tracing each one by hand. It is also a pattern for anyone building agents that act on data: let the model read and recommend, keep writes behind a human and a single audited query, and end every action with a query that proves it worked.

What I learned

  • Graphs make the question short. "Where did this money go, four hops out, after Tuesday?" is one Cypher pattern, not four joins.
  • Put safety in the database, not the prompt. GRAPH.RO_QUERY is a stronger guarantee than any instruction to "only read".
  • Verify the verifier. A proof that only checks the agent's own case can pass while money sits in an account the agent missed.
  • Give the model less, not more. Compact tool results, one-line summaries and a short required checklist beat long instructions on a small token budget.
  • Measure every prompt change. A rule that sounded better made the agent worse; only the eval showed it.

What's next

  • Upstream leak detection: flag a missed mule that feeds money into the ring, not only one that receives from it.
  • Streaming ingestion: real-time transaction feeds into FalkorDB, so investigations start the moment a pattern appears.
  • Real integrations: bank and UPI freeze APIs behind the same approval gate.

Try it

Needs Node.js 22.9+, Docker and a free Groq API key.

git clone https://github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker && cd ringbreaker
cp .env.example .env               # add GROQ_API_KEY
docker compose up -d               # FalkorDB on :6379, Browser on http://localhost:3000
(cd server && npm install) && (cd web && npm install)
npm run generate && npm run seed   # seeded synthetic graph into FalkorDB
(cd server && npm start)           # API on http://localhost:8080
(cd web && npm run dev)            # UI on http://localhost:5173

Open the UI, click ALT001, approve the freeze, and watch the open routes drop to 0.

Disclosures: all data is synthetic; no real people, accounts or UPI handles. Built with help from an AI coding assistant; I reviewed the code and can explain every part of the architecture and its safety model.

Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents by FalkorDB, Track 01. Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com · Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker

title: Building a liquid glass card with CSS
description:
A glass card can look great over a gradient and become unreadable the moment you put real content behind it. The blur is only one part of the effect. Tint, edge highlights and the backdrop matter just as much.

I built GradientDeck, formerly Gradienty.codes. Its liquid glass tool lets you adjust those pieces visually. Here’s a smaller, standalone CSS version you can use without the generator.

Start with something behind the glass

A flat background gives the filter very little to work with. This example uses two radial gradients so you can actually see the material.

<div class="scene">
  <article class="glass">
    <div class="glass-content">
      <h2>Make room for the good stuff.</h2>
      <p>A small glass card, built with plain CSS.</p>
    </div>
  </article>
</div>

.scene {
  min-height: 28rem;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  padding: 2rem;
  background:
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 20% 25%, #0d9488, transparent 60%),
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 80% 75%, #7c3aed, transparent 60%),
    #0f172a;
}

.glass {
  position: relative;
  width: min(100%, 24rem);
  box-sizing: border-box;
  padding: 2rem;
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 24%);
  border-radius: 1.75rem;
  background: #172033;
  color: #fff;
  box-shadow:
    0 20px 70px rgb(0 0 0 / 24%),
    inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 35%),
    inset 0 -1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 8%);
}

@supports ((backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) or
           (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1px))) {
  .glass {
    background: rgb(15 23 42 / 48%);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
    backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
  }
}

.glass-content {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1;
}

.glass h2 { margin: 0 0 0.75rem; }
.glass p { margin: 0; line-height: 1.6; }

The card starts with a solid background. Browsers that support backdrop filtering get the translucent version through @supports.

Add a highlight without washing out the text

The thin border defines the silhouette. The inset shadows catch the upper and lower edges. A separate highlight layer adds a little sheen:

.glass::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  pointer-events: none;
  background: linear-gradient(
    135deg,
    rgb(255 255 255 / 14%),
    transparent 45%
  );
}

Keep the highlight subtle. A bright white overlay across the entire card quickly makes the surface look cloudy.

Tune it in this order

  1. Backdrop: put the card over the actual page or image you plan to use.
  2. Tint: increase the background alpha until the text is comfortable to read.
  3. Blur: soften distracting detail without losing all the color behind it.
  4. Highlights: add enough light to define the edges.

A blur value alone won’t guarantee readable text. Check the card over both the brightest and busiest parts of the background, especially if content scrolls underneath it.

When nothing seems to blur

First, check that the card’s background is translucent and that there is something behind it.

Then inspect its ancestors. A parent with opacity below 1, a filter, a mask or its own backdrop filter can limit which pixels the child samples. Nested glass panels are a common place to encounter this. MDN explains the behavior in its backdrop-filter reference.

Use an alpha background color to make the surface translucent. Setting opacity on the whole card also fades its text and children.

Give people a solid option

Where the browser exposes the reduced-transparency preference, you can honor it with an opaque surface:

@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .glass {
    background: #172033;
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: none;
    backdrop-filter: none;
  }

  .glass::before { display: none; }
}

This also removes the decorative highlight. It doesn’t replace checking contrast in the default design.

For performance, start with one filtered surface. Avoid animating the blur radius, and be cautious about adding several overlapping blur layers to every card in a scrolling list. Check the result on the devices your readers actually use.

Try the settings visually

GradientDeck’s liquid glass generator has 20 presets, editable material controls and CSS and Tailwind CSS v4 exports. It’s free and doesn’t require an account. You can also preview the glass over an image from your device.

The example above recreates a glass-like appearance with CSS; it doesn’t implement optical refraction. Start simple, put it over your real UI, and let readability decide how transparent it should be.

title: Supabase SECURITY DEFINER RPC Callable by anon: Revoke It
description:
The short version

PostgreSQL grants EXECUTE to the PUBLIC role by default the moment CREATE FUNCTION runs. SECURITY DEFINER is the modifier that makes a function run with the privileges of the role that owns it rather than the role that called it. Create a write function with that modifier and leave it without an explicit REVOKE, and it becomes directly callable from the anon (unauthenticated) or authenticated role through Supabase's PostgREST layer.

  • Even with no GRANT written anywhere, EXECUTE for PUBLIC is there from the start
  • RLS policies on the table are irrelevant, because a SECURITY DEFINER function runs as the owner
  • Closing it means writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC explicitly and re-GRANTing only to the roles that need it

What it looks like

We created a function to push records for asynchronous delivery into a table called sync_outbox. Its definition pins search_path. search_path is the schema search path deciding which schema an unqualified object name resolves from inside a function, and pinning it to public is standard practice to stop a caller rewriting it so that a fake same-named object outside public resolves first.

create table if not exists public.sync_outbox (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  kind          text not null,
  ref_id        uuid,
  payload       jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
  status        text not null default 'pending'
                check (status in ('pending','sent','failed','dead')),
  attempts      int  not null default 0,
  -- (omitted)
);

alter table public.sync_outbox enable row level security;
create policy sync_outbox_staff_read on public.sync_outbox
  for select using (public.is_staff());

create or replace function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(p_kind text, p_ref_id uuid, p_payload jsonb)
returns uuid language sql security definer set search_path = public as $$
  insert into public.sync_outbox (kind, ref_id, payload)
  values (p_kind, p_ref_id, coalesce(p_payload, '{}'::jsonb))
  returning id;
$$;

The table's RLS says only "allow SELECT for the staff role". There is no policy anywhere permitting INSERT for anon. The function was written on the premise that only the app's backend (a cron worker) calls it. Pinning search_path was handled, but that guards a different kind of attack and does nothing for the problem here.

But this function is SECURITY DEFINER, and EXECUTE for PUBLIC is granted by default the instant CREATE FUNCTION runs. Supabase's PostgREST automatically exposes functions in the public schema at /rest/v1/rpc/<name>. It connects as anon or authenticated depending on the JWT the caller sends, and both roles inherit PUBLIC's privileges, so any function not explicitly revoked can be called directly by anyone.

That is what the review flagged. The table's RLS correctly narrowed reads to staff, and the function's execute privilege had never been narrowed at all.

Why

Three facts stack up.

① SECURITY DEFINER runs with the function owner's privileges

Not the calling role's privileges but those of the role that owns the function. That much is as specified.

② CREATE FUNCTION grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default

Even with no GRANT ever written, the function is callable by anyone the moment it is created. This is the opposite of tables, whose GRANT is closed by default (nobody can touch them without explicit permission): functions are open by default.

③ PostgREST automatically exposes public schema functions as RPCs

anon / authenticated are the connection roles Supabase provides, and they inherit PUBLIC's privileges as they are. With not a single GRANT on the table, one forgotten REVOKE on a SECURITY DEFINER function leaves a write path open that bypasses RLS entirely.

table GRANT        → closed by default → nobody touches it without explicit permission
function EXECUTE   → open by default   → anyone calls it unless explicitly revoked

This asymmetry is the cause of the oversight. Look only at the table and conclude "RLS protects this", and the hole on the function side goes unseen.

Fixing it

Strip the default PUBLIC privilege and re-allow only the roles that need it.

-- Close the SECURITY DEFINER write function to direct calls from anon/authenticated
-- (via PostgREST). Strip the default PUBLIC EXECUTE, allow only the backend (service_role).
revoke all on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) from public;
grant execute on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) to service_role;

REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC cuts off every inheritance source including anon / authenticated, and GRANT EXECUTE returns it to service_role alone, which actually needs to call it. The function definition itself is unchanged. All that happened is an open door was closed, with no effect on the intended calling path from the backend.

Checking it

Joining pg_proc and pg_roles gives you a function's owner and its execute privileges.

select p.proname, r.rolname as owner, p.proacl
from pg_proc p
join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner
where p.proname = 'enqueue_sync_outbox';

Look for EXECUTE for PUBLIC remaining in proacl (notation like =X/<owner>). Unless this check is run on every new SECURITY DEFINER write function, the same path opens once per function whose revoke was forgotten.

Making it not recur

This fix went in as an addition of revoke / grant to the existing migration file rather than recreating the function. Unless writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC paired with every SECURITY DEFINER function becomes the rule, the next write function added opens the same path.

  • Write REVOKE / GRANT directly beneath the creation SQL for any SECURITY DEFINER write function, so that adding only one of them is structurally impossible
  • Include the function's EXECUTE privilege in the same review item as the table's RLS review (on the premise of the asymmetry: tables closed by default, functions open by default)
  • Verify whether something is anonymously writable by actually querying pg_proc.proacl, not by reading the wording of a policy

However carefully the RLS policies are written, it means nothing if another door — the function's execute privilege — stands open. Another case shaped as an overlooked SECURITY DEFINER is in The function owner and the migration role. That one is about an intended bypass ceasing to work; this one about an unintended bypass working. Both start from the same property: SECURITY DEFINER behaviour is decided by who created the function, not by who called it.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.

The BigQuery Source plugin version 0.24.7 is available in Cloud Data Fusion version 6.11.0 and later. This release includes the following change:

Breaking

The Filestore agent volumes feature is available to all Google Cloud customers for evaluation and non-production use. To request access for your Google Cloud project, submit the Filestore agent volumes access request form.     • Fixed an issue in cm verify where verified findings could report "not found" or fail to persist confidence and status upon session completion or resumption.
    • Fixed syntax errors in generated verification scripts caused by invalid regex escaping in grep assertions during cm verify.
    • Prevented HTTP 409 lease conflict errors during long-running sessions by ensuring streaming HTTP connections are promptly released.

For more information, see CodeMender documentation.

title: What Amazon buying DuckDB's makers means for Aurora users
description:
Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the Amsterdam-based company behind the analytical database DuckDB, InfoQ reports. The first product result is already live. According to InfoQ, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL can now use DuckDB to run a single query across your live database rows and historical data stored in Amazon S3. The processing happens inside Aurora, and there is no extra fee: you pay only for the additional Aurora compute and the S3 requests those queries generate. That pricing and placement decides whether this story touches your bills and your pipelines.

The background you need

Databases do two broadly different jobs.

Transactional work, often called OLTP, is many small reads and writes: insert an order, update a user, fetch one profile. PostgreSQL is built for this. It stores each row's fields together, so grabbing or changing one record is fast.

Analytical work, often called OLAP, is the opposite. You scan millions of rows but only a few columns, as in total revenue by month for the last three years. Engines built for this store each column together. They read only the columns a query needs and process values in large batches. Running that kind of query on a row store works, but it is usually slow and expensive.

DuckDB is an open-source analytical database with that column-oriented design. Unlike most databases, it is built to run in-process. It lives inside another program instead of running as a separate server you connect to. People often describe it as SQLite for analytics. According to InfoQ, its creators are Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt, who co-founded DuckLabs. A non-profit, the DuckDB Foundation, oversees the project.

Aurora PostgreSQL is AWS's managed database service that is compatible with PostgreSQL. Your app talks to it like normal Postgres.

Some data lake vocabulary appears in the report without definitions:

  • Amazon S3 is object storage. Many teams move older data there because it is cheap to keep.
  • Parquet is a columnar file format, the on-disk version of the column-oriented idea above.
  • Apache Iceberg is a table format. It adds a metadata layer over a pile of Parquet files so they behave like one table, with a schema and a history of changes.
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog is a registry that records which tables exist and where their files live.
  • S3 Tables is an S3 offering designed specifically for storing Iceberg tables.

Finally, ETL (extract, transform, load) means copying data out of your app database into an analytics store. Reverse ETL goes the other way: it pushes data from the analytics side back into operational systems. According to InfoQ, AWS principal solutions architect Esra Kayabali describes the old approach this way: teams that needed recent Aurora data and historical S3 data together often built reverse ETL pipelines. Those pipelines duplicated data, raised infrastructure costs, and needed ongoing work to stay in sync.

Here is an analogy. Your current stock list sits at the shop counter and your archive sits in a warehouse across town. To answer a question that spans both, you used to pay a courier to keep copying boxes back to the counter. Now the clerk at the counter can read the warehouse shelves directly. The analogy breaks in two places. First, the clerk is still the same person, so the reading uses Aurora's own compute and is not free labor. Second, nothing gets copied, so the archive is only as current as whatever you have already written to S3.

What actually changed

These parts are new, according to InfoQ:

  • The acquisition. DuckLabs joins AWS. Mühleisen and Raasveldt will continue to lead the team and the open-source project's technical direction.
  • A DuckDB-powered feature in Aurora PostgreSQL. One query can combine live operational data with Iceberg tables managed through AWS Glue Data Catalog, plus Parquet and Iceberg data in S3 and S3 Tables. InfoQ says processing stays within Aurora, without additional network hops or ETL pipelines.
  • Availability and price. The feature is in all commercial regions and AWS GovCloud (US) at no additional charge. You pay for the incremental Aurora compute and S3 requests your queries create.

These parts were already true and stay true:

  • The license. DuckDB and the rest of what DuckLabs calls its Duck Stack, including DuckLake and Quack, remain free and open source under the MIT license. The DuckDB Foundation keeps supervising the projects.
  • The relationship. It is not new. In a post on Werner Vogels's blog, AWS distinguished engineer Andy Warfield writes that contact began while the S3 team was building S3 Tables. He says the teams collaborated for roughly two years, exploring AWS Lambda as a way to launch DuckDB queries quickly. They also smoothed integrations with AWS services through DuckDB's ATTACH and CONNECT commands.

So DuckDB could already reach AWS data from the outside. What changed is that DuckDB now runs inside a managed AWS database as a feature you can use from Postgres.

What it means if you deploy and run apps

The lever is simple. The analytical work now runs on your Aurora compute, and AWS charges no separate fee for the feature. That changes where your cost and risk sit.

Pipelines you might delete. You may run a scheduled job that copies S3 history into Postgres tables just so you can join it with live data. That job is now a candidate for retirement. You would stop maintaining sync code and stop storing the same data twice. Test with your real queries before you remove anything.

Costs move, they do not vanish. The pipeline's compute and duplicate storage go away. In their place you pay Aurora compute for each analytical query, plus S3 request charges. Analytical scans can be heavy. S3 request counts also tend to grow with the number of files a query touches, so data split into many small files can cost more to read.

Watch your database load. These queries run in the same service that serves your app. Before you point dashboards or reports at your primary instance, check the AWS documentation for where these queries can run. Then watch CPU and latency while you test.

If you use DuckDB on its own, in scripts, notebooks, or CI, InfoQ reports that the license and foundation oversight stay as they were. Community reaction was positive but cautious. One Reddit commenter quoted by InfoQ wrote: "I hope this doesn't slow the pace of innovation they have been doing". Release pace is worth watching.

AWS's broader pitch is about data size and AI agents. AWS technology VP Mai-Lan Tomsen Bukovec argues that DuckDB targets the majority of queries, which she says often run on 1 terabyte of data or less. She also argues that it suits AI agents that run many small exploratory queries. That is AWS's framing, not an independent measurement.

What to watch next: InfoQ calls Aurora PostgreSQL the first service to get a user-facing DuckDB feature. Expect announcements for other AWS services, though the report names none.

No additional charge does not mean free. According to InfoQ, you still pay for the extra Aurora compute and the S3 requests each query generates. Run a few of your real analytical queries on a test instance and check the bill and the instance metrics before you move production reports to it.

What we don't know yet

  • The deal terms. InfoQ's report does not give a price or financial terms.
  • Performance. The report includes no benchmarks for Aurora with DuckDB against a pipeline or a separate warehouse.
  • The details of use. The report does not say how you enable the feature, which Aurora PostgreSQL versions support it, or whether it can write to Iceberg tables as well as read them.
  • Isolation. It is unclear how analytical queries are kept from slowing transactional traffic on the same cluster.
  • Other engines. The report mentions only Aurora PostgreSQL. It says nothing about Aurora MySQL or standard RDS for PostgreSQL.
  • Long-term direction. The current assurances cover licensing and foundation oversight. How AWS priorities will shape DuckDB's roadmap over time is still an open question.

Cloud Billing

Feature

Spend cap budgets are now generally available for a limited set of services

For eligible services, you can configure a spend cap budget to automatically pause usage when your estimated spend exceeds the budget amount you set. You can manage spend cap budgets in the Budgets page in the Google Cloud console and using the Cloud Billing Budget API.

Spend caps are a cost control mechanism. A spend cap is enforced when usage costs exceed your budget target amount. When enforced, any new request to the eligible services, within the specified project, are paused and no further usage costs are accrued until the spend cap is lifted. You can manually lift an enforced spend cap, or wait until the start of the next month when the spend cap is automatically lifted.

Spend caps use gross, estimated costs to trigger the alerts and caps, enforcing a cap much faster than the actual costs are processed and appear on billing reports. Even though faster than reports, the enforcement of spend caps isn't instant and any cost overages are billed as normal.

More information about spend cap budgets

For managing spend cap budgets in the Google Cloud console, see:

  • How spend cap budgets work to help you control spend
  • Limitations of spend cap budgets
  • Configure a spend cap budget
  • Lift an enforced spend cap

For managing spend cap budgets using the Cloud Billing Budget API, see:

Feature

Object contexts with extended data are available in Preview. Google services attach these contexts to your objects during automated analysis, such as machine learning labeling. To retrieve a context and its extended data, use the viewFullContext JSON API method.

Feature

Storage Insights datasets include the Object Contexts Catalog view (object_contexts_catalog_view), which you can use to analyze object contexts in BigQuery. For more information, see Object contexts catalog and Analyze object contexts.

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.106.0 is available. This release adds support for flexible managed instance groups on static compute nodes, multiple network interfaces (multi-NIC) for Google Cloud Managed Lustre instances, and parallelism controls for Terraform to accelerate cluster deployment and teardown.

This release also introduces the cloud-build community module to build container images with Cloud Build.

Additionally, this release adds preflight checks for storage profiles when you submit jobs and cleans up gateways when you cancel jobs.

This update also scopes the --main-only flag in the gcluster job logs command to the main Pod and its default container.

For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can query regional views of global Compute Engine project and OS image resources by using the regional read-only projectViews and imageViews endpoints. Querying regional views isolates your control-plane read requests to a specific region, helping your workloads stay available during global API disruptions. For more information, see Use regional views for resilient control-plane reads and Access global resources regionally for high availability.

    • Manage Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform reasoning engines to deploy and run customized reasoning applications.

  • CloudDeployCustomTargetType

    • Manage Cloud Deploy custom target types to define custom deployment targets and rendering actions.

    • Manage Live Stream channels to ingest, encode, and distribute live video streams.

    • Manage Live Stream inputs to configure video ingestion endpoints.

    • Manage Map Management API style configurations to define custom map styles.

  • NetworkSecurityDNSThreatDetector

    • Manage Network Security DNS threat detectors to monitor and mitigate DNS-based threats.

Dataform

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for the Gemini Enterprise web app, mobile app, and AI developer tools.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. Gemini 4 Argon is supported in the web app and mobile app. For more information about turning on the model, see Manage features on the web app.
  • AI developer tools: Enabled by default for licensed users when Antigravity authorized models uses the default selection. If your organization specifies a custom model list, an administrator must manually select Gemini 4 Argon. For more information, see Configure AI developer tools settings.

Gemini Enterprise: Connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce

You can connect workflows in Workflow Builder to Microsoft Teams, Notion, and Salesforce to search data and automate actions across these third-party apps.

For more information, see Workflows overview.

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon is available in AlphaEvolve

AlphaEvolve experiments can generate candidate programs with Gemini 4 Argon in the global, us, and eu regions. To use it, specify gemini-4-argon in the models field of generationSettings. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Supported models and AlphaEvolve limitations.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Gemini 4 Argon in CodeMender (Preview)

CodeMender now supports Gemini 4 Argon. To use it, pass --model gemini-4-argon to cm find, cm verify, or cm fix. Gemini 3.8 Flash remains the default model.

For more information, see Specifying the model.

Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive

Gemini 4 Argon (gemini-4-argon) is available in General Availability (GA). Gemini 4 Argon is Google's frontier model that excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. It supports a unified 1,048,576-token input and output limit, configurable thinking levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), long decodes up to 1,048,576 tokens using continuation tokens on the GenerateContent API, and agentic video understanding in GA.

Gemini 4 Argon Cyber Permissive (gemini-4-argon-cyber-permissive), a version of Gemini 4 Argon for defensive cybersecurity use cases, is also available in GA behind the Fairwind Program allowlist.

  • Known issue (long decodes): Long decoding (continuation_token) on the GenerateContent API (generateContent and streamGenerateContent) is supported only in the v1beta1 API (not v1). The Google Gen AI SDK uses v1beta1 by default unless api_version='v1' is specified in http_options; for direct REST calls, use the v1beta1 endpoint path.

For more information, see Get started with Gemini 4 and the developer's guide to Gemini 4 Argon.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Google Cloud CCaaS prerelease notes 6.22

Here are the pre-release notes for what we expect to be the next version of Google Cloud CCaaS. When we release this version, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Feature

Campaign-based scheduled callbacks

Agents can now schedule a callback during an outbound campaign call. The callback belongs to the campaign, not to an individual agent, and the dialer calls the consumer back in the time slot they chose. Administrators set slot length, capacity, booking window, and expiry for each campaign, and supervisors can track upcoming, completed, and expired callbacks from the campaign list.

Feature

Transcript separation for chat

You can now configure Google Cloud CCaaS to deliver a separate transcript file for each participant segment in a chat, instead of one combined transcript per session. Under Settings > Chat > Chat Transcript, select Per Segment in Transcript Separation to generate individual transcript files for each agent, virtual agent, or supervisor who joins the chat—helpful for identifying which participant handled each part of a transferred or escalated conversation. Your consumers still receive a single, full-chat transcript regardless of this setting.

By default, this capability is inactive. Contact Google Cloud Support to turn it on for your instance.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where direct access point (DAP) greeting messages played twice when a call was deflected to an internal phone number due to queue overcapacity.

  • Fixed an issue where session metadata for top-level menu paths and selected menus was incorrectly displayed in English instead of the user's configured language.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed Salesforce lookup was incorrectly treated as having no matches, which resulted in the creation of duplicate records.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound transfer restrictions remained in force even after being hidden in the administrator interface, causing queues to become silently unreachable for transfers.

  • Fixed an issue where hold music continued to play throughout a call recording after a warm transfer was completed.

  • Fixed an issue where outbound virtual agent audio was prematurely truncated during multi-message turns.

  • Fixed an issue where the Real-time Monitoring Queues report didn't accurately count skill-matched agents for skills-based queues, often displaying zero available agents despite their availability.

  • Fixed an issue where calls deflected to an external phone number after entering a queue were incorrectly recorded as abandoned by the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where the credit card tokenizer was missing from the SmartActions menu during outbound callback calls.

  • Fixed an issue where mandatory call dispositions were discarded if an agent's voice connection dropped but their session remained active.

  • Fixed an issue where the text resize menu in the chat widget wasn't scrollable at 400% browser zoom, which prevented users from accessing all available text size options.

  • Fixed an issue where the system incorrectly prevented saving automatic call redirection settings when the target was a virtual agent-operated queue.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate call records were created for a single inbound call, causing incorrect wait times to appear in the real-time queue view.

  • Fixed an issue where empty data attributes caused an error in the agent interface during call connections.

  • Fixed an issue where the Transfer Restrictions destination picker provided no feedback when a queue was ineligible, making it indistinguishable from a typo or search error.

  • Fixed an issue where incoming calls were rejected with a SIP 603 error due to high database latency and connection timeouts.

  • Fixed an issue where the documentation for the Apps API and call session metadata schema didn't define the top-level parentId and finishReason fields.

  • Fixed an issue where certain inbound call failures were incorrectly reported as a busy signal.

  • Fixed an issue where the event processor service crashed during scaling or rebalancing of the system.

  • Fixed an issue where the conversation ID was missing from chat events during active sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where report exports didn't download or remained stuck in a processing state indefinitely.

  • Fixed an issue where agents could transfer calls to queues that were already closed if their transfer list was loaded while the queue was still open.

  • Fixed an issue where queued chats were assigned to agents after the end-user had become unresponsive without being prompted to check in.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls cold-transferred to an over-capacity queue generated duplicate reporting records and incorrect queue wait times if the callback leg failed.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls deflected to voicemail during after-hours played three separate audio prompts sequentially.

  • Fixed an issue where a single call was simultaneously assigned to two different agents if the pickup coincided with the cascade timer expiry.

  • Fixed an issue where direct inbound calls weren't projected to agents in a breakthrough-enabled status if another call was already waiting in their queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a gray empty area appeared below the chat container in the agent adapter when the iframe width was narrower than 449px.

  • Fixed an issue where several Kubernetes and Google Cloud service accounts were granted overly broad permissions, which could have allowed for unauthorized privilege escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's status sequence was recorded in the incorrect order following a brief connection loss during an active chat.

  • Fixed an issue where selecting a contact during a native campaign call didn't automatically open the corresponding record in the CRM.

  • Fixed an issue where AI-generated Smart Disposition suggestions were inconsistently displayed for outbound calls during the wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where call recordings became distorted or garbled when multiple holds were placed during a call.

  • Fixed an issue where audio uploads were accepted based on the file extension rather than the actual file content, which caused call disconnections when incompatible formats were played.

  • Fixed an issue where the call duration timer in the external call adapter didn't match the In-call status timer in the agent desktop for inbound calls.

  • Fixed an issue where the sentiment score was incorrectly displayed in the call adapter for calls escalated from a virtual agent, even when the Sentiment Analysis setting was disabled.

  • Fixed an issue where duplicate reporting rows were generated for call and wrap-up durations due to concurrent system events.

  • Fixed an issue where agents couldn't sign in or refresh their status if their account was linked to a deleted or unknown status.

  • Fixed an issue where the Manager API documentation for agent activity logs omitted 17 chat routing and activity values, leading to incomplete reporting data for customers.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR custom callback numbers for certain international regions, including Norway and Denmark, were incorrectly dialed with a +1 prefix.

  • Fixed an issue where metadata for calls deflected between virtual agent assignment and connection wasn't exported to the Cloud Storage bucket.

  • Fixed an issue where virtual agent to human chat escalations experienced delays of up to 300 seconds during agent assignment.

  • Fixed an issue where the Answer button didn't appear for dial-by-extension calls when other calls were already waiting in an agent's queue.

  • Fixed an issue where a supervisor's name didn't appear in the chat widget when joining a conversation using the monitor then barge workflow.

  • Fixed an issue where ending a chat session in one browser tab didn't automatically close the chat widget in other open tabs.

title: Stop Squinting at Messy LESS: How to Beautify Your Stylesheets in Seconds
description:
We've all been there. You inherit a project, open styles.less, and it looks like someone typed the whole thing in a single breath. Nested rules collapsed onto one line, mixins with no spacing, variables jammed against their values.

You can still read it. But every minute you spend decoding formatting is a minute you're not fixing the actual bug.

In this post I'll walk through what LESS is (quickly), why formatting matters more than people admit, and how a LESS beautifier can clean up a file in seconds. I'll also show you real before and after examples so you can judge for yourself.

Quick refresher: what is LESS?

LESS is a CSS preprocessor. It extends plain CSS with features like variables, nesting, mixins, functions and operations, then compiles down to regular CSS that browsers understand. The official LESS documentation is the best place to go deep on the language itself.

A tiny taste:

@primary: #3b82f6;

.button {
  background: @primary;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }
}

That nesting and the darken() function are what make LESS pleasant to write. But they're also what make badly formatted LESS painful to read, because the structure is the logic.

Why formatting matters more in LESS than in plain CSS

In plain CSS, a messy file is annoying. In LESS, a messy file can actually hide bugs. Here's why:

  • Nesting depth is meaning. A rule nested one level too deep (or too shallow) changes the compiled selector. If indentation doesn't match nesting, you can't see the mistake.
  • Mixins and guards are easy to miss. A mixin call buried in a long line is easy to overlook when you're debugging why a style is applied.
  • Missing braces are brutal. One unclosed } in a deeply nested block can break compilation, and the error message often points somewhere unhelpful.
  • Code review gets noisy. If every developer formats differently, pull requests fill up with whitespace changes that hide the real ones.

Consistent formatting isn't about being picky. It's about making the structure of your styles visible at a glance.

What does a LESS beautifier actually do?

A beautifier takes your LESS code and rewrites its whitespace and layout without changing what it means. Typically that includes:

  • Consistent indentation for nested blocks
  • One declaration per line
  • Sensible spacing around colons, braces and operators
  • Line breaks between rules so blocks are easy to scan

Crucially, it should not change your logic. Variables, mixins, operations and nesting stay exactly as you wrote them. Only the presentation changes.

A real before and after

Here's the kind of LESS you might get from a quick copy-paste, a minified export, or a teammate in a hurry:

@primary:#3b82f6;@radius:6px;
.mixin-card(@pad:16px){padding:@pad;border:1px solid #eee}
.btn{color:#fff;background:@primary;border-radius:@radius;&:hover{background:darken(@primary,10%)}.icon{margin-right:4px}}
.card{.mixin-card(24px);h2{font-size:1.25rem;a{color:@primary}}}

Technically valid. Practically unreadable. Now the same code after running it through a beautifier:

@primary: #3b82f6;
@radius: 6px;

.mixin-card(@pad: 16px) {
  padding: @pad;
  border: 1px solid #eee;
}

.btn {
  color: #fff;
  background: @primary;
  border-radius: @radius;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }

  .icon {
    margin-right: 4px;
  }
}

.card {
  .mixin-card(24px);

  h2 {
    font-size: 1.25rem;

    a {
      color: @primary;
    }
  }
}

Same code, same output once compiled, but now you can see that .icon lives inside .btn, that .card calls the mixin, and that the link color sits three levels deep. That last one is a good reminder to watch your nesting depth, which you'd never notice in the single-line version.

How to use an online LESS beautifier

When I just need to clean up a snippet or a single file, I don't want to configure a toolchain. An online tool is the fastest path. I put together the LESS Beautifier on 99tools for exactly this situation. The workflow is simple:

  1. Paste your messy LESS into the input box.
  2. Run the beautifier.
  3. Copy the cleaned-up result back into your editor.

No install, no config file, no setup. It's handy when you're:

  • Reviewing LESS from a client or a legacy project
  • Cleaning a snippet before sharing it in a bug report or Stack Overflow question
  • Reading code that was minified or exported from another tool
  • Teaching or learning LESS and wanting readable examples

A quick tip: as with any online tool, don't paste proprietary code or anything containing secrets if your company policy says otherwise. For sensitive projects, use a local formatter instead (more on that below).

Beautifier vs. linter vs. compiler

These three get confused a lot, so here's the short version:

Tool What it does Changes your code?
Beautifier / formatter Fixes indentation, spacing and layout Whitespace only
Linter Flags problems and style violations Usually no (some auto-fix)
Compiler (lessc) Turns LESS into CSS Produces new output

A beautifier won't catch a typo in a variable name, and it won't tell you your nesting is too deep. Use it alongside a linter like Stylelint and your normal compile step, not instead of them.

Best practices for clean LESS

Formatting is the baseline. Here are a few habits that keep LESS maintainable once it's tidy:

  • Keep nesting to 3 levels or fewer. Deep nesting creates overly specific selectors that are painful to override.
  • Group variables at the top or in a dedicated file so theme changes happen in one place.
  • Name mixins clearly and keep them small and single-purpose.
  • Agree on one style as a team (2 spaces vs 4, blank lines between rules) and automate it so nobody argues in code review.
  • Run a formatter before committing, so diffs show real changes only.

When an online tool isn't the right fit

I want to be upfront: an online beautifier is great for quick jobs, but it isn't the answer to everything.

If your team formats code on every commit, you'll be better served by an automated local setup, such as Prettier, which supports LESS, wired into your editor or a pre-commit hook. And if you're starting a brand new project, it's also worth knowing that native CSS now supports nesting, which covers some of what people originally reached for preprocessors to do. The MDN guide to CSS nesting is a good overview if you're weighing your options.

That said, LESS is still used in plenty of real projects, and a lot of us are maintaining it for years to come. For those moments, having a quick way to make messy code readable is genuinely useful.

Wrapping up

Readable code isn't a luxury. It's how you spot bugs sooner, review faster, and onboard people without a lecture. A LESS beautifier takes about ten seconds and removes one whole category of friction.

If you have a messy .less file sitting around, try the LESS Beautifier on it and see how the structure changes. And if you've got your own tips for keeping LESS clean, or a horror story from a legacy stylesheet, drop it in the comments. I'd love to hear it.

Happy styling! 🎨

Application Integration

Security

An Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in the AuthConfig validation and integration execution runtime in Application Integration versions prior to August 27, 2026. For more information, see the GCP-2026-068 security bulletin.

BigQuery

Feature

The Apache Hive catalog endpoint in the Lakehouse runtime catalog is now generally available (GA). This integration lets you use the metastore as a serverless, central metadata layer, enabling seamless data sharing and unified querying across Apache Spark, Apache Hive, and BigQuery.

For more information, see About the Hive catalog endpoint and Set up Spark and Hive with the Lakehouse runtime catalog.

Feature

Metadata migration from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse is now generally available (GA). You can perform a one-time backfill migration or dry run to migrate metadata from a Dataproc Metastore service to an Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint or a Hive catalog endpoint using the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, or the REST API.

For more information, see Migrate metadata from Dataproc Metastore to Lakehouse.

Feature

Conversational analytics now lets you create a conversation with all of the data sources in multiple projects, or create a conversation with a dataset. These features are generally available (GA).

Feature

You can publish a BigQuery Conversational Analytics agent in Gemini Enterprise. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

The AI.AGG function now supports the output_schema argument, which lets you specify the schema of the function output as a comma-separated list of fields. This feature is generally available (GA).

Certificate Manager

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Google Public CA (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates now rotate more frequently. This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. The transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Certificate Manager automatically manages both issuance and renewal.

For more information, see Google-managed certificates and Use Google-managed certificates.

Cloud Load Balancing

Change

Google-managed public SSL certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority (pki.goog) are gradually transitioning from a 90-day validity period to a 45-day validity period to improve security.

To align with modern industry-wide security standards and promote shorter certificate lifespans, Google-managed public certificates signed by Public Certificate Authority now rotate more frequently.

This proactive rotation enhances the overall security posture of load balancers. Transition requires no manual intervention or configuration changes as Google Cloud automatically manages issuance and renewal for both Certificate Manager and Compute Engine SSL certificates.

For more information, see Renew a Google-managed SSL certificate.

Feature

Service rate limiting policies are now available in Preview for regional internal Application Load Balancers and Secure Web Proxies.

Service rate limiting policies let you maintain service availability among trusted clients that might consume an inordinate amount of resources.

For more information, see the Service rate limiting overview.

Cloud SQL for MySQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL

Issue

When you enable the Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance created before April 18, 2026, the integration defaults to once a day instead of near real-time.

Near real-time updates upon Knowledge Catalog enablement aren't yet available for all existing instances. A new announcement will be published when this feature becomes available.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: When you reserve capacity by using future reservation requests, you can specify that Compute Engine delivers your reserved capacity as specifically targeted reservations. Specifically targeted reservations help you track and control which Compute Engine instances consume your reserved capacity. For more information, see About future reservation requests.

Feature

Generally available: You can increase the size of a Google Cloud Hyperdisk volume that's in multi-writer mode while the volume is attached to multiple instances. Previously, you had to detach the volume from all instances before you could resize it.

For more information, see Share disks between instances and Change the size or provisioned performance of a Hyperdisk volume.

Dataform

Feature

You can automatically preserve BigQuery data policies and data governance tags (Preview) applied to tables across Dataform executions by enabling the preserveGovernanceControls option in your table or workflow configuration. For more information, see Preserve access controls metadata. This feature is generally available (GA).

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 3.8 Flash regional availability in the United Kingdom

Gemini 3.8 Flash is generally available (GA) in the United Kingdom.

  • Location availability: Supported in the UK (europe-west2) in-country region with in-region at-rest data residency (DRZ) and machine learning processing (MLP).
  • App availability: Turned on by default in the web app for the UK region. Administrators can manage access with the Gemini 3.8 Flash toggle under Model availability.

For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Gemini 4 Argon available in Workflow Builder

Gemini 4 Argon is generally available (GA) for Workflow Builder. Gemini 4 Argon is also available in Workflow Builder workflow agents. Updates take up to a day to appear in workflow agents.

  • Location availability: Supported in global, us, and eu multi-regions, with data residency and ML processing support in us and eu. For more information, see Data residency for Gemini Enterprise.
  • App availability: Turned off by default. The toggle defaults to on beginning October 27, 2026. For instructions to turn on the model, see Manage features on the web app.

For more information, see Workflow Builder.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Priority PayGo support for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1

Priority Pay-as-you-go (PayGo) is available in General Availability (GA) for Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (gemini-nano-banana-2.1) on the global endpoint.

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.15.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Enhanced SARIF 2.1.0 reporting: Updated cm report SARIF output with standardized rule descriptors, severity properties, and repository-relative artifact locations for improved GitHub Code Scanning compatibility.
  • Model invocation metrics: Added model invocation tracking to cm stats --json, providing total, per-session, and per-turn invocation counts.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed an issue where token usage from completed turns was omitted from session logs during error or cancellation exit paths.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.

Feature

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is available in Public Preview

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from DeepSeek is available as a fully managed model (MaaS) in Model Garden. The model accepts text and image input, targets agentic and coding tasks, and supports a context window of up to 1M tokens.

For more information, see DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Google Cloud Armor

Feature

Cloud Armor supports service rate limiting. For more information, see Cloud Armor and service rate limiting. This feature is available in Preview.

Google Cloud Managed Service for Apache Kafka

Feature

Performance of the Cloud Storage Sink connector has been improved. The improvements include reduced out-of-memory errors, higher maximum throughput, and avoiding creating a large number of small files.

Fixed

Fixed an issue in GKE Sandbox where Pods using the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver could become indefinitely stuck in a Terminating state.

To resolve this issue, upgrade your node pools to GKE version 1.37.1-gke.1552000 or later and add the dev.gvisor.fuse.abort-on-teardown: "true" annotation to your Pod or Deployment metadata.

For more information, see About Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver for GKE and GKE Known Issues.
