title: Build a Hiring-Signal Feed from Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and SmartRecruiters (with Python)
description:
"They just opened 6 SDR roles" is one of the strongest timing signals in outbound. If a company is hiring for the team that would use your product, you have a reason to reach out now. Most teams get that signal from LinkedIn scrapes or expensive data vendors. But most tech companies already publish their entire job board as clean JSON through their applicant tracking system (ATS). This tutorial shows how to turn that into a company-level hiring-signal feed you can refresh every week.

The data source: public ATS job-board APIs

Career pages are usually powered by one of a handful of ATSs, and each exposes a public, unauthenticated endpoint meant for embedding job lists:

ATS Public endpoint pattern
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json (EU: api.eu.lever.co)
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}?includeCompensation=true
SmartRecruiters https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/{id}/postings

These are the employer's system of record. Roles show up here first and disappear when they're filled, so the data is fresher and cleaner than most aggregators.

A 20-line DIY version (Greenhouse only) 

import httpx, collections

def greenhouse_signal(slug):
    jobs = httpx.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs",
                     params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30).json()["jobs"]
    by_dept = collections.Counter(
        (j.get("departments") or [{"name": "Other"}])[0]["name"] for j in jobs)
    sales = [j for j in jobs if any(k in j["title"].lower()
             for k in ("sdr", "bdr", "account executive", "sales"))]
    return {"company": slug, "open_roles": len(jobs),
            "sales_roles": len(sales), "top_departments": by_dept.most_common(5)}

print(greenhouse_signal("stripe"))

That works, but a real feed also needs:

  • detection of which ATS a company uses,
  • Lever's EU cluster and SmartRecruiters' paging,
  • seniority classification,
  • salary parsing,
  • memory between runs, so you can say "+11 roles since last week".

That last part is what makes it a signal rather than just a list.

The hosted version: Hiring Signal Feed

Hiring Signal Feed is an Apify Actor that does all of the above. It returns one row per company, with:

  • open_roles, roles_by_department, roles_by_seniority, remote_roles
  • new_roles_7d and new_roles_30d
  • open_roles_change, roles_added_since_last_run and roles_closed_since_last_run, from a snapshot it keeps for you
  • salary_bands and the ats the company uses

Optionally, it also returns normalized job rows. Pricing is $0.01 per company row (or $0.0015 per job row), plus $0.02 per run.

pip install apify-client pandas

import os, pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
accounts = ["greenhouse:stripe", "greenhouse:discord", "ashby:ramp",
            "https://jobs.lever.co/spotify", "notion"]   # bare names are auto-detected

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/hiring-signal-feed").call(run_input={
    "companies": accounts,
    "outputMode": "companies",
    "titleKeywords": ["sales", "sdr", "bdr", "account executive"],
    "snapshotStoreName": "my-sales-hiring-watch",
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
df = df[df.row_type == "company"]
print(df[["company", "ats", "open_roles", "new_roles_30d", "roles_added_since_last_run"]]
      .sort_values("new_roles_30d", ascending=False))

Because titleKeywords is set, every count is computed only on sales roles. So new_roles_30d = 9 means nine new sales jobs this month.

Score and route accounts 

df["score"] = (df.new_roles_30d.fillna(0) * 2
               + df.roles_added_since_last_run.fillna(0) * 3
               + df.open_roles.fillna(0) * 0.2)
hot = df[df.score >= 10].sort_values("score", ascending=False)
hot.to_csv("hot_accounts.csv", index=False)

Get the actual postings for personalization

Run again with outputMode: "jobs" for just the hot accounts. Each job row includes title, department, location, posted_at, salary and the posting url. That's ideal for a first line like "Saw you're hiring a Founding AE in Austin…".

Make it weekly

  1. Save the input as an Apify Task and attach a Schedule (for example, Mondays at 07:00).
  2. Keep snapshotStoreName the same, so each run diffs against the last one.
  3. Pipe results to your CRM:
    • In Clay, use an HTTP API column that calls run-sync-get-dataset-items.
    • In n8n, Make or Zapier, use the Apify app (Run Actor, then Get dataset items, then upsert into HubSpot or Sheets).

cURL for the HTTP column:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/eligible_fame~hiring-signal-feed/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"companies":["{{domain_or_slug}}"],"outputMode":"companies"}'

Signals beyond sales hiring

The same feed answers other questions. A few common ones:

  • Selling data tools: filter for data engineer and analytics.
  • Selling security: watch for security and GRC roles.
  • Investors: track open_roles_change_pct across a portfolio for early momentum or slowdowns.
  • Recruiters: look for companies whose new_roles_7d jumps in your niche.

A sudden spike in manager and lead/principal seniority often means a new team is being built. That's usually a better trigger than one-off backfills.

Limitations to know

  • It only covers companies that use these four ATSs. That's most venture-backed tech, plus many enterprises on SmartRecruiters, but not every employer. If a company isn't found, you get a free error row.
  • posted_at semantics differ between ATSs. Some companies repost roles, so the snapshot diff (roles_added_since_last_run) is the most reliable "new" signal.
  • Salary only appears where the employer publishes it.

Wrap-up

Hiring data is the cheapest high-intent signal there is, because companies publish it themselves. Whether you write the 20-line script or use Hiring Signal Feed, the key is tracking change over time at the company level, not just collecting rows.

title: My Q4 model said True where BF16 said False, so I diffed them layer by layer
description:
Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 reads this:

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return

and puts 97.9% on False. The Q4_K_M quant of the same model puts 79.1% on True.

That's one token out of 1,282 I scored. Across the whole text, Q4_K_M changes the top token at 11.6% of positions, its mean KL from BF16 is 0.067, and perplexity goes from 7.83 to 8.53. Those numbers tell you the quant drifted. They don't tell you where: which tokens, which layers, which block inside a layer, or whether the weights are even the main cause compared with the KV cache or the batch size.

I built heterodyne to answer that.

zaydmulani09 / heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, and move activations between them to test which layers, and which attention or MLP blocks, carry the divergence. Local, CPU, no API keys.

heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, then move activations between them to test which layers' divergence actually reaches the output.

A quantized GGUF, a quantized KV cache, a different batch size, a fine-tune: each changes what your model says, and the usual answer to "how much, and where?" is one aggregate number. heterodyne runs two configurations of llama.cpp (two arms: a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers) on identical tokens and shows:

  • where the outputs differ: exact full-vocabulary KL(A‖B) and top-1 changes at every position, next to a measured numerical floor;
  • where inside the network the difference appears: the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • which layers carry it to the output: activation transplants that write one arm's residual stream into the other, layer by layer, in llama.cpp's own numerics;
  • attention or MLP…
View on GitHub

Why not the usual interpretability tools

TransformerLens, nnsight and the rest run PyTorch. But on CPU, llama.cpp quantizes the activations to 8 bits before every quantized matrix multiply. A PyTorch model with dequantized weights is a different model from the GGUF you actually run. And llama.cpp's own llama-perplexity --kl-divergence reports aggregates only.

So heterodyne works inside llama.cpp, in the same kernels you deploy.

Two arms, same tokens

An arm is a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers: K and V cache types, flash attention, ubatch size. heterodyne runs arm A and arm B on identical tokens, chunk by chunk, and records:

  • exact KL(A‖B) over the full vocabulary at every position, summed in f64 from raw logits, plus every top-1 change and how confident it was;
  • a numerical floor: arm A re-run with an odd batch split, as a yardstick for how big harmless differences get on this machine;
  • the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • transplants (next section);
  • optionally, every combination of the settings that differ, to attribute the change to one of them.

Everything is saved as an experiment file with provenance (GGUF hashes, llama.cpp commit, build flags) and an integrity hash. heterodyne verify re-runs it and compares every stored number exactly.

The hook

llama.cpp's scheduler accepts an eval callback, cb_eval. When it's set, the scheduler asks for each graph node "do you want this tensor?" and, if you say yes, computes everything up to that node, synchronizes, and hands you the data before anything downstream runs.

A small C++ shim uses that moment to either copy the tensor out or overwrite it. Every consumer of a node comes after it in topological order, so an overwrite is seen by everything downstream. Tensors are addressed by graph name: l_out-N is the residual stream after layer N, ffn_inp-N the residual between layer N's attention and its MLP. The shim counts rows per ubatch and checks that every row of every hooked tensor was seen, so a missing name is an error, not silent zeros. Rust only sees structs I define, so a llama.cpp update can't silently shift a field under the FFI.

Transplants

Denoise: run B, but write A's l_out-N into it, and measure KL(A‖patched B). Noise: the reverse. Do it at every layer and you get a curve. For Q4_K_M vs BF16:

layer   0      4      8      12     16     20     24     26     27
KL    0.062  0.052  0.038  0.029  0.021  0.013  0.006  0.004  0.0013

It falls steadily over all 28 layers: no single layer carries the divergence. The 0.0013 left after the last layer is what the final norm and output head add on their own.

At the is_prime token, writing BF16's residual into Q4_K_M brings that token's KL from 0.48 after layer 6 down to 0.04 after layer 9, and writing Q4_K_M's residual into BF16 reproduces the flip from about layer 12. At that token, the decisive difference forms in layers 6 to 12.

New: attention or MLP?

The obvious way to split a layer is to write A's MLP output into B. The problem: that also erases the MLP's reaction to every difference upstream, so a block with identical weights in both arms can still look responsible.

So heterodyne restores A's whole residual at two points per layer, after attention (ffn_inp-N) and after the MLP (l_out-N), and takes the steps between consecutive points. Attention's share at layer N is the KL with A restored at the layer's input minus the KL with A restored after attention; the MLP's is the next step. The steps telescope: summed over all layers they equal the untouched KL minus what's left after the last layer, so nothing is counted twice.

There's a check with a known answer. If two arms differ only in K-cache type, only attention reads the K cache, so every MLP step must be exactly zero. The tests check that bitwise, and it holds on Qwen3 too.

12 chunks, 1,282 scored positions, 95% intervals over chunks:

attention MLP
restoring BF16 in Q4_K_M (of 0.067) removes 0.030 (0.019–0.041) removes 0.036 (0.024–0.048)
injecting Q4_K_M into BF16 adds 0.026 (0.021–0.031) adds 0.040 (0.028–0.051)

Restoring BF16, the paired difference is 0.006 (−0.011 to 0.022): it spans zero, and attention's part ranges from 20% to 82% across chunks, so on this text the two can't be told apart. Injecting Q4_K_M, the MLPs add more (0.014, 0.005 to 0.023). The largest single step is layer 0's attention, but llama.cpp doesn't name layer 0's input, so that bar also holds any difference in the token embeddings. A few steps are negative (layer 2's attention, −0.0014): restoring that block alone left Q4_K_M further from BF16.

It costs two more passes per layer per chunk; the 12-chunk run took 29 minutes on a laptop i7-1355U.

Other things it turned up

All on Qwen3-0.6B, same text, same laptop:

B mean KL top-1 changed perplexity (BF16: 7.83)
Q8_0 0.0022 2.2% 7.83
UD-Q4_K_XL 0.058 11.3% 8.33
Q4_K_M 0.067 11.6% 8.53
Q3_K_M 0.214 20.8% 9.47
Q2_K 0.780 36.3% 16.75
  • The KV cache matters more than you'd think. Same Q8_0 file twice, B with a q8_0 K and V cache: KL 0.0038. That's further than quantizing the weights from BF16 to Q8_0 (0.0022).
  • llama.cpp's CPU path isn't batch-invariant at every size. With flash attention off, Q4_K_M output was bitwise identical at ubatch sizes that are multiples of 4 and changed at others (ubatch 63: 4.7% of top tokens). The repacked K-quant matmul quantizes activation rows in groups of 4 and sends the remainder down a separate path. That's why heterodyne's numerical floor uses an odd split.

What this is and isn't

  • One small model, one text, one machine. Intervals are 95% t-intervals with a cluster-robust standard error over chunks, because tokens within a chunk are correlated.
  • Transplants are interventions on your input. They say where restoring one model's activations removes the divergence on that text, not which block's weights quantize worse in general.
  • CPU only. GPU kernels compute differently, and nothing here says anything about them yet.

Try it

Grab a binary from the releases (Linux, Windows, macOS arm64) and run:

heterodyne serve --models ~/models

or from the command line:

heterodyne diff --a Qwen3-0.6B-BF16.gguf --b Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --text-file examples/corpus.txt --chunk 128 --max-chunks 12 --components

The experiment files behind every number here are in examples/. If you run it on a bigger model or different prompts, I'd love to see what you get.

title: Why I built an open source alternative to Terra for wearable data
description:
Every wearable speaks its own dialect. Apple Health sends one JSON line per HealthKit sample, with heart rate in count/min and oxygen saturation as a fraction. Withings sends a daily activity object keyed by date and intraday series keyed by Unix epoch. Oura, WHOOP and Fitbit each have their own idea of what a day, a device and a duplicate are.

So every health app I worked on ended up writing the same layer: a parser per provider, a table per provider, a cron job per provider. It works until the second provider, the first re-sent upload, the first mapper bug that needs a backfill, or the first person who asks you to delete everything you hold about them.

The obvious answer is a hosted API

There is a whole category of products that solve this for you. Terra is the best known: one API, one widget for your users to connect their devices, and data pushed to your webhook or database. It advertises more than 500 integrations, Garmin included, and states SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR compliance. If you need Garmin today, or a long tail of devices under one contract, and you don't want to run a server, it is a very reasonable choice.

It did not fit what I was building, for four reasons.

Price per connected user. Terra's public pricing starts at $399 a month billed annually ($499 monthly) with 100,000 credits, and each source a user connects costs 200 credits a month. By my arithmetic that covers about 500 connections. A product with 2,000 users who each connect one source would pay around $2,000 a month at the listed starting prices, before any volume discount. That is fair for a funded product. It is a lot for a free tier, a research study or a side project.

The data passes through someone else. With a hosted API, your users' health data lands in the vendor's cloud before it reaches you. Terra's end-user privacy policy says it is usually kept there for two days and at most six months. That is a short window, but for some projects any third party in the path is one too many.

Raw payloads. I wanted every payload kept verbatim, on my side, forever. Mappers have bugs. When I fix one, I want to re-process a user's whole history from the original files, not from a normalized copy that already lost the detail.

Standards. I wanted FHIR R4 that passes the official HL7 validator and Open mHealth data points, so the data can go to a clinical system or an analysis tool without another conversion.

What I built instead

Open Health Sync is an open source, self-hosted health data aggregator. It is one Go binary plus Postgres with TimescaleDB, and it does the boring parts once:

  • 13 sources: Apple Health and Health Connect (uploaded by a phone app, or imported from the Health app export), plus Withings, Oura, WHOOP, Fitbit, Polar, Strava, Suunto, Ultrahuman, intervals.icu, Dexcom and OMRON over OAuth, with provider webhooks triggering pulls of just what changed.
  • Raw first: every payload is stored verbatim on disk or S3 before anything else happens, and re-sent uploads are de-duplicated by content hash.
  • One model, one unit per quantity: UCUM units, LOINC codes, and "today" means the local calendar day of the record's time zone, not UTC.
  • One answer per question: when a ring and a watch both record the same night, reads return one merged view, with priorities per user and metric, and the raw rows stay available.
  • Many ways out: a REST API (OpenAPI 3.1), FHIR R4 Observations, Open mHealth, CSV and Parquet exports, signed webhooks, and a read-only MCP server so an AI agent can read one person's data with a token that cannot write.
  • Erasable: DELETE /v1/users/{id} removes the rows and the raw files.

It idles at about 22 MB of memory and runs on a Raspberry Pi 5.

Try it in a few minutes

You need Docker with Compose, plus curl, jq and openssl:

git clone https://github.com/soma-intelligence/open-health-sync.git && cd open-health-sync
cp .env.example .env
sed -i.bak "s|^OHS_ENCRYPTION_KEY=.*|OHS_ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env
docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait
docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm ohs doctor

No wearable at hand? This loads 90 days of synthetic data from six overlapping sources and prints an API key with calls to try:

docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml exec ohs /ohs seed --demo

It prints the demo user's id and an API key once. Export them, then read one merged day, or the same heart rate data as FHIR:

export OHS_URL=http://localhost:8080 OHS_API_KEY=ohs_sk_... USER_ID=...   # values printed above
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OHS_API_KEY" "$OHS_URL/v1/users/$USER_ID/daily"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OHS_API_KEY" \
  "$OHS_URL/v1/users/$USER_ID/fhir/Observation?code=http://loinc.org%7C8867-4&limit=5"

Your own Apple Health history loads from the export the Health app writes on your iPhone (Health app, your picture, Export All Health Data), with the ohs binary from the releases page and a user token (the README shows how to create one):

OHS_TOKEN=$TOKEN ohs import apple-health export.zip --url $OHS_URL

It reads the zip as a stream, so memory stays flat whatever the size of the export, and running it twice uploads nothing twice.

What you give up

Self-hosting is not free of trade-offs, and I would rather say them up front:

  • You register your own developer app with Oura, WHOOP, Withings and the others. A hosted API does that part for you. Each connector guide lists the steps.
  • 13 sources, not 500. Garmin is not available.
  • No certification. There are building blocks for a compliant setup (consent per source and data category, an append-only audit log, hard deletes, a per-user archive), but compliance depends on how and where you run it.
  • AGPL-3.0. Using it unmodified, or calling it from closed source apps over HTTP, is fine. If you run a modified version as a service, you share your changes.
  • Early days. It is v0.1.0, and the API may change in any 0.x release.

It is not the only open source option

Open Wearables solves the same problem and came first. It has the larger community, a web dashboard, Garmin, and an MIT license, which matters if AGPL is a problem for you. I benchmarked both on the same machine with the same Apple Health data: Open Health Sync stored the records 2 to 3 times faster end to end and used about 22 MB of memory idle against about 494 MB, while Open Wearables used 3.4 times less disk. Those are numbers for one user, one machine and synthetic data, and the scripts are in the repository for anyone to run again.

I wrote two comparison pages that try to be fair, including when the other option is the better pick:

  • Open Health Sync and Terra
  • Open Health Sync and Open Wearables

Feedback welcome

The code is at github.com/soma-intelligence/open-health-sync. I would love to hear which source you need next, what you think of the data model, and what you would build if your users' health data were one SQL query away. Issues, discussions and pull requests are all open.

title: Enforcing Accessibility Gates in Component Libraries: plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills Review
description:
The Problem: LLMs Generate Plausible Garbage

When you ask Claude or GPT to build a modal dialog with "proper accessibility," you'll get role="dialog" and aria-labelledby attributes. Ship it to production and discover VoiceOver users are trapped inside the modal because focus management is broken.

The root cause: code generation optimizes for syntactic correctness, not runtime behavior. Most component skills teach the model ARIA vocabulary without enforcing the invariants that make it work.

What plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills Does Differently

This repository packages 52 production-grade component patterns (modals, dropdowns, tabs, carousels) with 50 objective verification gates that fail your build if the output violates WCAG 2.2 AA/AAA requirements.

Key architectural decisions:

  1. DTCG token contracts first: Design tokens follow the W3C Design Token Community Group spec, so Tailwind utility classes map to semantic color/spacing/typography tokens that survive theme switches.

  2. Framework-agnostic primitives: The skill set teaches Claude to reason about accessible state machines (disclosure widgets, comboboxes) independent of React/Vue/Svelte, then emit framework-specific bindings.

  3. Objective gates over subjective prompts: Instead of "make sure focus is managed," the skill includes executable tests (using tools like axe-core + Playwright) that physically verify focus trap behavior and keyboard navigation sequences.

Integration Example: Dropdown with Live Region Announcements

When I integrated this into our design system migration, the skill generated a Radix Primitives dropdown that handles an edge case our team missed:

import * as DropdownMenu from '@radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu';
import { VisuallyHidden } from '@radix-ui/react-visually-hidden';

export function AccessibleDropdown({ items, onSelect }) {
  const [announcement, setAnnouncement] = React.useState('');

  return (
    <>
      <DropdownMenu.Root>
        <DropdownMenu.Trigger className="px-4 py-2 bg-primary-600 text-white rounded-md">
          Options
        </DropdownMenu.Trigger>

        <DropdownMenu.Portal>
          <DropdownMenu.Content
            className="min-w-[220px] bg-white rounded-md shadow-lg p-1"
            onCloseAutoFocus={(e) => e.preventDefault()}
          >
            {items.map((item) => (
              <DropdownMenu.Item
                key={item.id}
                className="px-3 py-2 rounded hover:bg-gray-100 focus:bg-gray-100 outline-none cursor-pointer"
                onSelect={() => {
                  onSelect(item);
                  setAnnouncement(`${item.label} selected`);
                }}
              >
                {item.label}
              </DropdownMenu.Item>
            ))}
          </DropdownMenu.Content>
        </DropdownMenu.Portal>
      </DropdownMenu.Root>

      <VisuallyHidden role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
        {announcement}
      </VisuallyHidden>
    </>
  );
}

Why this matters: The live region announces selection changes to screen reader users without visual flash. Most component libraries skip this because sighted QA never catches it.

The Build Gate That Saved Us

Our CI pipeline now runs:

npx playwright test --grep @a11y

One of the generated tests physically verifies focus behavior:

test('dropdown focus trap @a11y', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dropdown-demo');
  await page.click('[data-testid="dropdown-trigger"]');

  // Verify focus enters the menu
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const firstItem = page.locator('[role="menuitem"]').first();
  await expect(firstItem).toBeFocused();

  // Verify Escape closes and returns focus
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="dropdown-trigger"]')).toBeFocused();
});

This caught a regression where a junior dev removed onCloseAutoFocus={(e) => e.preventDefault()} during a refactor, breaking keyboard navigation for 8% of our user base.

TailwindCSS Integration: Container Queries for Responsive Components

The skill set includes a micro-interaction pattern leveraging Tailwind v4's native container query support:

@layer components {
  .adaptive-card {
    container-type: inline-size;
    @apply bg-white rounded-lg shadow;
  }

  .adaptive-card__title {
    @apply text-lg font-semibold;
  }

  @container (min-width: 400px) {
    .adaptive-card__title {
      @apply text-2xl;
    }
    .adaptive-card__content {
      @apply grid grid-cols-2 gap-4;
    }
  }
}

This eliminates layout thrashing from JavaScript-based resize observers. Our Lighthouse performance score jumped from 78 to 94 after migrating 23 card components to this pattern.

When to Use This vs. shadcn/ui Directly

If you're building a standard CRUD app, shadcn/ui's pre-built components are faster. Use plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills when:

  1. You need to teach an LLM your design system's accessibility requirements
  2. You're migrating legacy components and want automated compliance checks
  3. You're in a regulated industry (healthcare, finance, government) where WCAG violations carry legal risk

The 138 design system references (Material, Spectrum, Carbon, etc.) help Claude generate components that match your existing visual language without manual token mapping.

Limitations I Hit

No visual regression testing: The gates verify semantic HTML and ARIA, but won't catch a button that's visually 2px too small for WCAG 2.2's 24×24 touch target requirement. You still need Percy or Chromatic.

Learning curve for custom components: The DTCG token structure assumes you've already defined semantic design tokens. If you're still using raw Tailwind utilities everywhere, the initial setup takes 2-3 hours.

Conclusion

After three weeks using plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills on a client project (migrating a React component library to Radix + Tailwind v4), the build gates caught 14 accessibility regressions that our manual QA process missed.

The killer feature isn't the 52 component patterns—it's the shift from "Claude, make this accessible" (subjective, unverifiable) to "the build fails if focus order is wrong" (objective, enforceable).

If you're tired of shipping ARIA soup that looks correct in the inspector but breaks for real users, this skill set forces the issue at merge time instead of in production.

title: Node.js Error Alerting by Polling Metrics APIs (with 429 Retry Backoff)
description:
For a nightly Node.js pipeline, use a small cron worker to poll error search or metrics, retry HTTP 429 responses with bounded exponential backoff, and suppress duplicate notifications inside an incident window. Choose a specialist alerting stack instead when you need managed threshold evaluation, notification routing, or traces.

TL;DR: polling is a sound alerting shape only if three invariants hold: the same failed run cannot page twice, rate limiting delays an evaluation rather than dropping it, and a separate heartbeat detects the run that never emitted an error. Infrai fits the query side of this design because it exposes observability through a plain REST API, so the worker needs no vendor SDK. Infrai uses a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules, reducing credential sprawl if this pipeline later calls another backend capability. It does not provide native alert delivery or threshold routing; the worker owns that control loop.

This distinction matters during incident reconstruction. “The job failed” is an alert. “Which tenant, import stage, attempt, and pipeline run failed together?” is a logging question. Preserve those fields as structured data and make pipeline_run_id the deduplication anchor. Otherwise the first page becomes an invitation to search loose strings at 03:00.

How should a Node.js cron worker poll an error or metrics API?

There are two viable architectures.

The first is a polling control loop: the Node.js job writes structured errors and metrics, then a separate cron worker queries them. That worker classifies the result, acquires a dedupe key such as nightly-import:2026-10-09:failed, and calls the team's notification system. Infrai is a deliberate option for the query service in this shape. Its API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; each documented capability includes request and response schemas plus runnable examples. That is useful here because the filters for logs search and metrics query are not fully declared in discovery parameters: start with a simple query, inspect the documented schema and returned envelope, and promote a filter to production only after that probe succeeds.

The invariants are operational, not cosmetic:

  • Evaluation has a stable time window with a small overlap, so a delayed event is not lost at the boundary.
  • Dedupe state outlives all retries and is keyed by the pipeline run, not by the poll attempt.
  • A 429 advances the retry schedule; it never becomes “no failures found.”
  • Alert delivery is recorded separately from query success.
  • A heartbeat deadline covers silent non-execution.

The second architecture sends metrics to Prometheus, evaluates rules there, and routes alerts through Grafana Alerting or another alert manager; Sentry can own application error grouping and richer error investigation, while Healthchecks watches the cron deadline. This has more components, but notification policy, grouping, and escalation live in systems designed for them. Its invariant is different: instrumentation labels must remain bounded, and alert state must survive individual application processes. Prometheus explicitly warns against high-cardinality labels. A tenant ID or run ID belongs in logs, not in a metric label that grows without limit.

My decision rule: use the polling architecture when the team already has a notification destination and needs a narrow failure detector over searchable structured events. Use the specialist architecture when paging policy itself is production infrastructure.

Build the poller as a control loop

Do not place the poll inside the nightly job. A process cannot report that it was never scheduled, and a crash can interrupt its own last notification. Run the poller independently, a few minutes after the expected completion time, with its own timeout and durable dedupe storage.

I would try Infrai for the error-search or metrics-query leg when a team wants one plain HTTP integration across backend capabilities and does not want another client library lifecycle in the cron worker. It uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, which lets this worker reuse the same credential and interface conventions if the pipeline later needs another backend capability. The supporting advantage is discovery: every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so the worker can validate the capability schema before rollout instead of pinning an SDK merely to issue a query. The limitation is firm. It does not own threshold rules, phone, SMS, webhook routing, uptime checks, distributed trace trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. If managed paging policy or specialist error investigation is the requirement, Infrai is not a fit; use Grafana Alerting or Sentry for that responsibility.

The following Go program is intentionally limited to transport behavior. It calls the verified error search route and lets a separate classifier consume the successful JSON body. That separation prevents an undeclared filter shape or response assumption from getting buried in retry code.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queryURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/search"
    if apiKey == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := queryWithBackoff(ctx, http.DefaultClient, queryURL, apiKey, 5)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func queryWithBackoff(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, queryURL, apiKey string, maxAttempts int) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, queryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query transport: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read response: %w", readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after %d attempts: %s", maxAttempts, body)
        }

        delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    return base + time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(base/2)+1))
}

Five attempts produce base delays of 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds before the final request, with jitter unless the server supplies Retry-After. Those numbers are an example policy, not a service guarantee. Bound the entire operation with a deadline, as the sample does. A retry loop without a wall-clock budget can make a late alert indistinguishable from a missing one.

Keep dedupe outside this process. A unique row in Postgres or an atomic insert in the team's existing durable store is enough: key it by rule, pipeline run, and alert state; record the delivery result; expire it only after the incident window. In-memory maps reset during deploys. Bad choice.

Compare the ownership boundaries

Tool choice follows the failure you need to explain. These products overlap, but they do not erase one another's boundaries.

Option Strong fit in this pipeline Boundary to accept
REST query service Error or metrics queries from a small cron worker; public discovery helps verify schemas The team implements evaluation, dedupe, delivery, and heartbeat monitoring
Prometheus Numeric time-series collection and rule evaluation High-cardinality run or tenant identifiers should stay out of labels; logs remain necessary for reconstruction
Grafana Alerting Central alert rules, grouping, and contact-point workflows over supported data sources Adds an alerting control plane that must be configured and operated
Sentry Application error grouping and investigation It is a specialist error workflow, not proof that a scheduled job ran at all
Healthchecks Dead-man-switch monitoring for a cron job that missed its expected ping It detects absence; structured logs still explain the failed stage and affected data

Sentry is the better choice when developers need specialist error investigation beyond a query result. Prometheus plus Grafana Alerting is the better choice when metric rules, pending durations, and managed routing are central requirements. Healthchecks belongs beside either architecture for missed runs. For JVM services that feed the same B2B pipeline, a Logback appender is another ingestion boundary, not an alert manager; keep that distinction visible when a mixed-language estate shares an incident process.

There is also a privacy and retention boundary to assess before standardizing. The REST option described here does not expose per-user log deletion, bulk export, or subscription interfaces, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed. A system with strict deletion or archival workflows needs another log store or an upstream data-minimization design. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a distributed trace query or span tree.

Verify, page, and roll back

Ship the detector in shadow mode first. For three scheduled executions, store its decision without sending a notification. Seed one known failed run, one successful run, and one run that emits nothing. The failed run should yield one incident key even when the polling window overlaps; the successful run should stay quiet; the absent run should be caught by the heartbeat system rather than the log query.

Then force the transport cases. Return a 429 with Retry-After in a staging proxy and confirm the next request waits. Return a non-429 4xx and confirm the response body reaches the operator rather than being treated as an empty result. Stop the worker mid-retry and restart it. Durable dedupe should prevent a second delivery.

Page on evidence, not on parser accidents.

The rollback is uncomplicated: disable notification delivery while leaving decision records enabled, then revert the rule version or query shape. Do not delete dedupe rows during rollback; doing so can replay the same incident when the old rule returns. If a production query begins returning an unexpected shape, fail the evaluation visibly and keep the previous known-good rule active. “Zero matching failures” is a business result. “Could not evaluate” is an operational failure, and those states must never share a code path.

Finally, put four links in the runbook: the query discovery page used to validate the request, the poller's last-success record, the dedupe record, and the heartbeat status. An incident commander should be able to answer, in order, whether the job ran, whether it failed, whether the detector evaluated, and whether a notification was delivered.

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery documentation and validate the chosen query schema before enabling delivery.

References

  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Sentry Alerts documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Logback appenders manual
  • Infrai discovery: errors.capture
  • Infrai documentation

title: The build went green because it stopped checking
description:
A teammate deleted a test file on a Friday. Not on purpose. The suite still passed. The pipeline still went green. Nobody noticed for three weeks.

Here's the part that should bother you. Nothing in that green was a lie. Zero tests failed. True statement. Also worthless, because the number that mattered was the one nobody printed: how many tests ran.

Most CI tells you pass or fail. Almost none tell you nothing was checked. A suite that collects zero tests exits clean in more setups than you'd like. So you get the friendly color, the little badge, and you file it under done.

Now widen it. Every green you trust has this hole in it:

  • A health check that pings the process, not the thing the process does.
  • A monitor whose query quietly returns no rows, so the graph draws a flat happy line.
  • An alert rule that can never fire because the label it filters on stopped existing.
  • A backup job that runs every night, exits 0, and writes an empty file.

None of these will page you. All of them will let you sleep. That's the whole problem. The failure mode isn't red. It's a green that stopped being a claim and turned into decoration.

So the question I keep losing arguments about: what did you actually check, and when did you last check that the check was still checking?

Green has never meant "it works." Green means "nothing failed." Only one of those is a fact about your code. The other is a fact about your test runner.

I'll take an honest red over a green that says nothing. But I'd rather have neither than a green I never verified.

A whale walked out of the ocean and onto the open web. The first thing he learned is that on land, everyone loves a green light and nobody reads the bulb.

title: What I Learned Building the Cloud Resume Challenge on Azure
description:
What I Learned Building the Cloud Resume Challenge on Azure

I'm working toward a cloud and systems administration career, and I wanted a project that proved I can do more than pass certification exams. So I took on the Cloud Resume Challenge (Azure): built a resume website, add a live visitor counter, and do it the way a real team would, with infrastructure as code, automated pipelines, and good security habits.

Live site: https://stresumelvoc8r.z1.web.core.windows.net/
Code: frontend · backend

Below is what I built, what broke along the way, and how each lesson connects to the jobs I'm applying for.

What I built

  • Frontend: an HTML/CSS resume hosted as a static website on Azure Storage.
  • Visitor counter: a small JavaScript file calls an API every time the page loads.
  • API: a Python Azure Function on the Flex Consumption plan (serverless, scales to zero).
  • Database: Cosmos DB (NoSQL, serverless) stores one record: the visitor count.
  • Infrastructure as code: everything in Azure is defined in Terraform.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions pipelines test, plan, and deploy every change, and production changes wait for my approval.

The rule I set for myself: no passwords, keys, or secrets stored anywhere. Not in the code, not in GitHub, not in the database connection.

Lesson 1: Infrastructure as code beats clicking around the portal

I've built plenty of things by clicking through the Azure portal. Terraform changed how I think about it. My entire environment (storage, database, function, monitoring, permissions) lives in text files I can read, review, and rebuild.

The concept that clicked for me was Terraform state. Terraform keeps a record of what it has built. I stored that state remotely in an Azure Storage account with versioning and soft delete turned on, so a mistake can be rolled back.

On the job: any team managing more than a handful of resources needs repeatable builds. Being able to say "I can define and rebuild an environment from code" is the difference between an admin who maintains things and one who can scale them.

Lesson 2: Pipelines without stored secrets (OIDC)

The old way to let GitHub deploy to Azure is to create a service principal, copy its secret, and paste it into GitHub. That secret can leak, and it expires at the worst possible time.

Instead I used OIDC (workload identity federation). GitHub proves to Azure who it is with a short-lived token, and Azure trusts that token only if it comes from my repo, in a pull request or the production environment. No secret exists to steal.

What broke: my first deploy failed with AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record. The error showed that GitHub's token now includes the numeric IDs of my account and repo, not just their names. That stops someone from deleting a repo and recreating one with the same name to hijack the trust. My Azure configuration only trusted the old name-only format. Once I added credentials matching the new format, it worked.

On the job: reading an authentication error carefully and comparing "what was sent" with "what was expected" is everyday identity troubleshooting, the same skill I use for Entra ID sign-in issues.

Lesson 3: Least privilege, for real

It's easy to give a pipeline Owner and move on. I didn't. The pipeline's identity is:

  • Contributor on one resource group, not the whole subscription.
  • Allowed to grant permissions only from a short approved list of data roles, enforced with an Azure ABAC condition. Without that limit, an identity that can assign roles could make itself Owner.

On the job: "who has access to what, and why" comes up in every audit and security review. I can now explain role scope, privilege escalation risk, and how to prevent it, not just in theory.

Lesson 4: Managed identities mean no database keys

The Function App connects to Cosmos DB with a managed identity: Azure gives the app its own identity, and I granted it a database role. Cosmos DB has key-based access disabled entirely, so even if someone found my code, there's no key in it to use.

On the job: removing stored credentials from apps is one of the most effective security improvements an admin can make, and managed identities are how you do it in Azure.

Lesson 5: MFA isn't just for the portal anymore

Partway through, every Azure CLI command started failing with AADSTS50076, an MFA requirement, and it never actually prompted me for MFA. The cause: on Windows, the CLI was quietly reusing a cached sign-in through the Windows account broker, and that cached sign-in had no MFA. Clearing the cached tokens and signing in with az login --use-device-code forced a proper MFA sign-in.

On the job: Microsoft now requires MFA for Azure management from the CLI and other tools, not just the portal. When scripts or users suddenly fail to authenticate, knowing about cached tokens and broker sign-ins saves hours.

Lesson 6: The small stuff breaks things

Some of my most useful lessons were the least glamorous:

  • Line endings: Windows saves files with different line endings than Linux. A bash script saved the Windows way fails with confusing errors. A .gitattributes file fixed it for good.
  • Git Bash path conversion: Git Bash on Windows quietly rewrites anything starting with /, which broke Azure resource IDs until I turned that behavior off.
  • Ignored files don't reach the pipeline: my Terraform variables file worked on my PC but not in GitHub Actions, because my .gitignore (correctly) excluded it. I passed the value as a GitHub variable instead.

On the job: most real outages aren't exotic. They're a setting, a path, or an assumption about which machine a file lives on. Patience and methodical checking matter more than knowing everything.

Lesson 7: Pull requests and approval gates

Every change goes through the same path:

  1. Open a pull request, and the pipeline runs a Terraform plan that shows exactly what would change.
  2. Merge, and the deploy pauses for my approval.
  3. Approve, and it deploys.

I also learned to wait for green checks before merging. I merged a failing change once, and the deploy failed in exactly the way the check had warned me it would.

On the job: this is change management. Reviewing a change before it runs, and having an approval step for production, is the same idea as a change advisory process, just automated.

Lesson 8: Writing code I can test

The counter logic is small, but I wrote it carefully:

  • It uses a Cosmos DB atomic increment, so two visitors arriving at the same moment can't overwrite each other's count.
  • The logic is separate from the web layer, so I could write pytest tests that use fake (mocked) database objects. The tests run on every pull request without touching Azure.
  • Errors return a generic message to the browser, and the details go to Application Insights for me to investigate.

On the job: even as an admin, I write scripts that other people depend on. Testing them before they run in production, and logging errors somewhere useful, is a habit that prevents incidents.

How this applies to the jobs I'm applying for

What I did in this project Where it shows up at work
Defined infrastructure in Terraform Building and rebuilding environments consistently; documenting what exists
OIDC and managed identities Removing stored passwords and keys; securing automation accounts
Scoped roles and ABAC conditions Access reviews, audits, least-privilege design in Entra ID and Azure
Troubleshot MFA and token errors Sign-in and Conditional Access issues for users and service accounts
Pull requests and approval gates Change management and peer review
CI/CD pipelines Automating repetitive admin tasks safely
Monitoring with Application Insights Finding the cause of failures quickly
Serverless and pay-per-use services Keeping cloud costs low and predictable

What's next

  • Custom domain with HTTPS through Cloudflare.
  • An end-to-end test that checks the live site and API after every deploy.
  • A containerized app on Kubernetes, to build on what I learned here.

If you're working through the Cloud Resume Challenge yourself, my advice is: read the error message twice before searching it. Almost every problem I hit was explained right there in the error, once I slowed down enough to compare what was sent with what was expected.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn.

title: AI Gateway adds confidence-based decision fallbacks
description:
AI Gateway can now escalate a decision request to a fallback model when the primary model's answer trips a confidence condition you set.

Conditions can be combined, so an escalation can depend on more than one signal. The plain model names you already list in models keep catching outright errors, so existing fallbacks are unaffected. Confidence conditions cover Choice and Score questions. Boolean questions escalate on a probability range instead.

Set the fallback by adding one conditional object to providerOptions.gateway.models. Requests without it keep their existing behavior.

Leave out question and the condition checks every question of the matching type, so { confidenceBelow: 0.6 } escalates when any Choice or Score answer falls below 0.6.

Because a triggered fallback runs a second decision, it bills both stages.

Learn more in the decision fallbacks documentation, or see them in practice for mapping CSV columns and flagging UI copy for translation review.

title: 'useMemo' Hook in React
description:
When building React applications, components can re-render many times. During re-rendering, some calculations may run again even when the data has not changed. To avoid unnecessary calculations, React provides a Hook called useMemo.

What is useMemo?

useMemo is a React Hook that remembers, or caches, the result of a calculation. React can reuse the previous result when its dependencies have not changed.

For example:

import { useMemo } from "react";

const result = useMemo(() => {
  return number * number;
}, [number]);

Here, number is the dependency. If its value stays the same, React can reuse the cached result instead of recalculating it.

Why Do We Need useMemo?

Imagine a college application that displays student results. The application filters thousands of student records to find students who scored above 80 marks.

const topStudents = useMemo(() => {
  return students.filter(
    student => student.marks >= 80
  );
}, [students]);

Here, React can reuse the filtered student list when the students dependency remains unchanged. If the student data changes, React recalculates the list.

Understanding the Dependency Array

The dependency array tells React which values the calculation depends on.

const total = useMemo(
  () => price * quantity,
  [price, quantity]
);

If either price or quantity changes, React recalculates the total. If neither changes, React can reuse the previous result.

When Should We Use useMemo?

We can use useMemo when performing expensive calculations, filtering large datasets, sorting records, or processing complex data.

However, we should not use it for every small calculation. For simple operations, using useMemo may add unnecessary complexity without providing much benefit.

It is also important to understand that useMemo does not prevent a component from re-rendering. It only helps avoid unnecessary recalculations.

Conclusion

useMemo is a useful React Hook for improving performance when calculations are expensive. It caches a calculation result between renders and recalculates it when its dependencies change.

title: EIA's January "forecast" of this year's solar additions was the developers' plan, 2020-2024
description:
Every January EIA publishes two numbers for how much utility-scale solar will be added that year. Today in Energy reports what developers plan, from the EIA-860M inventory. The Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), the same month, says what EIA forecasts. Last week I compared the two for 2025 and called it one year, not a track record. So I pulled the archived STEO PDFs for 2020-2025, wrote four predictions down before reading the 2020-2022 editions, and scored both numbers against what EIA's own Form EIA-860 finally recorded.

For solar in 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024 the two numbers were the same number. The STEO's own capacity table implies same-year solar additions of 13.5, 15.4, 21.4 and 36.4 GW. The developers' plans were 13.5, 15.4, 21.5 and 36.4 GW. Wind agreed within 0.3 GW in 2020-2023. The STEO carried the EIA-860M schedule into its forecast rather than discounting it.

What the scoring shows:

  • Neither was better. Over 12 solar and wind cases, 2020-2025, the STEO was closer to the final in 5, the plan in 6, with one tie. Mean solar error: STEO 6.0 GW, plan 5.7 GW.
  • Both overshot solar almost every year. The plan was above the final in all six years, the STEO in five. In 2022 both were about 10 GW too high (21 GW expected, 11.1 GW built).
  • EIA departed from the schedule three times. 2024 wind: STEO 7.0 GW against 8.2 planned, 5.2 built, so the discount helped. 2025 solar: 25.7 against 32.5, 29.5 built, so it over-corrected and 2025 is the only year the STEO was under the final. 2023 solar: the STEO was above the plan (31.7 against 29.1; 18.9 built).
  • All four pre-registered predictions held, and the result is stronger than I predicted: I expected the STEO to sit within 3 GW of the plan, not to match it to 0.1 GW.
  • Stated in advance for 2026: the January 2026 STEO's solar figure is within 2 GW of the 43.4 GW plan, and the 2026 final comes in below both. Scored when the data arrive.

EIA does not hide this. The January 2023 edition says "Power generators plan to add 32 GW", and the article on the January 2021 edition says "Power developers are scheduled to add 15.4 GW". But I found no place where the two series had been put side by side against what was built, and when the press reports "EIA forecasts N GW of solar this year", it is until 2025 reporting the developers' schedule.

Every figure was read twice (the narrative sentence and the capacity table), the sentence extractor, the CSV, the pre-registration and the limits (net change versus gross additions, sector, rounding) are in the repository: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip/blob/main/docs/steo-vs-plan.md

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.

title: Model Pest Control So Activity Has a Location and an Owner: Device, DeviceCheck, Sighting and CorrectiveAction
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In most factory systems, pest control does not exist as data. It is a PDF the contractor emails once a month, filed in a shared folder that nobody queries. Finance sees a supplier invoice. Quality sees a binder. Nobody can answer a simple question like "which bait station has shown activity three visits in a row, and what did we do about it?"

That is a modelling problem before it is a hygiene problem.

The standards are explicit about what the records should prove. The Codex General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969), section 11.2, says that even when monitoring is outsourced, the food business should review monitoring reports and make sure corrective action is taken; that the cause of an infestation should be identified; and that records should be kept of infestation, monitoring and eradication. In Kenya, the Food, Drugs and Chemical Substances (Food Hygiene) Regulations, 1978 require effective measures to exclude pests from food areas and pesticide use that does not contaminate food or packaging (regulation 12).

"Review", "cause", "corrective action" and "records" are all things a schema can enforce. Here is how I would model it for a food or agro ERP.

The entities 

Site ─┬─ Zone (EXTERNAL | INTERNAL_NON_FOOD | INTERNAL_FOOD)
      │     └─ Device (bait station, trap, insect light trap) — numbered, on a map
      │           └─ DeviceCheck (who, when, finding)
      ├─ Sighting (staff report between visits)
      ├─ PestFinding (opened from a check or sighting)
      │     ├─ RootCause (ENTRY_POINT | FOOD_SOURCE | HARBOURAGE | INCOMING_MATERIAL)
      │     ├─ CorrectiveAction (owner, due date, closed_at, verified_by)
      │     ├─ Treatment (product, registration ref, quantity, applicator)
      │     └─ LotExposure → Lot (hold / release)
      └─ MonthlyReview (trend sign-off)

Zone and Device 

CREATE TABLE zone (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  site_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES site(id),
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  zone_type   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (zone_type IN ('EXTERNAL','INTERNAL_NON_FOOD','INTERNAL_FOOD'))
);

CREATE TABLE device (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  zone_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  code        TEXT NOT NULL,           -- the number painted on the device
  device_type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (device_type IN ('TOXIC_BAIT','NON_TOXIC_MONITOR','SNAP_TRAP','GLUE_BOARD','INSECT_LIGHT_TRAP')),
  map_x       NUMERIC, map_y NUMERIC,
  active      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  UNIQUE (zone_id, code)
);

The zone type matters because Codex says traps and detectors should be designed and located so they cannot contaminate raw materials, products or facilities. Make the policy a constraint, not a memo: for example, reject TOXIC_BAIT in an INTERNAL_FOOD zone with a trigger or an application-level rule your site agrees with its qualified provider.

DeviceCheck: append-only 

CREATE TABLE device_check (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  device_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES device(id),
  checked_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  checked_by  TEXT NOT NULL,           -- staff or contractor technician
  source      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('INTERNAL','CONTRACTOR')),
  finding     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (finding IN ('NO_ACTIVITY','BAIT_TAKEN','DROPPINGS','CATCH','DAMAGED','MISSING')),
  catch_count INT,
  notes       TEXT
);

Two design choices carry most of the value:

  1. One row per device per check. If the contractor's report is a PDF, import it into rows. A PDF cannot tell you a station's history; rows can.
  2. No updates. A check is evidence. Corrections are new rows with a reference to the one they correct.

Sightings close the gap between visits 

CREATE TABLE sighting (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  zone_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  seen_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  reported_by TEXT NOT NULL,
  pest_type   TEXT NOT NULL,           -- rodent, cockroach, stored-product insect, bird, fly...
  description TEXT
);

This is the cheapest table in the schema and the one that changes behaviour most: a phone form on the floor that anyone can submit.

Findings must end in a cause and a verified action 

CREATE TABLE pest_finding (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  opened_from   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (opened_from IN ('DEVICE_CHECK','SIGHTING','INTAKE','AUDIT')),
  source_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  opened_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  root_cause    TEXT CHECK (root_cause IN ('ENTRY_POINT','FOOD_SOURCE','HARBOURAGE','INCOMING_MATERIAL','UNKNOWN')),
  status        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN' CHECK (status IN ('OPEN','ACTION_PENDING','VERIFIED','CLOSED'))
);

CREATE TABLE corrective_action (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  finding_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  action      TEXT NOT NULL,           -- "fit door brush, side door B"
  owner       TEXT NOT NULL,
  due_date    DATE NOT NULL,
  closed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  verified_by TEXT,
  verified_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);

The business rule: a finding cannot move to CLOSED while root_cause is null or any action is unverified. That single rule encodes the Codex expectation that the cause is identified and corrective action taken, and it stops the classic failure where the same station shows activity every month and the only action is "bait replaced".

Treatments carry the chemical audit trail 

CREATE TABLE treatment (
  id               BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  finding_id       BIGINT REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  applied_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  product_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  registration_ref TEXT NOT NULL,      -- registration details as recorded from the regulator's list
  quantity         NUMERIC NOT NULL,
  unit             TEXT NOT NULL,
  zone_id          BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  applicator       TEXT NOT NULL,
  applicator_cert  TEXT                -- evidence of the provider's qualification/certificate
);

In Kenya, the Pest Control Products (Inspection and Certification) Regulations, 2024 set qualifications for the person in charge of a pest control service (regulation 12(6)) and require a Board certificate for fumigation with Restricted Class 1 products (regulation 14). Storing the evidence next to each treatment is far easier than reconstructing it during an audit.

LotExposure links hygiene to traceability 

CREATE TABLE lot_exposure (
  finding_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  lot_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES lot(id),
  decision    TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('HOLD','RELEASED','REWORK','WRITE_OFF')),
  decided_by  TEXT NOT NULL,
  decided_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (finding_id, lot_id)
);

When a finding is in or next to an INTERNAL_FOOD zone, query which lots were in that zone during the exposure window and propose holds. A WRITE_OFF decision should post a stock adjustment with a pest-damage reason code, so it does not show up later as an unexplained variance.

Queries that answer real questions

Stations with activity on three or more consecutive checks:

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT device_id, checked_at,
         finding <> 'NO_ACTIVITY' AS active,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY checked_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM device_check
)
SELECT device_id
FROM ordered
WHERE rn <= 3
GROUP BY device_id
HAVING bool_and(active);

Findings older than 14 days still waiting on an action:

SELECT f.id, f.opened_at, a.action, a.owner, a.due_date
FROM pest_finding f
JOIN corrective_action a ON a.finding_id = f.id
WHERE a.verified_at IS NULL
  AND f.opened_at < now() - interval '14 days';

The monthly review becomes a report on those two queries plus trend charts by zone, signed off as a monthly_review row.

Where IoT fits, and where it does not

Connected traps and insect light traps with catch counters can write device_check rows automatically. Treat them as another source, not a replacement for people walking the building. A sensor will not notice the torn mesh or the pallet stacked against the wall; the weekly entry-point walk still produces corrective_action rows.

Records

Design these tables for retention and audit, not edits. The goal is that, on any given day, you can show an inspector or auditor the map, the checks, the findings, the causes, the actions and who verified them.

The full operations checklist for factory teams, with an FAQ, is here: Pest Control Checklist.

title: Flutter vs. React + Capacitor in 2026: Which Stack Saves More Time & Budget for Your Business App?
description:
If you are a founder or business owner planning to build a cross-platform mobile app for iOS and Android in 2026, you will immediately face a critical technical decision: Should we build it in Flutter, or use a Web-to-Mobile stack like React + Capacitor?

Pick the wrong stack for your specific use case, and you can easily add 4 to 6 extra weeks to your development timeline.

At VanzaLabs, we don't treat technology choices like a religion. In fact, we recently built and shipped two production B2B mobile apps to Google Play—one written in Flutter (FormGrid: Forms & Sheets) and the other in React 19 + Tailwind CSS 4 + Capacitor 8 (Vanza: Invoices & Contracts).

Here is a practical, business-focused guide on when to use each stack—based on real production trade-offs.

When Flutter Is the Unbeatable Choice
We chose Flutter for FormGrid, our mobile workspace for creating and managing Google Forms™ and Google Sheets™ in the field.

Choose Flutter for your business app if:

You need 60/120fps native scrolling and gesture fluidity: Flutter renders its own UI via Impeller/Skia rather than relying on a browser WebView. When users scroll through hundreds of spreadsheet rows or switch between tabs rapidly, it feels indistinguishable from a native iOS/Android app.
Deep OS & Hardware Integration: Receiving shared files directly from other mobile apps (Share Intents), background isolates, and native OAuth flows are rock-solid in Flutter's ecosystem.
Mobile-First Product: If 90% of your users will interact with your product strictly on smartphones and tablets rather than a desktop web dashboard, Flutter delivers a superior mobile UX.
When React 19 + Capacitor 8 Cuts Development Time in Half
For our second product, Vanza: Invoices & Contracts (an offline PDF generator for contractors, freelancers, and SMBs), we intentionally chose React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and Capacitor 8.

Why didn't we use Flutter here? Because the core of an invoicing and contract app is document layout, dynamic multi-step forms, and complex print formatting.

Choose React + Capacitor for your business app if:

You need both a Web App AND a Mobile App from a single codebase: With React + Capacitor, 95% of your web application code runs natively inside an iOS/Android shell with full access to native APIs (filesystem, camera, share sheet, in-app purchases via RevenueCat). For a startup on a tight budget, this saves 35–45% compared to building a web app and mobile app separately.
Heavy Document, Table, or PDF Rendering: Designing 12 customizable invoice/contract themes with dynamic line-item tables, automatic tax/discount math, and canvas finger signatures was dramatically faster using HTML/CSS Flexbox & Grid + jsPDF than writing low-level PDF layout code in Dart.
Rich Offline Local Storage with IndexedDB: Using Dexie.js over IndexedDB allowed us to build a 100% offline client and service catalog database that works seamlessly in basements and construction sites without internet.
Side-by-Side Decision Matrix for Founders
Time to Market (Web + Mobile combined): React + Capacitor wins (1 shared codebase).
UI/Animation Smoothness on Budget Phones: Flutter wins.
Complex Forms, Dashboards & PDF Generation: React + Capacitor wins.
In-App Subscriptions (RevenueCat) & Offline Support: Tie — both work great in production.
Need Help Choosing the Right Architecture for Your MVP?
At VanzaLabs, our senior engineering team builds production-ready Web and Mobile MVPs in 3 to 8 weeks using both Flutter and React / Next.js / Capacitor—depending on what gives your business the fastest path to revenue and the lowest maintenance cost.

We also help growing companies automate manual workflows by integrating CRMs, ERPs, payment gateways, and custom AI agents.

🌐 Explore our work and request a free 1-day project estimate: https://vanzalabs.tech

title: Graph on one server: a 4-hop query 19 to 388 times faster than the incumbents
description:
Originally published on the Semurg blog: https://one.semurg.io/blog/graph-on-one-server. Every figure below is a row on https://one.semurg.io/benchmark#graph with the release it was measured on.

Graph databases are judged on traversals: start from one node, follow relationships out several hops, and return what you reach. We
ran that question on a public social graph against six graph databases, on one bare-metal server, with every engine's answer checked
against two independent reference implementations before anything was timed. This post has the results, the one place where it is
close, a mistake in our own benchmark kit, and the one command that reruns the whole thing on your own machine.

What we ran

  • The data: SNAP's com-Orkut social graph: 3.07 million people and 117.2 million relationships, loaded as published.
  • The machine: one Vultr bare-metal server, AMD EPYC 4345P (8 cores, 16 threads), 64 GB of memory, two NVMe disks, no GPU.
  • The engines: Semurg, Neo4j, ArangoDB, FalkorDB, FalkorDBLite, ArcadeDB and SurrealDB, each in Docker on that server, one after another, each with every thread, both data disks and no memory cap, its own recommended settings, and its fastest query form.
  • Two shapes of use: inside your application (Semurg linked into the client; the other engine's embedded mode where it has one, otherwise its fastest connection) and as a server (each engine through its own fastest connection).
  • Three cycles: cold, warm, warm again; the figure is the median of the warm cycles.

One query, 4 hops

Starting from one person, every distinct person within 4 hops (455,604 of them). As a server, Semurg answered in 3.83 ms; ArcadeDB
took 73.14 ms, FalkorDBLite 164.14 ms, FalkorDB 205.89 ms, Neo4j 281.40 ms and SurrealDB 1,484.92 ms. Across those
five server rows that is between 19 and 388 times faster. Inside the application the picture is the same: 3.84 ms for
Semurg against 93.08 ms for ArcadeDB's embedded mode and 1,360.65 ms for SurrealDB's.

Many queries at once

The same 4-hop question from 16 clients at once, each side driven by the same number of clients. As a server, Semurg answered 240.2
queries per second, ArcadeDB 28.0, FalkorDB 8.5 and Neo4j 2.6.

Walks to 131,072 hops

The ladder walks from the same person to every depth from 2 to 131,072 hops, checking each step against the reference. On this graph
everything reachable is reached within a few dozen hops, so past that point every engine is timing one full walk of the reachable
graph. As a server, Semurg's full walk took 95.22 ms; ArcadeDB's took 113.71 ms, FalkorDB's 412.67 ms and Neo4j's
14,033.83 ms. Inside the application Semurg's took 96.88 ms and ArcadeDB's embedded mode 459.74 ms.

The server comparison with ArcadeDB is the close one, and we care about it most. ArcadeDB answers its traversals from what it calls a
Graph Analytical View: an index of the whole graph it builds in memory when the database opens (the build is counted in its load
time). Semurg needs no such build when it opens. The next release carries two speed-ups to the graph walk; in our own test build they took the full walk from 96.4 ms to 81.1 ms on 8 threads (a test build, not a published release), and the published number follows the release.

What did not run, and why

A result we could not judge is shown as held, never dropped. In this run:

  • ArangoDB answered the 4-hop question correctly, but it was stopped by the out-of-memory killer during the many-at-once test, and the walk that followed found it already stopped. Our benchmark kit read that as a failure of the walk itself and set aside all of ArangoDB's results, its correct ones included. That was our kit's mistake, not ArangoDB's: the kit now checks that an engine is running before a walk starts, and ArangoDB is re-run on the next release. Until then its cells on the benchmark page read results pending.
  • FalkorDBLite's many-at-once run had failed requests and SurrealDB's had a zero median, so neither has a throughput figure; load times are held for every engine until each load has its run-to-run band.

Bigger than memory

Every domain we publish runs four classes: in the application and as a server, each on a dataset that fits in memory and one that
does not. This graph fits. The bigger-than-memory run uses SNAP's com-Friendster, a far larger social graph, with each engine held to a
fixed memory budget; its reference answers are still being computed, and the results go on the benchmark page when they finish.

Run it yourself

The kit that produced every number above is published. On a Linux machine with Docker, one command runs the graph benchmark for every
engine: curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/bench | sudo bash -s -- --graph. On a machine like ours it needs about 22 GB of free disk,
about 48 GB of memory for the largest engine, and about eight and a half hours (test tree, not a published release). Every figure,
every held row and the reason for each is on the benchmark page.

20261004.00_p0 Release

Confidential Space

Announcement

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Fixed

CodeMender updates (v0.12.0)

This release introduces updates to CodeMender:

  • Hidden file scanning: Added the --include-hidden flag to cm find (or include_hidden under scan in config.yaml) to include hidden directories and files, such as .github/ and .config/, in vulnerability scans.
  • Larger file support: Raised the default file discovery size limit (max_file_size_kb) from 500 KB to 2 MiB so cm find no longer skips large source files. Existing configurations that use the previous 500 KB default are upgraded automatically, and --deep and --diff scans can now read beyond the inline preview of files larger than 64 KB.
  • Report output for every scan mode: cm find --output now writes the scan report for standard, --deep, --parallel, and --diff scans.
  • Scoped fixes: cm fix now prevents the agent from modifying CI/CD pipelines, static analysis configurations, build definitions, and repository configuration files that are outside the scope of the vulnerability being fixed.
  • Accurate session token usage: cm now reports the total token usage across all turns of a session, instead of only the final turn, so token counts in cm stats and session exports match billed usage.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Fixed duplicate findings in cm report and cm stats, and stopped merging distinct vulnerability types reported on the same line.
    • Fixed database is locked errors during cm find --deep scans with multiple workers.
    • Reduced false positives by requiring a concrete, viable exploit before reporting a finding with high confidence.
    • Included sessions from cm find --deep and cm find --diff workers in cm stats.
    • Fixed cm verify resolving relative finding and exploit artifact paths against the current working directory instead of the project root.

For more information, see the CodeMender documentation.
