title: I Built Kiver: A Discovery Marketplace for Telegram Bots and Mini Apps
description:
Building a Telegram bot is one thing. Getting people to discover it is another.

That problem is what led me to build Kiver.

"https://www.getkiver.com" (https://www.getkiver.com)

The problem I wanted to solve

Telegram has an ecosystem of bots and Mini Apps for almost everything: AI assistants, productivity tools, finance, education, gaming, automation and more.

Developers spend time building these products, improving their features and trying to attract users. But once a bot is ready, discovery becomes a challenge of its own.

A Telegram link is useful, but it doesn't always give a product the broader visibility it needs. Potential users may not know the bot exists, and developers need more ways to put their work in front of relevant audiences.

I wanted to build something that could help bridge that gap.

What is Kiver?

Kiver is a discovery marketplace for Telegram bots and Mini Apps.

The idea is straightforward: help users find useful Telegram tools and give makers a public place to showcase what they've built.

On Kiver, users can:

  • Browse Telegram tools across different categories.
  • Search for bots by name, username or use case.
  • Explore individual product pages.
  • Upvote tools they find useful.
  • Open listed bots directly in Telegram.

For developers and makers, Kiver provides a way to turn a Telegram link into a dedicated, shareable product listing.

Giving Telegram tools a public home

One part of Kiver I'm particularly interested in is discoverability beyond Telegram itself.

A maker can submit a public Telegram link, review the listing details, select a category and publish a product page.

That page gives the tool a dedicated URL that can be shared in communities, included in documentation or discovered through search engines.

The goal is to create another discovery channel for Telegram products instead of relying entirely on someone already knowing a bot's username or receiving its link from another person.

Of course, a public page doesn't guarantee search rankings or new users. The challenge is building a useful directory that people actually want to visit.

I'm still growing it

Kiver is an early-stage project, and I'm starting to see traffic coming to the website.

It's not massive traffic, and I'm not going to pretend it is. But seeing people visit a product you're building is useful feedback. It gives me a reason to keep improving the experience, expanding the directory and thinking more carefully about how users discover and evaluate tools.

The next challenge is turning visits into something more meaningful: people finding useful products, makers getting discovered, and visitors returning because the directory helps them.

That's the kind of growth I want to build toward.

What I'd like to improve

There are several areas I'm interested in developing further:

  • Better discovery: Helping users find relevant tools without having to know their names beforehand.
  • More useful listings: Making it easier to understand what a bot does before opening it.
  • More makers: Bringing more developers into the directory so users have a wider selection of tools.
  • A stronger community: Making product feedback and voting more useful for both users and builders.

The important part is making the directory valuable to both sides. More listings are useful, but only if people can find tools that genuinely solve their problems.

Try Kiver

If you've built a Telegram bot or Mini App, you can explore the directory and submit your own project.

Website: https://www.getkiver.com

Browse the directory, see how listings work, or launch your own Telegram tool on the platform.

I'm building Kiver in public and would appreciate feedback from developers, indie hackers and anyone working in the Telegram ecosystem.

If you build Telegram tools, what is the biggest challenge you've faced when trying to get your first users?

I'd be interested to hear what has worked for you.

title: Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis
description:
title: "Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-11T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [nodejs, redis, backend, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Producers And Consumers: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Delayed And Recurring Jobs: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency Control: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Exponential Backoff Retries: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Producers and consumers, delayed and recurring jobs, concurrency control, exponential backoff retries, and monitoring queue health with Arena."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Working with S3 Object Tags in Buckets: SET, MERGE and CLEAR
description:
A practical walkthrough for keeping Amazon S3 objects organized without changing what is inside the files.

Object tags are easy to overlook when you are busy uploading and moving files around S3. But once a bucket starts filling up, a few consistent labels can make objects easier to organize and manage. The part that matters is how you update them: replacing a tag set is not the same as adding a tag to what is already there.

I used Buckets by Serverless Creed to explore three useful actions—SET, MERGE and CLEAR—and checked the results in the AWS S3 console. I also compared the downloaded files with their original SHA-256 hashes to make sure the contents stayed exactly the same.

A quick look at object tags

An S3 object tag is a key-value pair attached to an object. For example, env=test, team=intern or phase=review can describe where a file belongs or how it is used. These are separate from the file itself and from ordinary user-defined object metadata. S3 allows up to ten tags per object.

Tags can be useful for organizing data and for AWS features that are configured to use them, including lifecycle rules and some access-control policies. That is why updating tags deserves a little more care than simply changing a filename.

Start with a small sample folder

I worked with a handful of harmless text files in a private S3 bucket:

  docs/readme.txt
  b.txt
  c.txt
  control.txt

The files were small enough to inspect easily. The bulk operations shown below target only b.txt and c.txt. I left control.txt with a separate control=keep tag so there was always an object to compare against the ones being updated.

The sample files as they appear in the Buckets object browser.

SET: replace the existing tags

SET is the option to choose when an object needs a completely new tag set. In Buckets, select the files, open the bulk tagging action and choose Set (replace). For this example, I entered team=intern.

The important word is replace: tags that were on the object before, but are not included in the new set, will be removed. Before applying the change, the dialog shows the exact object keys being updated. It is worth reading that list rather than assuming every visible folder or file is included.

SET preview in Buckets, with the new team tag and the exact object list.

The operation completes and Buckets displays the update result.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for SET.

I then opened the object details in AWS. The tag panel showed one tag, team=intern, which is the state I expected after a replacement.

AWS S3 shows the new tag set after SET.

MERGE: add a tag without losing the others

MERGE is more useful when the existing labels should stay. I kept team=intern, switched to Merge, and entered a new tag: phase=review. I left the remove-keys field empty.

That should leave both tags on the objects. If a tag key already exists, MERGE updates that key; keys not mentioned are preserved. This is usually a safer option for incremental changes than rebuilding the full tag list by hand.

MERGE adds phase=review while preserving the other tag keys.

The MERGE action completes successfully.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for MERGE.

The AWS object details now displayed both team=intern and phase=review. Checking the entire tag list is useful here: seeing only the new key would not prove that the earlier one survived.

Both team and phase are visible in the AWS object-tag panel.

CLEAR: remove tags, not the object

CLEAR does exactly what the name suggests: it removes the object’s tag set. In Buckets, choose Clear all after selecting the intended files. The confirmation makes the scope explicit and warns that tag-dependent lifecycle rules or policies may no longer match.

This is the step where I would be most careful in a real bucket. Clearing tags does not delete a file, but tags may be used by other AWS configurations. Always check the objects listed in the confirmation before proceeding.

CLEAR warns about removing all tags and shows the affected object keys.

Buckets confirms that the tag-removal operation completed.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for CLEAR.

Afterward, the AWS object details showed Tags (0). The AWS object details still identified b.txt; the wider Buckets capture also shows readme.txt remaining in the browser after tag removal. That distinction is important: removing tags is not the same thing as deleting objects.

The S3 tag section is empty after CLEAR.

A wider view of the Buckets object browser after tag removal.

The AWS object details page still shows the file and its empty tag set.

Independent verification and SHA-256 integrity checking

I kept control.txt out of the tagging changes. Its control=keep tag was still there at the end, which was a quick check that the untouched object had retained its original tag.

The control object keeps its original tag.

For file contents, I recorded SHA-256 hashes of the original text files before uploading them. After the tagging sequence, I downloaded the S3 objects into a separate folder and compared them with that original hash list. Run the check from the download folder, with the original hash list one directory above it:

shasum -a 256 -c ../original-hashes.txt

All four downloaded files match their original SHA-256 hashes.

The output was:

docs/readme.txt: OK
b.txt: OK
c.txt: OK
control.txt: OK

The AWS Console screenshot lists CRC64NVME as its stored checksum function. The SHA-256 verification here is a separate local comparison of the downloaded bytes against the original files.

All four checks returned OK. That gives two independent views of the outcome: the AWS Console shows how the tags changed, and the hash check shows that the downloaded file bytes matched the originals.

A few habits worth keeping

Three things made this workflow straightforward. First, use SET only when replacing the full tag set is intentional; use MERGE when existing labels should remain. Second, review the exact object list before any bulk operation, especially when folders and nested files are involved. Third, check the resulting tags in S3 rather than relying on a success message alone.

For a small example like this, the difference between SET, MERGE and CLEAR is easy to see. On a busy bucket, choosing the right operation—and verifying the final state—can save a lot of confusion later.

title: Accelerating Spatio-Temporal Attention for Video Diffusion on TPUs
description: To address the quadratic latency bottleneck of self-attention in high-resolution video diffusion models, developers implemented Sparse VideoGen (SVG) to dynamically route attention heads to highly structured spatial or temporal sparse masks. Translating this algorithmic sparsity into physical hardware speedups on TPUs required optimizing the Splash Attention kernel by bypassing empty memory tiles, restricting exact coordinate masking strictly to boundary tiles, and permuting token memory layouts into temporal-major order for contiguous access. By aligning these sparse masks with actual hardware tile execution, the combined optimizations significantly reduced wasted matrix operations and achieved up to a 1.69x end-to-end inference speedup for 1440p video generation.

title: GST Helper: a local-first GSTR-1 preparation assistant
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

I built GST Helper, a local-first AI workspace that helps a small business prepare selected GSTR-1 values from sales invoice PDFs.

The demo company is BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. The user starts by loading outward-sales invoice PDFs. GST Helper reads the invoices, extracts values, shows page evidence, and turns the documents into a guided GSTR-1 review flow.

The current app prepares these GSTR-1 sections:

  • Table 4A regular domestic B2B invoices
  • Table 12 B2B HSN/SAC summary
  • Table 13 document numbers issued

It shows the invoice value including tax, taxable value, IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST, cess, total tax, and invoice count for the supported B2B scope. It also creates a reference PDF tied to the saved review revision, so the user can inspect the same values before downloading the file.

The problem is simple: small business owners and bookkeepers often do this first pass manually. They read invoice PDFs, copy values into spreadsheets, check invoice numbers, and then use those figures while working in the GST Portal. That work is slow, error-prone, and full of accounting language that is not friendly to a non-expert.

GST Helper is meant for a small business owner, bookkeeper, or accountant who wants a faster way to prepare and review the numbers before portal entry. The paid version could charge for private local workflows, more GST sections, accountant review packs, and better import and export support.

The app does not file a return, connect to the GST Portal, or claim that the whole GSTR-1 return is complete. Other GSTR-1 sections must be handled separately. That boundary is visible in the product because tax software needs trust more than magic.

Demo

Video demo: https://youtu.be/RFq9whXetRg


The demo shows the full BharatBiz flow:

  1. Load sample sales invoice PDFs.
  2. Confirm the seller GSTIN, tax period, and turnover band.
  3. Review invoice fields with page evidence.
  4. Save the reviewed values.
  5. Inspect the Table 4A totals.
  6. Generate a verified reference PDF.
  7. Use the review chat beside the final PDF.

Code

Repository: https://github.com/sonu0702/pgst

sonu0702 / pgst

GST Helper

GST Helper is a local-first GSTR-1 preparation app for BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. It turns outward-sales invoice PDFs into reviewed values, a clear summary for the supported GSTR-1 sections, and a reference PDF the user can inspect before downloading.

This release prepares only regular B2B invoices in Table 4A, the B2B HSN/SAC summary in Table 12, and documents issued in Table 13. It does not prepare a complete GSTR-1 return, connect to the GST Portal, submit or file a return, or decide GST treatment. Other applicable GSTR-1 sections must be prepared separately. The GST Portal accepts a JSON workflow through its offline tool, but the portal still validates the account and return when the user uses that file.

What the app does

  • Starts with outward-sales PDFs, then suggests seller GSTIN and tax period with page evidence before asking for return details.
  • Shows observed invoice-number…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The app is a single repository with a React frontend and a FastAPI backend.

Tech stack:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Local AI: Ollama with Gemma 4
  • PDF processing: Python PDF extraction with optional local OCR support
  • Export artifacts: reference PDF and supported-section JSON
  • Storage: no database in this prototype. Reviews live in temporary process memory.

The user flow starts with source documents, not a chatbot. That choice matters. Invoices are the source of truth, so the app first reads the PDFs and creates a review workspace from them.

The backend extracts invoice fields and line items, keeps compact evidence snippets, and builds a temporary GSTR-1 review case. The frontend lets the user inspect and edit each value. When the user saves, the backend runs local checks for the supported sections and returns readiness results.

Gemma 4 is used through Ollama for a narrow review task. It can answer questions about values already in the review or prepare a proposed edit from invoice evidence or from a value the user states. It cannot decide tax treatment, calculate GST, approve filing, or submit anything.

The user stays in control:

  • The model proposes changes.
  • The user applies the proposal.
  • The user reviews the form.
  • The user saves the revision.
  • The user regenerates the PDF if anything changed.

The reference PDF is tied to the saved revision. The app renders the PDF back in the browser and verifies the expected content before the user downloads it.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters here because tax preparation needs transparency, local control, and the ability to inspect the workflow.

A closed hosted API can produce a polished answer, but that is not enough for this use case. A small business owner needs to know where a number came from and what the app did with the source document. GST Helper keeps the review path visible: invoice evidence, editable fields, saved revision, local checks, and a reference PDF.

Open-weight local AI also changes the privacy story. In this prototype, Gemma 4 runs locally through Ollama. The app does not need to send invoice details to a hosted model API. That made it possible to build an AI-assisted review flow that still respects sensitive business documents.

Open-source tools also made the project practical for a hackathon:

  • FastAPI made the backend small and inspectable.
  • React and Vite made the review UI fast to iterate.
  • Ollama made local Gemma 4 setup approachable.
  • Python PDF tooling made extraction and reference PDF generation possible without building a document pipeline from scratch.

The project is not trying to replace a tax professional or the GST Portal. It is trying to make the preparation step clearer, safer, and more reviewable.

My Agent Session

I used Codex as an AI coding agent throughout the build. The agent helped with product scoping, GSTR-1 flow design, FastAPI and React implementation, sample invoice generation, UI polish, PDF review, and the demo walkthrough.

The most useful part was not code generation alone. The agent helped keep the product narrow. Whenever the app started to look like a generic invoice-review demo, I pushed it back toward one clear filing workflow: GSTR-1 preparation from sales invoices.

That made the final project stronger. It has a specific user, a specific filing task, a clear supported scope, and visible review boundaries.

Team

Feature

Kubernetes 1.36 support

Apigee hybrid v1.16.10 adds support for Kubernetes 1.36 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Google Distributed Cloud Virtual for VMware (vSphere), Google Distributed Cloud Virtual for bare metal, Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, and Rancher Kubernetes Engine (RKE2).

For more information, see Supported platforms.

Feature

Forward proxy support for AI policies

Apigee hybrid v1.16.10 adds forward proxy support for AI policies, such as the Model Armor and semantic caching policies. Outbound calls from these policies can now be routed through an HTTP forward proxy.

For more information, see Configure a forward proxy, Get started with the Model Armor policies, and Get started with semantic caching policies.

Cloud SQL for MySQL now automatically enables point-in-time recovery (PITR) in a separate, asynchronous operation after disaster recovery (DR) switchover and replica failover operations complete. Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4D machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by AMD EPYC Turin processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4D instances are purpose-built for low core usage and high storage density workloads such as:

  • SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • Data analytics and data warehouses
  • Search
  • Parallel file systems for AI/ML

The Z4D machine series delivers up to 3 TB of memory and 42,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4D also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4D instances are available in predefined standardlssd and highlssd machine shapes.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.34.900-gke.135 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade a cluster. Google Distributed Cloud 1.34.900-gke.135 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.900-gke.135:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between Reconciling and Running states if the management cluster configured a different pod density than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where gkectl diagnose and preflight validations failed to locate PersistentVolume datastores for user clusters deployed in a separate vSphere datacenter from the admin cluster (cpNodesInAdminDatacenter: true).
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could get stuck because the node pool controller attempted to recreate machine resources while deletion was in progress.

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.34.900-gke.135 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.34.900-gke.135 runs on Kubernetes v1.34.7-gke.200.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.34.900-gke.135:

  • Fixed vulnerabilities listed in Vulnerability fixes.
  • Fixed an issue where the status for Ingress resources was not updated when using bundled Ingress.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster had a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could get stuck because the node pool controller attempted to recreate machine resources while cluster deletion was in progress.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.18 will roll out to Looker (original) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, September 21, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 4, 2026

Looker 26.18 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom content theme fonts were improperly applied to the Look edit mode bar. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where downloading a dashboard as a CSV or ZIP file could result in a 500 error if any dashboard elements lacked an explicit title. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where links created using the LookML link parameter could return a 500 error if no label was specified. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard filter token chips didn't display an active highlighted background when a filter value was selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the Git connection test could fail to recognize Git credentials as sufficient if a branch protection rule on the Git provider restricted temporary branches. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where analytic models that referenced cross-database, schema-qualified, or dot-delimited table names failed to compile in BigQuery and Snowflake DDL generation. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where custom tooltips in Single Record visualizations appeared at the bottom of the Explore panel rather than directly beneath the selected row. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dashboard filter tokens and popover menus could fail to inherit fonts from custom themes. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where dragging series between Y-axes on pivoted Cartesian charts could cause the Explore page to crash or prevent visualization configurations from being saved. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in Explores where you couldn't scroll within the Chart Config Editor dialog when editing JSON visualization configurations. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where scheduled PDF deliveries to Cloud Storage could produce corrupted files and unexpectedly replace spaces in filenames with underscores. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where attempting to visualize pivoted query results in SQL Runner resulted in a TypeError configuration error. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

API requests that target a LookML project whose files or directories aren't found on the instance now return a 404 Not Found error instead of a 500 Internal Server Error.

Fixed

In Conversational Analytics, the Open in Explore button and sidebar exploration links are now hidden or disabled with explanatory tooltips when you lack explore permissions for the underlying model.

Fixed

The embed preload page now supports custom theming using the theme URL query parameter.

Fixed

Donut Multiples visualizations now automatically hide overlapping value labels.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed in self-service analytics where CSV and Excel uploads to BigQuery and Snowflake could fail or corrupt data when files contained multiline headers, leading numeric characters, UTF-8 BOM markers, or special characters. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where creating a shared branch based on the production branch in a bare repository project could initialize from stale remote commits, causing the Looker IDE to immediately report the branch as being behind production. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where scheduled deliveries intermittently failed with permission errors such as Cannot send all results because user permissions were incorrectly cached across scheduled jobs on worker threads. This feature now performs as expected.

NetApp Volumes

Feature

Organization Policy Service custom constraints are available for Google Cloud NetApp Volumes. You can use custom constraints to control how NetApp Volumes is used in your organization. For example, you can restrict storage pool or volume capacity, or enforce that storage pools are created only with Premium or Extreme service levels.

For more information, see Custom organization policy constraints.

Oracle Database@Google Cloud

Feature

For Exadata Database Service, Oracle Database@Google Cloud is available in europe-west12 (Turin, Italy) region.

For a list of supported locations, see Supported regions and zones.

Secure Web Proxy

Feature

Secure Web Proxy supports distributed tracing by integrating with Cloud Trace. With distributed tracing, you can track the lifecycle of outbound requests from internal workloads through your Secure Web Proxy gateways to external endpoints. This integration helps you detect latency bottlenecks and troubleshoot connectivity errors.

This feature is available in Preview.

Spanner

Feature

Spanner queues are generally available (GA). Spanner queues provide transactional messaging to help you manage asynchronous work. The feature pairs this capability with the scalability and reliability of Spanner, letting you build event-driven applications. For more information, see the Spanner queues overview.

title: Synthetic Data vs Fake Data: What's the Difference and When Should You Use Each?
description:
Developers often use the terms fake data, dummy data, mock data, and synthetic data as if they all mean the same thing.

Sometimes that is harmless.

Sometimes it causes real confusion.

Consider these two records:

{
  "name": "Test User",
  "email": "test@test.com",
  "city": "Test City"
}

and:

{
  "name": "Anna Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "city": "Hamburg",
  "country": "DE",
  "postalCode": "20095"
}

Both are not real customer records.

But they serve very different purposes.

The first is obviously placeholder data.

The second is designed to resemble the structure and relationships found in real data.

That difference becomes important when you're testing applications, APIs, imports, forms, analytics pipelines, or databases.

So what exactly is synthetic data, and how is it different from ordinary fake data?

What is fake data?

Fake data is any information created specifically for testing, demonstrations, development, or other non-production purposes.

It can be extremely simple:

John Doe
123 Fake Street
test@example.com

Or even:

foo
bar
123

The goal is usually not realism.

The goal is simply to have something to put into a field.

For example, if you're testing whether a form submits correctly, this might be enough:

{
  "firstName": "Test",
  "lastName": "User",
  "email": "test@example.com"
}

Nothing about that record needs to resemble a real user.

It only needs to satisfy the basic input requirements.

What is synthetic data?

Synthetic data goes a step further.

It is generated data designed to imitate the properties, structure, distributions, or relationships of real data without copying actual records.

For a simple customer profile, that could mean:

{
  "firstName": "Anna",
  "lastName": "Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Hamburg",
  "postalCode": "20095"
}

The person is not meant to represent a real customer.

But the record is internally plausible.

The fields relate to each other in a meaningful way.

That makes synthetic data useful for testing systems that behave differently depending on realistic combinations of values.

Fake data can be intentionally unrealistic

Sometimes unrealistic data is exactly what you want.

Suppose you're testing whether a username field accepts a value.

This may be perfectly fine:

test123

You do not need a sophisticated identity generator.

Likewise, if you're testing a calculator:

2 + 2 = 4

there is no benefit in generating realistic financial records.

Simple fake data is often best for:

  • unit tests
  • simple form tests
  • exact business rules
  • predictable fixtures
  • small examples
  • documentation

The simpler the test, the simpler the data should usually be.

Synthetic data is useful when relationships matter

Now imagine a checkout system.

You may need:

name
country
city
postal code
phone number
currency
tax rules
shipping options

If every field is generated independently, you might get:

{
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Tokyo",
  "postalCode": "SW1A 1AA",
  "phone": "+1 212 555 0100"
}

Every individual value looks valid.

Together they make little sense.

If your application uses those relationships, your tests become less useful.

Synthetic data can preserve context.

For example:

{
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Hamburg",
  "postalCode": "20095",
  "phone": "+49 40 12345678"
}

That is much more useful for testing country-aware behavior.

Dummy data is usually simpler

The term dummy data usually refers to placeholder information.

Examples:

John Doe
Company ABC
123456
example@example.com

It is often used for:

  • screenshots
  • demos
  • temporary UI development
  • prototypes
  • documentation

Dummy data does not necessarily try to reproduce real-world distributions or relationships.

It just fills space.

That makes it useful.

But it is not automatically realistic.

Mock data is slightly different

Mock data often appears in the context of mocked systems.

For example, a frontend may call an API that does not exist yet.

Instead of making a real request:

const response = await fetch("/api/users");

the frontend might receive a mocked response:

{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Anna",
  "plan": "pro"
}

The important concept is not whether the values are realistic.

The important concept is that the response stands in for another system.

Mocking is about replacing dependencies.

Synthetic data is about generating realistic data.

They can absolutely be used together.

A mocked API can return synthetic data.

Test fixtures are about repeatability

A fixture is data prepared for a test.

For example:

const user = {
  id: "user-42",
  plan: "pro",
  balance: 100
};

Fixtures are often deliberately static.

That is useful because the expected state is obvious.

If a test fails, you know exactly what the input was.

Synthetic data can also be used as a fixture, especially when it is seeded.

For example:

seed = checkout-user-42

The generator can recreate the same synthetic customer every time.

That combines realism with reproducibility.

Realism should match the test

One mistake developers make is assuming that more realistic data is always better.

It isn't.

Suppose you're testing this function:

function addTax(price, rate) {
  return price + price * rate;
}

You probably want a test like:

expect(addTax(100, 0.19)).toBe(119);

Generating a realistic customer, address, order, product catalog, and payment method adds nothing.

But if you're testing a full checkout flow, realistic synthetic data becomes much more useful.

A simple rule:

Use the least complicated data that still tests the behavior you care about.

Production data is not test data

There is another category developers sometimes use:

copied production data.

For example:

export 1,000 customers
import into staging

This may create realistic test conditions.

It also creates privacy and security risks.

Production data can contain:

  • names
  • emails
  • addresses
  • phone numbers
  • account identifiers
  • transaction histories
  • internal notes
  • sensitive metadata

Once copied into development, that information may appear in:

  • local databases
  • logs
  • screenshots
  • test exports
  • bug reports
  • backups
  • developer laptops

Synthetic data avoids this problem by generating new records rather than copying actual customers.

Synthetic does not automatically mean anonymous

This distinction is important.

If you take real customer data and simply replace:

John Smith

with:

User 123

the dataset is not necessarily synthetic.

Other attributes may still allow the person to be identified.

For example:

location
age
transaction history
rare job title
specific timestamp

can potentially reveal identity when combined.

Truly synthetic data should be generated rather than merely renaming real individuals.

Format-valid data is another category

Sometimes realism means following a technical format.

For example:

UUID
IBAN
MAC address
IMEI
IP address
phone number
email

A useful test value may need to satisfy structural rules.

For example, this:

DE123

is not very useful for testing a real IBAN validator.

You may instead need an identifier that follows:

country length
BBAN structure
checksum rules

That makes the test data technically realistic.

But an important distinction remains:

Format-valid does not mean real-world verified.

A generated IBAN can satisfy structural checks without representing an existing bank account.

A generated device identifier can match the expected format without representing an actual device.

Synthetic data can preserve distributions

For some applications, individual realistic records are not enough.

Imagine testing analytics.

Production data might contain:

70% free users
20% standard users
10% premium users

A naive generator could produce:

33% free
33% standard
33% premium

That may create misleading results.

A more advanced synthetic dataset could preserve the intended distribution:

free: 70%
standard: 20%
premium: 10%

Likewise, synthetic datasets can model relationships such as:

country → currency
country → phone format
product → price range
subscription → feature usage
age group → behavior

This becomes useful for:

  • analytics
  • machine learning testing
  • load testing
  • dashboards
  • data pipelines
  • BI systems

Synthetic data can still contain edge cases

Realistic does not mean normal.

Good test datasets should include unusual scenarios.

For example:

very long names
empty optional values
Unicode characters
leap-day dates
zero-value orders
duplicate records
minimum values
maximum values
unusual postal formats

These cases often expose more bugs than ordinary records.

A good synthetic-data system should allow realism and deliberate edge cases to coexist.

Example: signup testing

For a simple unit test, this may be enough:

{
  "email": "test@example.com"
}

For integration testing:

{
  "firstName": "Anna",
  "lastName": "Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE"
}

For edge-case testing:

{
  "firstName": "A".repeat(100),
  "lastName": "Schneider",
  "email": "anna+very-long-alias@example.com",
  "country": "DE"
}

Different tests deserve different data strategies.

Example: API testing

Imagine this endpoint:

POST /customers

The API expects:

{
  "name": "string",
  "email": "string",
  "country": "string",
  "phone": "string"
}

A basic fixture could be:

{
  "name": "Test",
  "email": "test@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "phone": "123"
}

That may be enough to test JSON parsing.

But it is not very useful for testing phone validation.

A realistic synthetic fixture could be:

{
  "name": "Anna Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "phone": "+49 40 12345678"
}

Now the same payload exercises more realistic application behavior.

Example: database testing

Suppose you need 100,000 customer rows.

Writing static fixtures is obviously impractical.

A synthetic generator can create:

100,000 records
multiple countries
different subscription plans
varied signup dates
different order histories

That is useful for:

  • query testing
  • pagination
  • indexing
  • search
  • analytics
  • performance testing

For this kind of workload, synthetic data becomes much more valuable than simple dummy records.

Seeds make synthetic data reproducible

Pure generation introduces a problem:

run 1 → dataset A
run 2 → dataset B
run 3 → dataset C

If dataset A exposes a bug, you may want it again.

That is where seeds help.

For example:

seed = regression-42

can produce the same synthetic dataset repeatedly.

Then a CI failure can report:

Generator: customer
Seed: regression-42

A developer can recreate the exact input locally.

This makes synthetic data much more practical for automated testing.

Don't use synthetic data everywhere

Synthetic data is not the answer to every problem.

Use static fixtures when:

  • exact values matter
  • the test is small
  • readability is important
  • business rules are simple

Use synthetic data when:

  • realistic variation matters
  • you need many records
  • relationships between fields matter
  • you want multiple locales
  • you need performance datasets
  • production data should not be copied

Use deliberately invalid data when:

  • testing validators
  • testing error messages
  • testing edge cases
  • testing defensive code

The best test suite usually combines all three.

A practical hierarchy

I like to think about test data in layers.

Level 1: Placeholder data 

foo
bar
123

Useful for very simple tests.

Level 2: Static fixtures 

{
  "email": "test@example.com",
  "plan": "pro"
}

Useful for predictable business logic.

Level 3: Synthetic records 

{
  "name": "Anna Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Hamburg"
}

Useful for realistic application testing.

Level 4: Synthetic datasets 

10,000 related records
multiple countries
weighted distributions
edge cases

Useful for analytics, system testing, and performance testing.

The higher the level, the more complexity you introduce.

Only move up when the test actually benefits from it.

Where tools like Genory fit

Developer tools such as Genory focus on generating synthetic test data and structured developer fixtures without requiring real customer records.

For example, you can work with:

  • synthetic profiles
  • custom datasets
  • addresses
  • UUIDs
  • format-based test identifiers
  • validators
  • developer utilities

For more complex fixture generation, you can start with the Genory test-data tools.

For programmatic workflows, the current API documentation is available at genory.dev/docs.

The goal is not to replace explicit test fixtures.

The goal is to make realistic test data easier to create when realism actually helps.

A simple rule

When choosing test data, ask:

Does this test care about the exact value?

If yes:

Use an explicit fixture.

If no, ask:

Does realism matter?

If no:

Use simple fake data.

If yes:

Use synthetic data.

And if the test must be reproducible:

Use a seed.

Final thought

Fake data and synthetic data are not enemies.

They solve different problems.

Fake data is often simple, obvious, and predictable.

Synthetic data is useful when your tests benefit from realistic structure, relationships, variation, or scale.

The mistake is not choosing one over the other.

The mistake is using complicated data where simple fixtures would work — or using meaningless placeholders when your application depends on realistic relationships.

Choose the data based on the behavior you're trying to test.

Not based on which generator looks more impressive.

title: What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing
description:
What We Learned Building Cross-Channel Message Routing for Chatbots

Sooner or later, every chatbot project hits the same wall: customers don't stay on one channel. A user asks a question on Instagram, follows up on WhatsApp, and expects the Telegram bot to know what happened. If each channel runs its own isolated logic, you end up with duplicated flows, lost context, and replies that arrive twice or not at all.

This is a behind-the-scenes post about how we approached cross-channel message routing for chatbots, the mistakes we made, and the patterns that held up. By the end you'll know how to design a normalized message format, build channel adapters, route messages reliably, and avoid the failure modes that cost us the most time.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • What is cross-channel message routing?
  • Lesson 1: Normalize messages before you route them
  • Lesson 2: Keep channel quirks inside adapters
  • Lesson 3: Build the router around rules, not channels
  • Lesson 4: Make delivery idempotent
  • Lesson 5: Plan for fallbacks and human handoff
  • Mistakes we'd avoid next time
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

You don't need a full production stack to follow along. It helps to have:

  • [ ] Basic familiarity with webhooks and REST APIs
  • [ ] Node.js 18+ and TypeScript (the examples use them, but the ideas are language-agnostic)
  • [ ] An account or sandbox for at least two messaging channels (e.g., WhatsApp Business API, Telegram Bot API, Instagram Messaging)
  • [ ] A queue or job system (Redis, RabbitMQ, SQS, or similar)

What is cross-channel message routing?

Cross-channel message routing is the layer that sits between your messaging channels and your bot logic. It receives inbound messages from any channel, decides where they should go (a flow, an AI agent, or a human), and delivers the reply on the right channel in the right format.

Why it matters: without a routing layer, every new channel multiplies your logic. With one, adding a channel means writing an adapter, not rewriting your bot.

Here's the high-level shape:

[WhatsApp] [Telegram] [Instagram]
     \         |         /
      \        |        /
     [ Channel Adapters ]
              |
     [ Normalized Message ]
              |
        [ Routing Engine ]
         /     |      \
   [Flow]  [AI Agent]  [Human]
              |
     [ Outbound Dispatcher ]

Lesson 1: Normalize messages before you route them

Our first version passed raw webhook payloads around. It worked until we added the second channel and every if (channel === "...") branch started leaking into business logic.

The fix was a single internal message schema that every channel converts into:

type Channel = "whatsapp" | "telegram" | "instagram";

interface NormalizedMessage {
  id: string;              // our internal ID
  externalId: string;      // the channel's message ID
  channel: Channel;
  contactId: string;       // stable ID across channels (when known)
  channelUserId: string;   // the user's ID on that channel
  type: "text" | "image" | "audio" | "button_reply" | "other";
  text?: string;
  mediaUrl?: string;
  receivedAt: string;      // ISO timestamp
  raw: unknown;            // keep the original payload for debugging
}

Two small decisions paid off immediately:

  • Keep raw. When a channel changes its payload format, you'll want the original to debug against.
  • Separate contactId from channelUserId. This is what later lets you recognize the same person on different channels.

Lesson 2: Keep channel quirks inside adapters

Every channel has its own rules: message length limits, button formats, media handling, and messaging windows. We moved all of that into adapters with the same interface:

interface ChannelAdapter {
  channel: Channel;
  parseInbound(payload: unknown): NormalizedMessage;
  send(to: string, message: OutboundMessage): Promise<SendResult>;
}

class TelegramAdapter implements ChannelAdapter {
  channel: Channel = "telegram";

  parseInbound(payload: any): NormalizedMessage {
    const msg = payload.message;
    return {
      id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      externalId: String(msg.message_id),
      channel: "telegram",
      contactId: "", // resolved later by the contact service
      channelUserId: String(msg.from.id),
      type: msg.text ? "text" : "other",
      text: msg.text,
      receivedAt: new Date(msg.date * 1000).toISOString(),
      raw: payload,
    };
  }

  async send(to: string, message: OutboundMessage) {
    // Telegram-specific formatting and API call live here
    return { ok: true };
  }
}

Rule of thumb: if a line of code mentions a specific channel, it should live in an adapter.

A useful side effect is that you can test routing logic with a fake adapter and no network calls.

Lesson 3: Build the router around rules, not channels

Our early router asked, "Which channel did this come from?" The better question turned out to be, "What does this conversation need?"

We switched to declarative rules evaluated in priority order:

interface RoutingRule {
  name: string;
  priority: number;
  when: (msg: NormalizedMessage, ctx: ConversationContext) => boolean;
  to: "flow" | "ai_agent" | "human";
  target?: string;
}

const rules: RoutingRule[] = [
  {
    name: "human-takeover-active",
    priority: 1,
    when: (_m, ctx) => ctx.humanAssigned,
    to: "human",
  },
  {
    name: "keyword-support",
    priority: 2,
    when: (m) => /refund|complaint|cancel/i.test(m.text ?? ""),
    to: "human",
  },
  {
    name: "default-ai",
    priority: 99,
    when: () => true,
    to: "ai_agent",
    target: "general-assistant",
  },
];

function route(msg: NormalizedMessage, ctx: ConversationContext) {
  return [...rules]
    .sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority)
    .find((r) => r.when(msg, ctx))!;
}

Because rules don't care about the channel, the same logic works on WhatsApp, Telegram, and Instagram. You can still add channel-aware rules when you need them, such as a rule for a channel's messaging window.

Lesson 4: Make delivery idempotent

Webhooks get retried. Networks fail. If you don't plan for this, users get duplicate replies. Two protections helped us the most:

  1. Deduplicate inbound messages using channel + externalId.
  2. Use idempotency keys on outbound sends so a retried job doesn't send twice. 
async function handleInbound(msg: NormalizedMessage) {
  const key = `inbound:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`;
  const isNew = await redis.set(key, "1", "EX", 86400, "NX");
  if (!isNew) return; // duplicate webhook, ignore

  await queue.add("route-message", msg, {
    jobId: `route:${msg.channel}:${msg.externalId}`,
  });
}

Acknowledge the webhook fast and do the real work in a queue. Channels penalize slow responses, and long AI calls shouldn't block your HTTP handler.

Lesson 5: Plan for fallbacks and human handoff

Things that will go wrong: a channel API times out, a message is rejected, or the AI isn't confident. Decide the behavior in advance:

  • Retry with backoff for transient errors (timeouts, 5xx).
  • Don't retry permanent errors (blocked user, invalid recipient). Mark them and move on.
  • Hand off to a human when confidence is low or the user asks for one, and make the router respect that state (see the human-takeover-active rule above).
  • Log every routing decision with the rule name, so you can answer "why did the bot do that?" later. 
async function dispatch(adapter: ChannelAdapter, to: string, msg: OutboundMessage) {
  try {
    return await adapter.send(to, msg);
  } catch (err) {
    if (isTransient(err)) throw err;   // let the queue retry
    await markUndeliverable(to, err);  // permanent failure
  }
}

Mistakes we'd avoid next time

  • Routing on raw payloads. Normalize first, always.
  • Treating identity as an afterthought. Decide early how you'll link a user across channels.
  • Skipping decision logs. Debugging a routing bug without them is guesswork.
  • Assuming channels behave alike. Message windows, formats, and rate limits differ more than the docs suggest.

Replace this section with 1-2 real incidents from your build (a bug, a surprising channel behavior, a number you measured) before publishing.

Conclusion

The main takeaways from building cross-channel message routing for chatbots:

  • Normalize every inbound message into one schema.
  • Isolate channel-specific behavior inside adapters.
  • Route on conversation needs using ordered rules, not on channel names.
  • Make both inbound and outbound delivery idempotent.
  • Design fallbacks and human handoff from day one.

These patterns take time to get right, and many teams would rather spend that time on the customer experience than on plumbing. That's the problem platforms like Botsailor aim to take off your plate, with omnichannel automation across WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram, and more, so you can focus on conversations instead of webhooks. If you're building your own, we hope these lessons save you a few late nights.

How do you handle routing across channels? Share your approach or your worst webhook horror story in the comments.

title: TypeSafe AI's Jev 1.14 is now available on AI Gateway
description:
Jev 1.14 from TypeSafe AI is now available on AI Gateway.

Jev is a decision model for software. You pass it state and a set of questions, and it returns typed Choice, Score, and Boolean answers with probabilities instead of free-form text. It answers every question in one request, in parallel, for classification, routing, scoring, and automated verification.

Jev 1.14 accepts images as part of the state, and has an experimental long-context mode for documents, logs, or conversation histories that are too long for a standard request.

Use typesafe-ai/jev-1.14.0 as the model name.

Image input

Pass an image as a file part alongside text in state. This example reads a local PNG and asks a Boolean question about its color:

Long context

Enable long-context mode with providerOptions.typesafe.longContext: true. This example reads a support log and checks whether it reports a damaged delivery:

Jev supports Zero Data Retention and No Training, which you can enable per request. Decision calls also appear in logs and custom reporting, count toward budgets, and accept other Gateway provider options in the same providerOptions.gateway object.

Read the documentation on decision models on AI Gateway for more details, discover practical use cases for Jev, and browse resources in the knowledge base.
