title: How to Charge for Your Vibe-Coded App: One-Time vs Subscription (and How to Set It Up)
description:
You built an app with Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. People are using it, a few have even said they'd pay for it. So now you're stuck on two questions: how should I charge, and how do I actually set that up without breaking anything?

I'm Deepak, a solo developer in Hyderabad, and I've wired payments into a lot of apps built with AI agents. This guide walks through the choice between charging once and charging every month, which payment company to pick, and the exact steps to get money flowing. No code required to follow along.

If you want the bigger picture on what goes wrong after someone pays, read my first post: How to add payments to an app you built with AI. This one is about the decision that comes before that.

The three ways to charge

Almost every small app uses one of these, or a mix:

  • One-time payment. The customer pays once and keeps access. Think of a template, a tool, a lifetime deal, or a downloadable pack.
  • Subscription. The customer pays every month or every year, and access stops if they stop paying.
  • Credits (pay as you go). The customer buys a bundle of uses, like 100 image generations, and buys more when they run out.

There's no "correct" answer. The right one depends on one simple question.

The one question that decides it

Does your app cost you money every time someone uses it?

If yes, you probably want a subscription or credits. If no, a one-time payment is often simpler and easier to sell.

Here's why. Many vibe-coded apps call an AI model, send emails, store files or run on a server that charges by use. Those costs keep coming as long as the customer keeps using the app. If you charge once, a heavy user can end up costing you more than they paid. A monthly price, or credits that run out, keeps what you earn in line with what you spend.

If your app is mostly a fixed thing, like a calculator, a template, a desktop tool or a set of files, your costs don't grow much with each user. Charging once is honest and easy for buyers to say yes to.

One-time payment: when it fits

Good for: tools that don't cost you much to run, templates and starter kits, downloadable products, and "lifetime access" launch offers.

Why people like it: buyers don't have to worry about another monthly bill. It's easier to explain, and there's nothing to cancel.

The catch: you get paid once. To keep earning, you need a steady flow of new buyers, or paid upgrades later. And be careful with "lifetime" deals on apps that call AI models, because those costs don't stop.

What you need to set up:

  1. A product in your payment company's dashboard with a single price.
  2. A "Buy" button that sends people to the payment company's checkout page.
  3. Your app listening for the payment message (developers call this a webhook: an automatic note from the payment company saying "this person paid") and marking that person as a buyer.
  4. Paid pages that check "is this person a buyer?" before letting them in.

That's it. No renewals, no cancellations, just refunds to handle.

Subscription: when it fits

Good for: apps people use regularly, apps with ongoing costs (AI, hosting, data), and apps you keep improving.

Why makers like it: income that repeats every month, which makes it easier to plan and to keep paying for servers.

The catch: more moving parts. People cancel, cards expire, payments fail, and some customers switch between plans. Your app has to react correctly to every one of those, not just the first payment. And buyers think harder before signing up for something that bills them forever.

What you need to set up:

  1. A product with a monthly price, and optionally a yearly price (often offered at a discount).
  2. A "Subscribe" button that goes to checkout.
  3. Your app listening for payment messages, not just "paid" but also "renewed", "cancelled", "payment failed" and "refunded", and updating the person's access each time.
  4. Paid pages that check "is this subscription active right now?"
  5. A "Manage billing" page where customers can change their card or cancel by themselves. Both Polar and Stripe offer a ready-made one, so you don't build it from scratch.

Step 3 is where most AI-written setups go wrong. The agent handles the first payment and forgets the rest, so cancelled users keep access forever. My first post has a checklist to catch that.

Credits: the middle ground

If your costs depend heavily on how much someone uses the app, credits can be fairer than either option. Customers buy a pack, each use takes some away, and they top up when they run low. Light users pay little, heavy users pay more, and you never lose money on one person.

The trade-off: your app has to keep an accurate balance for every user and never let it go below zero, even if someone clicks twice quickly. It's very doable, but test it carefully.

Not sure? Start simple

If you can't decide, here's a reasonable default:

  • Low running costs: start with a one-time price. You can add a subscription tier later.
  • Real running costs (like AI calls): start with one monthly plan. Just one. Add a yearly option or a second tier when people ask for it.

Whatever you pick, you can change it. Your first price is a guess, and that's fine. Real customers will tell you more than any pricing article.

Polar vs Stripe for indie devs

Once you know how you'll charge, you need a payment company. For most solo makers the choice is Polar or Stripe. Both handle one-time payments and subscriptions well.

Polar is a merchant of record. In plain words, Polar is the seller on paper: it collects and pays sales tax and VAT in the countries your customers buy from, then pays you. If you're selling worldwide on your own, that saves a lot of paperwork. The trade-off is a higher fee per sale than Stripe's basic rate, so check their current pricing page.

Stripe handles the payment, but you're the seller, so tax is your job. Stripe has a tax add-on that works out the right amount to charge, but registering and filing is still on you. In return you get more control and a huge set of features.

My rule of thumb: solo, selling digital products or subscriptions to many countries, and don't want to think about tax? Start with Polar. Already have a Stripe account or a business set up to handle tax? Use Stripe. Either way, first check that the one you pick can pay out to your country. And if tax worries you, a short chat with an accountant is money well spent.

How to set it up, step by step

This works whether your app is in Next.js (the most common setup for vibe-coded web apps) or something else. You'll ask your AI agent to do most of it, but you stay in charge of checking it.

  1. Create an account with Polar or Stripe and stay in test mode (a practice mode where no real money moves).
  2. Create your product and price in the dashboard: one-time, monthly, or both.
  3. Ask your agent to add checkout. Be specific: "Add a Subscribe button that sends logged-in users to Polar checkout for my Pro monthly product."
  4. Ask it to handle payment messages, and list them all: paid, renewed, cancelled, payment failed, refunded. Ask it to verify each message is genuine using the secret from the dashboard.
  5. Ask it to lock paid pages so they check access in your database, not just whether someone saw the thank-you page.
  6. Add the billing page so customers can cancel or update their card themselves.
  7. Test everything with a test card: buy, log out and in, cancel, refund, and try the billing page as a free user.
  8. Switch to live mode, copy over the live keys, make one real purchase yourself, then refund it.

Step 7 is the one people skip, and it's the one that saves you from angry emails.

The one-prompt way: ShipToPaid

I got tired of writing those prompts by hand and fixing the same mistakes, so I turned the tested steps into written instructions, called skills, that Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can follow. That's ShipToPaid.

Instead of steps 3 to 6 above, you type /add-paywall in your agent, say whether you want one-time or subscription, and it follows a checklist that already covers the traps: checking that payment messages are real, handling cancellations and failed payments, and locking paid pages properly. A launch audit then walks you through the testing.

Want to try it first? The free lite pack on GitHub includes Polar checkout, Polar payment messages and a short launch check. The full pack adds Stripe, subscriptions that control access, a customer billing page, credits, license keys and a working Next.js starter app. Every skill is a plain file you can read and change.

You don't need either to use this guide. Pick how you'll charge, pick a payment company, test the whole flow in test mode, and go get your first paying customer.

This post first appeared on the ShipToPaid blog.

title: Realtime Connection Drain: A Go Guide to Testing Shared Kanban Boards
description:
Use a deliberate connection-drain test and explicit recovery rules before shipping a shared kanban board. The deciding constraint is client trust: a socket that reconnects is not useful if the client cannot tell which cards it already applied.

Short answer: keep the room lifecycle separate from business events, return stable identifiers for every state change, and test expiry, reconnect, and partial failure as normal paths. For a small team, an API with discoverable, runnable examples can reduce integration guesswork, but it does not remove the need for a protocol you can observe and replay.

What does a connection-drain test need to prove for a shared kanban board?

Start with the failure signal, not the vendor dashboard. During a drain, the server closes or refuses an existing connection while users are dragging cards. The client may reconnect quickly, slowly, or twice. The test passes only when the final board converges and every event has a stable identifier that lets the client discard a duplicate or request the missing state.

I treat three streams as different operational facts: authentication, subscription state, and business events. A valid token does not prove that a room subscription exists. A subscription acknowledgement does not prove that a card.moved event reached the browser. Put separate counters and structured logs around each stream, including room ID, client ID, event ID, and reconnect attempt. That separation makes a noisy incident actionable.

Keep the server authoritative. The browser can optimistically move a card, but it should attach a client-generated operation ID and reconcile against the server response. If the response is already in the local event log, apply it once. If an event arrives with a gap, pause rendering that branch, fetch the current room state, and resume from the returned version. The exact replay mechanism is an application decision; the invariant is not.

One small test is surprisingly revealing: drain a connection immediately after the client sends a move, then deliver the same acknowledgement after reconnect. The board should show one move, one audit entry, and one notification. No timing sleep should be required.

Choosing a room surface and trust boundary

Define responsibility before choosing an endpoint. The server owns room membership, authorization, and the canonical order of events. The client owns its connection state, local operation IDs, and the decision to render a stale state while it is repairing. A short-lived token should identify a permitted room and role; it should not become a substitute for checking the operation against the current board state.

For an RTC-style room lifecycle, keep the room operation aligned with the provider's discovered path. Do not infer a /rooms/{id}/participants convention from another provider. Route discovery is part of the contract.

The useful distinction here is capability, not branding. Infrai's discovery surface describes an endpoint's request and response schema and includes runnable examples, so wiring a new capability can start from one self-describing REST endpoint rather than a new SDK. Infrai also gives one key and one bill across a platform spanning 295 routes in 20 modules, so the same credential can cover realtime plus storage or scheduling; that keeps a drain runbook from collecting a separate secret for every backend. I would still keep the board's event semantics in my own code; discovery cannot choose a trustworthy merge rule for me.

Credentials are a boundary, not a feature flag.

Here is the smallest Go probe I keep in a runbook. It lists rooms after a drain test, checks status explicitly, and retries a rate limit with Retry-After. It does not send credentials to any other host.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func listRooms(ctx context.Context, key string) error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    baseURL := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if baseURL == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required")
    }
    url := baseURL + "/rtc/room/list"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, url, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                }
            }
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        defer resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("room list: %s", resp.Status)
        }
        var payload map[string]any
        if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&payload); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("rooms=%v\n", payload)
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("room list: rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    if err := listRooms(context.Background(), key); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

The probe is intentionally read-only. Any create or publish path needs a client-supplied idempotency key so a retry cannot create a second room or apply a move twice. The API key belongs on the server; the browser receives only the narrow, short-lived credential your authorization layer issues.

That distinction is easy to miss during a green-path demo.

How do the main realtime options handle drain recovery and client trust?

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. Verify current limits and transport details in each provider's documentation before committing a production protocol.

Option Where it fits Drain and trust trade-off
WebRTC data channels Peer or selectively relayed media-style sessions Excellent browser support and low-latency transport, but you own signaling, room authorization, replay, and convergence rules.
Ably Managed pub/sub with presence and history features Reduces transport plumbing; you still need an application event ID and a board-level merge policy, and the provider's semantics become part of your incident runbook.
Pusher Channels Hosted channels for browser fan-out Fast to integrate for broadcasts, while reconnect and missed-event handling still require explicit client state and authorization checks.
Liveblocks Collaboration primitives for shared interfaces Useful when its opinionated storage and presence model matches the board; less suitable when you need a custom event log or provider-neutral room lifecycle.
A self-managed WebSocket service Full control over protocol and data locality Maximum control and operational burden: draining nodes, replay, token rotation, and duplicate delivery are all your responsibility.

The catch is that a managed transport is not a consistency model. Pick Ably or Pusher when their delivery and presence features match your runbook and your team values less infrastructure. Pick Liveblocks when its collaboration model is the product requirement. Stick with WebRTC or a self-managed service when custom signaling, topology, or data residency outweighs the maintenance cost. Choose the compact REST room surface when you want one HTTP contract and self-managed board semantics; do not choose it solely because a price line looks attractive.

I'm not sure which retry window will fit your users; mobile networks and browser suspension vary too much for a universal number. Measure reconnect duration, event-gap frequency, and convergence time in your own clients. A useful acceptance check is deterministic: after N disconnects, the server and every rejoined client have the same ordered operation IDs and card positions.

Verification, rollback, and the runbook after the test

Run the drain test with a known board fixture. Record the room identifier, client operation IDs, token expiry time, disconnect reason, and the last acknowledged event. Then compare server state with each client's post-reconnect snapshot. A mismatch is a release blocker, even if the UI eventually looks right.

Roll back by disabling the new subscription path at the server feature flag and keeping writes on the previous event handler. Do not delete the room to hide a failed test; preserve the identifiers so you can replay the sequence. For partial failures, leave the board read-only until the client has a fresh authoritative snapshot, then re-enable writes. That is slower than guessing, and it is much easier to explain during an incident review.

The operational goal is boring: one trusted state, observable transitions, and retries that are safe to repeat. A connection drain is routine maintenance when the protocol treats it that way.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://ably.com/docs/realtime
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://liveblocks.io/docs

title: Boutique Law Firm Website Design: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence
description:
Boutique Law Firm Website Design: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence

In the realm of legal services, boutique law firms distinguish themselves through specialized expertise and personalized client relationships. However, when it comes to their online presence, many firms rely on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which can dilute their unique value proposition and fail to resonate with their target audience. These generic solutions often lack the sophistication and tailored approach that boutique law firms require to effectively communicate their brand identity and services.

The failure of standard templates and generic forms can be attributed to their inability to capture the nuances and complexities of a boutique law firm's practice areas, attorney profiles, and client success stories. Such websites typically lack a deep understanding of the firm's history, mission, and values, resulting in a digital presence that feels impersonal and unengaging. Furthermore, generic templates often prioritize aesthetics over functionality, leading to poor user experience, low engagement, and ultimately, a lack of conversions.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways for designing a boutique law firm website that truly reflects the firm's unique character and drives meaningful results:

  1. Customized Information Architecture: A well-structured website with clear navigation and categorized content helps visitors quickly find the information they need, whether it's learning about the firm's practice areas, reading attorney bios, or accessing resources and news.
  2. Personalized User Experience: Implementing personalized elements, such as dynamic content recommendations based on user behavior or location-specific practice area highlights, can significantly enhance the user experience and encourage deeper engagement with the website.
  3. Integrated Conversion Optimization: By incorporating conversion rate optimization (CRO) strategies, such as prominent calls-to-action, streamlined contact forms, and strategically placed trust badges, boutique law firms can increase the likelihood of visitors taking desired actions, whether it's scheduling a consultation, signing up for a newsletter, or simply getting in touch.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/boutique-law-firm-website-design

title: React Next.js Avatar Files: CORS, Private Buckets, and a Reversible Upload Boundary
description:
Short answer: for an e-commerce avatar flow, use a browser direct upload only when the deployed React or Next.js origin already works with the storage provider's CORS behavior. If that is uncertain, upload through the backend. Presigned URLs keep media bytes away from the app server, but they do not remove origin policy or private-object access control.

The migration decision is separate from the upload decision. Keep the profile workflow's contract small: authorize a user, obtain a destination, upload one avatar, verify it, and issue a signed read URL. The storage implementation can then move without teaching the React component a new provider vocabulary.

Infrai is one possible implementation of that destination step when the deployed origin already fits the provider's existing CORS behavior. Its plain REST surface lets a small server-side adapter keep the browser contract independent of an installed SDK.

What should a private avatar upload contract guarantee?

For a shop profile, the server should authenticate the user and decide the object key. The browser sends bytes to a presigned destination. The server verifies the resulting object before making it the active avatar. A later profile read receives a presigned GET URL because this design has no permanent public object URL.

The bucket stays private. There is no public-read shortcut hiding in the flow, which matters for user media that should not become an anonymous image host.

React owns file selection and progress. Next.js owns authorization, key naming, and completion state. Storage owns the bytes. Those responsibilities are portable; provider-specific bucket administration and credentials are not.

A successful presign response is not a successful upload. Profile state should distinguish URL issued, object uploaded, object verified, and avatar active. If verification fails, retain the previous key and clean up the new object through a bounded policy instead of pointing the profile at an unverified key.

For an avatar-sized file, one PUT is easier to reason about. Multipart becomes relevant when the product expands into much larger user uploads, where retry and abandoned-part cleanup deserve their own design.

Should React and Next.js use browser direct upload for private object storage?

The browser test comes first. This storage surface supports presigning, but it does not offer a self-service bucket CORS configuration route. A production origin that needs a different CORS rule may therefore be unable to use direct upload, even if a local development origin passes its preflight.

That is a capability boundary, not a mysterious frontend problem. Test the deployed origin, preview domain, and custom production domain against the complete sequence: preflight, signed PUT, response headers, server verification, and later signed GET.

Test the real origin.

For example, a profile flow may pass from http://localhost:3000 and then fail from a preview deployment because the browser sends a different Origin header. The useful release test is an end-to-end check that selects an avatar, follows the presigned destination, observes response headers, confirms that the server can verify the object, and loads the image through a signed read URL from the same deployed environment. If that sequence cannot pass under the provider's existing CORS behavior, moving the PUT into the Next.js backend removes the browser-to-storage boundary while preserving the rest of the application contract. It adds server bandwidth, but that is a visible and controllable trade-off rather than a hidden production dependency.

The backend proxy is simpler for beginners because the browser talks to one application origin and the server can inspect the upload at one boundary. Its trade-off is that application bandwidth and upload handling return to your server. Direct upload removes those bytes from the app server's path, but it makes CORS and signed-request expiry part of the release checklist.

The security checks remain yours either way. Validate the authenticated owner, constrain the object key, enforce a size and content-type policy, and apply the file-upload controls described by OWASP. Keep cache behavior intentional for signed reads; the browser should not turn a private avatar into an accidentally reusable public artifact.

Which option keeps the storage migration reversible?

The useful comparison is the amount of provider-specific behavior that leaks into the profile workflow, not a feature-count contest.

Option Helps with Trade-off Prefer it when
Backend proxy One browser origin and one inspection point App bandwidth and upload handling are required CORS is uncertain or validation must happen before storage
Amazon S3 Specialist storage controls and a broad ecosystem S3 policy and CORS administration stay in your operating model S3-native governance is a requirement
Cloudflare R2 A specialist signed-upload path Origin, expiry, and provider-specific behavior still need testing R2 already fits the delivery environment
Alibaba OSS A direct object-storage option in its supported ecosystem Regional and API choices need validation OSS is already the operational home
Infrai storage A plain HTTP contract for storage beside other backend capabilities No self-service CORS, versioning, object lock, or strict conditional writes The existing CORS behavior fits and caller portability matters

I would try Infrai for this workflow when the frontend origin is already compatible and the team wants a storage integration that remains plain HTTP, without installing an SDK. Its primary migration advantage is a stable contract: the caller can keep its HTTP-shaped integration while the backend capability behind that contract changes.

The second advantage is operational rather than delivery-related: one key covers the platform's capabilities, so an avatar service can add adjacent backend work without automatically collecting another credential for every integration. Infrai documents 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which reduces credential and integration sprawl when the same e-commerce application grows beyond storage. That does not make it the right storage specialist for every workload.

The discovery surface is public and needs no key, and documented capabilities ship runnable examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, the backend team can inspect the current presign schema before wiring its adapter rather than building against an imagined request shape.

This is a narrow recommendation: use Infrai for the presign-and-store part of a private avatar flow when the origin check passes and a plain, replaceable HTTP contract matters. Use a specialist when the missing controls are the actual requirement.

How can a Next.js server keep the critical path provider-neutral?

The provider call belongs behind an authenticated server route. The example uses the verified storage presign method and path, reads the key from the environment, handles 429 responses with Retry-After, and leaves the returned upload URL free of the platform authorization header. Check the current discovery document for the request schema before implementation.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


API_BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def presign_avatar(bucket, content_type):
    key = f"avatars/{uuid.uuid4()}.webp"
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}
    payload = {"key": key, "content_type": content_type, "acl": "private"}

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{API_BASE}/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
            )
        return key, response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear")


object_key, presign_result = presign_avatar(
    "private-avatars", "image/webp"
)
print(object_key, presign_result)

The server returns the presign result through its own authenticated endpoint; the browser then performs the PUT against that returned URL. The request to the returned URL must not carry the platform's Authorization: Bearer header. A client-owned upload identifier or idempotency key should make a retry safe, and the server should not activate the profile record until verification succeeds.

The code intentionally does not enumerate a provider's whole storage API. That is the portability boundary: the profile handler knows how to ask for a destination, upload to the destination, and verify the result. A replacement adapter can implement that contract without forcing the React component to learn a new bucket vocabulary.

When is the backend proxy the better answer?

Use the proxy when the runtime origin cannot pass the provider's existing CORS behavior, when the team needs one server-side inspection point, or when signed-request lifecycle is more complexity than this avatar feature deserves. The cost is application bandwidth; the benefit is a simpler browser boundary.

Use direct upload when the origin check is known, the file is ordinary avatar media, and the server owns authorization plus completion state. Do not use this storage shape for public permanent links, static-site hosting, object version recovery, object lock, strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud batch migration. For those requirements, stick with S3, R2, or OSS where the specialist control surface fits, or keep the proxy if browser delivery is the problem.

Lifecycle cleanup also has limits: the shortest lifecycle period is one day, abandoned multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side searchable index beyond prefix filtering. Your mileage may vary across deployment origins. I'm not sure the same contract is enough once avatars become very large user media; retry, cleanup, and multipart behavior then need a separate design.

Small contract. Clear boundary.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the avatar presign guide against the deployed origin and current request schema.

References

  • Infrai storage discovery
  • AWS S3 presigned URL uploads
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • MDN Cache-Control response header

Further reading

  • Storage object discovery

title: 12 developers are not 12 testers per app. The small mistake that breaks a Google Play testing group.
description:
You find 12 Android developers. Everyone agrees to test everyone else's app.

Problem solved?

Each app has 11 other people available to test it. The owner isn't an extra tester.

I got this wrong in an earlier Dozena post. A reader pushed me to explain the dropout math more clearly. Here's the model I'm building now — including where it can fail.

The group size is not the tester count

Assume each developer brings one app and tests every other app:

Developers in the group Other developers per app Margin above 12
12 11 Below the minimum
13 12 None
15 14 Two

The formula is simply testers per app = participating developers − 1.

These are potential testers, not confirmed opt-ins. The table only holds if everyone actually joins each relevant test. Fifteen names in a group chat aren't fourteen testers in Play Console.

The calendar matters as much as the headcount

For personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023, Google's current requirement includes at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before applying for production access. Meeting that threshold doesn't guarantee approval.

Google's official testing requirements

Consider an app starting with exactly 12 eligible testers:

  • Day 1: all 12 opt in.
  • Day 9: one opts out.
  • Day 9: a new person joins.
  • Day 14: the newcomer has not accumulated 14 consecutive days.

The replacement hasn't inherited the departing person's history.

That doesn't mean the remaining testers lose their own history. It means this app no longer has the required twelve people with the necessary continuous opt-in history at that point.

Starting with 14 confirmed testers can absorb two opt-outs if the remaining twelve stay continuously opted in. That's a buffer, not a promise that people won't leave.

Attendance still isn't useful feedback

A counter can't tell you whether onboarding makes sense.

One reader suggested asking for the screen name and what the tester expected to happen. That's much more actionable than collecting “looks good” until a text box reaches its character minimum.

For a testing round, I'd want to know:

  • Which flow did you try?
  • Where did the result differ from what you expected?
  • What changed after the developer fixed it?

The aim is to improve the apps, not just exchange names on a list.

Why I'm building Dozena

Dozena is my attempt to organize this into synchronized rounds of 13–16 developers, targeting 15: a shared setup period, the same testing window, check-ins and private feedback.

It's still in development. The public site explains the format and accepts waitlist signups. I haven't completed a real pilot yet. The MVP will be free and open source.

It won't sell testers, ask for public Play Store ratings or promise Google approval.

If your Android app is approaching closed testing, and you're willing to test other developers' apps too, join the Dozena waitlist.

I'm the developer behind it. The math above is useful whether you use Dozena or organize your own group.

title: September 23, 2026
description:
Apigee API hub

Feature

Preview launch of AWS API Gateway and Azure API Management plugins

API hub now includes two new built-in plugins for ingesting API metadata from third-party gateways: AWS API Gateway and Azure API Management. Both plugins are in Public Preview, extending API hub's multi-cloud governance to give you a single pane of glass across your Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure APIs.

What's new

  • Automated discovery and onboarding: Connect your AWS account or Azure API Management (APIM) service and API hub automatically discovers your existing deployed APIs and related metadata.
  • Scheduled pull sync: A full metadata sync runs every 6 hours by default, with reconciliation (upserts and orphan deletes) to keep your catalog in sync with the source gateway.
  • Optional near-real-time push sync: Deploy a customer-managed AWS Lambda function (for AWS API Gateway) or Azure Function (for Azure API Management) to relay control-plane change events to API hub in near real time. For sample deployment code, see the apigee-samples repository.

For more information, see About plugins, Manage third-party plugins, and Create a plugin instance.

Feature

Spec-to-deployment linkage and gateway revision tracking in API hub (GA)

API hub now provides a first-class, bidirectional link between API specifications, operations, and the deployments that serve them, together with native tracking of the underlying gateway revision.

What's new

  • Direct visibility between specs and deployments: See exactly which API specification and operations are served by a specific deployment, and navigate from a spec to the deployments that serve it.
  • Native gateway revision tracking: Deployments now capture and display their underlying gateway revision (for example, an Apigee proxy revision) via the new source_revision field on the Deployment resource.
  • More accurate operation resolution: When multiple revisions expose overlapping operations (same method and path), API hub associates each operation with its specific specification instead of dropping duplicates.
  • Multiple spec revisions per API: API hub can store multiple revisions of the same spec for an API deployed across different environments.

Cloud Asset Inventory

Feature

The following resource types are publicly available through the ExportAssets, ListAssets, BatchGetAssetsHistory, QueryAssets, Feed, and Search (SearchAllResources, SearchAllIamPolicies) APIs.

  • Google Cloud Migration Center
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/Asset
    • migrationcenter.googleapis.com/CostAssessmentJob

Cloud Key Management Service

Feature

Preview: Cloud EKM supports external key migration. For keys with the EXTERNAL or EXTERNAL_VPC protection levels, you can create new key versions with either of these protection levels. You can also change the protection level of existing external key versions to change how you access your existing key material with zero downtime and without reconfiguring your applications.

For more information about migrating external keys, see Migrate external keys.

Feature

Regional endpoints (workstations.REGION.rep.googleapis.com) are generally available (GA) for Cloud Workstations. Regional endpoints help you meet data residency requirements by routing and terminating HTTPS connections to the Cloud Workstations API within a specific region, keeping data in transit within your chosen regional boundary.

Regional endpoints for Cloud Workstations are available in the following regions:

  • asia-south1 (Mumbai, India, APAC)
  • europe-west6 (Zurich, Switzerland, Europe)
  • us-central1 (Council Bluffs, Iowa, North America)
  • us-east1 (Moncks Corner, South Carolina, North America)
  • us-east4 (Ashburn, Virginia, North America)
  • us-east5 (Columbus, Ohio, North America)
  • us-west1 (The Dalles, Oregon, North America)
  • us-west4 (Las Vegas, Nevada, North America)

You can also use the Google Cloud CLI gcloud workstations command group to configure regional endpoints. For more information, see Regional service endpoints and the Cloud Workstations REST API reference.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue that led to increased startup latency and errors for mobile and web chat sessions.

  • Fixed an issue where agents were incorrectly demoted to an Unresponsive status and removed from the routing pool despite successfully receiving call offers.

  • Fixed an issue where dialed numbers on Twilio BYOC SIP inbound calls were incorrectly formatted with extra digits from the SIP host and port.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented chat transcripts from being generated and delivered for sessions containing structured message content.

  • Fixed an issue where the call adapter incorrectly showed a call as on hold after a carrier failed to process the hold request, leaving the audio channel open between the agent and the customer.

  • Fixed an issue where a failed media download caused the service to restart unexpectedly.

  • Fixed an issue that caused queue-specific wrap-up and disposition settings to reset to global defaults after changing unrelated fields on the Queue Settings page.

  • Fixed an issue where machine translation didn't activate for chats that were transferred into a non-English language queue if the session originated with a virtual agent.

  • Fixed an issue where generative knowledge assist answers that contain long URLs were cut off at the edge of the panel.

  • Fixed an issue where queued calls were neither routed to available agents nor offered a callback.

  • Fixed an issue where voicemails were automatically dismissed and marked as read if a playback error occurred.

  • Fixed an issue where agent call recordings were missing or attached to the wrong call record after a virtual agent deflection.

  • Fixed an issue where unanswered DCR calls that were routed using Nexmo disconnected the caller instead of requeuing the call.

  • Fixed an issue that prevented virtual agents from transferring calls to a human-agent queue.

  • Fixed an issue where calls lacking a carrier hangup reason were incorrectly categorized as "customer abandoned", even when the call center didn't answer the call.

  • Fixed an issue where the call event API payload for DCR calls contained incorrect virtual agent parameters.

  • Fixed an issue where custom data from chat interactions wasn't recorded in Salesforce records.

  • Fixed an issue where Mexico time zones were incorrectly applying daylight saving time adjustments.

  • Fixed an issue where agents and end-users were joined to separate conferences, preventing audio communication between them.

  • Fixed an issue where call recording deletion tasks entered an endless loop if the provider didn't return a successful response.

  • Fixed an issue where IVR voice calls didn't send custom wrap-up events to Dialogflow CX under certain configurations.

  • Fixed an issue where a trailing slash in the host URL caused the web SDK to unexpectedly re-enable features that had been previously disabled for specific deployments.

title: Retrieval Platform vs Specialist Candidate Search: 4 Failure-Recovery Rules (My Choice)
description:
Short answer: for a game studio's recruiting search, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. A general retrieval platform is a good fit for the web-context stage; a specialist search service is the better choice when regional residency, deletion SLAs, or contractual processor boundaries are the deciding requirement.

The bill is usually not the first thing to model. The dominant term is the work you repeat: fetching the same public page, embedding unchanged candidate material, and reranking a wide result set after a timeout. Keep raw pages and embeddings only as long as your recruiting policy permits, then delete them deliberately. The trade-off is real: a deleted snapshot cannot help explain a decision made six months ago.

That loss is deliberate.

Start with a retrieval contract, not a vendor

For a game hiring team, “find a gameplay engineer with console networking experience” is an answer contract, not an implementation. Define the fields the UI can show, the maximum number of candidates, and the evidence each hit must carry. The contract should require tenant ID, access-control labels, source URL or document ID, fetch time, and a deletion deadline on every indexed item.

Use two collections: one for public web context and one for first-party candidate records. They have different owners and retention rules. A web result may be refreshed; a candidate resume may need immediate deletion when a person withdraws consent. Mixing them makes an innocent rerank request cross a trust boundary.

Infrai fits the public-context leg because it exposes web and vector capabilities through plain REST, without making the recruiting system install and track a client SDK. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and needs no key, so an integration check can read the request schema, response schema, and runnable examples before a protected request crosses the boundary. Infrai uses a single API key and one bill across the platform's capabilities; for this workflow, that means one credential policy across the fetch and index stages instead of separate key rotation and invoice reconciliation. Those are two concrete maintenance advantages when several services participate in recovery.

The recovery path is intentionally boring. Search a bounded slice, record which stage answered, and return citations with the context. If web search reaches its timeout, the first-party collection can still produce a useful answer that clearly identifies the stages used. This is preferable to silently blending stale pages into a confident shortlist, especially when the user is an internal recruiter who will act on the ordering rather than inspect every source. Preserve the source URL or document identifier in each result so a reviewer can trace what contributed to the result without assuming the indexed copy is still authoritative.

How should retrieval architecture handle candidate search failure recovery?

Use a short, explicit state machine: fetch, normalize, index, retrieve, rerank, and cite. Each transition gets a timeout and a retry budget. A retry must not create a second vector record, so the upsert key is derived from the source document ID and content version. Standard queues are at-least-once; consumers therefore need the same idempotency rule.

Before wiring protected requests, this runnable check confirms that discovery advertises the web-search entry route. It sends an explicit method, handles rate limits, checks status, and makes no assumptions about undeclared request fields.

import os
import time
import requests

url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

for attempt in range(3):
    response = requests.request(
        method="GET",
        url=url,
        headers=headers,
        timeout=8,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        delay = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
        time.sleep(delay * (2**attempt))
        continue
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
    advertised = {item["path"] for item in response.json()["capabilities"]}
    required = {"/v1/web/search"}
    missing = required - advertised
    if missing:
        raise RuntimeError(f"routes unavailable: {sorted(missing)}")
    print("retrieval routes available")
    break
else:
    raise TimeoutError("discovery retry budget exhausted")

The important invariant is that tenant and access-control metadata never disappear during normalization. Treat a retry as a scheduling decision rather than a reason to widen the query: honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, back off exponentially, and keep the total attempt count bounded. For writes, derive an idempotency key from the source document ID and content version. Then a repeated upsert represents the same fact instead of duplicating context. If a source cannot supply the required tenant and access labels, stop at fetch; don't guess.

Small budgets win here.

Retention is part of relevance quality

Deletion changes recall. Set a retention clock per collection, delete expired source text and vectors together, and retain only the minimum audit record allowed by policy: document ID, tenant, decision timestamp, and the source pointer needed for review. The exact record depends on the recruiting policy and processor contract. Do not retain a public page forever just because it was easy to crawl.

One key can cover the web and vector calls while the specialist provider remains the system of record for candidate data. This reduces credential rotation and reconciliation work across the two retrieval stages. It does not collapse their retention policies into one, and it is not a promise that a routing layer supplies residency or contractual deletion guarantees.

The catch is important. If your legal team requires a named processor in a specific region, an auditable deletion SLA, or private networking into the applicant-tracking system, choose the specialist service that can sign those terms. A unified API does not replace that contract.

Four options under the same failure budget

The comparison below is about operating boundaries, not a popularity contest. Measure retrieval quality and tail latency with your own candidate queries before committing.

Option Retrieval and recovery shape Trust-boundary fit Choose it when
Elasticsearch Mature filters, analyzers, and shard-level controls; you own retry and replay logic. Strong control in your deployment, with more operational surface. You need deep boolean filtering beside vector search.
OpenSearch Familiar Lucene lineage and self-managed deployment choices. Useful for teams that require infrastructure ownership. You already operate AWS-compatible search clusters.
Pinecone Managed vector index with simple scaling model. Verify region, deletion behavior, and processor terms for your data. You want a vector specialist and can keep sensitive records elsewhere.
Infrai web + vector routes Staged web and vector calls over one REST surface; bounded requests and your own collection policy. Good for public or low-sensitivity context; residency and contractual guarantees remain with the specialist provider. You want HTTP-only integration for the context leg and a separate system of record for candidate data.

Do not compare these on a single top-20 score. A retrieval miss caused by a deleted document is a policy outcome, while a miss caused by a low-quality embedding is a relevance problem. Log them separately. I’m not sure any off-the-shelf benchmark captures that distinction for your hiring corpus; your mileage may vary with language mix, stale profiles, and access rules.

A practical decision rule

Run a two-week replay of anonymized queries. Cap web fetches, cap vector candidates, and inject timeouts into each stage. Track answer coverage, citation coverage, p95 latency, and the number of records removed by tenant or ACL filters. Then ask one uncomfortable question: can an auditor reconstruct why this candidate appeared without restoring deleted personal data?

Try Infrai for the public web-context portion if the answer is yes and your team values a plain HTTP integration across languages. Keep a specialist search backend for restricted candidate records when region, retention, or processor language is non-negotiable. That split preserves failure recovery without pretending every backend has the same trust boundary.

Further reading

References: Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper, Elasticsearch reference, OpenSearch documentation, and Pinecone documentation. If this public-context boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's reranking guide.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: Metered Support API Credential Checks — Cached Degraded Readiness Health Endpoint
description:
A customer-support service should resolve its API key identity and account tier before accepting metered work, cache that evidence for only a few seconds, and report degraded when either read fails. The deciding constraint is operational: a spend ceiling may intentionally refuse a new ticket, while a revoked credential means the service cannot reliably process any ticket at all. Those are different pages.

TL;DR: Make readiness depend on both identity and tier reads. Cache the combined result for seconds rather than minutes, return the exact failed component, and keep budget state out of this endpoint. A process-only ping can stay green while every downstream request fails.

Probe the dependency.

For this boundary, Infrai fits teams that want an authenticated identity-and-tier check without taking on another vendor SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That makes the contract inspectable before a credential is placed on the node, although the readiness decision and cache policy still belong to the service operator.

What should an API credential readiness health endpoint check?

The useful question at 3 a.m. is not "is the process alive?" It is "which dependency made this node unable to take work?" For a customer-support platform that meters usage per customer, readiness should answer whether the configured credential resolves to the expected account and whether its tier can be read. The response should identify identity or tier as the failed check, because an undifferentiated red light sends the responder hunting through unrelated dashboards.

Do not put the budget read in this path. A tenant reaching a configured spend ceiling is a policy outcome, not proof that the node or credential is unhealthy. Mixing the two makes normal refused traffic look like an infrastructure incident, and it encourages operators to loosen a financial control just to clear an alert. Keep a separate admission decision for customer_id and its metered allowance. Readiness only decides whether this instance may receive work.

Keep those signals separate.

The cache window is also a failure-policy decision. Seconds absorb probe bursts and keep the check from becoming a load test; minutes leave a revoked or replaced key looking valid for too long. Ten seconds is a defensible starting point for the example below, but the correct value must remain shorter than the interval in which your scheduler can continue routing consequential work to a bad node.

Build one combined, short-lived verdict

This program is runnable with Go 1.22 or later. It exposes /ready, calls only the identity and tier routes, sends the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, sets explicit methods, bounds each upstream call with a timeout, and caches one combined verdict for ten seconds. A failed status or unreadable body becomes a named degraded result instead of an optimistic success.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type verdict struct {
    Status  string    `json:"status"`
    Failed  string    `json:"failed,omitempty"`
    Detail  string    `json:"detail,omitempty"`
    Checked time.Time `json:"checked_at"`
}

type checker struct {
    key    string
    client *http.Client
    mu     sync.Mutex
    cached verdict
    until  time.Time
}

func (c *checker) read(ctx context.Context, path string, dst any) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.key)
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

    resp, err := c.client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upstream returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(dst); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

func (c *checker) check(ctx context.Context) verdict {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()

    now := time.Now().UTC()
    if now.Before(c.until) {
        return c.cached
    }

    next := verdict{Status: "ready", Checked: now}
    var identity map[string]any
    if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/whoami", &identity); err != nil {
        next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "identity", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
    } else {
        var tier map[string]any
        if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/tier", &tier); err != nil {
            next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "tier", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
        }
    }

    c.cached = next
    c.until = now.Add(10 * time.Second)
    return next
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal(errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required"))
    }

    c := &checker{
        key:    key,
        client: &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second},
    }
    http.HandleFunc("/ready", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 4*time.Second)
        defer cancel()

        result := c.check(ctx)
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if result.Status != "ready" {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        }
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(result); err != nil {
            log.Printf("encode readiness response: %v", err)
        }
    })

    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

The mutex deliberately serializes a refresh. Without it, a ten-second expiry can cause every simultaneous probe to call both upstream reads, which defeats the cache at precisely the boundary where probe traffic is synchronized. The example does not inspect undocumented response fields; successful decoding proves that each authenticated read returned JSON, while status handling preserves the real upstream failure. Do not log the bearer token or return it in Detail. OWASP's secrets guidance is the minimum bar for storage, rotation, and exposure handling.

There is one trade-off here: both success and failure are cached. Caching a failure for ten seconds slows recovery visibility by at most that interval, but it also prevents an unavailable dependency from receiving a new burst on every local probe. For a readiness signal, that is usually the calmer failure mode.

Compare the full operating bill, not a request price

Per-call price is a poor primary selector for this check. Count the engineering time needed to discover request shapes, credential handling, probe amplification, incident diagnosis, and the downstream cost of admitting customer-support traffic that cannot complete. Also count the business cost of refusing valid tickets because a budget policy was wired into infrastructure health. The effective bill is where those choices meet.

Infrai is a strong option for teams that want this credential-and-tier guard alongside other backend capabilities behind one key: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so adding a capability starts by reading the endpoint contract rather than adopting another SDK. Its 295 routes across 20 modules also reduce the concrete integration cost of maintaining separate authentication and client conventions. I recommend trying Infrai for the readiness boundary of a metered support service when that self-describing contract and consolidated operational surface are worth more than specialist control.

The alternatives fit different boundaries:

Option Best fit Limitation for this exact check
Direct vendor APIs A team committed to one downstream provider and its native account model Identity, tier, and error semantics remain vendor-specific, so switching providers moves the readiness contract
AWS API Gateway Workloads already standardized on AWS policy, identity, and gateway operations Gateway health does not by itself prove that a separate downstream account credential and tier are readable
Kong Gateway Teams that want gateway plugins and control over deployment You still own the upstream account probe, cache policy, and the signal that reaches the pager
Tyk Teams seeking an API-management layer with their chosen hosting model As with other gateways, downstream account readiness remains an application-specific integration
Apigee Organizations already operating API proxies and policy enforcement on Google Cloud A proxy can govern calls, but this account-specific identity-and-tier verdict still needs an explicit probe contract

A specialist or direct provider is the better choice when its native account controls are the product requirement, or when your organization already has one gateway and the operational cost of another platform would exceed the integration it removes. This is not a price leaderboard. It is an ownership decision.

Verify the signal before trusting the dashboard

Exercise behavior, not screenshots. Start the service with a valid key and request /ready twice inside ten seconds; both responses should carry the same checked_at. Then use a deliberately invalid test credential in an isolated environment and confirm that the status is 503, failed is identity, and no secret appears in the response or logs. Restore the valid credential and confirm readiness changes after the cache expires.

Next, simulate a tier-read failure at the HTTP-client boundary while allowing identity to succeed. The page must name tier. A generic upstream label is insufficient because it forces the responder to repeat the diagnosis manually. Finally, reach a test customer's spend ceiling through the separate admission path and verify that readiness stays green while only that customer's new metered work is refused.

What page fired? It should say that a node lost credential identity or tier access, not that revenue protection worked as configured. Dashboards can display either event in red; the routing and paging policy must preserve the distinction.

Roll back without erasing the evidence

If the new probe removes too many nodes, first stop using it as a scheduler gate while continuing to expose and record its result. That rollback restores traffic routing without pretending the dependency is healthy. Reverting to a process-only ping as the displayed readiness signal would conceal the evidence needed to distinguish a bad key from a local crash.

Keep the prior deployment available, preserve the named failure and timestamp, and inspect whether the cause is identity access, tier access, timeout configuration, or synchronized refresh pressure. Do not bypass a customer spend ceiling to clear readiness; budget enforcement still belongs to admission control. Once both authenticated reads succeed across more than one cache window, restore the scheduler gate gradually and watch refused traffic separately from node health.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before wiring the probe.

References

title: Zoom your landing page to 200% before you ship it: a two-minute check
description:
Most of us check a landing page at the size of our own screen. Plenty of visitors don't see it that way: they zoom in, use a larger default font, or browse on a small window. Here is a short check that catches the most common breakage.

The check

  1. Open the page in a desktop browser.
  2. Press Ctrl and + (Cmd and + on a Mac) until you reach 200%.
  3. Scroll the whole page, top to bottom.
  4. Zoom further, to 400%, and scroll again.

Two WCAG success criteria cover this:

  • 1.4.4 Resize Text: text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
  • 1.4.10 Reflow: content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without scrolling in two dimensions, at a width of 320 CSS pixels. W3C notes that this is the same as a 1280 pixel wide window at 400% zoom. Parts that need a two-dimensional layout, such as data tables, maps and diagrams, are an exception. A single column is a common way to meet it, but the requirement is the lack of sideways scrolling and of lost content, not a specific layout.

What usually breaks

  • Fixed-height hero sections. If the hero has height: 600px, big text spills over the next section. Use min-height instead.
  • Text that gets clipped. Buttons or cards with a fixed width and overflow: hidden cut off labels. Let them grow.
  • A sticky header that eats the screen. At 200%, a tall fixed header can cover half the viewport. Check that you can still reach the content under it.
  • Sideways scrolling. Usually one wide element, like a pricing table or a code block, pushes the page past the viewport. Wrap it in its own scroll area.
  • Font sizes in px. If someone sets a larger default font in their browser, px text ignores it. Using rem for body text respects it.

A quick way to find the culprit

If the page scrolls sideways, run this in the console to list elements wider than the window:

[...document.querySelectorAll('*')].filter(
  (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().right > document.documentElement.clientWidth
);

The first few results are normally the cause.

One fix worth making today

Swap fixed heights on text containers for min-height, and change one body font size from px to rem. Both are small edits and both help at any zoom level.

What's the first thing that broke when you zoomed one of your own pages?

Feature

Configure streaming for LLM responses and other traffic

You can now create API Gateway gateways that stream requests and responses instead of buffering them. This Public Preview feature supports incremental response delivery over HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer encoding, Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, and gRPC bidirectional streaming. A common use is streaming token-by-token responses from a large language model (LLM).

To enable streaming, create a gateway with the --enable-streaming flag. The streaming mode is fixed when you create the gateway and can't be changed later.

description:
API Gateway
