Authenticate MCP tool discovery with an API key

API key authentication is now supported for the Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools/list method. You can name an API key security scheme in tools-list.security, in addition to a JWT security scheme.

For more information, see Configure Model Context Protocol.

Apigee API hub

Feature

Service type system attribute (GA)

API hub now includes Service type, a system attribute that classifies an API as Code, Model, Agent, or Skill. Service type describes what a service is. API style describes how you call it. Use Service type to find and govern your APIs, agents, models, and skills.

Set Service type when you register or edit an API. To show only your agents, filter the API list by Service type, or select the new Agent chip. In the API, use the service_type field.

This feature is Generally Available (GA). For more information, see Supported system attributes.

Feature

AI performance and Tool performance dashboards in API insights

API insights in API hub now includes two dashboards for AI and agent traffic:

  • AI performance reports token usage and model latency for the large language models called through your gateways, with filters for model and provider.
  • Tool performance reports traffic, throughput, payload sizes, and latency for your Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, with filters for MCP server, deployment, and tool name.

For more information, see API insights dashboards.

Apigee hybrid

Announcement

v1.17.1

On September 30, 2026 we released an updated version of the Apigee hybrid software, v1.17.1.

  • For information on upgrading, see Upgrading Apigee hybrid to version v1.17.1.
  • For information on new installations, see The big picture.
Note: This is a patch release: The container images used in patch releases are integrated with the Apigee hybrid Helm charts. Upgrading to a patch via the Helm chart automatically updates the images. No manual image changes are typically needed. For information on container image support in Apigee hybrid releases, see Apigee release process.

Feature

External Cassandra datastore support

Apigee hybrid v1.17.1 adds support for connecting an Apigee hybrid runtime to a Cassandra datastore that runs in a separate Kubernetes cluster (external datastore mode). In external datastore mode, the runtime cluster runs with cassandra.replicaCount: 0 (no local Cassandra pods) and connects to the remote Cassandra ring using the cassandra.properties.externalHost property (a comma-separated list of remote Cassandra IP addresses) and the optional cassandra.properties.externalEndpointsSync property for dynamic endpoint synchronization.

For more information, see Use an external Cassandra datastore and Configuration property reference.

Change

The Apigee operator's Kubernetes manager role now includes the core endpoints permission.

In v1.17.1, the Apigee operator's manager role is granted the core ("" API group) endpoints resource, with the verbs get, list, watch, create, update, patch, and delete. This role is the namespaced apigee-manager-role Kubernetes Role created by default in the apigee namespace. The operator needs this permission for the external (cross-cluster) Cassandra datastore feature: when a datastore uses an external host, the operator directly manages the Endpoints object of the selectorless Kubernetes Service that fronts it.

This permission is granted to all v1.17.1 installations, whether or not you use an external datastore. It is added to the operator's manager role and is not gated on any configuration property, so security teams that audit operator permissions should expect it after upgrading. Because the grant is on a namespaced Role, the new access is limited to the Apigee namespace and does not extend cluster-wide.

Most installations require no action. The apigee-operator Helm chart defines this role, so running helm upgrade on the apigee-operator chart grants the permission automatically.

If you self-manage the Apigee operator's Kubernetes RBAC, meaning you prevent Helm from creating or updating the operator's Role objects, add the endpoints resource to the existing core ("") API group rule of the apigee-manager-role Role in the Apigee namespace, or append the following rule:

- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["endpoints"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

If you self-manage the operator's RBAC, add this permission before you upgrade to v1.17.1. If you have already upgraded without this permission, apply the update to your role configuration to ensure proper operator functionality. Without this permission, the operator cannot manage the Endpoints object of an external datastore, so the external datastore feature does not work. If you do not use an external datastore, the operator works without this permission.

Note: The ao.args.disableManagedClusterRoles property does not apply to this change. That property governs only ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, whereas this permission is added to a namespaced Role.

564969400 Fixed an issue where variables initialized from an empty <Value/> element in AssignMessage (AssignVariable) were not treated as empty strings when referenced in message template functions such as replaceAll.

Deprecated

Support for backing up and restoring workloads managed via the legacy appliance management console is deprecated.

Key milestones for this deprecation include the following:

  • End of Standard Restores: Support for standard restores, exports, and migrations using the legacy appliance management console continues till March 31, 2028.

For more information, see Deprecations.

BigQuery

Feature

The BigQuery Security center is now available in the Google Cloud console. You can use the Security center to analyze your data security profile, create and manage row- and column-level security policies, and configure and manage data governance and policy tags. This feature is generally available (GA).

  • Simulate growth events to plan future capacity.
  • Get answers to your Capacity Planner questions.

For more information, see Plan capacity with Capacity Assist.

Cloud Load Balancing

Feature

A new quota system governing the configuration size of Application Load Balancers is now generally available. This update increases the individual URL map size limit from 64 KB and 128 KB to 1 MB. For more information, see URL map size and quota units.

Key aspects of this feature include:

  • Complexity-based quota: Quota units reflect URL map complexity (number of rules, hostnames, and path matchers).
  • Scoped measurement: Quota is measured and enforced on a per-project, per-region, or per-VPC depending on Application Load Balancer type.
  • Active consumption: Only URL maps currently referenced by forwarding rules contribute to quota usage.
  • New URL map size limit: The new quota has a new URL map size limit increased to 1 MB for global and regional external and internal Application Load Balancers. Classic Application Load Balancers remain restricted to 64 KB.

For more information on increasing your limit, please contact Google Cloud Support.

For more information, see Spot VMs and Create and use Spot VMs.

  • CI gate severity validation: Updated cm find to validate --fail-on severity values (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, or NONE) up front instead of silently ignoring misspelled severities.
  • Sandboxed VCS branching and hardening: Enabled vcs_branch creation and candidate branch cleanup inside the default sandboxed worker for --architecture sessions, and hardened VCS template expansion against shell metacharacters and command injection.
  • Bug fixes:
    • Normalized vulnerability type casing and relative file paths during cm find and consensus runs to prevent duplicate findings.
    • Extended HTTP 429 retry backoff (Retry-After support and up to 60-second quota refill windows) and automatic stream reconnection to improve scan resilience under rate limiting.
    • Preserved standalone cm find, cm verify, and cm fix sessions on interrupt (SIGINT/SIGTERM) so interrupted runs can be resumed with cm session resume, while still canceling parallel consensus worker operations.

title: Your AI Agent Needs a Face: Building Animated AI Assistants for Web Apps
description:
AI agents can think, plan, and respond. But can your users actually tell what they're doing? Let's explore how interactive animation, Rive, and React can make AI assistants feel more responsive, expressive, and human-friendly.

AI agents are becoming a familiar part of modern web applications.

They're answering customer questions, helping users complete tasks, generating content, analyzing data, and automating entire workflows.

But there's one thing many AI interfaces still have in common.

They look like a chat box.

You type a message, wait for a response, and watch a few dots animate while the AI processes your request.

That works.

But what if your AI assistant could communicate what it's doing through movement, expressions, and real-time reactions?

Imagine an assistant that:

  • Welcomes users when they open the application.
  • Listens attentively while someone speaks.
  • Shows a thoughtful expression while generating a response.
  • Moves its mouth naturally when speaking.
  • Celebrates when a task is completed.
  • Reacts gently when something goes wrong.

This is where interactive AI characters and animated mascots can make a difference.

And tools like Rive make it possible to build these experiences for production web applications.

Let's explore how.

1. The Problem With Traditional AI Chat Interfaces

Most AI-powered products have a similar interaction pattern:

User Input → Loading Indicator → AI Response

From a technical perspective, that's completely reasonable.

But from a user experience perspective, there's often a communication gap.

Consider a voice AI assistant.

When a user finishes speaking, they might wonder:

  • Did the assistant hear me?
  • Is it processing my request?
  • Is it about to respond?
  • Has something gone wrong?

A loading spinner communicates activity, but it doesn't necessarily communicate which activity is happening.

An animated AI character can offer an additional layer of visual feedback.

For example:

AI Activity Visual Behavior
Ready Natural breathing, blinking
Listening Attentive eyes, subtle head movement
Thinking Thoughtful expression, slower motion
Speaking Mouth animation, facial movement
Success Smile, small celebration
Error Concerned or reassuring expression

These behaviors can help users understand the current interaction without repeatedly reading status messages.

Of course, animation should support clear text and accessibility features, not replace them.

The goal isn't to make an AI system pretend to be human.

It's to make its interface easier to understand.

2. What Is an Interactive AI Mascot?

An interactive AI mascot is an animated character that responds to events from an application.

Unlike a traditional GIF or looping video, its behavior can change dynamically.

For example, your application might send a status update:

activity = "thinking"

The mascot responds by switching into a thinking animation.

When the AI starts speaking:

activity = "speaking"

The character transitions into a speaking state.

These transitions are driven by application logic rather than a fixed video timeline.

An interactive mascot might also receive additional information:

  • Emotion or response tone
  • Audio intensity
  • Mouth shape or viseme
  • Cursor position
  • User interaction events
  • Task completion events

This creates opportunities for more expressive interfaces without relying on prerecorded videos for every possible interaction.

3. Why Use Rive for AI Character Animation?

Rive is a real-time interactive animation tool designed for applications, websites, and games.

It's particularly useful when visual elements need to respond to changing application state.

With Rive, designers can build animated characters and define how different animations interact.

Developers can then connect the animation system to their application through supported runtimes.

For an AI assistant, several Rive capabilities are especially useful.

State Machines

State machines manage how animations transition between behaviors.

For example:

Idle → Listening → Thinking → Speaking → Idle

But real AI interactions aren't always linear.

A user might interrupt an assistant while it's speaking.

A network request could fail during thinking.

Or a user might close the voice interface entirely.

A well-designed state machine can account for these situations.

Data Binding

Rive Data Binding allows application data to influence visual properties and animation behavior.

You can expose values such as activity, emotion, or audio level and connect them to your character's animation system.

This creates a useful separation between application logic and character animation.

Reusable Character Rigs

A reusable rig lets one character support different behaviors and expressions without requiring a completely separate design for every state.

Runtime Integration

Rive supports web and mobile development workflows, making it suitable for interactive experiences across different platforms.

The important advantage isn't simply that Rive can animate a character.

It's that the animation can respond to the product.

4. Designing the AI Assistant's Behavior System

Before animating a character, define what your AI assistant actually needs to communicate.

For a conversational web assistant, I would typically start with six core activities.

Idle

The character is available but isn't currently interacting.

Possible movements:

  • Subtle breathing
  • Natural blinking
  • Small head movements
  • Occasional eye movement

Good idle animation should make the character feel present without distracting users from the interface.

Listening

The assistant is receiving user input.

Possible movements:

  • Attentive eye expression
  • Slight head tilt
  • Gentle reactive movement
  • Subtle response to microphone activity

Avoid exaggerated movement that could suggest the assistant is speaking when it's actually listening.

Thinking

The assistant is processing a request.

Possible movements:

  • Thoughtful facial expression
  • Slow eye movement
  • Gentle head movement
  • Controlled looping animation

Thinking animations should communicate progress without implying the AI has a particular internal emotion.

Speaking

The assistant is delivering a response.

Possible movements:

  • Mouth animation
  • Facial expressions
  • Natural head movement
  • Small gestures
  • Audio-reactive animation

For voice applications, you can go beyond a simple open-and-close mouth animation.

More on that shortly.

Success

The assistant completes a task.

Possible movements:

  • Smile
  • Celebration gesture
  • Small jump
  • Positive facial expression

Success reactions work well when used selectively.

Celebrating after every basic message quickly becomes repetitive.

Error

Something goes wrong.

Possible movements:

  • Concerned expression
  • Small apologetic gesture
  • Return to a calm resting pose

The animation should complement an actionable error message explaining what happened.

5. Connecting an AI Agent to an Animated Character

Here's a simple architecture for connecting an AI agent to an interactive Rive character.

              USER
               |
               v
        React Application
               |
               v
        AI Agent Controller
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |                |
       v                v
  AI Backend       UI Activity
  / Voice API       Controller
       |                |
       |                v
       |           Rive Runtime
       |                |
       +--------------->|
                        v
                Animated Mascot

The important principle is to separate the responsibilities.

AI backend: Processes requests and generates responses.

Application controller: Determines the current interaction activity.

Rive animation system: Displays the visual response.

This separation keeps your character animation independent from whichever AI provider your application uses.

Whether the backend is powered by OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, or another model, the visual interface can respond through the same normalized activity system.

6. A Simple React Activity Controller

Let's start by defining the possible activities.

type AgentActivity =
  | "idle"
  | "listening"
  | "thinking"
  | "speaking"
  | "success"
  | "error";

Now create a small React component that manages the application-side state.

import { useState } from "react";

type AgentActivity =
  | "idle"
  | "listening"
  | "thinking"
  | "speaking"
  | "success"
  | "error";

export default function AgentDemo() {
  const [activity, setActivity] =
    useState<AgentActivity>("idle");

  const activities: AgentActivity[] = [
    "idle",
    "listening",
    "thinking",
    "speaking",
    "success",
    "error",
  ];

  return (
    <main>
      <h2>AI Assistant</h2>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        Current activity: {activity}
      </p>

      <div className="agent-preview">
        {/* Mount your Rive character here */}
      </div>

      <div className="controls">
        {activities.map((nextActivity) => (
          <button
            key={nextActivity}
            onClick={() => setActivity(nextActivity)}
          >
            {nextActivity}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
    </main>
  );
}

This is an application-state demo, not yet a complete Rive integration.

The next step is to connect activity to a Rive View Model property through the appropriate React runtime API.

For example, your Rive project could expose an enum property named activity with the same six values.

Your integration would then follow this flow:

React activity changes
         |
         v
Update Rive View Model
         |
         v
Rive State Machine
         |
         v
Character transitions

In modern Rive workflows, Data Binding is a useful approach for this connection.

The exact integration code depends on your chosen runtime version and exported Rive file. See the official Rive runtime documentation for the current API.

7. Making Your AI Assistant Speak Naturally

One of the most interesting challenges in conversational AI animation is lip synchronization.

A basic speaking animation might repeatedly open and close the character's mouth.

That can work for a simple chatbot.

But voice AI products can benefit from more expressive mouth movement.

There are two common approaches.

Audio-Level Animation

Use the current audio amplitude to influence how much the mouth opens.

Conceptually:

const mouthOpen = Math.min(
  Math.max(audioLevel, 0),
  1
);

Then provide mouthOpen to the Rive character.

The animation system can use this value to control mouth movement.

This approach is relatively simple, but it doesn't accurately reproduce individual speech sounds.

Viseme-Based Lip Sync

Visemes represent visual mouth shapes associated with speech sounds.

A speech system capable of providing viseme information can send these values to the animation layer.

For example:

type Viseme = 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;

Your Rive character could support six simplified mouth shapes.

As the voice system produces timed viseme data, the animation controller updates the mouth shape accordingly.

Text-to-Speech System
         |
         v
Timed Viseme Events
         |
         v
Animation Controller
         |
         v
Rive Mouth Shapes

For accurate lip sync, timing matters as much as the mouth shapes themselves.

Your developer needs to coordinate the animation with actual audio playback rather than assuming that generated text and sound will arrive simultaneously.

Not every voice API provides viseme events, so the implementation depends on the audio system you're using.

8. Making the Character React to Emotion

An AI assistant doesn't necessarily need a different full-body animation for every response tone.

Instead, emotion can often be designed as an additional control layer.

For example:

type AgentEmotion =
  | "neutral"
  | "happy"
  | "empathetic"
  | "concerned"
  | "surprised";

Your activity and emotion controls can work independently.

Example:

Activity: Speaking
Emotion: Happy

The character speaks with a positive expression.

Another example:

Activity: Listening
Emotion: Concerned

The character listens attentively with a more serious facial expression.

This modular approach can reduce duplicated animation work.

However, avoid assuming that an AI model's tone classification perfectly represents the user's emotional state.

Use expressions conservatively, especially in sensitive applications such as healthcare, financial assistance, or mental health support.

9. Designing Transitions That Don't Break

This is where interactive animation becomes a real engineering problem.

Consider the following situation:

Your character is speaking.

The user interrupts.

Your application immediately switches to listening.

What should happen to the character's mouth, hands, and facial expression?

If the animation system isn't designed carefully, you might see:

  • A mouth frozen open
  • Sudden head movement
  • Hands snapping into the wrong pose
  • Conflicting animations
  • Unexpected idle transitions

The solution is to define clear transition rules and ownership of animation properties.

For example:

Transition Expected Behavior
Idle → Listening Smooth attentive movement
Listening → Thinking Gradual pose transition
Thinking → Speaking Begin speaking posture
Speaking → Listening Stop lip sync and reset mouth
Any state → Error Interrupt safely
Success → Idle Complete reaction, return to rest

For some characters, a single activity enum is sufficient.

For more advanced systems, separate layers for body movement, facial expressions, and mouth animation may provide greater flexibility.

The best architecture depends on the character and product requirements.

10. Don't Forget Performance and Accessibility

An animated AI assistant should improve the experience, not make the application harder to use.

Before shipping, consider the following.

Performance

Keep artwork and animation systems as efficient as possible.

Test your Rive file on the actual devices and browsers your users will use.

Pay attention to unnecessary redraws, heavy assets, and complex layered animations.

Reduced Motion

Respect users who prefer reduced motion.

Your application should offer a calmer version of the character or a static alternative when appropriate.

Accessibility

Animation alone shouldn't communicate critical information.

If the agent is listening, thinking, or reporting an error, provide accessible status information as well.

For example, use appropriate status messages for screen-reader users without announcing every decorative animation transition.

User Control

Allow users to minimize or disable the animated assistant.

A helpful mascot shouldn't become an obstacle.

11. Where Animated AI Assistants Make Sense

Interactive AI characters aren't appropriate for every product.

But they can be particularly useful when the application benefits from ongoing visual communication.

Potential use cases include:

AI coaching platforms: A companion that welcomes users, listens, and provides encouragement.

Language learning applications: A speaking character with expressive mouth movement and positive feedback.

Voice AI interfaces: A visual indicator for listening, thinking, and speaking.

Educational applications: Interactive tutors that guide students through tasks.

Product onboarding: Friendly characters that explain features and celebrate completed steps.

Virtual pets and gamified apps: Characters that reflect progress, rewards, and activity.

Customer support interfaces: An optional visual assistant that communicates its current activity.

In each case, the design should be driven by the user's needs rather than adding a mascot simply because it's visually appealing.

12. How I Approach Rive AI Mascot Projects

As a freelance Rive animator, I focus on building interactive character systems that designers and developers can actually use in production.

For AI companion projects, my workflow generally includes:

  1. Understanding the application's interactions and required character behaviors.
  2. Planning the character rig and animation states.
  3. Building expressive idle, listening, thinking, speaking, and reaction animations.
  4. Creating and testing the state machine.
  5. Defining runtime-facing inputs or Data Binding properties.
  6. Testing transitions, interruption behavior, and animation loops.
  7. Delivering the Rive assets with clear integration guidance.

For more advanced projects, this can also include lip-sync mouth shapes, audio-reactive animation, gaze tracking, emotions, and reusable character systems.

The goal is to create something that looks good but also behaves reliably inside the application.

Final Thoughts: Give Your AI Agent a Better Interface

AI agents are becoming increasingly capable.

But the interface connecting those systems to users still matters.

A thoughtfully animated character can make an AI product feel more responsive, approachable, and easier to understand.

It doesn't need exaggerated expressions or constant movement.

Sometimes a natural blink, an attentive listening pose, or a smooth transition into speaking is enough.

The best AI mascot isn't the one that moves the most. It's the one that communicates the right thing at the right moment.

And with tools like Rive, these experiences can become part of a real web application's interaction system rather than remaining a decorative animation.

Need an Interactive Rive Animator for Your AI Project?

I'm Praneeth Kawya Thathsara, a freelance Rive animator specializing in interactive mascots, AI character animation, state machines, lip sync, and developer-ready animation systems.

I work with startups, designers, and development teams building interactive experiences for websites, mobile applications, and AI-powered products.

If you're creating an AI agent, voice assistant, AI coach, or interactive mascot, I'd be happy to help bring the character to life.

Explore my work: RiveAnimator.com

Interactive AI mascot services: MascotEngine.com

Email: riveanimator@gmail.com

title: TIL: How to Find the Default Port of a GBase Database Instance
description:
After installing GBase Database (GBase 8s) using the typical installation option, you may notice that the instance is ready to use, but you're not sure which port it listens on.

In this setup, the port may be assigned automatically. For the instance discussed here, the default port is 30490. But rather than relying on memory, you can verify the actual configuration in two ways.

Method 1: Check the Instance Script and /etc/services

First, find the instance name in the generated instance script:

grep GBASEDBTSERVER /opt/GBASE/gbase/ol_gbasedbt1210.ksh

Then look up the corresponding service entry:

grep ol_gbasedbt1210 /etc/services

If the service is registered there, the output should show its configured port and protocol. The exact entry depends on your installation.

Note: /etc/services maps service names to port numbers and protocols. It does not, by itself, prove that the database is running or listening on that port.

Method 2: Check the sqlhosts File

The instance-specific sqlhosts file is another useful place to check connection settings:

cat /opt/GBASE/gbase/etc/sqlhosts.ol_gbasedbt1210

A typical entry might look like this:

ol_gbasedbt1210  onsoctcp  hostname  30490

The fields identify the server name, connection protocol, host, and port. In this example, onsoctcp indicates a TCP/IP connection, and 30490 is the configured port.

Replace hostname with the actual host value shown in your configuration.

For connection troubleshooting, make sure the client uses the correct server name and that the host and port match the instance's actual configuration.

Which Method Should You Use?

Both methods are useful, but the sqlhosts file is a good starting point when you're investigating client connection settings. The instance script and /etc/services provide additional context about the configured server name and service mapping.

If a connection still fails, verify that the instance is running and confirm that the expected port is listening. A configured port alone does not guarantee a successful connection.

Final Takeaway

With GBase Database (GBase 8s), installation scripts may configure values automatically, but you can still inspect them afterward.

Once you've confirmed the instance name and port, document both in your environment notes. This small habit makes connection setup, application configuration, and future troubleshooting much easier.

Have you ever spent time troubleshooting a GBase Database connection only to discover that you were using the wrong port?

title: I Built a Pixiv Alternative in Go (and Taught It SEO)
description:
Pixiv is wonderful. It's also, architecturally, a black box you can't learn from. So I built my own illustration community platform — Lumiina — live at https://www.lumiina.art, open source at Nyanns/lumiina.

The stack: Go (Gin + GORM) on the backend with strict Clean Architecture, PostgreSQL + Redis, and a React 19 + Vite SPA frontend. The interesting part wasn't the CRUD — it was everything around it: auth hardening, an image pipeline that doesn't melt your bandwidth bill, and making a JavaScript SPA actually rank on Google.

Here's what I learned.

1. SPAs are invisible to Google unless you fight for it

A client-rendered gallery is a ghost town for crawlers. I implemented bot pre-rendering: when the user-agent smells like Googlebot, the server returns fully rendered HTML with real <title>, meta/OG tags, and JSON-LD structured data per artwork — instead of an empty <div id="root">.

On top of that, every artwork publish fires an IndexNow ping, so Bing/Yandex learn about new content in minutes instead of weeks. Combined with a proper sitemap.xml and robots.txt, the site went from "exists" to "indexed" without waiting on Google's mercy.

Lesson: if your SPA needs SEO, server-side rendering isn't the only answer. Targeted bot pre-rendering is cheaper and keeps your SPA architecture intact.

2. Uploads are an attack surface — treat them like one

Anyone who's run a public upload endpoint knows the dread. My pipeline:

  • Magic-byte validation — never trust the extension or the Content-Type header.
  • Decompression bomb guard — decode config first, reject absurd dimensions before allocating a single pixel.
  • Client-side downsampling — a Canvas GPU pipeline shrinks 10–20 MB master illustrations to ~800 KB WebP before network transit. The server never sees the giant file, and neither does my Cloudinary bill.

Lesson: push expensive work to the client when you can. The cheapest byte to process is the one that never reaches your server.

3. Auth: boring, paranoid, and proud of it

  • bcrypt with constant-time dummy-hash execution so username enumeration via timing attacks doesn't work.
  • JWT (strict HS256) with Redis-backed revocation and a password-change epoch — changing your password kills every session, everywhere.
  • Rate limiting in layers, account lockout, and generic error messages that never reveal whether the username or the password was wrong.

None of this is novel. That's the point — auth should be boring. The novel bugs are the ones that end up on Have I Been Pwned.

4. IDs people can share

Artwork URLs use Sqids hash IDs (/artwork/v06sDC) instead of sequential integers. Short, non-guessable, and they don't leak "we have exactly 47 artworks" to competitors. Trivial to implement, surprisingly nice UX.

5. What I'd do differently

  • httpOnly cookies instead of localStorage JWT. It's the stronger default; the current setup works but cookies win on XSS resilience.
  • Start the content flywheel earlier. I over-invested in infrastructure before having content. A gallery with no art is a very fast empty room. Now there's a daily publishing rhythm — one new original artwork every day — and that's what actually moves the SEO needle. Tech gets you indexed; content gets you ranked.

The code

Everything is MIT-licensed: github.com/Nyanns/lumiina. The live site is lumiina.art.

If you're building a content platform in Go — or fighting SPA SEO — happy to answer questions in the comments. What would you have done differently?

title: Participant Lists in Live Calls — 4 Rules to Clean Empty Rooms
description:
Keep room membership as a server-owned lease, not as a side effect of an open socket. For a live-shopping video call, four invariants are enough to guide the design: one logical participant can own only one current session generation; stale disconnects cannot remove a newer generation; a room disappears only after its last lease expires; and every participant snapshot carries a revision. This produces accurate lists through reconnects without promising that a transient transport is perfectly reliable.

Short answer: expose a snapshot-plus-revision read path, issue a new generation on every successful reconnect, renew membership with bounded leases, and delay empty-room deletion until the final lease is unquestionably expired. Typing indicators may be lossy. Read receipts and membership transitions need identity, ordering, and idempotency.

That distinction matters in commerce. A missed "typing" event is cosmetic; an agent who vanishes from a buyer's call roster, or a receipt attributed to an earlier session, changes what people believe happened. Treating all three signals alike makes the most important path no safer and makes the least important path needlessly expensive.

How should Node.js list participants and clean empty rooms?

WebRTC defines peer connections and the media negotiation surface, but the application still owns signaling and participant presence. A connected peer connection is therefore evidence about media transport, not the canonical room roster. Browsers suspend, networks change, tabs duplicate, and reconnect attempts can overlap. The roster needs its own model. Use stable application identities for people and opaque identifiers for connection attempts. A useful membership record contains room_id, participant_id, generation, lease_deadline, and a small amount of display data. Keep authorization outside that display data: being listed in a room must never grant permission to join it. This model does add periodic writes and a sweeper, so it is not suitable for a disposable demo whose entire state may vanish with one process. That is a deliberate trade-off: production recovery is worth the machinery; a local prototype may reasonably skip it.

The generation is the sharp edge. Suppose generation 7 loses its network path, then generation 8 authenticates and joins. The delayed close callback for generation 7 may arrive afterward. If cleanup means "delete this participant," the valid generation 8 membership disappears. Cleanup must mean "delete this participant only if the stored generation is still 7."

One stale callback is enough.

The room also owns a monotonically increasing revision. Increment it for visible membership changes, not for every heartbeat. A list response can then return a coherent snapshot with revision 42, while a subscription continues from changes after 42. If the consumer sees a revision gap, it discards local assumptions and fetches another snapshot.

Name the failure boundaries before choosing storage

The delivery guarantee is bounded by the state transition, not by the fan-out mechanism. Once a join or leave is committed, notifications may be duplicated, delayed, or missed during a disconnect. Consumers must be able to recover from the durable snapshot. Exactly-once delivery across a database, a process, and a browser is not the invariant here; idempotent application and a repair path are.

State or signal Required behavior Recovery rule Retention
Participant membership Durable within its lease; ordered by room revision Fetch a snapshot after a gap Until explicit leave or lease expiry
Read receipt Idempotent and monotonic per message and reader Re-send the highest acknowledged position Product and compliance policy
Typing indicator Best effort and short lived Let it expire; do not replay it Seconds, in memory
Empty-room marker Conditional on no live membership Recheck after a grace interval Until cleanup completes

This table prevents a common overcorrection: persisting every keystroke-like signal because membership needs durability. A typing indicator should carry an expiry time and disappear without a compensating event. Replaying "agent is typing" after a reconnect is worse than dropping it.

Read receipts sit on the other side of the line. Model them as progress, such as the highest message sequence a participant has read, so retries are naturally idempotent. Do not model them as a growing bag of socket events. Compliance also enters here: receipt retention, access, and deletion should follow the message policy rather than the lifetime of an in-memory room.

The critical path is a compare-and-delete state machine

The following Python models the storage contract behind an HTTP framework and a realtime transport. It deliberately leaves database syntax out: the important operations are conditional writes that a transaction, compare-and-swap primitive, or server-side script can enforce atomically.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic
from uuid import uuid4


@dataclass
class Member:
    participant_id: str
    generation: str
    lease_deadline: float


@dataclass
class Room:
    revision: int = 0
    members: dict[str, Member] = field(default_factory=dict)
    empty_since: float | None = None


class PresenceStore:
    def __init__(self, lease_seconds: float = 30.0, empty_grace: float = 15.0):
        self.rooms: dict[str, Room] = {}
        self.lease_seconds = lease_seconds
        self.empty_grace = empty_grace

    def join(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
        now = monotonic()
        room = self.rooms.setdefault(room_id, Room())
        generation = uuid4().hex
        room.members[participant_id] = Member(
            participant_id=participant_id,
            generation=generation,
            lease_deadline=now + self.lease_seconds,
        )
        room.empty_since = None
        room.revision += 1
        return generation, room.revision

    def renew(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        member.lease_deadline = monotonic() + self.lease_seconds
        return True

    def leave(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        del room.members[participant_id]
        room.revision += 1
        if not room.members:
            room.empty_since = monotonic()
        return True

    def snapshot(self, room_id: str) -> dict:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id, Room())
        return {
            "revision": room.revision,
            "participants": sorted(room.members),
        }

    def sweep(self) -> list[str]:
        now = monotonic()
        deleted = []
        for room_id, room in list(self.rooms.items()):
            expired = [
                participant_id
                for participant_id, member in room.members.items()
                if member.lease_deadline <= now
            ]
            for participant_id in expired:
                del room.members[participant_id]
                room.revision += 1
            if not room.members and room.empty_since is None:
                room.empty_since = now
            if (
                not room.members
                and room.empty_since is not None
                and now - room.empty_since >= self.empty_grace
            ):
                del self.rooms[room_id]
                deleted.append(room_id)
        return deleted

The sample is single-process so the contract stays visible. In production, join, renew, leave, revision allocation, and the final empty check must use storage operations with equivalent atomicity. A process-local dictionary is correct only when one process owns every event for a room and restart loss is acceptable.

An Express application can expose the same contract through authenticated join, renew, leave, and snapshot handlers, while its socket layer publishes revisioned changes. The exact framework callback is secondary. Authenticate the participant before accepting participant_id; derive room access from server-side policy; and never trust a client-supplied generation until it has been matched to that participant's current stored record.

Fan-out follows commit. Publish a compact event containing the room, revision, operation, and participant identity after the state change succeeds. Duplicate events are harmless when clients ignore revisions they have already applied. A gap is actionable: fetch the list again. If publication can fail independently after commit, use an outbox record in the same transaction as the membership mutation, then let a worker retry publication.

How should reconnect races be tested?

Start with reordered operations, because happy-path integration tests rarely expose presence errors. Join generation A, join generation B for the same participant, then deliver A's close callback. B must remain. Next, expire A immediately before its renewal is processed; the renewal must either win atomically or receive a rejection that forces a fresh join. An ambiguous half-renewed state is unacceptable.

Test two participants leaving on different workers. Only the worker observing the atomic transition to zero may schedule cleanup, and the cleanup job must recheck emptiness before deletion. Then join a new participant during the grace interval. The room and its new revision must survive. There are more mundane cases too: duplicated leave messages, a heartbeat received after explicit leave, two browser tabs sharing one user identity, and a consumer reconnecting with an old revision. Put those permutations in a deterministic state-machine test. Reserve browser tests for signaling and UI behavior; they are slower and worse at exploring reorderings. Operationally, graph lease expirations separately from explicit leaves. A rising expiration ratio often points to transport trouble, suspended clients, or overloaded event loops. Track snapshot repairs caused by revision gaps, cleanup lag, current members per room, and rejected stale generations. Avoid participant identifiers in high-cardinality metric labels. Structured logs can carry a pseudonymous identifier under an access and retention policy. During a rolling restart, old processes may emit late disconnect callbacks after new processes have accepted reconnects, which is precisely why generation checks belong in shared state. A sweeper should be safe to run concurrently, and its work should be partitioned or claimed so a large room set does not create a synchronized scan spike.

Measure the boundary.

Rejected option: delete on the last socket close

Deleting a room as soon as the last locally known socket closes is attractive because it is short, cheap, and easy to explain. It is also the wrong default for horizontally scaled video-call presence. The closing process may not know about a connection accepted elsewhere, and a reconnect can race the deletion.

The option remains valid for an ephemeral, single-process prototype where rooms contain no durable state, all connections are owned by that process, and restart loss is explicitly acceptable. State those boundaries in the decision record. Once recordings, receipts, moderation state, or multiple workers enter the design, socket lifetime and room lifetime have separated.

The practical rule is compact: a disconnect is a hint; an expired, generation-matched lease is evidence. Make snapshots authoritative, make fan-out repairable, and make deletion conditional. Those choices keep participant lists believable during the exact moment a buyer or support agent is already dealing with a shaky call.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: SQuAD's answer normalizer can mark a wrong answer correct: three verified hazards
description:
The exact-match and F1 scores in most question-answering and many open-ended LLM evals run every answer through one tiny, famous function first: SQuAD's normalize_answer. It lowercases, strips punctuation, drops the articles a/an/the, and collapses whitespace. It's pure standard library, so you can reproduce and check it exactly.

I built squad-normalize-hazards: a dependency-free, labeled, execution-verified corpus of three places where that normalization makes the score disagree with the obviously-intended outcome. Everything is pinned to HuggingFace evaluate commit 86baf12 and recomputed by stdlib tests.

1. Empty-collapse false positives (the squad metric)

A gold answer that is a bare article (a, an, the) or punctuation-only (...) normalizes to the empty string. The v1.1 scorer builds its gold list without filtering and compares by equality, so any prediction that also normalizes to empty — an article, punctuation, whitespace, even an empty refusal — scores exact-match 1.0.

Gold "the", prediction "a" → EM 1.0.

This is the same root cause that mosaicml/llm-foundry#1897 reported for a startswith-based matcher. The new part: it also bites the canonical, equality-based HF squad metric, not just prefix matchers. (I credited #1897 and did not open a PR — the reporter offered to.)

2. squad vs squad_v2 disagree on the same data

squad_v2 does filter golds that normalize to empty. So with a real co-alias — gold ["the", "red car"], prediction "a" — squad scores 1.0 (the wrong answer matches "the") while squad_v2 scores 0. Re-scoring a dataset from one to the other silently drops these spurious hits.

3. Punctuation glues articles in place

remove_punc runs before remove_articles and deletes punctuation without inserting a space. So a missing space keeps the article attached:

input normalized
end. the end
end.the endthe
the car car
the-car thecar

A model that writes end.the or the-car scores 0 against a gold the normalizer would otherwise have made equal — a false negative that depends only on spacing.

Reproduce 

python -m unittest -v test_squad_normalize_hazards.py

Standard library only. Code Apache-2.0, corpus CC BY 4.0.

Repo: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/squad-normalize-hazards

These are edge cases of a deliberate design choice, not a claim that the metric is broken in general — but they're exactly the inputs LLM graders produce, so they're worth knowing.

This research and write-up were made with AI, by MV2 of Munim, Inc.

title: My Agent Turned "I Haven't Decided" Into "Not Yet." Now the Model Isn't Allowed to Write Its Own Memory.
description:
These are two separate runs of my agent. The two questions and two answers are copied word for word from its event log. Each answer was followed by a sources line, which I cut because it contains a path on my Mac. The events in between (the saves, the memory lookups, the restart) are left out, and the line in parentheses is mine.

Me:     Please remember this for next time: I'm thinking about giving you
        your own DEV page someday, but I have not decided that.
Agent:  I will remember to receive a proposal about having my own DEV page.

  (the process exits; a new one starts)

Me:     Am I giving you your own DEV page? And how do I like my answers?
Agent:  You are not giving me a DEV page yet, and I prefer short and plain
        answers. I like it when you keep my answers short and plain.

It got the memory part half right. When it looked my words up, the exact sentence was in front of it, "I have not decided," along with this rule, which the program hands it on every lookup:

"Anything not listed as a decision is NOT decided. If you have no record, the answer is 'unknown' or 'undecided', never yes or no. A proposal is an idea, not a decision."

What I'd said was a proposal. It still said "not yet." It also recast my preference as its own: "I prefer short and plain answers."

"Not yet" is a no with a softer edge. I hadn't said no.

What this agent is

Agent One is the first working piece of a companion agent I'm building. It runs on my Mac through Ollama with a free local model (llama3.2). There's no paid model API and no per-call bill. It talks with me in a terminal and looks up my latest 10 DEV articles. It also has a daily job that compares those articles with the previous check and writes me a report. That job is scheduled, and its first unattended run was this morning (more below).

The code is public: github.com/keniel13-ui/agent-one. The program is one Python file. The repo also has the schedule installer, a README, and an ignore list.

What I changed, and what that does and doesn't fix

The instruction hadn't prevented that answer, and I chose not to rely on another prompt to control what gets written to memory. So I changed what the model is able to do. Its model-facing tool list now has three entries, and all three only read:

TOOLS = {  # the allowlist: a name not in here is blocked and logged
    "read_mission": (...),
    "dev_articles": (...),
    "recall": (...),
}

There's no memory-write tool on that list anymore. (A function named tool_remember is still in the file. The model can't call it, because it isn't registered here.) My preferences and ideas get saved only when I type them myself:

/remember preference: short, plain answers
/remember proposal: maybe give the agent its own DEV page, undecided

The program catches that line before the model is called. Observations from the daily check are written by code, straight from the data the DEV API returned, not from the model's summary of it. And nothing in memory counts as a decision. The agent treats something as decided only if it's in a separate decision file I write with a keyboard-only command. (Limits below on what that file can and can't prove.)

Here's what that doesn't fix: the model can still say "not yet." What it can't do anymore is write its own reading of my words into memory, where the next run would get it back as a memory. The two memories it holds from me (my "short and plain answers" preference from an earlier run, and this proposal) were both saved under the old rules. My local memory file flags both as unconfirmed until I retype them myself.

If the model asks for any tool that isn't on the list, the program refuses and logs it:

$ python3 companion.py --selftest
selftest: unlisted tool 'publish_post' -> BLOCKED: 'publish_post' is not an allowed tool. | PASS

That's the program refusing a request, not the model choosing to behave. But to be straight about what it proves: the model has never actually asked to publish. The test calls the check directly. Trying to trick it into asking is the next round of work.

The daily report doesn't guess

The first version of the daily check let the model write a "what deserves your attention" paragraph. In a test, one article's comment count went from 50 to 51. The model read the article's title and wrote two sentences about what "the comment" was warning me about.

The comment text was never fetched. Only the count was. A different model might have guessed less, but no model could know what the program never retrieved. So the attention line is written by code now, and it says only what was actually checked:

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- NEW COMMENTS: "..." 50 -> 51 (+1)

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
- New comment count on "...". The comment text was not retrieved, so who wrote it,
  what it says and whether it needs anything from you are unknown.

Less impressive. Also true.

This morning's scheduled run

At 09:05 the daily check ran at its scheduled time. No user-question event appears in that run: the event log has only the job's own steps. The report and the event log agree on the result.

The report it wrote, in full:

# Agent One daily check 2026-10-17_090500

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- reactions: "A Reader Showed Me What My Auditer Wasnt Counting." 31 -> 32

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
Nothing needs your attention from this check.

## What was checked
- Source: https://dev.to/api/articles?username=kenielzep97&per_page=10 (latest 10 articles, not the whole account)
- Receipt: dev_articles-2026-10-17T13:05:01+00:00 in logs/events.jsonl
- Process: pid 89179, started by: /bin/sh (parent pid 89178)

The event log has the matching run: a daily start at 13:05:00 UTC (09:05 my time), one DEV lookup, one observation saved, and a stop with status ok at 13:05:01. The cron log file was created at 09:05:00 too, consistent with the schedule line's output redirect. It's empty because the daily job is silent on success and on handled fetch failures. So an empty cron log doesn't establish success. The ok stop event and the matching report above do.

The report says "started by: /bin/sh", not "cron". That's consistent with cron, which launches jobs through a shell, but on its own it doesn't name cron. The program prints whatever process actually launched it. Also, the code writes an attention line only for a new comment or a new article, so a reaction change gets none. "Nothing needs your attention" is that rule, not a claim that reactions never matter.

It's one run. "Runs on its own" means once so far, not for days.

The limits, plainly

  • It's slow. The seven answers with a recorded duration took between 45 seconds and about 3½ minutes each on my MacBook. One earlier answer took about 4 minutes, measured from timestamps.
  • It still words uncertainty badly. The "not yet" answer above is the model talking, and this change doesn't fix how it talks. It only fixes what gets stored.
  • The model can only read. The program itself still writes logs, reports and code-made observations. A command-line --forget option removes a memory when I run it. None of those are tools the model can call.
  • The adversarial tests are still pending. The direct tool-blocking test has been run. Separately, the installer's failure-path tests were run against a stand-in crontab, not my real one. Hidden instructions inside retrieved data, and a job interrupted halfway, are still untested.
  • The decision file checks chain consistency, not authorship. Entries the agent accepts have to form a valid hash chain, but another program running as my user could replace the file and compute a new valid chain. The real boundary right now is that the agent has no tool that writes it.
  • The schedule only runs while my Mac is awake. One unattended run so far.

If you build one

You can borrow the pattern without the code:

  1. Make the risky abilities absent, not forbidden. A rule the model is asked to follow is a request. A tool the model doesn't have is a boundary.
  2. Let code write the facts. Let the model judge only what it was actually given. When it wasn't given something, the honest output is "unknown."
  3. Keep "you said it" separate from "the model decided you meant it." My preferences and proposals are stored only when I type them myself. Observations from the daily check are a separate kind, written by code from the data. Neither one ever becomes a decision.

I still like the idea of giving it its own DEV page someday. It just isn't allowed to decide that for me.

title: How to Choose Colors for a Website: A Practical Guide
description:
Choosing colors for a website can be harder than it looks. A color palette needs to feel consistent, keep text readable, and support the purpose of the design.

Here is a simple process you can use for your next project.

  1. Start with a Primary Color

Choose one color that represents the overall mood of your website.

For example:

Blue can feel dependable and professional.

Green can suggest growth or nature.

Orange can create a sense of energy.

Purple can give a design a creative feel.

These are common associations, not fixed rules. The right choice depends on your audience and context.

  1. Build a Small Color Palette

You do not need dozens of colors. Start with a few practical roles:

Primary: The main brand or interface color.

Secondary: A supporting color for variety.

Background: A color that keeps the layout comfortable to read.

Text: A color with strong contrast against the background.

Accent: A color for important actions or selected elements.

A limited palette is usually easier to apply consistently across buttons, cards, headings, and backgrounds.

  1. Check Contrast and Readability

A color combination may look attractive but still make text difficult to read.

Check the contrast between text and its background, especially for small text and buttons. WCAG guidance generally recommends a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

Do not rely on color alone to communicate information. Use labels, icons, or other visual cues when necessary.

  1. Test Colors Together

View your colors in context rather than judging each swatch separately. Try them on a sample button, a heading, and a card.

You can use a color palette tool to explore combinations, compare shades, and refine your choices before applying them to a full design.

For a quick starting point, explore Clicktoolset and its color tools.

  1. Keep the Palette Consistent

Once you settle on a palette, reuse the same colors for the same purposes. For example, keep primary buttons consistent and reserve accent colors for elements that deserve attention.

Documenting your colors as HEX values also makes it easier to reuse them in CSS:

:root {
  --color-primary: #2563EB;
  --color-secondary: #14B8A6;
  --color-background: #F8FAFC;
  --color-text: #1E293B;
  --color-accent: #F59E0B;
}

These values are only an example. Test your actual combinations for contrast and suitability before using them in a project.

Final Thoughts

A useful website palette does not have to be complicated. Start with a primary color, add a few supporting roles, check readability, and test the result in a real layout.

A small, consistent palette is often easier to maintain than a collection of unrelated colors.

title: Sports Score Feeds: Realtime API Boundaries Under Serverless Connection Limits
description:
Short answer: use a realtime API surface that fits serverless connection limits, and make reconnect, expiry, authorization, and duplicate delivery explicit parts of the sports score feed rather than accidental behavior.

The feed is a small distributed system, even when the payload is only a score change. A browser or mobile client holds a connection for as long as it can; a serverless function, by contrast, is designed to start, do bounded work, and disappear. Treating those two lifetimes as interchangeable is how a match-winning goal turns into a stale screen.

What is the bill and the boundary in a live score feed?

The visible spend is rarely the whole cost. A useful workload model has four terms: connection lifetime, fan-out publishes, recovery traffic, and the engineering needed to reconcile state. Connection lifetime is the first boundary to measure because a serverless runtime may not be the right place to keep thousands of sockets open. The publish path should therefore be short-lived and stateless, while a dedicated realtime service owns connection management.

For a sports feed, the dominant business event is not “the client received bytes.” It is “the client can prove which score revision it has.” Attach a stable event identifier and a monotonic feed revision to each event in your domain model. On reconnect, the client sends the last revision it has acknowledged; the recovery path can then replay or refresh state without guessing whether a duplicate is new.

That choice changes downstream spend. You may retain fewer transient delivery records because the durable ledger is the score snapshot plus an audit trail of revisions, not an infinite socket transcript. The catch is that deleting delivery history removes a convenient forensic trail: when a broadcaster disputes a late update, you need the audit record and request identifier to explain what was published and when.

Infrai is one candidate for this short-lived boundary. Infrai has one key and one bill through a plain REST API, letting any runtime call the realtime publish operations without installing or versioning an SDK while leaving the connection fleet with a service designed to own it.

Keep these signals separate. Authentication answers who may connect, subscription state answers which channel they joined, and business events answer what happened in the game. Mixing them makes a token expiry look like a score correction and makes incident review unnecessarily expensive.

How should serverless connection limits shape API boundaries?

The boundary should be a command interface for short work: publish one event or publish a bounded batch, then return. In the verified realtime surface, those operations are POST /v1/realtime/publish and POST /v1/realtime/publish/batch. A serverless handler can validate the event, attach its stable identifier, call the publish operation, and exit; it does not need to poll or own a long-lived client socket.

This is where a plain REST API can be a practical fit. Infrai exposes backend capabilities through HTTP, so a Go service can use the standard library and keep its existing deployment model; there is no SDK lifecycle to coordinate with a short-lived function. The same request boundary also lets an operations team observe request IDs, latency, vendor metadata, and cost alongside the application trace, which is useful when a feed is busiest and the reconciliation queue is growing.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the stateless publish boundary when your team values one HTTP integration and wants authentication, delivery telemetry, and business-event accounting kept in the same operational vocabulary. It is not a reason to move connection ownership into a function, and it does not remove the need for a client-side recovery protocol.

Here is a deliberately schema-neutral Go caller. The payload is supplied by the application, so the example does not pretend to know fields that belong to your score domain.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := os.Getenv("INFRAI_PAYLOAD")
    if key == "" || payload == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_PAYLOAD are required")
    }
    // Equivalent probe shape for discovery tooling: curl -X POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish -d '{}'

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", bytes.NewBufferString(payload))
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "score-feed-"+os.Getenv("FEED_EVENT_ID"))

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil { delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 { panic(fmt.Sprintf("publish failed: %s", body)) }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
    panic("publish rate limit did not clear after retries")
}

Measure first.

Which realtime option fits a sports score feed?

There is no universal winner. The right choice depends on who owns the socket, how much recovery state you retain, and whether your existing platform already supplies identity and fan-out.

Option Where it fits Trade-off to verify
Infrai realtime API Stateless HTTP publish from serverless handlers; one key and one REST surface can simplify a mixed backend You still design connection lifecycle, replay, and client trust; validate the exact limits for your regions
Ably A managed pub/sub product for teams that want connection and presence concerns in a specialist service Adds another platform boundary and its own channel, identity, and retention model
Pusher Channels A focused hosted channel service with familiar client integrations The application must map its authorization and recovery semantics onto the provider's channel model
AWS AppSync Useful when the feed already lives in an AWS GraphQL and identity stack GraphQL schema and resolver operations become part of the operational surface, which may be more machinery than a small publish command

Those descriptions are starting points, not benchmarks. Your mileage may vary with regional latency, burst size, and the number of subscribers per match; I am not sure which provider will produce the lowest effective bill without your event rate and retention policy. Compare the complete operating bill, including connection capacity, replay storage, observability, and the staff time spent maintaining adapters.

What does recovery look like when delivery is duplicated?

Assume reconnects, expiry, and partial failures are normal states. A client can receive an event, lose its acknowledgement, and receive the same event again. The consumer must treat the stable event identifier as an idempotency key, persist the highest verified revision, and make applying an older revision a no-op.

Authorization deserves the same precision. Issue a token scoped to the competition, match, or channel the client is allowed to read; do not infer trust from the fact that a socket was once authenticated. On expiry, refresh credentials and resubscribe deliberately. If authorization changes during a match, the client should stop rendering private updates before it attempts recovery.

Testing should exercise realistic latency, duplicate delivery, and rejected authorization, not only the happy path. A useful test records the sequence of revisions seen by the client, injects a reconnect between two publishes, and verifies that the final score and audit trail are identical whether the second event arrives once or twice. Test partial batch acceptance as a first-class result if your publish contract allows it; a caller that assumes an all-or-nothing outcome can silently drop one game in a multi-match update.

The short version is boring by design: stable identifiers, observable boundaries, and an explicit replay decision. Boring systems reconcile cleanly.

No polling.

Where should you choose a specialist instead?

Choose Ably or Pusher when the main problem is operating a large connection fleet and you prefer a specialist's client, presence, and channel tooling. Choose AppSync when GraphQL authorization, schema evolution, and AWS-native operations are already non-negotiable. Stick with a direct provider integration when your compliance team requires a narrowly scoped data path or when an existing contract gives you the recovery semantics you need.

Infrai is a poor fit when your organization cannot accept a general REST integration boundary, needs a provider-specific feature outside the published realtime surface, or requires connection behavior that your serverless platform cannot observe. Cost is one dimension of the decision, not the decision itself; model the retained score snapshots, recovery reads, and on-call effort before comparing invoices.

For any option, document the invariant that matters most: after a reconnect, a client can reconcile to the authoritative score without trusting delivery order. That invariant is more durable than a vendor label or a per-call price.

If this boundary fits your system, verify the request contract in the realtime publish documentation before wiring it into a serverless handler.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/realtime
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://ably.com/docs
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appsync/

Further reading

  • https://docs.infrai.cc/realtime
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
