title: Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · 1. What an agent is, minus the marketing
description:
Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · Chapter 1 of 14 · AI Engineering · new chapter every Sunday morning

By the end of this chapter: Reduce an agent to a loop, a model and a set of tools.

The problem

Say you are a senior backend engineer at a fintech startup. You have been asked to prototype an “autonomous ticket‑triage” service that will read incoming support emails, decide whether they need a human, and, if not, reply with a drafted resolution. You spin up a small Python script that calls the OpenAI gpt‑4o‑mini model, feed it the email body, and print the model’s answer.

When you run the script against a handful of real tickets you see two symptoms:

  • The script prints the same generic apology for every ticket, never reaching the “human‑escalate” branch you coded.
  • After a few minutes the process is killed by the OS with MemoryError.

You have spent a day writing the script, a half‑day debugging the model’s output, and you have delayed the sprint by two days because the team cannot rely on the prototype. You need a concrete mental model that tells you what an agent actually is – not a marketing buzzword – so you can reason about loops, state, and tool integration without reinventing the wheel each time.

Before you start

  • Python ≥ 3.11 (tested on 3.11.8)
  • openai package == 1.30.0 (pip install openai==1.30.0)
  • rich package == 13.7.0 (for pretty logging, optional)
  • An OpenAI API key with access to gpt‑4o‑mini (set as environment variable OPENAI_API_KEY)

Verify the environment with a single call that should succeed without error:

python - <<'PY'
import os, openai
assert os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"), "Set OPENAI_API_KEY"
client = openai.Client()
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"}],
    max_tokens=5,
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content.strip())
PY

Expected output:

Hello!

If you see the word “Hello!” the setup is correct and you can continue.

What does the loop look like?

Question: How does an agent repeatedly interact with its model and external tools?

An agent is nothing more than a deterministic while‑loop that:

  1. Collects input (e.g., a new ticket).
  2. Builds a prompt that includes the current state and a tool contract description.
  3. Calls the LLM and receives a structured response (often JSON).
  4. Interprets the response – either taking an action (calling a tool) or producing a final output.
  5. Updates its internal state (e.g., remembering that ticket #123 was escalated).

The loop terminates when the model returns a special finish action.

Why this matters: the loop is the only place where time and cost accumulate. Each iteration incurs an API call (cost per token) and latency (network + model compute). Understanding the loop lets you bound the number of iterations, predict cost, and avoid runaway execution.

How to confirm: Insert a counter and a log statement inside the loop. When you run the prototype, you should see the counter increase once per model call and stop at the finish action.

iteration = 0
while True:
    iteration += 1
    print(f"[iteration {iteration}]")
    # … rest of loop …
    if action["type"] == "finish":
        break

If the counter climbs indefinitely, you have a logic error (see “When this breaks”).

What does the model provide?

Question: What part of the agent’s behaviour is delegated to the LLM, and what guarantees does it give?

The model is a stateless transformer that, given a prompt, returns a probability distribution over tokens. In an agent context we treat it as a function:

f(prompt) → structured_action
  • Deterministic enough – with temperature=0 the model will return the same token sequence for the same prompt, which is essential for reproducibility.
  • No memory – any notion of “remembering” must be supplied by the agent (e.g., a Python dict).
  • Limited context window – gpt‑4o‑mini has a 128 k token window (≈ 96 k tokens of usable text after system messages). Exceeding it yields a context_length_exceeded error.

The contract you write for the model must be explicit: you ask it to output JSON with a known schema. The model does not guarantee syntactic correctness, but with a tight schema and temperature = 0 the failure rate drops below 1 % in practice (observed on 10 k test prompts, see OpenAI release notes 2024‑09‑12).

How to confirm: Run the model with a deliberately malformed prompt and check that it still returns valid JSON.

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "You must output JSON with fields `type` and `payload`."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Just say hi"}],
    temperature=0,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.parsed)   # should be a dict, not raw text

If parsed raises an exception, you need to tighten the system prompt or add a post‑processing validator.

How do tools become contracts?

Question: How does an agent invoke external code safely and predictably?

A tool is a pure function that the agent may call, described to the model via a tool contract:

Field Meaning
name Identifier used in the model’s JSON ("type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web").
description Human‑readable sentence explaining purpose.
parameters JSON Schema describing expected arguments.

The contract is sent to the model as part of the system prompt. When the model decides to call a tool it returns:

{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "search_web",
  "arguments": {"query": "refund policy"}
}

Your agent then dispatches to a Python function matching the name, validates arguments against the schema, runs the function, and feeds the result back into the next prompt.

Why a contract matters: it isolates the LLM from arbitrary code execution. The agent never evaluates raw model output as code; it only calls functions you have explicitly registered.

How to confirm: Register a dummy tool and deliberately send a malformed argument; the dispatcher should reject it before the function runs.

from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    return f"Results for {query}"   # placeholder

tool_schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["query"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

def dispatch(action):
    if action["type"] != "call_tool":
        raise RuntimeError("Unexpected action")
    if action["name"] != "search_web":
        raise RuntimeError("Unknown tool")
    try:
        validate(instance=action["arguments"], schema=tool_schema)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid arguments: {e.message}")
    return {"result": search_web(**action["arguments"])}

Run a test:

bad_action = {"type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web", "arguments": {"q": "test"}}
dispatch(bad_action)   # should raise "Invalid arguments: 'q' is a required property"

If the validation passes only for correct schemas, your contract is enforced.

Build it

Below is a minimal, runnable agent that demonstrates the three components: loop, model, tools. It processes a single ticket, decides whether to reply or escalate, and terminates.

# agent_loop.py
import os, json, sys
import openai
from rich import print as rprint
from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

client = openai.Client()

# ---------- 1. Tool definitions ----------
def reply_ticket(ticket_id: str, answer: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to send a reply; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} replied with: {answer}"

def escalate_ticket(ticket_id: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to flag for human; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} escalated to human"

tools = {
    "reply_ticket": {
        "func": reply_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "ticket_id": {"type": "string"},
                "answer": {"type": "string"},
            },
            "required": ["ticket_id", "answer"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Send an automated answer to the user.",
    },
    "escalate_ticket": {
        "func": escalate_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"ticket_id": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["ticket_id"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Hand the ticket to a human operator.",
    },
}

# ---------- 2. Prompt construction ----------
def build_system_prompt():
    tool_desc = "\n".join(
        f"- `{name}`: {info['description']}"
        for name, info in tools.items()
    )
    return f"""You are an autonomous support agent. You have access to the following tools:
{tool_desc}

When you decide on an action, output JSON with the following schema:
{{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "<tool name>",
  "arguments": <object matching the tool's schema>
}}
If you have reached a final answer, use the tool `reply_ticket`. If you think a human is needed, use `escalate_ticket`. Do not output anything else."""

SYSTEM_PROMPT = build_system_prompt()

# ---------- 3. Agent loop ----------
def run_agent(ticket_id: str, ticket_body: str):
    state = {"history": []}
    iteration = 0
    while True:
        iteration += 1
        rprint(f"[bold cyan]Iteration {iteration}[/]")

        # Build user message
        user_msg = f"""Ticket ID: {ticket_id}
Content:
{ticket_body}

Current state (JSON):
{json.dumps(state, indent=2)}"""

        # Call the model
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
            ],
            temperature=0,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )
        action = resp.choices[0].message.parsed
        rprint("[green]Model action:[/]", action)

        # Dispatch
        if action["type"] != "call_tool":
            rprint("[red]Unexpected action type[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        tool_name = action["name"]
        args = action["arguments"]
        if tool_name not in tools:
            rprint(f"[red]Unknown tool {tool_name}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Validate arguments
        try:
            validate(instance=args, schema=tools[tool_name]["schema"])
        except ValidationError as e:
            rprint(f"[red]Invalid arguments for {tool_name}: {e.message}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Execute tool
        result = tools[tool_name]["func"](**args)
        rprint("[magenta]Tool result:[/]", result)

        # Update state
        state["history"].append({"action": action, "result": result})

        # Termination condition: we consider a reply or escalation final
        if tool_name in ("reply_ticket", "escalate_ticket"):
            rprint("[bold green]Agent finished.[/]")
            break

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    ticket_id = "12345"
    ticket_body = """I was charged twice for my last purchase and need a refund."""
    run_agent(ticket_id, ticket_body)

How to run 

python agent_loop.py

You should see a short log, ending with either a “replied” or “escalated” message. The loop will have executed exactly one model call per iteration; with the simple ticket above it terminates after two iterations (one reasoning step, one tool call).

When this breaks

Symptom Cause Fix
MemoryError raised inside the loop after a few iterations. The state["history"] list grows without bound because the agent never reaches a terminating tool. Add a hard iteration cap (if iteration > 10: break) and ensure your system prompt explicitly tells the model to use a tool to finish.
context_length_exceeded from OpenAI API. The accumulated state JSON plus the ticket text exceeds the 128 k token window. Summarise history (e.g., keep only the last 3 actions) or store older entries in an external DB and only inject a short summary into the prompt.
Invalid arguments ValidationError from the dispatcher. The model returned a JSON field that does not match the tool’s schema (common when temperature>0). Set temperature=0 for deterministic output, and add a fallback that asks the model to retry with corrected schema (re‑prompt with the validation error).
Model returns plain text instead of JSON (no parsed attribute). response_format not honoured because the model version does not support it (e.g., using an older model). Switch to a model that supports JSON mode (gpt‑4o‑mini or later) and verify the API version (client.api_version).
Infinite loop – iteration counter climbs forever, never hitting a tool. Prompt does not contain a clear “finish” instruction, so the model keeps asking for clarification. Refine the system prompt: “You must either call reply_ticket or escalate_ticket on every turn. Do not ask questions.”

After applying the fix, re‑run the script and confirm the iteration count stops as expected.

What it costs

Aspect Cost / Trade‑off
Latency One API call per iteration; with gpt‑4o‑mini typical round‑trip ≈ 150 ms. More iterations linearly increase total latency.
Monetary gpt‑4o‑mini costs $0.15 / M tokens (prompt + completion). A 2‑iteration ticket of ~200 tokens each costs ≈ $0.00006. Scaling to 100 k tickets per day ≈ $6 / day.
Memory Storing full history in‑process grows O(N) with N iterations. For long‑running agents you must prune or externalise.
Debuggability JSON contracts make failures explicit, but you still need to handle schema mismatches and token‑limit errors.
Flexibility vs Safety Tight contracts prevent arbitrary code execution, but they also limit dynamic behaviour (e.g., you cannot ask the model to generate new tool definitions at runtime).

If your use‑case tolerates a few seconds of latency and a few dollars per day, this minimal loop is acceptable. If you need sub‑100 ms response times or have strict cost ceilings, you must either cache model outputs, batch tickets, or move to an on‑premise LLM.

In the interview

Typical interview prompt:

“Explain how you would decompose a support‑ticket triage agent into its core components. What are the trade‑offs of using a language model as the decision engine?”

Weak answer: “An agent is just a loop that calls a model and then does something.” – It lacks concrete terminology, ignores tool contracts, and does not discuss cost or failure modes.

Strong answer:

  1. Loop – deterministic while‑loop with a hard iteration cap to bound latency and cost.
  2. Model – stateless function f(prompt) → JSON; set temperature=0 for reproducibility, respect the 128 k token window.
  3. Tools – pure functions described by a JSON‑Schema contract; the model only ever returns call_tool actions, preventing arbitrary code execution.
  4. Trade‑offs – each iteration adds API latency and token cost; the model provides flexibility but no built‑in memory, so the agent must manage state.
  5. Failure modes – token overflow, schema violations, infinite loops; mitigated by iteration caps, summarisation, and strict validation.

Senior vs junior expectations:

  • Junior: should be able to name the three pieces (loop, model, tools) and sketch a simple Python example.
  • Senior / Staff: must discuss iteration caps, token budgeting, schema validation, and cost analysis, and propose monitoring (e.g., Prometheus metrics for iteration count).
  • Director / Engineering‑manager level: the interview probes strategic impact – “When would you replace the LLM with a rule‑engine?” – expecting a discussion of long‑term maintainability, compliance, and total cost of ownership.

Follow‑up that separates experience from theory:

“Describe a real incident where the model returned malformed JSON under load and how you resolved it.”

A candidate who mentions adding response_format and lowering temperature, plus a retry‑loop with error‑aware prompting, demonstrates hands‑on experience.

Your tasks

  1. Add a summariser tool

    Implement a summarise_history(state) function that returns a one‑sentence summary of the last two actions. Register it as a tool and modify the system prompt to allow the model to call it. Verify that after 5 iterations the prompt size stays under 10 k tokens.

    Done when the agent runs three tickets, each completing in ≤ 4 iterations, and the logged prompt length never exceeds 10 k tokens.

  2. Introduce a hard cost budget

    Add a per‑ticket token budget of 500 tokens. If the model’s cumulative token usage for a ticket exceeds this, the agent must automatically call escalate_ticket. Use the usage field from the OpenAI response to track tokens.

    Done when a deliberately verbose ticket triggers escalation after the budget is breached, and the log prints “Token budget exceeded – escalating”.

  3. Break and diagnose

    Remove the JSON schema validation for reply_ticket and run the agent against a ticket that contains a newline in the answer field. Observe the failure, then restore validation and add a sanitisation step that strips newlines before calling the tool.

    Done when the agent no longer crashes and the final reply contains a single‑line answer.

  4. Scale test

    Write a script that spawns 100 parallel ticket processes (using concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor). Measure average latency and total cost (use the usage data). Report whether the average latency stays below 500 ms.

    Done when the report shows average latency ≤ 500 ms and total cost is ≤ $0.10 for the batch.

  5. Add a retry policy

    Implement exponential back‑off for transient API errors (RateLimitError, ServiceUnavailableError). The agent should retry up to 3 times before giving up and escalating.

    Done when a forced RateLimitError (mocked by raising the exception) results in two retries followed by escalation, with logs showing the back‑off intervals.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.

Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems

Chapter 1 of 14. New chapter every Sunday morning.
Next: Tool definitions as a contract.

title: September 22, 2026
description:
Access Approval

Feature

Developer Connect is generally available (GA).

Access Transparency

Feature

Developer Connect is generally available (GA).

BigQuery

Feature

You can now publish a BigQuery data agent in Gemini Enterprise by registering the agent with Agent Registry and importing it using default Google-managed credentials. When BigQuery and Gemini Enterprise are in the same Google Cloud project and configured with a matching Agent Gateway region, you don't need to manually copy the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) JSON card or configure OAuth client credentials.

These features are in Preview.

Bigtable

Feature

You can use the Google Cloud console to create and manage protobuf schemas (schema bundles) for your Bigtable tables. You can also view schema bundle definitions in Bigtable Studio. This feature is generally available (GA). For more information, see Create and manage protobuf schemas.

Cloud NGFW

Feature

You can now use Cloud NGFW Enterprise advanced threat prevention with cross-region internal Application Load Balancers (Preview).

You can configure global network firewall policies with security profile groups to inspect incoming traffic targeting load balancer forwarding rules. This integration supports intrusion detection and prevention service and Advanced malware sandbox (WildFire) to protect workloads and backends.

For more information, see Supported load balancers. This feature is available in Preview.

Cloud Trace

Feature

The following remote Google Cloud MCP servers automatically generate a trace span for tools/call operations.

  • Identity and Access Management
  • Organization Policy Service
  • Policy Analyzer
  • Security Command Center
  • Spanner
  • Unified Maintenance

These spans can help you understand the behavior of your agentic applications. For more information, see Investigate MCP calls using Trace.

Feature

You can use Terraform to configure resources managed by the Observability API. For example, you can use Terraform to create and update observability buckets, create links on datasets, and configure default settings.

For more information, see the following documents:

  • Set defaults for observability buckets
  • Create observability buckets
  • Update observability buckets
  • List buckets and manage datasets

Cluster Toolkit

Feature

Cluster Toolkit v1.104.0 is available. This release adds agent skills to let you debug Kueue workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and migrate from the Accelerated Processing Kit (XPK).

It also adds optional support for managed instance groups on static compute nodes and Private Service Connect interfaces on Slurm nodesets and login nodes.

Additionally, gcluster now validates placement policies, reservations, and queues when you submit GKE jobs.

This update also runs the Lustre Networking (LNet) setup script only when Lustre is enabled and prevents LNet errors from causing deployments to fail. For more information, see the release announcement on GitHub.

Compute Engine

Deprecated

As of September 15, 2026, NVIDIA P100 (nvidia-tesla-p100 and nvidia-tesla-p100-vws) GPUs have reached end of support (EOS) and are shut down. You can no longer create, launch, or access Compute Engine instances or other Google Cloud resources that use NVIDIA P100 GPUs.

For information about migrating your workloads to supported GPU alternatives such as the G2 (NVIDIA L4) or G4 (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) machine series, see NVIDIA P100 end of support.

Deprecated

NVIDIA T4 (nvidia-tesla-t4 and nvidia-tesla-t4-vws) and NVIDIA P4 (nvidia-tesla-p4 and nvidia-tesla-p4-vws) GPUs are deprecated and will reach end of support (EOS) on August 1, 2027. After August 1, 2027, you won't be able to create, launch, or access Compute Engine instances or other Google Cloud resources that run NVIDIA T4 or P4 GPUs. In addition, you can no longer purchase or renew 3-year committed use discounts (CUDs) for NVIDIA T4 or P4 GPUs.

To transition your workloads to supported GPU models such as the G2 (NVIDIA L4) or G4 (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000) machine series before the EOS date, see NVIDIA T4 end of support and NVIDIA P4 end of support.

Developer Connect

Announcement

The Secret Manager API is no longer enabled by default when you enable the Developer Connect API. For Git repository connections, you must enable the Secret Manager API explicitly.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: D&B Risk Analytics data store

The D&B Risk Analytics data store is generally available (GA) in Gemini Enterprise. You can connect D&B Risk Analytics to run third-party and counterparty risk workflows against your D&B Risk Analytics tenant using natural language. Supported workflows include KYB onboarding, counterparty due diligence, sanctions and adverse media screening, and supplier and financial risk assessment. The data store also supports actions, such as creating an entity, starting a screening, and updating tags and custom fields.

For more information, see Connect D&B Risk Analytics.

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: New data store (Preview)

The following data store is available in Gemini Enterprise:

  • DirectBooker

This data store is in Public Preview. For more information, see Connect a third-party data source.

Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform

Feature

Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5

Claude Opus 5.5 is available in Model Garden.

Network Intelligence Center

Feature

Connectivity Tests analyzes firewall policy rules that use Google Threat Intelligence data.

title: Search trace spans from the Vercel CLI
description:
You and your coding agents can now search a project’s trace spans from the terminal with vercel traces search.

Each span represents one step in a request, helping you investigate errors, latency, and security-related behavior without opening the dashboard.

By default, vercel traces search returns up to 100 spans from the last hour, newest first, so you can search without first finding a request or trace ID. Filter results by environment, service, span name, status, deployment ID, request ID, trace ID, or span ID, or narrow the time range with --since and --until:

For filters without a dedicated option, use --query with Vercel's supported subset of Kibana Query Langugage (KQL). It supports fields such as duration, along with span and resource attributes:

Add --json to output one JSON object per span, giving scripts and agents structured data to analyze.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade, then run vercel traces search --help to see all available options. Learn more in the vercel traces documentation.

title: AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity
description:
AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity

The failure class, not just the identifier

CVE-2026-107282 is one entry in a batch of fixes published for AsyncHttpClient (AHC), the Java library that a large share of JVM services use to make outbound HTTP calls. The batch matters more than any single item because every entry in it has the same shape: the client decides who it is, or who it is talking to, from state that was computed for a different request. The result is a library that is diligent about authentication and still sends credentials to the wrong place.
The headline issue, affecting versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1, concerns cross-host request replay. When AHC re-issues a request against a different host, it updates the current request object but leaves the target request and the associated proxy context pointing at the original host. Path, Host header, Authorization credentials, or a cleartext body computed for host A can therefore be transmitted to host B.

Why that is a credential disclosure rather than a cosmetic bug

Consider a service that talks to an internal API and, after a redirect or a retry against a different endpoint, replays a request. The Authorization header was minted for the first host. The second host may be a third-party service, a different tenant's endpoint, or an attacker-controlled redirect target. Because the client decided the request was a replay, from its point of view nothing unusual happened; from the receiving end, a valid bearer token for an unrelated system just arrived in plaintext or in a header the receiver can read.
The same reasoning applies to the body. A replayed POST whose payload was assembled for the original destination can carry internal identifiers, query fragments or credentials to a host that was never meant to see them. In a microservice mesh where dozens of internal services trust bearer tokens issued by a shared issuer, a single misplaced header is enough to move laterally.
The practical lesson is about the object model, not about HTTP. Replay is inherently a copy operation, and every field of the copy has to be re-derived for the new destination. When one field is treated as immutable context, the copy is incomplete, and the incompleteness is invisible to any test that only checks whether the retry succeeded.

The rest of the batch

CVE-2026-107281 is arguably the more interesting sibling. The HTTP/1.1 connection pool key excludes the authenticated principal when connection-oriented NTLM or Negotiate authentication is in use, in versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1. A pooled connection that was established under one identity can therefore be handed to a different identity. Connection reuse is the entire point of a pool, and NTLM authenticates the connection rather than each request, so the substitution is not visible at the request layer. Any multi-tenant service that authenticates to a downstream system with NTLM through a shared client instance is exposed, and the failure is silent on both ends.
CVE-2026-107283, rated Low, is a cryptographic hygiene defect: Realm.Builder generates the HTTP Digest client nonce with ThreadLocalRandom rather than a cryptographically secure source, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. A predictable nonce weakens the replay protection that Digest was designed to provide, which makes an unrelated credential-exposure bug worse rather than better.
CVE-2026-107284, also Low, concerns WebSocketHandler.upgrade: a handshake whose Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or invalid is aborted, but the handler continues into pipeline installation. Failing to stop on a failed validation is exactly the pattern that turns a validation routine into a formality.
CVE-2026-107285, Medium at 5.9, involves proxy authentication on WebSocket requests tunnelled through CONNECT, where NettyRequestFactory.newNettyRequest and requestUri decide whether to attach proxy credentials, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. The details differ from the cross-host replay case, the reasoning does not: a decision about credentials is made from context that does not describe the request actually being sent.
A related defect in a different Java client shows how common the shape is. CVE-2026-107314 describes pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, in versions 42.7.11 through 42.7.13: when the requireAuth connection property excludes every authentication method the driver knows, for example by listing them all with negation, the driver enforces nothing and accepts any method the server offers. A configuration intended to restrict authentication produces no restriction at all. The score is 5.9 and the consequence is a downgrade to whatever the server proposes.

What to do

Upgrade. The AHC fixes are in 3.0.13 and 2.16.1 for the replay and pool-key issues, and in 3.0.12 and 2.16.1 for the proxy and WebSocket items, so the practical target is the newest build in the line you maintain. Because the library is a transitive dependency in most projects, the version that matters is the one resolved into the final artifact, not the one you typed.
Inventories should be resolved dependency trees, not dependency files. Ask the build for the effective version of org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client in every deployable, and rerun the query after a framework upgrade, because spring and cloud libraries routinely pin the version for you.
If NTLM or Negotiate authentication to a downstream system is in play, treat CVE-2026-107281 as the priority. It is the item that can cross an identity boundary inside your own infrastructure without any external redirect, and it will not appear in a request log that only records that a 200 was returned.
Review your own use of copies. Where your code builds a request for one destination and then reuses it for another, verify that the URI, Host header, credentials and body are all recomputed. The library fix closes the library's path; application-level copies have the same failure mode.
Rotate where exposure was possible. Any deployment that ran an affected version between the release of the fix and the upgrade may have delivered a credential to a host that should never have received it, and rotating is cheaper than reasoning about whether it did.

title: Building a trustworthy photo-upload flow for AI-powered ecommerce
description:
AI features in ecommerce are often introduced as a model problem: choose a model, connect an API, render the result. In a customer-facing product, the surrounding flow matters just as much. A shopper needs to understand why an image is requested, what happens while the system works, what the result means, and how to return to the original product.
I’m building Trylume, a photo-based virtual try-on experience for fashion ecommerce. A shopper starts from a product page and uses a personal photo to create a garment preview. Working on this product has made me think about the integration as a sequence of trust decisions rather than a single image-generation call.

  1. Explain the input before requesting it A file picker with no context creates uncertainty. Tell users what kind of image is useful and what the feature will do with it. Keep the explanation close to the upload control, not hidden in a distant policy page. Be clear about what the generated preview can and cannot tell them. For clothing, a visual preview should not be presented as a size or fit guarantee. Product measurements and size guidance still matter.
  2. Treat loading and failure states as part of the product Image processing is not instant. The interface should show that work is happening, avoid duplicate submissions, and explain what a user can do if generation fails. If there is a retry, give it a clear label. If the system is still processing, do not leave the shopper wondering whether the click worked. A useful failure state should preserve the product context. The customer should not lose the item they were considering or be forced to restart the whole store session.
  3. Keep the result connected to the source product A generated preview is most useful when the shopper can confirm which garment and variant they selected. The experience should provide a path back to product details, color selection, size information, and checkout. Otherwise the feature can feel like a separate image generator rather than part of shopping.
  4. Minimize the data path Before launch, map what is sent to the store, the application, the model provider, and storage. Decide which images need to persist and for how long. Make the public explanation match the actual implementation, including failure cases, backups, and third-party processing. Never use a privacy promise just because it sounds reassuring.
  5. Measure the whole funnel Track more than successful generations. Useful events include the feature being shown, opened, upload started, upload accepted, result completed, retry or failure, return to product details, add-to-cart, and purchase. Compare against a baseline and remember that a try-on interaction alone does not prove additional revenue. The lesson for me is that AI output quality is only one part of the experience. Trust, recovery, privacy, and the path back to shopping all affect whether a customer will use the feature again. I’m continuing to test Trylume with real product images and want feedback from developers who have built image-upload workflows: what edge case did you wish you had tested earlier? https://trylume.tech/

title: Postgres Logical Replication: Slots, DDL, and Failover
description:
At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, a client's reporting replica silently stopped applying changes. The publisher kept accepting writes. The replica kept answering read queries. And a logical replication slot sat inactive for six hours, pinning WAL files until the disk hit 96 percent. Nobody got paged because "replication is running" was a monitoring lie I had set up myself: a check for the slot's existence, not its health. That night taught me that logical replication is not a feature you turn on. It is a pipeline you operate.

This is the guide I wish I had that night. It covers what logical replication is actually good for, how to watch replication slots so they do not eat your disk, why schema changes are the quiet killer, and what happens when the primary fails.

What logical replication is (and is not)

Logical replication in PostgreSQL replicates data changes at the level of rows and transactions, not disk blocks. A publisher marks tables in a publication. A subscriber creates a subscription, and the publisher streams decoded write-ahead log (WAL) entries through an output plugin, pgoutput by default, as a replication protocol stream. Subscribers apply those changes with normal SQL, which means the data arrives through ordinary tables, triggers, and constraints.

That design choice is the source of both its power and its traps:

Aspect Logical replication Physical (streaming) replication
Unit of replication Row changes, per table Whole database cluster, block level
Target Any Postgres instance, any major version within reason Same major version, same architecture
Selectivity Per table, per row, per column All or nothing
DDL (schema changes) Not replicated Replicated
Writes on subscriber Allowed Not allowed
Conflict detection Minimal, async only None needed

The official logical replication documentation is the primary reference, and the restrictions section is required reading; every claim about defaults in this post traces back to them.

For a small business, the practical meaning is this: logical replication is the right tool when you want a subset of data somewhere else, on infrastructure you do not fully control, or in a version you cannot upgrade in lockstep. It is the wrong tool when you want a byte-for-byte standby for disaster recovery. Use physical replication for that.

Use cases that justify the operational cost

I only recommend logical replication when one of these is true. Each one I have run in production.

Reporting and analytics offloading

Point your BI tool at a subscriber that holds only the tables analytics needs, optionally with row filters and column lists (available since PostgreSQL 15). Writers keep their I/O profile; readers stop hammering the OLTP primary. This is the most common and the most forgiving use case.

Zero-downtime major version upgrades

Upgrade the replica to the newer Postgres major version, subscribe it to the old primary, let it catch up, flip a connection string, and drop the old node. Logical replication works across major versions in the direction old-to-new. This is the standard escape hatch when pg_upgrade's downtime window is unacceptable.

Cross-region read scaling and consolidation

A subscriber in another region serves local reads, or pulls data from several publishers into one warehouse-shaped database. Because replication is per-table, you can consolidate five regional databases into one reporting node without shipping every byte. For teams evaluating multi-datacenter latency, our analysis of multi-region architecture maps out routing tradeoffs and read-replica replication lag.

Selective data sharing

Expose a subset of rows to a partner, a contractor, or a staging environment without granting anyone access to the full primary. Row filters make this defensible; you are not copy-pasting exports that go stale.

If your need is "a copy of everything, fast, automatically," use streaming replication and stop reading. If your team is still choosing a database stack, our breakdown of building a small business tech stack from scratch covers where Postgres fits among managed and self-hosted options.

Replication slots: the part that bites you

Every logical subscription consumes a replication slot on the publisher. The slot's job is to guarantee that the WAL the subscriber has not consumed yet is not recycled. That guarantee is unconditional. If the subscriber falls behind or dies, the slot holds WAL, and WAL accumulates on disk until either the subscriber catches up or the disk fills.

PostgreSQL exposes everything you need in the pg_replication_slots view. These are the columns I alert on:

  • active: false for more than a few minutes means the consumer is down or stuck.
  • inactive_since: tells you exactly when the slot went quiet.
  • wal_status: anything other than reserved means trouble. unreserved means WAL is about to be removed; lost means the slot is dead and the replica needs a rebuild.
  • restart_lsn and confirmed_flush_lsn: the gap between current LSN and these values is your disk-usage clock.
  • conflicting and invalidation_reason: if invalidation_reason is set, the slot has already failed and the reason tells you which protection (max_slot_wal_keep_size, idle_replication_slot_timeout) killed it.

One short query covers a morning health check:

SELECT slot_name, active, inactive_since, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_type = 'logical';

Set max_slot_wal_keep_size to a value your disk can survive (a few GB, not -1) so a runaway slot errors instead of filling the volume. Pair it with idle_replication_slot_timeout for slots from decommissioned environments. Yes, a slot that overruns its budget invalidates and forces a resync of that subscriber. That is the correct trade. An invalidated slot is a bad afternoon. A full disk is a bad week.

WAL retention pressure is only one flavor of the resource problem. If you are also scaling write capacity across database clusters, our database sharding for Postgres SaaS guide breaks down partitioning, replication boundaries, and horizontal distribution patterns.

Schema changes: the quiet killer

Logical replication does not replicate DDL. Add a column on the publisher and nothing breaks immediately, because the subscriber simply never sees the new column. Rename a column and the subscriber starts erroring on apply, the subscription halts, and the slot begins retaining WAL while your on-call rotation sleeps.

The failure pattern I see most often: a migration framework (Flyway, Alembic, a hand-rolled migration directory) deploys schema changes to the primary without any awareness of subscribers. The team finds out at 9 a.m. from a disk alert.

The playbook that works:

  1. Additive changes only, subscriber first: add new columns and new tables to the subscriber before the publisher, never the reverse. Dropping is the dangerous direction.
  2. Treat renames and type changes as two-step operations: add the new column, backfill, switch writes, then drop the old one later.
  3. Expand and contract: write code that tolerates both schemas during the transition window.
  4. Wire migrations into deployment order: subscribers get DDL before publishers, enforced by your pipeline, not by memory.
  5. After any migration, check pg_stat_subscription_stats on the subscriber for apply errors before you call it done.

Column lists and row filters (publication options, PostgreSQL 15 and later) make some of this easier: if the subscriber declares a column list that matches its local schema, publisher-side additions do not break apply. Row filters deserve the same care, because a filter that silently excludes rows on the subscriber is a data bug that no error message will surface.

What happens when the primary fails

Here is the blunt version most tutorials skip: logical replication has no automatic failover. If the publisher dies, your subscriptions stop, full stop. Subscribers keep serving stale reads, happily, with no error that your application will notice.

Since PostgreSQL 17, there is a supported path for surviving planned and unplanned failover of the publisher: create the subscription with failover = true, and the primary synchronizes the logical slot to its physical standby. When the standby is promoted, the slot is already there and the subscriber reconnects to the new primary. The requirements are strict, per the logical replication failover documentation:

  • You need a physical standby of the publisher anyway.
  • The slot sync is asynchronous. You must verify, before promoting, that the slots on the standby report synced and not invalid. The docs provide verification queries for exactly this.
  • The standby must be ahead of the subscriber, or data written after the slot's confirmed position is lost from the replication stream.

Miss the verification step and you get a promoted primary whose logical slots are behind your subscriber's confirmed flush position. That gap is silently dropped data. Not corrupted, dropped: transactions committed on the old primary but never decoded will never reach the subscriber, and nothing raises an error.

For planned failovers, use synchronized_standby_slots and check failover readiness on the standby before switching. For unplanned ones, accept that you may need to re-sync subscribers if the standby was behind. And test this. A failover drill on a staging cluster takes an afternoon and is the only way to find out your slots were never syncing. We follow a similar recovery-testing protocol in our playbook on business internet and infrastructure failover.

What most guides get wrong

Three claims repeat across vendor blogs, and all three cost me production time before I stopped believing them.

First: "logical replication is simple streaming with a filter." No. It is a decoding pipeline with persistent state (the slot) that couples the publisher's WAL retention to the subscriber's health. The filter is the easy part. The slot is the product.

Second: "just monitor lag." Lag, meaning apply delay on the subscriber, is the metric everyone graphs, and it is nearly useless as an early warning. Slot WAL retention on the publisher fills your disk long before apply lag becomes dramatic, and a dead subscriber has zero lag and an ever-growing WAL pile. Watch wal_status and the LSN gap on the publisher, then apply errors on the subscriber via pg_stat_subscription_stats. If you run security audits on your infrastructure and data layer, the same discipline applies in our web security fundamentals: the real vulnerability is almost never the headline metric.

Third: "failover = true fixes HA." It fixes one narrow scenario, publisher failover with a physical standby present, and only if you verified slot sync before promoting. It does nothing for subscriber failure, network partitions, or the dropped-transaction gap. Guides that present it as a checkbox are selling comfort, not reliability.

Operator's checklist

Run this daily, automate what you can, page on the starred items:

  • [ ] * wal_status = reserved for every logical slot; anything else is an incident
  • [ ] * Disk headroom above the max_slot_wal_keep_size budget on the publisher
  • [ ] confirmed_flush_lsn gap below your agreed rebuild threshold
  • [ ] pg_stat_subscription_stats shows no apply_errors
  • [ ] inactive_since null, or slot retention policy (idle timeout) in place for exceptions
  • [ ] For failover-enabled subscriptions: synced = true on the standby and invalidation_reason null
  • [ ] Migration runbook confirms subscriber-first DDL for any deploy touching published tables

Conclusion

Logical replication earns its keep for reporting offload, version upgrades, selective sharing, and cross-region consolidation, but only if you operate the slot as a first-class citizen: alert on wal_status and retention, not lag; run additive, subscriber-first migrations; and treat failover slot sync as a verified procedure, not a parameter. The failure modes are quiet until they are expensive, which is exactly why this is the checklist you build before the 2 a.m. page, not after.

title: The Geometry of Shadows: What a Bridge Railing Taught Me About the Mathematics of LLMs
description:
While running one morning, I found myself staring at the shadows cast by a stone bridge railing. The railing had a series of identical, carved镂空 (hollowed-out) structures. As I ran past, the angle of the sun shifted, and the shadows on the ground transformed.

At one moment, the shadow looked like a swimming fish; a few steps later, it looked like a rolling wave; later still, it was just an abstract, elongated blob.

It struck me that I was witnessing a perfect physical metaphor for how human language—and Large Language Models (LLMs)—generate meaning.

The stone bridge hole is the concept. The sunlight is the context. The shadow on the ground is the utterance.

This realization perfectly mirrors the "Central Problem" of language modeling, beautifully stripped of its usual jargon in Joseph L. Breeden’s paper, The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models.

The Problem of the Single Shadow

In his paper, Breeden highlights a fundamental flaw in early AI approaches: treating words as static, unchanging symbols. He uses the classic example of the word "bank":

  1. "I deposited money at the **bank." (a financial institution)
  2. "We walked along the river **bank." (the land beside a river)
  3. "The plane **banked* sharply left."* (tilted)

If we assign a single, fixed vector to the word "bank" in a high-dimensional space, we are essentially trying to capture all three meanings in one static shape. But as Breeden points out, a fixed vector for "bank" cannot simultaneously be close to "money," "river," and "tilt."

In my running metaphor, a single, fixed vector is like looking at the bridge hole only at exactly high noon. You get one specific shadow. But language is dynamic. The meaning of "bank" depends entirely on the "angle of the light" provided by the surrounding words.

The Mathematics of Light: Learned Weighted Averaging

How does an LLM solve this? Breeden explains that the core mechanism of a Transformer is not magic; it is Learned Weighted Averaging.

Let’s map Breeden’s mathematics to the bridge railing:

1. The Bridge Hole (The Token Embedding, $e$)
Before any context is applied, the word "bank" is just an initial embedding vector ($e$). It is the physical stone structure itself. It contains the potential for all its meanings, but it is currently unshaped by the environment.

2. The Angle of the Sunlight (Influence Scores, $a_i \cdot b_j$)
To determine what the shadow will look like, we need light. In an LLM, the "light" comes from the surrounding words (the context).
Breeden explains that the model computes an influence score between the target word and its context. It does this by projecting the vectors through learned matrices ($W^A$ and $W^B$).

  • When the context is "deposited money," the "light" hits the bridge hole from a financial angle.
  • When the context is "river," the light hits it from a geographical angle. The dot product ($a_i \cdot b_j$) measures how perfectly the angle of the light aligns with the shape of the hole.

3. The Shadow on the Ground (Context-Dependent Representation, $h_i$)
Finally, the light passes through the hole and casts a shadow. Mathematically, the model takes a weighted average of the context vectors (using the content projection $W^C$), resulting in a brand new vector ($h_i$).
This new vector is the shadow. It is a context-dependent representation. The "bank" in the first sentence is mathematically pulled toward the geometry of finance; the "bank" in the second sentence is pulled toward the geometry of nature. They are the same material, but entirely different products.

Why This Metaphor Matters

What makes Breeden’s explanation so profound is that it removes the anthropomorphic jargon of "Queries," "Keys," and "Values." There is no little homunculus inside the computer "looking up" information in a database.

There is only geometry and light.

When an LLM reads the sentence "The plane banked sharply left," it doesn't "know" what a plane is. Instead, the high-dimensional vectors for "plane" and "sharply left" act as a specific angle of light. This light passes through the "bank" bridge hole and casts a shadow that aligns perfectly with the geometric region of "physical motion" in the model's latent space.

Furthermore, this explains the difference between languages. In English, "bank" is a single, multi-purpose bridge hole that requires complex, dynamic lighting (Attention mechanisms) to cast the right shadow. In Chinese, the language has already carved three separate, distinct bridge holes: 银行 (bank), 岸 (riverbank), and 倾斜 (to tilt). The Chinese model requires less "light manipulation" because the physical structures themselves are already disentangled.

Conclusion: Meaning is a Projection

As I finished my run, I realized that the bridge railing wasn't just casting shadows; it was performing a physical projection.

Large Language Models do not store a dictionary of definitions. They store a high-dimensional geometry of concepts. Meaning is not a static object you can hold in your hand; it is a projection. It is the dynamic, mathematical shadow cast when the light of context passes through the structure of language.

And just like the shadows on the pavement, the beauty of language lies not in the stone itself, but in how it changes with the light.

References:
Breeden, J. L. (2026). The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models. CRC Working Papers.

title: These are ALL you NEED to get started with Python PANDAS
description:
Pandas is a Python library used for data manipulation, analysis, and cleaning. It provides fast and flexible data structures designed to work with tabular data (similar to an Excel spreadsheet or a SQL table)

Dataframes and Series

  • DataFrame: A 2-dimensional labeled data structure with rows and columns (a complete table)
  • Series: A 1-dimensional labeled array capable of holding any data type (like a single column in a spreadsheet).

Before getting started with pandas we need to install it first.

pip install pandas

import pandas as pd

# 1. Create a simple DataFrame
data = {
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Age': [25, 30, 35],
    'City': ['New York', 'London', 'Paris']
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# 2. Load data from an external file
# df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

# 3. View the first 5 rows
print(df.head())

Reading files in pandas

CSV Files (.csv): Use pd.read_csv() to import comma-separated values.

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

Excel Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls): Use pd.read_excel() to load spreadsheets. You can specify a sheet using the sheet_name parameter.

df = pd.read_excel('budget.xlsx', sheet_name='Q1_Report')

JSON Data (.json): Use pd.read_json() to convert JSON strings or files into tabular format.

df = pd.read_json('users.json')

Parquet Files (.parquet): Use pd.read_parquet() for highly optimized, columnar storage files common in big data workflows.

df = pd.read_parquet('large_dataset.parquet')

SQL Database Tables: Use pd.read_sql() to pull data directly into Pandas via a database connection (e.g., utilizing an engine from the SQLAlchemy project)

import sqlalchemy
engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine('sqlite:///my_database.db')
df = pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM employees', con=engine)

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) using Pandas is the foundational step in any data science workflow. It allows you to understand the structure, distributions, relationships, and anomalies within a dataset before moving to modeling

.head()

  • first n rows of a DataFrame or Series. It is primarily used to quickly inspect and verify the structure, column names, and data types of a dataset after loading it.
  • Inside the brackets you can put the number of rows you want to inspect. 
df.head()
df.head(10)

.tail

  • The df.tail() method in pandas returns the last n rows of a DataFrame or Series. 
df.tail()

.shape

  • df.shape is an attribute that returns a tuple representing the dimensions of a DataFrame or Series. It provides a quick way to see how many rows and columns your dataset contains. 
df1.shape

Output:

(5632, 27)

Structural & Descriptive Summaries

  • Before analyzing trends, verify how data types are registered and look at basic statistical summaries. 
# Check data types, memory usage, and non-null counts
df.info()

Output:

# Summary statistics for numerical columns (mean, min, max, quartiles)
df.describe()

Output

# Summary statistics for ALL columns (including categorical frequencies)
df.describe(include="all")

Output

Exploring Single Variables

  • Examine individual variables to understand their distribution, frequency, and pull out any categorical unique counts 
# For Categorical Data: Count frequencies of unique values
df["category_column"].value_counts()
df["category_column"].unique()  # List unique entries
df["category_column"].nunique()  # Total number of unique entries

# For Numerical Data: Quick pandas native plotting
df["numeric_column"].hist(bins=20)  # Check skewness and distribution
df["numeric_column"].plot(kind="box")  # Identify outliers

Data Cleaning

  • Before cleaning is done, a quick EDA must be done to know the areas to clean and what to clean. Below is a sample code to have a sneek- peek of what to actually clean. 
# Find duplicate rows and drop them
print(df.duplicated().sum())
df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)

# Find missing values
print(df.isnull().sum())

Deal with missing values

  • Missing values in a dataset can either be dropped or imputed depending on the size of the data, importance and number of missing values.
  • Here are some of the ways to deal with missing values: 
df.dropna(subset=["critical_column"], inplace=True)  # Drop missing rows

df["numeric_column"] = df["numeric_column"].fillna(
    df["numeric_column"].median()
)  # Impute with median

Dealing with DataTypes

  • Values may be recorded in a datatype which may not be fit for them. In anycase this occurs, they can be changed to the correct datatypes.

  • Using pd.to_numeric() Best for converting text or mixed-type columns into numbers. Use errors='coerce' to turn unconvertible entries (like random text or symbols) into NaN.

df['price'] = pd.to_numeric(df['price'], errors='coerce')
  • Using pd.to_datetime() Converts date and time strings into proper datetime64 objects 
df['sale_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['sale_date'], errors='coerce')
  • Dealing with mixed date formats e.g dd/mm/yyyy, mm/dd/yyyy, yyyy/mm/dd 
df1['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    df1['order_date'],
    format='mixed',
    errors='coerce'
)

df1['payment_method'] = df1['payment_method'].str.strip().str.capitalize()
  • replace(), used when you want to change items inside a column to ensure consistency in values recorded and reliability. 
df1['payment_method'] = df1['payment_method'].replace({
    'Mpesa' : 'M-pesa',
    'Visa': 'Card'
})
  • If the column has mixed characters and values for example here in unit_price, you can also use replace function to standardize the column and maybe change the datatype if need be. 
df1['unit_price_kes'] = df1['unit_price_kes'].str.strip().str.replace(r'[^0-9]','', regex = True).astype(float)

Creating new columns

  • You can also be required to create a new column maybe from from a condition as below or from a calculation. In such a scenario, here's how to deal with it. 
df1['phone_validity'] = np.where(df1['customer_phone'].astype(str).str.len() == 10, 'valid', 'invalid')

# Calculate total cost (multiplication)
df['total_cost'] = df['price'] * df['quantity']
  • The code above will create a new column called total_cost.

Deleting columns

  • You can delete columns from a DataFrame using .drop() 
# deleting a single column
df = df.drop(columns=['B'])

#  deleting multiple columns
df = df.drop(columns=['C', 'D'])

Aggregation in pandas

  • Aggregations in Pandas reduce a collection of numerical or categorical values into a single summary value (such as a sum, mean, or count). You can perform these operations on an entire Pandas DataFrame, specific columns, or groups of data using the groupby() 
# Clean, flat DataFrame output with custom column names
clean_summary = df.groupby('Department').agg(
    total_salary=('Salary', 'sum'),
    average_bonus=('Bonus', 'mean'),
    employee_count=('Employee', 'count')
).reset_index()

Concatenation and Merging in Pandas

Concatenation (pd.concat)

  • Use pd.concat() when your datasets have the same structure and you want to glue them together along an axis. • axis=0 (Default): Stacks DataFrames vertically (appends rows). • axis=1: Stacks DataFrames horizontally (appends columns) aligned by their index. 
import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [5, 6], 'B': [7, 8]})

# Stack vertically (Row-wise)
vertical_stack = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)

# Stack horizontally (Column-wise)
horizontal_stack = pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)

Merging (pd.merge)

  • Use pd.merge() when you have different datasets that share a common identifier column (like an ID or SKU) and you want to align them side-by-side. 
left = pd.DataFrame({'User_ID': [1, 2, 3], 'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']})
right = pd.DataFrame({'User_ID': [1, 2, 4], 'Salary': [50000, 60000, 70000]})

# Merge on a matching column
merged_df = pd.merge(left, right, on='User_ID', how='inner')

Saving the final dataframe

  • You can save a Pandas DataFrame to different file formats in Python using specific df.to_*() export methods 
import pandas as pd

# Assume 'df' is your existing DataFrame
# 1. Save as CSV (excluding the default index)
df.to_csv("data.csv", index=False)

# 2. Save as Excel
df.to_excel("data.xlsx", index=False)

# 3. Save as JSON
df.to_json("data.json", orient="records")

# 4. Save as Parquet (requires pyarrow or fastparquet)
df.to_parquet("data.parquet")

# 5. Save as Pickle
df.to_pickle("data.pkl")

Conclusion

Python pandas is the foundational, industry-standard tool for modern data manipulation, cleaning, and analysis. Built around its core DataFrame and Series structures, it transforms raw, messy data into structured, tabular insights by providing powerful, intuitive functions for merging datasets, handling missing values, and performing complex aggregations like groupby. While it integrates seamlessly with the broader Python ecosystem—including NumPy, Matplotlib, and scikit-learn—pandas does suffer from high memory usage and reduced performance when processing massive, multi-gigabyte datasets. Despite these scaling limitations, it remains an indispensable cornerstone of data science workflows, unmatched for exploratory data analysis and rapid prototyping.

title: Anatomy of a Paid AI Video Job: What Happens Between Upload and MP4
description:
A walkthrough of the lifecycle behind a two-photo trend video generator: validation, quotes, credit holds, async rendering and data expiry.

Consumer AI video looks like a single button: upload photos, get a clip. Behind that button sits a long-running, paid, failure-prone job, and most of the product work goes into making that job predictable for someone who just wants a funny video of their friends.

This post follows one job through AIHotelLobby.win, a single-purpose tool that recasts the Hotel Lobby trend video with two uploaded portraits. It makes a good example because its public guides, help page, terms and privacy policy spell out every stage, from upload checks to how long each file lives. Everything below is based on those pages; the snippets are simplified sketches of the behavior they describe.

Stage 1: Reject bad input before anything expensive happens

A GPU minute costs far more than a file check, so the cheapest quality control is at the upload box. Each photo has to be a JPG, PNG or WebP, at least 512 × 512 pixels and no larger than 10 MB, showing one clearly visible adult.

const ACCEPTED = ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'];
const MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024;

function checkPhoto(type: string, bytes: number, w: number, h: number): string | null {
  if (!ACCEPTED.includes(type)) return 'Use a JPG, PNG or WebP image';
  if (bytes > MAX_BYTES) return 'Keep the file under 10 MB';
  if (w < 512 || h < 512) return 'Use an image at least 512 × 512 pixels';
  return null;
}

Two details worth noting. Metadata is stripped when the images are prepared, which removes location data people forget their phones attach. And the docs are explicit that these checks only cover the file: they do not verify identity, age or consent. Being honest about what validation can't do is part of the design.

Stage 2: Keep the draft alive through the login wall

Users can pick both photos, assign left and right, and choose length and sound before creating an account. The draft is kept on the device while they sign in, so the login wall doesn't throw away their work. Signing out clears it.

This is a conversion detail as much as a technical one. The moment someone is asked to sign in is the moment they are most likely to leave, and making them redo the upload afterwards doubles that risk.

Stage 3: Quote first, then hold the credits

After sign-in, the photos upload privately and the server returns a quote: length, format and credit cost. Prices are fixed per length (5 seconds is 30 credits, 10 is 50 and 15 is 70), and the quote is pinned to the task.

type Quote = {
  durationSeconds: 5 | 10 | 15;
  aspect: '16:9';
  audio: 'original' | 'silent';
  credits: 30 | 50 | 70;
  configRevision: string; // the model, template and price recorded for this task
};

The terms make the pinning explicit: prices and models can change for new requests, but an existing task keeps the provider, settings and price recorded in its quote. Confirming the quote reserves the credits. They are captured only after a valid video has been stored, and released if the task definitively fails. Buying credits is a separate flow and never starts a job by itself.

Stage 4: Hand off to the model, then let the user leave

The configured model is Kling 3.0 Omni, accessed through KIE as the API provider. (A second model, Seedance 2.0 Mini, is integrated but not enabled for customers.) The provider receives the two photos, the reference video and the instructions for that task.

From here everything is asynchronous. The published examples list render times from about three to seven and a half minutes, which is far too long to hold a browser tab hostage. The user can close the page; the task keeps running and shows up in My videos on any device signed in to the same account.

The hard case is a timeout during submission: the provider may or may not have accepted the job. Releasing the credits risks giving away a video that will finish anyway; capturing them risks charging for nothing. The answer here is a holding state:

type Job =
  | { state: 'reserved' }
  | { state: 'running' }
  | { state: 'needs_review' } // submission outcome unknown; credits stay held
  | { state: 'completed'; videoKey: string } // credits captured
  | { state: 'failed' }; // confirmed failure; credits released

The page on credits and task recovery tells users what this means for them: losing the connection does not stop generation, an uncertain task keeps its credits reserved while it is checked, and they should follow that same task rather than start a duplicate. Credit returns and cash refunds are also kept separate, which saves a lot of support confusion.

Stage 5: Deliver briefly, then delete

Personal photos are a liability the moment you no longer need them, and the retention schedule reflects that:

Data How long it stays
Validated photos never submitted for a task 24 hours
Photos needed by an active or uncertain task Up to 48 hours
Task inputs after the task reaches a final state Scheduled to expire within 24 hours
Finished videos 7 days
A download link 5 minutes

Downloads use short-lived signed links. Deleting a file stops new links from being issued, though a link already handed out can work until it expires, and the privacy policy says so plainly. It also notes that provider copies and backups follow their own schedules, which is the kind of caveat most products leave out.

What's worth copying

  • Validate cheaply, and say what validation can't check.
  • Let the draft survive authentication.
  • Pin the quote to the task, so a price or model change never rewrites a job already in flight.
  • Model the unknown state explicitly instead of guessing between refund and charge.
  • Publish retention times as numbers, not "as long as necessary".

None of this is specific to trend videos. Any product that runs a slow, paid job on someone's personal media faces the same five stages, and users notice when one of them is handled carelessly.

AIHotelLobby.win is an independent service. It is not an official Kling, Seedance or KIE product and is not affiliated with the artists behind "Hotel Lobby". Details come from its public pages as of October 18, 2026.

title: Voyage Rerank 3 and Rerank 3 Lite are now available on AI Gateway
description:
Rerank 3 and Rerank 3 Lite from Voyage AI by MongoDB are now available on AI Gateway.

The models reorder search results by relevance before passing documents to a language model. The series improves retrieval quality across domains, with the largest gains on long documents and code.

Rerank 3 focuses on accuracy, while Rerank 3 Lite is optimized for latency and cost. Both handle up to 32K tokens per query-document pair and follow instructions in the query to guide ranking.

To use Rerank 3, set the model to voyage/rerank-3:

For Rerank 3 Lite, change the model to voyage/rerank-3-lite.

Try Voyage Rerank 3 in the AI Gateway model playground, or explore the model catalog.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

Read more
